description: Vault._calcDeposit() initializes the first deposit's share count using `shares = max(amount0, amount1) - 1000`. For the WBTC/USDC vault where token0=WBTC (8 decimals) and token1=USDC (6 decimals), the first depositor who provides e.g. 1 WBTC (1e8) and 100,000 USDC (100_000e6 = 1e11) receives shares proportional to max(1e8, 1e11) - 1000 = 1e11 - 1000. The initial share price is therefore set based on raw token amounts without any price normalization. This means 1 share is worth approximately 1e-11 USDC or 1e-8 WBTC worth of underlying — a share price anchored to USDC units. Subsequent depositors who provide different token0/token1 ratios will receive shares calculated against these initial balances via the cross-product formula, but the initial share issuance has no economic meaning because it mixes raw amounts of tokens with different decimals. An attacker who performs the first deposit with dust token0 and large token1 (or vice versa) sets a share price that causes subsequent depositors to receive wildly incorrect shares relative to their economic contribution.

collectFees() passes mainPosition.tickUpper instead of vestPosition.tickUpper when collecting fees for the vesting position. Because vestPosition stores its own tickUpper (set at addVestingPosition time), but a subsequent rebalance will move mainPosition.tickUpper to a different value, the fee collection call operates on the wrong tick range — a position that does not exist at those ticks. The call to burn(vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper, 0) on a non-existent position returns 0 fees silently. All vesting position fees are permanently lost (never collected into idle balances) for every collectFees() call after a rebalance has moved mainPosition.tickUpper.

checkPoolActivity() iterates observations from index 1 to observationCardinality inclusive. On the last iteration (i == observationCardinality), the index formula `(observationCardinality + currentIndex - i) % observationCardinality` evaluates to `currentIndex % observationCardinality` which equals `currentIndex` (since currentIndex < observationCardinality). This re-reads the same observation slot that was used to seed `nextTimestamp` / `nextCumulativeTick` at the start of the function (before the loop). The resulting tick delta between two identical observations is `(nextCumulativeTick - tickCumulative) / (nextTimestamp - timestamp)` where both cumulative values are equal, producing tick = 0 (or division by zero if timestamps are equal). This can cause the loop to report a spurious zero tick or underflow, making the price-within-range check unreliable on its final iteration.

_setSecondaryPositionsTicks() can set tickLower >= tickUpper for the secondary position when `modulo == 0` (tick falls exactly on a tick-spacing boundary) and the `bal0in1 < bal1` branch is taken. In that branch:
  secondaryPosition.tickLower = mainPosition.tickLower
  secondaryPosition.tickUpper = tick - modulo = tick
If mainPosition.tickLower == tick (which can happen when the main position is symmetric and tick is exactly the border), the secondary position has tickLower == tickUpper. Uniswap V3 pool.mint() requires tickLower < tickUpper and will revert if this invariant is violated, bricking subsequent rebalances. Even when tickLower < tickUpper, the secondary position may overlap the main position (both share tickLower), causing double-counting of liquidity in balances().

In addVestingPosition(), the vesting position ticks are copied from mainPosition at the time of the call (lines 433-434). However, if rebalance() is subsequently called, mainPosition.tickLower and tickUpper are updated to a new range, while vestPosition.tickLower and tickUpper remain at the old values. The vesting position liquidity is correctly tracked in Uniswap at the old ticks, but _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() calls _removeFromPosition(liquidityToRemove, vp.tickLower, vp.tickUpper) using the stale (but actually correct) vestPosition ticks. The BUG is in collectFees() at line 167, which ignores vestPosition.tickUpper and uses mainPosition.tickUpper instead (see LIB-01), causing the fee-collection step to operate on a different tick range than _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition uses. This inconsistency means: fees are collected from the wrong range, but principal removal happens at the correct range. Protocol fee is applied to the wrong fee income, and users may be under-compensated.

pullFunds() transfers real underlying tokens out of the yToken contract without updating reserve.underlyingBalance. This causes a permanent divergence between the accounting state (underlyingBalance) and the actual ERC20 balance held by the yToken contract. After pullFunds is called, reserve.availableLiquidity() returns a value higher than the real token balance. Any subsequent borrow call that passes the availableLiquidity check but exceeds the actual ERC20 balance in the yToken will cause the ERC20 transfer to revert. More critically, if the borrow amount is within the actual remaining balance, the borrow succeeds but underlyingBalance becomes doubly incorrect (it should have been decremented for pullFunds but wasn't, and now is decremented for borrow). The inflated underlyingBalance propagates to exchangeRate calculations, causing new depositors to receive fewer yTokens than they deserve (they pay for liquidity that isn't there).

pushFunds() transfers real underlying tokens INTO the yToken contract without updating reserve.underlyingBalance. This is the symmetric counterpart of FH-01. After pushFunds, underlyingBalance is understated relative to actual ERC20 balance. This means the yTokenToReserveExchangeRate() is lower than true value, so lenders who redeem right after pushFunds receive FEWER underlying tokens than they are entitled to (the excess sits in the yToken contract unaccounted). The 'stranded' tokens can never be recovered through normal protocol flows since underlyingBalance is never incremented for pushFunds.

In _deposit(), the exchange rate for minting yTokens (reserveToYTokenExchangeRate) is computed AFTER updateState() but BEFORE the actual token transfer completes. However, the critical ordering issue is: the capacity check (checkCapacity) uses totalLiquidity which depends on underlyingBalance. If pullFunds was previously called without updating underlyingBalance, the capacity check passes using an inflated total, potentially allowing deposits beyond the real reserve capacity. Combined with FH-01, this means reserveCapacity is effectively bypassed when pullFunds leaves underlyingBalance inflated.

In _updateIndexes(), interest accrual uses the stored currentBorrowingRate but this rate was computed at the PREVIOUS interaction's utilization. Between two interactions, neither underlyingBalance nor totalBorrows changes, so the interest accrued is correct. However, there is a subtle ordering issue in _deposit(): updateState() is called first (which accrues interest and increases totalBorrows), THEN checkCapacity() is called using the post-interest totalLiquidity. This means the capacity check includes accrued interest as part of total liquidity, slightly underestimating available deposit headroom. More importantly: the capacity check in checkCapacity uses totalLiquidity BEFORE the new deposit is added, but the require is `totalLiquidity + depositAmount <= reserveCapacity`. After updateState() inflates totalBorrows (by accrued interest), the totalLiquidity used in checkCapacity is already higher, potentially causing legitimate deposits to revert even when the reserve is not actually at capacity in terms of real principal.

The yToken burn flow in _redeem() has a subtle state ordering issue: burn() is called on the yToken contract which (1) burns yTokens from msg.sender (lendingPool contract) and (2) transfers underlying to the recipient. The yToken totalSupply decreases during the burn. However, underlyingBalance is decremented AFTER burn() returns (line 150). During the yToken.burn() execution, if there were any callback (e.g., ERC777-style or custom receive), the exchange rate would be computed with decreased totalSupply but not-yet-decreased underlyingBalance — inflating the exchange rate. In the current implementation, yToken uses plain ERC20 (no hooks), so this is not directly exploitable. But the pattern is dangerous if the underlying asset has transfer hooks (e.g., USDT-with-hooks, ERC777). More concretely: `yToken.burn(to, yTokenAmount, underlyingTokenAmount)` sends tokens to `to` (receiverOfUnderlying). If `to` is a contract that calls back into lendingPool during receive(), the exchange rate is artificially high (supply down, balance not yet down).

In _updateIndexes(), when interest is applied, the code computes:
  newTotalBorrows = newBorrowingIndex * reserve.totalBorrows / reserve.borrowingIndex
This is correct. However, in borrowedLiquidity() (a view function), it computes:
  liquidity = latestBorrowingIndex(reserve) * reserve.totalBorrows / reserve.borrowingIndex
Both use the same formula. After updateState() is called, reserve.borrowingIndex IS updated to newBorrowingIndex and reserve.totalBorrows IS updated to newTotalBorrows. So after update:
  borrowedLiquidity = latestBorrowingIndex(newIndex) * newTotalBorrows / newIndex
Since latestBorrowingIndex() checks `lastUpdateTimestamp == block.timestamp` and returns `reserve.borrowingIndex` directly (no further compounding), this correctly returns newTotalBorrows. BUT: if two operations happen in different blocks without updateState() being called between them, the view correctly accumulates. The bug scenario is: if a malicious actor triggers two borrows in the same block after a long idle period. The first borrow calls updateState() which updates indexes. The second borrow in the same block also calls updateState() but latestBorrowingIndex() returns current borrowingIndex (no change since same block). This is correct behavior. ACTUAL FINDING: The `repay` function accepts repayment even when paused (by design, comment says so). But repay DOES NOT check `notPaused`. So when paused, ONLY repay is allowed. However, `pullFunds` and `pushFunds` also lack the `notPaused` modifier — meaning the leverager can still move funds even during emergency pause. This bypasses the pause safety mechanism intended to freeze the system in emergency.

In _deposit(), when the yToken totalSupply is 0 (first deposit), 1000 yTokens are burned to DEAD_ADDRESS to defend against inflation attacks. However, the check `totalSupply == 0` is performed AFTER the yToken exchange rate is computed and AFTER tokens are transferred from the depositor to the yToken contract. The yToken amount to mint is calculated as:
  yTokenAmount = amount * exchangeRate / PRECISION
where exchangeRate = reserveToYTokenExchangeRate() = PRECISION (returns PRECISION when totalSupply == 0). So yTokenAmount = amount. Then 1000 is burned to dead. But the check for dust amount `require(yTokenAmount > MINIMUM_YTOKEN_AMOUNT)` happens BEFORE the burn branch. This means if a user deposits exactly 1001 units, they get 1001 yTokens computed, the dust check passes (1001 > 1000), then 1000 are burned to dead, and the user gets 1 yToken. But the original dust check was supposed to ensure the user gets a meaningful amount. With 1 yToken, on subsequent deposits the exchange rate favors the first depositor. The true inflation attack mitigation is the dead address burn, but the dust check at line 120 only checks `yTokenAmount > MINIMUM_YTOKEN_AMOUNT` BEFORE the burn deduction, so a deposit of 1001 units passes the dust check but the user receives only 1 yToken — effectively the dust check is wrong; it should check `yTokenAmount - MINIMUM_YTOKEN_AMOUNT > 0` or more explicitly `yTokenAmount > 2 * MINIMUM_YTOKEN_AMOUNT` for meaningful first deposits.

In repay(), the state is updated (totalBorrows decremented, underlyingBalance incremented) BEFORE the ERC20 transferFrom executes. While nonReentrant prevents reentrant calls to repay() itself, if the underlying token is a rebasing or fee-on-transfer token, the amount credited to underlyingBalance may exceed the amount actually received. Specifically:
  1. reserve.totalBorrows -= amount  (state update)
  2. reserve.underlyingBalance += amount  (state update)
  3. IERC20(asset).safeTransferFrom(leverager, yToken, amount)  (actual transfer)
If the token charges a transfer fee, the yToken receives less than `amount`, but underlyingBalance is incremented by full `amount`. This overstates available liquidity. This is the classic "state before external call" pattern where the accounting assumes the transfer sends exactly the specified amount.

`feeRecipient` is declared public at line 47 but there is no setter function anywhere in Leverager.sol. It is never initialized in the constructor, and no `setFeeRecipient` function exists. Whenever `liquidationFee > 0`, the code at lines 328-329 calls `safeTransfer(feeRecipient, ...)` which resolves to `address(0)`, permanently burning the protocol's fee tokens. This is a complete loss of fee revenue — not just an access issue but a permanent fund-burning bug.

In `withdraw()` at line 232, when the borrowed denomination is token1, the conditional expression uses `amountOut0` instead of `amountOut1` to compute `repayFromWithdraw`. The line reads:
  `uint256 repayFromWithdraw = amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount;`
When `amountOut1 < owedAmount` (the common case where the withdrawn token1 is less than owed), `repayFromWithdraw` is set to `amountOut0` (token0 amount) instead of `amountOut1`. This causes `owedAmount` to be reduced by the wrong quantity and `amountOut1` to be under-reduced. The user then must pay `owedAmount` (incorrectly computed) from their wallet, and `amountOut1` returned to them is also wrong. In extreme cases this can cause underflow or force users to overpay by up to the full token0 withdrawal amount.

In `liquidatePosition()` at line 318, `borrowedValue` is computed as:
  `owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()`
The denominator uses `.decimals()` which returns the raw uint8 (e.g., 6 for USDC, 8 for WBTC, 18 for WETH). It should be `10 ** ERC20(...).decimals()` to convert to actual token units. Using the raw decimal value (e.g., 6 instead of 1_000_000) massively over-inflates `borrowedValue` by several orders of magnitude. This makes `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` almost never true, meaning the protocol-fee branch is never entered AND the liquidation health check may behave incorrectly. Effectively, liquidators will almost always see `totalValueUSD <= borrowedValue` even for healthy positions, causing the liquidation to proceed as if there is never any profit — fee recipient gets nothing AND the position's collateral may be returned incorrectly.

`_sweepTokens(token0, token1)` at the end of `openLeveragedPosition` (line 198) transfers the ENTIRE balance of token0 and token1 held by the Leverager contract to `msg.sender`. If any residual token balance exists in the contract from prior transactions (e.g., from partial liquidations, leftover denomination tokens after borrow/repay cycles, or tokens accidentally sent to the contract), an attacker can drain them by opening a minimal leveraged position. The only cost is the gas and the minimal collateral required for the position (which is returned).

`initVault()` at line 75 guards against double-initialization with:
  `require(!vaultParams[vault].leverageEnabled, "already enabled");`
However, `toggleVaultLeverage()` at line 536 can set `leverageEnabled = false` (disabling the vault). After disabling, the `initVault` guard no longer fires, allowing the owner to call `initVault` again on the same vault. This re-runs all initialization including `forceApprove` with unlimited allowances. While only callable by the owner (Ownable), this is still a surprising state inconsistency — the guard is supposed to be "set once" but is easily bypassable by first toggling the vault off. A governance error or a compromised owner could reset vault params (overwriting maxUsdLeverage, maxTimesLeverage, minCollateralPct, maxCumulativeBorrowedUSD) while existing positions remain open under the old parameters.

The `collectFees` modifier (line 494) is applied to `liquidatePosition` before `nonReentrant`. The modifier calls `IStrategy(strat).collectFees()` on the strategy contract derived from the position's vault. Since this external call occurs BEFORE the reentrancy lock is set, a malicious vault/strategy that implements `collectFees()` with a callback could reenter `liquidatePosition` or other Leverager functions. Although positions are tracked by storage, a reentrant call on the same `_id` before the first call deletes the position could lead to double-liquidation or double withdrawal of vault shares.

collectFees() uses the wrong tick upper bound when collecting fees for the vesting position. Line 167 calls `collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper)` but the vesting position was minted at `(vp.tickLower, vp.tickUpper)` which equals `(mainPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper)` at the time of creation. Using `mainPosition.tickUpper` for the upper tick might seem correct, BUT the lower tick also needs to be `vestPosition.tickLower`, not `mainPosition.tickUpper` for the upper. More critically, after a rebalance the `mainPosition.tickUpper` can change, making the pair (vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper) a position key that was never minted. The pool's burn/collect will silently operate on a non-existent or wrong position, so vesting position fees are never collected and the protocol loses fee revenue. Also, _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() uses vestPosition.tickLower/tickUpper correctly, but collectFees() does not — creating an inconsistency that accumulates uncollected fees inside the wrong Uniswap slot, causing protocol fee accounting to be wrong on subsequent fee collections.

_withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() uses the wrong denominator when computing the pro-rata liquidity to remove. The formula at line 467 is:
  liquidityToRemove = vp.initialLiquidity * (lastValid - vp.lastUpdate) / (vp.endTs - vp.startTs)
The denominator `(vp.endTs - vp.startTs)` is the TOTAL vesting duration. However, the numerator uses the elapsed time since the LAST update. If the function is called multiple times, the correct denominator for incremental vesting should be the remaining time span, not the original total span. Because `vp.lastUpdate` advances but `vp.startTs` is fixed, later calls compute a smaller fraction of `initialLiquidity` per time unit than earlier calls. This means: - Early partial withdrawals vest MORE liquidity per second than intended. - Late partial withdrawals vest LESS liquidity per second than intended. - The total across all calls does NOT equal `initialLiquidity` unless only called once or
  the position is fully elapsed.
In the worst case, if collectFees() is called frequently, the vested amounts per call are tiny (since the elapsed window is small) and the total vested across the full duration will be much less than `initialLiquidity`, causing the remaining liquidity to never fully vest even after `endTs`, because each call reduces `remainingLiquidity` by a small but incorrectly computed amount. However, note that when `lastValid == vp.endTs` it uses `vp.remainingLiquidity` (drains the rest), so on the final call it corrects itself — but intermediate distributions are wrong.

checkPoolActivity() reverts with "timestamp 0" when it encounters an uninitialized observation slot (timestamp == 0). Uniswap V3 pools initialize their observations array lazily: slots beyond the initial cardinality of 1 are only populated as trades occur. The function iterates over ALL `observationCardinality` slots, but not all slots may be written. Specifically, observations are stored in a ring buffer and the currently active cardinality may have slots that were never populated (timestamp=0) if the cardinality was recently increased via `increaseObservationCardinalityNext`. This causes `_requirePriceWithinRange()` to permanently revert, completely blocking `rebalance()` and `compound()` — a denial of service on the core protocol operations.

uniswapV3MintCallback() only checks `msg.sender == pool` (the stored pool address). The Strategy grants infinite approval (`forceApprove(vault, type(uint256).max)`) to the vault in the constructor. However, the mint callback grants the pool permission to receive tokens. The trust boundary issue is: if `pool` is a malicious or upgradeable contract, it can call `uniswapV3MintCallback` with arbitrary `amount0`/`amount1` and drain all token0/token1 from the Strategy. In practice, for a known Uniswap V3 pool this is unlikely, but the Strategy has no mechanism to verify that the callback is only called during an active `mint` (no reentrancy lock or call-depth tracking). A compromised or fake pool address set at deployment could drain the entire strategy. More practically: the callback transfers `amount0` and `amount1` to `pool` unconditionally. If the pool misbehaves and requests more tokens than needed, Strategy will send them all. There is no check that `amount0` and `amount1` are bounded by the liquidity being minted.

_setSecondaryPositionsTicks() can set tickLower >= tickUpper for the secondary position, creating an invalid Uniswap V3 position. When `bal0in1 >= bal1` (more token0 value), the secondary position should be above the current price (all token0 will be deposited). The code sets `secondaryPosition.tickLower = tick - modulo + tickSpacing` and `secondaryPosition.tickUpper = mainPosition.tickUpper`. However, `mainPosition.tickUpper = tickBorder + halfWidth` from `_setMainTicks`. If the computed `tick - modulo + tickSpacing` is >= `mainPosition.tickUpper`, the position is invalid (tickLower >= tickUpper). This can happen when `positionWidth` is very small (e.g., 2 * tickSpacing) and the tick is near the upper boundary of the main position. When this invalid position is passed to `IUniswapV3Pool(pool).mint(...)`, Uniswap V3 will revert with "TLU" (tick lower must be less than tick upper), causing the entire rebalance() to fail.

The Strategy grants infinite token approval to the vault (`forceApprove(vault, type(uint256).max)`) at construction time. The vault address is stored as a plain `address public vault` and is NEVER validated or changeable after construction. If the vault contract is upgradeable (proxy), a malicious upgrade could use this approval to drain all tokens from the Strategy via `transferFrom(strategy, attacker, balance)`. The infinite approval is necessary for `Vault.withdraw()` to pull tokens, but creates a permanent trust dependency on the vault's integrity. Since `vault` is not updatable, if the vault is compromised, the strategy's entire balance is at risk with no defensive mechanism.

Strategy.collectFees() calls collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper) for the ongoing vesting position, but it should use vestPosition.tickUpper as the upper tick. The vesting position was created at (vestPosition.tickLower, vestPosition.tickUpper), which matches (mainPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper) at creation time. However, after a rebalance, mainPosition.tickUpper changes while vestPosition.tickUpper remains fixed. Once any rebalance occurs after a vesting position is created, collectFees() calls burn/collect on a tick range (vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper) that no longer corresponds to any real Uniswap position. Uniswap returns 0 fees for this non-existent range. The actual vesting position fees (vestPosition.tickLower, vestPosition.tickUpper) are never collected. Because _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() removes liquidity using the correct vestPosition ticks, the underlying liquidity is properly removed, but any accumulated fees on that position are permanently lost — neither transferred to the feeRecipient nor to vault depositors.

In Vault._calcDeposit(), the initial share calculation for the first deposit is `shares = (amount0 > amount1 ? amount0 : amount1) - 1000`. This compares raw token amounts from two tokens with different decimals (WBTC has 8 decimals, USDC has 6 decimals) without any price normalization. The larger raw amount determines the initial share supply. In the WBTC/USDC pool, 1 WBTC = 1e8 and 100,000 USDC = 1e11, so the first depositor always gets a share count based on USDC raw units regardless of actual market value. More critically, this means the initial depositor can manipulate the initial share price: by depositing a tiny amount of one token and a large amount of the other, they control the totalSupply relative to the vault's actual asset value. This allows the first depositor to create an inflated share price that causes subsequent depositors to lose tokens to rounding.

Strategy.balances() does not include the vesting position's liquidity in its output. It sums only idle balances + main position + secondary position. When an ongoing vesting position exists, the tokens locked in that position are invisible to balances(). Since Vault.deposit() and Vault.withdraw() both use balances() to calculate share prices, the vesting position's tokens are systematically excluded from the vault's asset valuation. This means: (1) depositing while a vesting position is active gives more shares than warranted (the denominator is deflated), diluting existing holders; (2) withdrawing while a vesting position is active gives less tokens than the user's true proportional share of total assets. The larger the vesting position relative to the vault's total assets, the more significant this mispricing becomes.

In Strategy.collectFees(), the `ongoingVestingPosition` branch collects fees for the vesting position using `mainPosition.tickUpper` instead of `vestPosition.tickUpper`. This was noted in Strategy context. From Vault.sol's perspective, any call to Vault.deposit() or Vault.withdraw() invokes `IStrategy(strategy).collectFees()` first. Since collectFees() silently returns 0 fees for the wrong tick range (the non-existent Uniswap position), the preBal/afterBal delta used to compute protocolFees is 0 for the vesting position's contribution. This means protocol fees are NOT collected from vesting position fees, even though those fees accumulate in the pool. The impact from Vault's perspective: every deposit and withdrawal during an active vesting position bypasses the fee collection for that position. Over time, vesting position fees become permanently inaccessible — trapped in the Uniswap pool at ticks that nobody is tracking.

In `withdraw()`, when `borrowed == up.token1`, the `repayFromWithdraw` is computed using `amountOut0` instead of `amountOut1`. This is a copy-paste error from the token0 branch directly above. As a result, when the borrowed token is token1 (e.g. USDC), the contract uses the token0 balance to cap the repayment rather than the actual token1 withdrawal proceeds. If amountOut0 < owedAmount (token0 balance is small), the user is forced to pull more denomination token from their wallet than necessary. Conversely, if amountOut0 is large, repayFromWithdraw is set to owedAmount but amountOut1 is never decremented by the actual repay amount — leaving surplus token1 in the contract instead of returning it to the user, or causing an incorrect accounting of amountOut1 that gets transferred.

In `liquidatePosition()`, line 318, the borrowed value in USD is computed as:
  `uint256 borrowedValue = owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals();`
This uses the raw return of `decimals()` (e.g. 8 for WBTC, 6 for USDC) as the divisor instead of `10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` (e.g. 1e8, 1e6). Every other place in the contract uses the correct form:
  - Line 131: `up.initCollateralUsd * (10 ** ERC20(lp.denomination).decimals()) / bPrice`
  - Line 401: `totalValueUSD * (10 ** ERC20(pos.denomination).decimals()) / bPrice`
With the raw `decimals()` value (e.g. 8), `borrowedValue` is inflated by a factor of `1e8 / 8 = 12,500,000x`. This makes `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` nearly always FALSE, so the protocol fee block is skipped and `feeRecipient` receives nothing. More critically, the comparison is also used implicitly in the broader liquidation logic: the condition determines whether there is profit to charge a fee on. With enormously inflated `borrowedValue`, the liquidator effectively always liquidates positions "at a loss" from the fee perspective, receiving the full collateral with no protocol cut.

In `_getTokenIn()`, the `while` loop calls `path.skipToken()` but NEVER reassigns the result back to `path`. `Path.skipToken(bytes memory path)` returns a new `bytes memory` value — it does NOT mutate the input in-place. The `using Path for bytes` declaration means `path.skipToken()` is syntactic sugar for `Path.skipToken(path)`, but the return value is discarded. Therefore: (a) If the path has multiple pools, `path.length` never decreases, `hasMultiplePools()`
    always returns true, and the loop runs forever — consuming all gas (infinite loop).
(b) Even for single-pool paths (the only working case), the function returns `tokenIn`
    which is `tokenB` from `decodeFirstPool`. For exactOutput swaps, the path encoding
    is `[tokenOut, fee, tokenIn]`, so `decodeFirstPool` returns `(tokenOut, tokenIn, fee)`.
    Thus `tokenIn` is correctly `tokenB` for single-hop. The bug only manifests with
    multi-hop paths, causing a DoS/revert via out-of-gas.

`feeRecipient` (declared at line 47) is never initialized in the constructor or any setup function. It is only used in `liquidatePosition()` to transfer protocol fees. Since `feeRecipient` defaults to `address(0)`, any `safeTransfer` to `feeRecipient` will either silently succeed (sending tokens to the zero address, burning them) or revert depending on the ERC20 implementation. As a result, all liquidation fees are permanently lost rather than going to the protocol. There is no `setFeeRecipient` function defined in the contract (the `liquidationFee` can be set via `setLiquidationFee`, but there is no corresponding setter for `feeRecipient`).

In `withdraw()`, when `wp.hasToSwap` is true and `swapParams1.amountIn > 0`, the contract deducts `swapParams.amountIn` from `amountOut0` (line 249):
  `amountOut0 -= swapParams.amountIn;`
However, the `exactInput` swap is called with arbitrary `swapParams` decoded from user input, and the user sets the `recipient` of the swap. There is no check that `amountOut0 >= swapParams.amountIn` before the subtraction. If the user specifies an `amountIn` larger than `amountOut0`, this underflows (in checked arithmetic context) and reverts. But more subtly — there is also no check that the approval given (`IERC20(up.token0).forceApprove(swapRouter, swapParams.amountIn)`) is backed by actual token0 balance. The contract could approve more than it holds. While this would revert at transfer time, the swap recipient is user-controlled, allowing the user to specify swapParams that route tokens back to themselves, and to set amountIn to the full token0 balance including tokens that were already designated for repayment in the token0 branch (though that branch only runs when denomination == token0). Additionally, in `liquidatePosition()` the same swap handling is present but with no check that `amount0 >= swapParams.amountIn` before `amount0 -= swapParams.amountIn` (line 356), which can underflow if swap input exceeds available collateral.

In `withdraw()`, when `wp.pctWithdraw == 1e18` (full withdrawal), the position is deleted and the NFT burned. However, the `repay` call uses `amountToRepay` (= `owedAmount` = the pct-scaled portion of total debt), which for pctWithdraw=1e18 equals `totalOwedAmount`. This is correct.
But the partial-withdraw path updates `positions[wp.id].borrowedAmount` to `totalOwedAmount - amountToRepay` (line 289). This is the NEW total owed after repay, normalized to `bIndex`. This looks correct in isolation.
However, `positions[wp.id].initCollateralValue` is decremented by `up.initCollateralValue * wp.pctWithdraw / 1e18` (line 288), which represents the ORIGINAL collateral value at open time. But the `borrowedAmount` is updated to the CURRENT owed value (with accrued interest). This creates a mismatch: after a partial withdrawal, the ratio of `borrowedAmount / initCollateralValue` no longer reflects the original leverage ratio. This affects `isLiquidateable()` which computes `base = owedAmount * 1e18 / (vp.maxTimesLeverage - 1e18)` and caps it at `pos.initCollateralValue`. If `initCollateralValue` is decremented proportionally but `borrowedAmount` grows due to interest, `base` may be capped at a lower value than intended, making the liquidation threshold more lenient (harder to liquidate) over time.

pushFunds() permanently inflates underlyingBalance when called without a matching pullFunds(). pushFunds() executes IERC20(asset).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, yTokenAddress, amount) which deposits tokens into the yToken contract, BUT never updates reserve.underlyingBalance. pullFunds() likewise never decrements underlyingBalance. The net result is: after any pullFunds(X)/pushFunds(X) cycle, underlyingBalance is unchanged (correctly). But if pushFunds(X) is called WITHOUT a prior pullFunds, the yToken contract receives X extra tokens while underlyingBalance stays the same — meaning the actual yToken balance is HIGHER than underlyingBalance tracks. Conversely, if the leverager only calls pullFunds without ever calling pushFunds (e.g., due to a revert in the leverager), underlyingBalance remains HIGHER than actual yToken balance permanently, allowing the reserve to issue redemptions that will fail on transfer because the yToken contract does not hold enough tokens. The yTokenToReserveExchangeRate will return a value based on the stale (too-high) underlyingBalance, so lenders believe they have more value than they can withdraw.

pushFunds() does not update reserve.underlyingBalance when tokens are pushed back. The function only does a safeTransferFrom into the yToken address, without calling reserve.updateState() or modifying underlyingBalance. This is the mirror bug of WC-01: during the pullFunds/pushFunds window, any call that reads underlyingBalance (such as deposit, redeem, borrow, exchangeRateOfReserve, utilizationRateOfReserve) operates on a stale, incorrect value. Specifically, between pullFunds(X) and pushFunds(X), the underlyingBalance still shows the pre-pull amount, making the pool appear to have MORE available liquidity than it actually holds. This causes borrowingRate to be computed at a lower value than reality (lower apparent utilization), which disadvantages lenders who should be earning higher rates during the gap.

A whitelisted leverager can borrow and repay within the same block, paying ZERO interest. In latestBorrowingIndex(), when reserve.lastUpdateTimestamp == block.timestamp, the function returns reserve.borrowingIndex immediately with no accrual. In _updateIndexes(), the new borrowing index is only updated if reserve.totalBorrows > 0 BEFORE the call. The sequence is: 1. borrow() → updateState() → no interest accrued (zero borrows before) → totalBorrows += amount 2. repay() in same block → updateState() → lastUpdateTimestamp == block.timestamp → no interest The leverager effectively gets a free intra-block loan with no interest charged. Since the leverager is a single trusted contract, this is a design-level risk: if the leverager can be front-run or manipulated to borrow + repay within the same block (e.g. through flash loan callback composability), lenders earn nothing on those borrowed funds.

pullFunds() skips reserve.updateState() and reserve.updateInterestRates(), causing interest rates to remain stale while the pool's actual available liquidity has dropped to zero. When funds are pulled without updating state, the stored currentBorrowingRate reflects the old utilization (lower). Any subsequent call that reads currentBorrowingRate for interest accrual (calculateCompoundedInterest) uses this stale rate. This means lenders earn interest at a lower rate than the pool's actual utilization warrants during the time funds are pulled. The borrow() function updates state before lending, but pullFunds() does not. This is an asymmetry that systematically undercharges borrowers and underpays lenders during active leverager operations.

setLeverager() can only be called once and cannot be changed. If the leverager contract is compromised, has a bug, or is intentionally malicious, the LendingPool has no mechanism to rotate the leverager address. Furthermore, if the leverager calls pullFunds() and then self-destructs or gets paused, the funds are permanently stuck: pullFunds() removed tokens from the yToken contract without tracking this in underlyingBalance, and pushFunds() can only be called by msg.sender == leverager. With the leverager destroyed, pushFunds can never be called again. The funds in transit are permanently lost. The nonReentrant modifier on pullFunds/pushFunds prevents same-tx callbacks, but does nothing to prevent cross-transaction leverager compromise scenarios.

The _deposit() function computes the exchange rate (reserveToYTokenExchangeRate) BEFORE updating underlyingBalance. The exchange rate uses totalLiquidityAndBorrows which reads reserve.underlyingBalance (the old value). Then IERC20.safeTransferFrom sends tokens to the yToken contract. Then yTokenAmount is computed. Then underlyingBalance += amount. The issue: the exchange rate is computed against the PRE-deposit balance. This is correct for a pure deposit (each depositor gets pro-rata share). However, if tokens have been sent directly to the yToken contract (outside the normal deposit flow), then underlyingBalance does not reflect the actual yToken balance. Such a direct token donation increases the yTokenToReserveExchangeRate (lenders get more per yToken) without the donor receiving any yTokens. But crucially, underlyingBalance does not track the donation, meaning subsequent deposits compute exchange rates against the stale (lower) underlyingBalance. The donated tokens are effectively "lost" from the accounting perspective — they exist in the yToken contract's ERC20 balance but are never reflected in underlyingBalance, so they accrue to existing yToken holders forever without being properly tracked. A related issue: pushFunds() sends tokens to yToken without incrementing underlyingBalance, so tokens pushed this way create the same permanent accounting divergence.

liquidatePosition() uses `ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` (returns uint8, e.g. 8 for WBTC) instead of `10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` (1e8) when computing borrowedValue. For WBTC (decimals=8), this divides by 8 instead of 100_000_000, overstating borrowedValue by a factor of ~12.5 million. The result: `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` is almost never true, so the protocol fee branch is skipped, but more critically the denominator error means `borrowedValue` is absurdly large — positions look insolvent on paper even when they are healthy. Combined with `isLiquidateable()` (which uses the correct 10**decimals), the borrowedValue computed inside liquidatePosition is inconsistent. When `totalValueUSD <= borrowedValue` (which is nearly always due to the bug), the zero-fee path is taken — this is acceptable. But when denomination is a token with large decimals (e.g. WETH, 18 decimals), dividing by 18 instead of 1e18 yields a borrowedValue ~55 quadrillion times larger than reality, guaranteeing totalValueUSD < borrowedValue always — making fee collection impossible and masking protocol revenue, but NOT reverting. The true DoS consequence is that for tokens where `decimals()` < actual scale, the transfer to feeRecipient is skipped, reducing liquidator incentive and protocol accounting. However the most direct DoS: if `feeRecipient == address(0)` (uninitialized, per prepass signal), a non-zero `pf0` or `pf1` causes `safeTransfer` to address(0) which reverts in OZ SafeERC20, completely bricking all liquidations whenever `liquidationFee > 0` is set.

In withdraw(), when `borrowed == up.token1`, the code at line 232 computes `repayFromWithdraw = amountOut0 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount` instead of using `amountOut1`. It then subtracts `repayFromWithdraw` from `amountOut1` on line 234. Since `amountOut0` can be larger than `amountOut1`, this will cause an arithmetic underflow revert at line 234 (`amountOut1 -= repayFromWithdraw`) whenever `amountOut0 > amountOut1`. In WBTC/USDC pools this is almost always the case (1 WBTC = 100,000 USDC in value terms but amountOut0 in raw units is tiny compared to amountOut1 in 1e6). This permanently blocks withdrawal for any position that borrowed USDC (token1).

In `liquidatePosition()`, line 318 computes borrowedValue incorrectly: `uint256 borrowedValue = owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` ERC20.decimals() returns uint8 (e.g., 8 for WBTC, 18 for WETH, 6 for USDC). The correct divisor is `10 ** decimals` (the token unit scale). For WETH (18 decimals): divides by 18 instead of 1e18 — borrowedValue is 5.5e16x larger than the real value. For USDC (6 decimals): divides by 6 instead of 1e6 — borrowedValue is ~166,666x too large. Consequence: `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` is almost never true for any realistic position, so the protocol fee branch (lines 321–331) is never entered. This means no fees are ever transferred to feeRecipient — a denial of service against the protocol's revenue mechanism. Additionally, the completely wrong `borrowedValue` figure means the profit/loss accounting during liquidation is broken, potentially allowing liquidators to profit in unexpected ways or preventing liquidations from being profitable enough to incentivize callers.

The ERC721 `_mint()` call in `openLeveragedPosition()` at line 197 uses the standard OZ ERC721 `_mint()` which does NOT call `onERC721Received` on the recipient. However, in `withdraw()` and `liquidatePosition()`, the NFT is burned using `_burn()`. There is no issue with _mint itself. BUT: the `_isApprovedOrOwner` check in `withdraw()` at line 211 calls `ERC721.ownerOf(tokenId)` which reverts if the token does not exist. An attacker can call `withdraw()` with a non-existent position ID, causing a revert from ownerOf() (token doesn't exist). This is expected behavior. The real DoS is that once a position is burned (deleted), a griefing attacker with an approved address could call withdraw() on a burnt ID — ownerOf reverts, permanently wasting gas. This is a minor issue. The stronger DoS: if for any reason `_burn` is called on an already-burned token (double burn), OZ _burn reverts. The `delete positions[wp.id]` and `_burn(wp.id)` order means if `_burn` reverts, positions remain deleted but ERC721 is inconsistent. Actually the more significant vector: `collectFees` modifier (line 494) calls `IVault(up.vault).strategy()` then `IStrategy(strat).collectFees()`. If `up.vault` is address(0) (because position doesn't exist or was deleted), this will revert with a call to address(0), blocking the liquidation modifier from completing.

pullFunds() and pushFunds() do not update reserve.underlyingBalance, creating a permanent accounting desync. borrow() correctly decrements underlyingBalance and repay() correctly increments it, but pullFunds/pushFunds move the same underlying tokens WITHOUT touching underlyingBalance. After pullFunds(asset, X), the yToken contract holds (underlyingBalance - X) actual tokens but reserve.underlyingBalance still reports the original (higher) value. This causes availableLiquidity() to return a stale inflated number, allowing borrow() to pass its liquidity check even when actual tokens are insufficient, and causing exchangeRateOfReserve() to compute a higher-than-real rate, overpaying redeemers who may drain the yToken.

pushFunds() does not update reserve.underlyingBalance. It is the mirror of pullFunds: tokens come back into the yToken contract but underlyingBalance is never incremented. The pair pullFunds/pushFunds is designed to be used together (comment says "Should always push the same amount back"), but neither leg updates accounting. Combined with LH-01, a pull followed by a push leaves underlyingBalance correct by accident (both wrong in opposite directions), but any partial push or any interaction between pull/push and other operations will leave the accounting in an inconsistent state. Specifically, if pushFunds is called WITHOUT a prior pullFunds (e.g., leverager repays extra collateral), underlyingBalance stays stale (too low), causing the utilization rate to be computed incorrectly (too high), driving up borrowing rates for all lenders unnecessarily.

pullFunds() uses a memory copy of ReserveData (`DataTypes.ReserveData memory reserve`) rather than a storage reference. This means even if someone tried to add accounting updates inside pullFunds, writing to `reserve` would have no effect on state. The same issue exists in pushFunds(). By contrast, borrow(), repay(), _deposit(), and _redeem() all use `DataTypes.ReserveData storage reserve` (via `getReserve()` which returns a storage reference). The memory/storage divergence is the root cause of why accounting updates are silently discarded — a developer who added `reserve.underlyingBalance -= amount` inside pullFunds() would see it compile without errors but have zero effect on chain state.

pullFunds() lacks the notPaused modifier that borrow() has. Both functions transfer underlying tokens OUT of the yToken contract to the leverager. When the owner pauses the protocol (emergencyPauseAll()), the intention is to halt all outflows of funds. borrow() correctly respects this: it has the `notPaused` modifier. But pullFunds() does not — the leverager can continue pulling funds from any reserve even when the system is paused. This defeats the purpose of the emergency pause mechanism for the pull/borrow path.

pullFunds() does not check if the reserve is frozen. borrow() checks `!reserve.getFrozen()` and `reserve.getBorrowingEnabled()` before proceeding. pullFunds() skips both checks. A frozen reserve is supposed to prevent NEW borrows and deposits while allowing only repays and redeems — but pullFunds bypasses the freeze entirely. Similarly, if borrowing is disabled via disableBorrowing(), borrow() will revert, but pullFunds() will succeed. This creates an inconsistency: an admin action (freeze/disable) intended to stop fund outflows only partially works.

The core accounting invariant of the LendingPool is:
  reserve.underlyingBalance == actual ERC20 balance held by yToken contract
This invariant is maintained by deposit (+amount to both), redeem (-amount from both), borrow (-amount from both), and repay (+amount to both). But pullFunds and pushFunds break this invariant: they move actual ERC20 tokens WITHOUT updating underlyingBalance. The result is that all derived quantities — totalLiquidity, utilizationRate, exchangeRate, availableLiquidity — are computed on stale data after any pull/push. In particular, a user can deposit, have a leverager pull funds, and then redeem for more underlying than actually exists in the yToken (because the exchange rate uses stale inflated totalLiquidity). The burn() call in yToken will then safeTransfer an amount that reverts, permanently blocking redeems.

pullFunds() calls yToken.transferUnderlyingTo() which physically moves tokens out of
the yToken vault. However, it never decrements reserve.underlyingBalance. After the call,
the reserve storage records more available liquidity than exists in the yToken contract.
This "phantom" underlyingBalance inflates totalLiquidityOfReserve() and the
yTokenToReserveExchangeRate(). Because availableLiquidity() reads underlyingBalance
(not the real token balance), subsequent borrow() calls pass the liquidity check but
revert at the actual token transfer — permanently DoS-ing borrows. Worse, the first
lender to redeem steals from later lenders who find the vault empty.

Root cause: LendingPool.sol pullFunds() has NO underlyingBalance update.
Contrast with borrow() which correctly does: reserve.underlyingBalance -= amount.

The same underlyingBalance accounting failure applies to all three reserves.
A single fuzzer property that checks all three at once maximises coverage
and catches cross-reserve interactions where pull on one reserve masks solvency
issues on another.

pushFunds() transfers tokens INTO the yToken vault via safeTransferFrom but never
increments reserve.underlyingBalance. The pushed tokens are physically in the yToken
but are invisible to the reserve accounting:
  - availableLiquidity() still reads the old (lower) underlyingBalance
  - The exchange rate is not improved for existing lenders
  - The tokens cannot be borrowed (borrow checks underlyingBalance)
  - The tokens cannot be redeemed (redeem uses underlyingBalance-derived exchange rate)
The pushed tokens are permanently locked in the yToken contract.
This is the mirror of H001: pullFunds makes actual < accounted;
pushFunds makes actual > accounted.

The protocol has an emergency pause mechanism (paused flag, notPaused modifier).
borrow() correctly checks notPaused. However, pullFunds() — which moves tokens out of
the yToken vault with equivalent effect to a borrow but WITHOUT recording any debt —
has no notPaused check. The leverager can continue draining the yToken vault while
all other operations are halted. An admin who pauses the contract to stop an exploit
cannot stop the leverager from pulling remaining funds.

pushFunds() is callable while the contract is paused. Unlike repay() (which has an
explicit comment explaining why it must work while paused so borrowers can unwind),
pushFunds() injects arbitrary token amounts into the yToken vault WITHOUT the deposit
validations (capacity check, state update, yToken minting). This bypasses the paused
state's intent of halting all asset movements, and because underlyingBalance is never
updated by pushFunds(), tokens pushed during a pause are permanently locked.

When a reserve is frozen (freezeReserve()), the intent is: no new deposits or borrows,
but lenders may still redeem and repay. borrow() correctly checks reserve.getFrozen().
pullFunds() — which moves tokens out with the same effect as a borrow — has no frozen
check. A leverager can continue extracting liquidity from a frozen reserve, leaving
lenders unable to redeem what the frozen reserve promised to protect.

borrow() enforces: require(amount <= reserve.availableLiquidity()).
pullFunds() has NO such check. The leverager can call pullFunds with amount equal
to the entire yToken balance — more than the tracked underlyingBalance if there are
discrepancies — and the tokens leave without ANY debt being recorded in totalBorrows.
This creates a completely undetected capital drain: no borrow event, no debt entry,
no utilization rate change. The protocol cannot detect or recover from this via
normal repayment flows since there is no corresponding totalBorrows to repay.

yTokenToReserveExchangeRate() = totalLiquidity / totalYTokenSupply.
totalLiquidity = underlyingBalance + borrowedLiquidity.
After pullFunds(X), underlyingBalance is NOT decremented, so totalLiquidity is overstated
by X, making the exchange rate appear higher than the actual backing per yToken.
Consequence: the first lenders to redeem receive their entitled amount (backed by
phantom liquidity), but the tokens are already gone from the vault for later redeemers.
The total redeemable obligations encoded in the exchange rate exceed the actual vault
balance, enabling a bank-run dynamic where early redeemers profit at late redeemers'
expense.

Quantitative bound: sum of (yTokenBalance[user] * exchangeRate / PRECISION) over all
holders must be <= actual yToken vault balance + totalBorrows (recoverable).

After pullFunds drains the yToken vault without updating underlyingBalance, the vault
may not hold enough tokens to honor redemptions. The exchange rate is phantom-inflated,
so the _calculated_ redemption amount may exceed the actual vault balance. Lenders'
yTokens become worthless (or cause a revert) even though the protocol's accounting
shows a healthy reserve.

The invariant: for any individual holder with balance B yTokens, the vault must
hold at least B * exchangeRate / PRECISION underlying tokens to honour their redeem.
At minimum, the lender seeded with the full reserve in Setup should always be
able to redeem their balance.

The ReserveLogic library's availableLiquidity() function returns reserve.underlyingBalance
directly (line 37: `return reserve.underlyingBalance`). This value is only updated in
_deposit, _redeem, borrow, and repay — NOT in pullFunds or pushFunds. As a result,
underlyingBalance becomes a stale oracle that diverges from the true vault balance
after any pull or push operation. All downstream computations that depend on it
(totalLiquidity, utilization rate, borrowing rate, exchange rate, capacity checks)
are corrupted. The protocol's entire economic model is predicated on this value
being accurate.

borrow() and pullFunds() both call yToken.transferUnderlyingTo() to move tokens out.
borrow() also:
  (1) checks notPaused
  (2) checks reserve.getBorrowingEnabled()
  (3) requires amount <= reserve.availableLiquidity()
  (4) increments reserve.totalBorrows (records debt)
  (5) decrements reserve.underlyingBalance (maintains accounting)
  (6) calls reserve.updateInterestRates()
pullFunds() does NONE of these. It simply transfers tokens out. This asymmetry means
pullFunds is a completely unguarded backdoor for extracting vault liquidity without
triggering any of the economic or security invariants that borrow() enforces.

repay() has: `if (amount > reserve.totalBorrows) { amount = reserve.totalBorrows; }`.
When totalBorrows == 0, amount is clamped to 0. Then underlyingBalance += 0 and
safeTransferFrom(0) are called — both are no-ops. So calling repay while no borrows
exist is harmless. However, the combination with pullFunds creates a scenario where
the leverager can create a deficit (pullFunds) that can NEVER be resolved via repay
because repay only adjusts totalBorrows (which pullFunds never incremented).
There is no path to restore underlyingBalance after pullFunds except for a new deposit
by a lender, which would be at a phantom exchange rate.

FullMath.mulDiv uses XOR (^) instead of exponentiation (**) for the initial Newton-Raphson seed: `uint256 inv = (3 * denominator) ^ 2`. In Solidity, `^` is bitwise XOR, not exponentiation. The correct seed should be `(3 * denominator) * denominator` (i.e., 3*d^2 mod 2^256). The XOR-2 gives a completely wrong starting value, causing the modular inverse computation to diverge or converge to a wrong value. This only affects the 512-bit code path (when prod1 != 0, i.e., when a*b >= 2^256). Any mulDiv call that overflows 256 bits in the intermediate product will return a wrong result. This affects share calculations, liquidity math, and any downstream pricing that uses FullMath.mulDiv with large inputs.

The `balances()` function in Strategy.sol (called by Vault.deposit and Vault.withdraw to compute share prices) does NOT include the vesting position's liquidity in the reported balances. It only sums idle + main + secondary. However, the vault has real tokens locked in the vesting position on Uniswap. When a user deposits, the denominator (total value) is understated, so they receive more shares than they should. When the vesting position is withdrawn (collectFees -> _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition), those tokens flow into idle balances, which instantly increases the value of all existing shares — including the ones minted with the understated denominator. This allows any depositor to receive free value from the vesting position by depositing right before a vest withdrawal event.

In `_calcDeposit`, when both balances are nonzero, the code calculates `cross = min(depositAmount0 * bal1, depositAmount1 * bal0)` and then rounds UP both `amount0 = (cross - 1) / bal1 + 1` and `amount1 = (cross - 1) / bal0 + 1`. This over-collects tokens from the depositor (both are rounded up independently). The user pays slightly more than their actual proportional share of either token, but only receives shares computed as `cross * totalSupply / bal0 / bal1` which truncates down. The tiny excess tokens are effectively donated to the vault on every deposit. While individually small, this is systematic and happens on every non-first deposit with nonzero balances on both sides.

The `withdraw()` function in Vault.sol calls `_burn(msg.sender, shares)` (line 89) BEFORE checking slippage (line 101). If `collectFees()` triggers a reentrancy or if the strategy's `withdrawPartial()` reverts, the shares are already burned but no tokens are returned. However, `_burn` follows the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern correctly for reentrancy. The more subtle issue: `withdraw()` reads `totalSupply` AFTER burning (line 88 captures it before burn, then burn happens at line 89). Wait — looking carefully: line 88 is `uint256 totalSupply = totalSupply();` and line 89 is `_burn(msg.sender, shares);`. The totalSupply snapshot is taken BEFORE burn. Then `withdrawAmount0 = totalBalance0 * shares / totalSupply` uses the pre-burn totalSupply. This is correct for proportional withdrawal. BUT: the `safeTransferFrom(strategy, msg.sender, withdrawAmount0)` requires that the strategy has pre-approved the vault to spend its tokens. This approval is granted in Strategy constructor via `forceApprove(vault, max)`. However, if the strategy's approval is ever revoked or consumed (e.g., by a future upgrade or approval race), `safeTransferFrom` will revert AFTER shares are already burned. The user loses their shares permanently.

The `_withdrawPartOfVestingPosition()` function computes `liquidityToRemove` using `vp.initialLiquidity * (lastValid - vp.lastUpdate) / (vp.endTs - vp.startTs)`. This accumulates rounding error each time it is called. Each call to `collectFees()` (triggered on every deposit/withdraw) calls this function. If `(lastValid - vp.lastUpdate)` is small relative to `(vp.endTs - vp.startTs)`, the integer division truncates to 0, meaning NO liquidity is removed despite time having passed. This causes the vesting to stall for short time intervals, allowing the vesting position to effectively never fully vest if collectFees is called very frequently. Meanwhile `lastUpdate` advances but `remainingLiquidity` stays the same. Over many calls, the total removed liquidity may be less than `initialLiquidity`, leaving residual liquidity permanently stuck in the vesting position (since the endTs check uses `remainingLiquidity` for the final withdrawal).

In `Vault._calcDeposit()`, the first-deposit share calculation is: `shares = (amount0 > amount1 ? amount0 : amount1) - 1000`. This takes the MAX of two raw token amounts which have different decimals (WBTC has 8 decimals, USDC has 6 decimals). The raw number `1e8` WBTC represents 1 WBTC (~$60k) while `1e8` USDC represents 100 USDC (~$100). By taking the max of the two raw values, the first depositor's share count depends entirely on which token has the larger raw integer value. This is economically meaningless and can be gamed: a first depositor can deposit 1 wei of token0 and a huge amount of token1, getting shares denominated in token1 units. The second depositor then gets shares at the same ratio, creating a wildly imbalanced share price. More concretely, if someone deposits `1e8` WBTC and `1` USDC, they get `1e8 - 1000 = 99999000` shares, but the vault has very little USDC. The next depositor must match the ratio and gets far fewer shares per dollar of value.

Path.skipToken() returns a new bytes slice but the caller in _getTokenIn never captures the return value. Because `path` is a `bytes memory` value type, the assignment never updates `path`, so `path.hasMultiplePools()` remains true forever for any multi-hop path, causing an infinite loop (OOG) on every exactOutput multi-hop swap. For single-pool paths the while loop body is never entered, so `decodeFirstPool` still reads the FIRST token instead of the last, returning the wrong tokenIn (tokenOut of the swap), causing the denomination check to fail and blocking all multi-hop leveraged positions.

In `withdraw()` at line 232, when the borrowed denomination is token1, the ternary expression `amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount` uses `amountOut0` in the true branch instead of `amountOut1`. When `amountOut1 < owedAmount` (the common case where withdrawal proceeds are less than the owed debt), `repayFromWithdraw` is set to `amountOut0` (the token0 amount) rather than `amountOut1`. Then `owedAmount -= repayFromWithdraw` can underflow or produce wrong accounting: more (or less) repayment is credited than the token1 balance actually supports, and `amountOut1 -= repayFromWithdraw` may revert with underflow if repayFromWithdraw > amountOut1.

In `liquidatePosition()` at line 318, the denominator for `borrowedValue` uses `ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` (the raw uint8, e.g. 8 for WBTC or 6 for USDC) instead of `10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` (the scaling factor 1e8 or 1e6). This makes `borrowedValue` massively over-inflated (by 1e8/8 = 12.5 million times for WBTC). As a result: (a) `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` is almost always FALSE, so no protocol fee is ever collected; (b) `repayAmount` (which equals `owedAmount`) is computed correctly but `borrowedValue` used for fee logic is wrong. When `totalValueUSD < borrowedValue` (which is nearly always because borrowedValue is hugely inflated), no fee is taken, meaning `feeRecipient` receives nothing.

`feeRecipient` is declared as a public state variable at line 47 but is never initialized in the constructor or any setup function. There is no `setFeeRecipient` function. As a result, `feeRecipient` is permanently `address(0)`. In `liquidatePosition`, when the protocol fee condition is met (and would be if LIB-03 were fixed), `IERC20(up.token0).safeTransfer(feeRecipient, pf0)` sends tokens to address(0), burning them. The protocol collects no liquidation fees.

In `_getTokenIn`, `Path.skipToken()` is a pure function that returns a NEW bytes slice (the remainder after skipping one token+fee element). The library function does NOT mutate the input `path` in-place — Solidity `bytes memory` is passed by reference in the sense of pointer, but `skipToken` calls `BytesLib.slice()` which allocates a fresh memory region and returns it. Since `path.skipToken()` at line 568 discards the return value, `path` never changes, `path.hasMultiplePools()` never becomes false, and the function loops infinitely (gas exhaustion) for any multi-hop path. For a single-hop path, the loop body is skipped, and `decodeFirstPool` is called on the original undivided path — but because exactOutput paths are encoded in REVERSE (tokenOut...tokenIn), `decodeFirstPool` reads the FIRST address which is tokenOut, and the SECOND address which is the intermediate/tokenIn. For a 1-hop path this happens to be correct. The bug is entirely about multi-hop paths causing infinite loops.

In `withdraw()` at line 232, the wrong variable is used for the repay-from-withdraw calculation when denomination is token1. When `amountOut1 < owedAmount` (true branch), the code sets `repayFromWithdraw = amountOut0` (token0 amount) instead of `amountOut1` (token1). Then at line 234, `amountOut1 -= repayFromWithdraw` uses `repayFromWithdraw = amountOut0`. If WBTC (8 decimals, much smaller unit value) amount is large, e.g. 1 WBTC = 1e8 units, and USDC amount is say 50_000e6 = 5e10, then `amountOut1 -= 1e8` still works. But if `amountOut0 > amountOut1`, arithmetic underflow reverts with SafeMath, and the full withdrawal becomes impossible — a denial of service on any USDC-denominated position partial withdrawal.

pullFunds() and pushFunds() do not update reserve.underlyingBalance. The leverager can pull tokens from the yToken contract and push back a different amount (or push back nothing in an error path), causing underlyingBalance to permanently diverge from the actual token balance held by the yToken contract.  Because availableLiquidity() returns underlyingBalance verbatim, future borrow(), redeem(), and deposit() operations will use a stale accounting value.  If underlyingBalance exceeds the true balance, borrow/redeem will call transferUnderlyingTo or safeTransfer for more tokens than the yToken holds, reverting with ERC-20 insufficient-balance and bricking the reserve.

The deposit() function mints yTokens based on the exchange rate `yTokenAmount = amount * exchangeRate / PRECISION` and then requires `yTokenAmount > MINIMUM_YTOKEN_AMOUNT` (1000).  Because the exchange rate uses totalLiquidity = underlyingBalance + borrowedLiquidity (including accrued interest), as interest accumulates the exchange rate drops (fewer yTokens per underlying token).  For low-decimal tokens (token0, 8 decimals = 1e8 per token), once the exchange rate falls below 1000/amount * PRECISION, deposits of that size revert with "deposit is dust amount".  A borrow followed by time-skipping causes interest accrual, which increases totalLiquidity relative to totalYTokens, reducing the yToken-per-underlying rate.  At extreme utilization the exchange rate approaches 0 (many underlying per yToken), making medium-sized deposits impossible.

setLeverager() can only be called once (guarded by `require(leverager == address(0), "leverager can only be set once")`). If the leverager contract is upgraded, exploited, or becomes broken, there is no way to update it.  Any borrow(), repay(), pullFunds(), and pushFunds() calls will then route through the broken leverager address and either fail or be permanently blocked.  Additionally, if the leverager is a contract that self-destructs or has a critical bug, the LendingPool's borrow/repay functionality is permanently disabled with no recovery path for the owner.

In `_updateIndexes`, after computing the new borrowing index, there is a hard require: `require(newBorrowingIndex <= type(uint128).max)`. If this condition is ever violated (via extreme borrowing rates set by admin + long time without state updates), ALL state-mutating operations on that reserve permanently revert: deposit(), redeem(), borrow(), repay() all call reserve.updateState() which calls _updateIndexes. The only exception is repay() which also calls updateState() first, so even repay is blocked.  There is no way to reset the index or skip the check.  The reserve becomes permanently frozen for all operations. While this requires extreme rates + very long time, it represents a permanent irrecoverable DoS with no admin escape hatch.

The checkCapacity() function in ReserveLogic.sol uses a bare require() with no error message: `require(totalLiquidity + depositAmount <= reserve.reserveCapacity)`. This is a usability issue but more importantly, if reserveCapacity is set to 0 by the admin (or is inadvertently set too low), all deposits will revert silently.  The deposit() function provides no way to check whether a deposit will succeed before submitting, and the revert provides no diagnostic information.  If the admin calls setReserveCapacity(asset, 0), all deposits are permanently blocked with no on-chain indication of why.

The redeem() function has the notPaused modifier. When the contract is paused via emergencyPauseAll(), depositors cannot redeem their yTokens to get back their underlying assets. The pause has no time limit and no automatic expiry. Combined with the fact that pausing is a unilateral admin action (single owner key), all depositor funds are frozen indefinitely at the admin's discretion. repay() intentionally omits notPaused (the comment says "Modified from original version to accept repayments even when contract is paused") but redeem() does not receive the same treatment.

The initReserve() function checks `reserves[asset].lastUpdateTimestamp == 0` to prevent double-initialization. The internal initReserve() sets `lastUpdateTimestamp = uint128(block.timestamp)`. If block.timestamp is ever 0 (only possible on block 0 of a chain, or in a Foundry test with default timestamp), the check passes and a reserve can be re-initialized, overwriting borrowingIndex, yTokenAddress, and all config fields. Re-initializing an existing reserve with active deposits would replace yTokenAddress with a new yToken contract, making all existing yToken holders unable to interact with the reserve (wrong yToken for approval/ burn), permanently locking their funds.

Strategy.collectFees() contains the following call for the vesting position:
  collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper)
The second argument MUST be vestPosition.tickUpper, not mainPosition.tickUpper.
At vesting-position creation both values are identical (addVestingPosition stores
mainPosition.tickLower/tickUpper into vestPosition), but after any subsequent
rebalance() the mainPosition ticks are recalculated while the vestPosition struct
retains its original ticks.  After the first rebalance post-creation,
mainPosition.tickUpper != vestPosition.tickUpper.
collectFees() then calls burn(0) + collect() on the pair
  (vestPosition.tickLower, NEW_mainPosition.tickUpper)
which is not the position the strategy owns.  Uniswap V3 silently returns 0 for
both calls on a non-existent position, so vesting-position fees are never credited
to idle balance in the protocol-fee window.  The actual vesting liquidity is only
touched later in _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition, which uses the correct struct
ticks but runs AFTER protocol fees are taken — so all vesting trading fees bypass
the protocolFee deduction entirely.

Strategy.balances() returns:
  amount0 = idle0 + main0 + secondary0
  amount1 = idle1 + main1 + secondary1
The vesting position (vestPosition.remainingLiquidity) is never included.
Vault.deposit() prices new shares using these understated balances, so new
depositors pay fewer tokens per share than the true NAV warrants.  Existing
shareholders suffer dilution: their proportional claim on total assets decreases
with every new deposit made while a vesting position is active.
The magnitude of dilution equals (vesting_position_value / total_true_NAV) per
deposit, compounding with each subsequent depositor.

strategy.rebalance() and strategy.compound() both gate execution with
_requirePriceWithinRange(), which verifies that spot price is within tickTwapDeviation
of the TWAP and that consecutive oracle observations have not moved beyond
maxObservationDeviation.  Vault.deposit() and Vault.withdraw() perform no such check.
Both call strategy.balances(), which reads sqrtPriceX96 from pool.slot0() (spot price)
to convert position liquidity into token amounts via LiquidityAmounts.getAmountsForLiquidity.
A flash-loan attacker can push the pool price in one direction within a single block,
call deposit() with a skewed balance report to receive inflated shares, then restore
the price — all atomically.  The slippage guards (amount0Min / amount1Min) protect
the vault from receiving too few tokens but do NOT constrain the share count minted,
which is derived from the manipulated balances.

_calcDeposit for the first deposit (totalSupply == 0) sets:
  shares = max(depositAmount0, depositAmount1) - 1000
For a WBTC/USDC vault (8 / 6 decimals), depositing 1 WBTC (1e8) + 100,000 USDC (1e11)
yields shares ≈ 1e11 − 1000.  The 1000 burn shares represent a fraction of
1000 / (1e11) = 1e-8 of total supply — effectively zero inflation protection.
Compare with depositing 1 WBTC alone (1e8 units): shares ≈ 1e8 − 1000, where the
burn fraction is 1000 / (1e8) = 1e-5, still tiny but ~1000× larger.
The same BTC value gives 1000× fewer shares depending solely on whether USDC is
included, because USDC raw units dominate.  This makes the initial share price
arbitrary and the anti-inflation seed deposit negligible for any USDC-heavy first deposit.
A first depositor who controls the deposit mix can choose the denomination that gives
the most shares per unit of actual value, skewing the exchange rate for all future
depositors.

_calcDeposit contains:
  assert(totalSupply == 0 || bal0 > 0 || bal1 > 0);
A failing assert in Solidity 0.8 raises Panic(0x01) and consumes ALL remaining gas,
unlike require() which refunds unused gas.  The condition can be violated when
totalSupply > 0 AND bal0 == 0 AND bal1 == 0.
This state is theoretically reachable: the permanent BURN address holds 1000 shares,
so totalSupply can never reach zero.  If all positions are emptied (e.g., full
withdrawal by the last real depositor combined with precision-loss rounding in Uniswap
V3 liquidity → token conversion), both bal0 and bal1 could round to 0 while
totalSupply remains 1000.  Every subsequent deposit() call would then hit the assert,
spending the full gas stipend and reverting — permanently bricking the vault.
Additionally, assert should never be used for invariant checks that depend on external
state (pool price, precision rounding); only require() is appropriate there.

The deposit flow in Vault.deposit() is:
  1. safeTransferFrom(user → strategy, depositAmount0)   [tokens leave user]
  2. safeTransferFrom(user → strategy, depositAmount1)   [tokens leave user]
  3. if (depositFee > 0) shares -= shares * depositFee / 10_000
  4. require(shares > 0)
  5. _mint(msg.sender, shares)
The slippage guards (amount0Min, amount1Min) protect only against token-amount
slippage, not against share-count slippage.  A user cannot specify a minimum
acceptable share count.  If the owner calls setDepositFee() to raise the fee in the
same block (front-running or coincident transaction), the user's tokens are fully
transferred but fewer shares are minted than expected — with no mechanism to detect
or reject this outcome.  The fee is capped at 0.1% (10 BPS), so loss per call is
bounded but the pattern creates a silent value transfer from depositors to existing
holders whenever the fee is non-zero and changes unexpectedly.

Vault.withdraw() uses the condition:
  if (idle0 < withdrawAmount0 || idle1 < withdrawAmount1)
to decide whether to call strategy.withdrawPartial().  When exactly one idle balance
is sufficient but the other is not, withdrawPartial() is still invoked.  Inside
withdrawPartial(), the proportional idle allocation is:
  amount0Out += bal0 * shares / totalSupply
  amount1Out += bal1 * shares / totalSupply
where bal0/bal1 are idle balances at the time of the call.  The "sufficient" idle
token is partially removed from the position AND added as idle proportion, effectively
double-counting it relative to the direct idle-transfer path.  The resulting
withdrawAmount0/withdrawAmount1 returned by withdrawPartial() may differ from the
simple proportional calculation (totalBalance * shares / totalSupply) used in the
non-partial path, creating a discontinuity at the boundary where idle0 == withdrawAmount0
but idle1 < withdrawAmount1.  Users whose withdrawal happens to straddle this boundary
receive a slightly different amount than the pure proportional formula predicts,
inconsistent with the non-partial path.

In withdraw(), when the borrowed asset is token1, the repayFromWithdraw variable is assigned using amountOut0 instead of amountOut1 in the ternary condition. This means the amount actually deducted from amountOut1 is wrong: it either uses too much (amountOut0 > owedAmount when amountOut1 < owedAmount) or too little. The user pays incorrect amounts and the accounting of amountOut1 sent back to the user is corrupted, leading to either an undercharge or overcharge of repayment and incorrect token1 transfer to the user.

In liquidatePosition(), the borrowedValue computation divides by ERC20(up.denomination).decimals() (e.g. 8 for WBTC, 6 for USDC) instead of 10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals() (i.e. 1e8 or 1e6). This produces a borrowedValue that is astronomically larger than the real USD value of the debt. For WBTC with 8 decimals, borrowedValue is overstated by a factor of 1e8/8 = 12,500,000x. As a result: (1) the fee logic `if (totalValueUSD > borrowedValue)` is almost always false, so protocol fees are never collected; (2) even if it were true, fee calculations would be wildly wrong; (3) borrowedValue is not used for the actual repay decision but a future maintainer or auditor reading this code would expect the logic to be coherent.

feeRecipient is declared as a public state variable at line 47 but is NEVER initialized and there is NO setter function for it anywhere in the contract. It permanently remains address(0). When liquidationFee > 0 and the fee condition is met, protocol fees (pf0, pf1) are transferred to address(0) — effectively burned. The protocol can never collect liquidation revenue. Even if the owner later tries to set liquidationFee to a non-zero value, all fees are burned.

The `currBorrowedUSD` accounting in VaultParams tracks borrowed USD at position-opening prices. During partial withdrawal, it decrements by `initBorrowedUsd * pctWithdraw / 1e18`, using stale opening-time USD values. This means the running cumulative borrow cap (maxCumulativeBorrowedUSD) does not reflect current market value. Over time with many partial opens/closes and price movement, the tracked currBorrowedUSD can diverge significantly from actual outstanding exposure. While documented as intentional for simplicity, this allows the vault to silently exceed its intended USD exposure limit when borrowed asset prices increase significantly after position opening.

In openLeveragedPosition(), the borrowedAmount is computed as `lp.maxBorrowAmount - denomBalance` where denomBalance is the entire denomination token balance of the Leverager contract BEFORE repayment. If the Leverager contract holds any pre-existing balance of the denomination token (e.g. from a previous incomplete operation, or from tokens swept back), the borrowedAmount recorded in the position will be understated. The comment in the code acknowledges this: "if for some reason there have previously been a large amount of tokens stuck, this could fail". More subtly, even small residual balances will silently reduce the recorded borrowedAmount, meaning the position accrues less debt than was actually borrowed — a free subsidy from the protocol.

In isLiquidateable(), the base computation at line 408 uses `owedAmount * 1e18 / (vp.maxTimesLeverage - 1e18)`. If maxTimesLeverage is set very close to 1e18 (e.g. 1.001e18), the denominator becomes very small (0.001e18 = 1e15), causing `base` to be astronomically large. The min() with initCollateralValue then always picks initCollateralValue. While this doesn't immediately break, the liquidation threshold calculation `vp.minCollateralPct * base / 1e18` becomes exactly `minCollateralPct * initCollateralValue / 1e18`, which means near-1x leverage positions with small minCollateralPct can never be liquidated even when they are deeply underwater. More critically, if maxTimesLeverage == 1e18 exactly, the division by zero causes a revert in isLiquidateable(), which is called from liquidatePosition(), making liquidation permanently impossible and causing bad debt accumulation.

The `withdraw()` function does not update `positions[wp.id].initCollateralUsd` when doing a partial withdrawal, only `initCollateralValue` and `initBorrowedUsd`. The `initCollateralUsd` field is set at position opening and never updated. This field is not directly used in post-open calculations (isLiquidateable uses on-chain vault balances), but it creates a misleading state where the stored position data does not reflect the current position size.
