An attacker can liquidate ANY position — even perfectly healthy ones — because the check `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` will almost always be false (borrowedValue is ~1e10 times larger than it should be for WBTC).

The `feeRecipient` state variable at line 47 is declared but never initialized. It remains address(0) for the lifetime of the contract (no setter exists in the owner-only functions). In liquidatePosition(), protocol fees are transferred to feeRecipient at lines 328-329. These fees are permanently burned (sent to address(0)) on every liquidation. A secondary impact is that a malicious liquidator can trigger this to silently drain the fee entitlement rather than having it reach the protocol.

In `withdraw`, when the borrowed denomination is token1, the `repayFromWithdraw` variable is computed as `amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount`. This is a copy-paste bug: when `amountOut1 < owedAmount` the branch should use `amountOut1` (the available token1 amount), but instead uses `amountOut0` (the token0 / WBTC amount expressed in 8 decimals). The subsequent subtraction `amountOut1 -= repayFromWithdraw` can massively underflow or incorrectly account the repayment, allowing the user to repay less than required while receiving more tokens than they should, or causing a revert that prevents legitimate withdrawals.

In `liquidatePosition`, the `borrowedValue` is computed as `owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` instead of `owedAmount * bPrice / (10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals())`. `decimals()` returns the raw uint8 decimals value (e.g. 6 for USDC, 8 for WBTC), NOT the scaling factor. Dividing by 6 or 8 instead of 1e6 or 1e8 massively overestimates `borrowedValue` by a factor of ~1e5 to ~1e7, causing the `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` check to almost always be false, so the protocol never charges liquidation fees — the fee logic is permanently bricked.

`feeRecipient` is declared as a public state variable at line 47 but is never initialized — there is no constructor assignment and no setter function. It permanently remains `address(0)`. Any liquidation fees computed (when the decimals bug WC-02 is fixed) would be sent to `address(0)` (burned), causing permanent loss of protocol revenue. Additionally, `safeTransfer` to `address(0)` may revert on some token implementations.

In `openLeveragedPosition`, `_sweepTokens` is called at the very end and transfers ALL remaining balances of token0 and token1 back to `msg.sender`. Because the Leverager holds pre-approved max allowances to the vault and lendingPool for all vault tokens (set in `initVault` / `enableTokenAsBorrowed`), any leftover tokens from previous transactions accumulate and are swept to the NEXT position opener. If a prior operation leaves residual tokens (e.g. due to slippage in exactOutput swaps, or partial flash loan repayment edge cases), the next caller captures them. This creates a griefing/frontrunning vector where attacker can seed dust and then open a position to drain them.

In `withdraw`, when `wp.hasToSwap` is true, the code decrements `amountOut0` by `swapParams.amountIn` (line 249) and `amountOut1` by `swapParams.amountIn` (line 259) WITHOUT first checking whether `amountOut0` or `amountOut1` is sufficient to cover the swap input. If the user supplies a `swapParams.amountIn` larger than `amountOut0` (or `amountOut1` after the debt repayment reduction), the subtraction underflows (Solidity 0.8 reverts). But more critically: there is no check that the tokens being approved for the swap actually came from the withdrawal. The contract blindly approves `up.token0`/`up.token1` for `swapParams.amountIn` from its own balance — which could include tokens from OTHER users' pending withdrawals if reentrancy protections are partially bypassed through the ERC721 callback in `_burn` or via `onERC721Received`.

In `openLeveragedPosition`, the denomination token approval check has an edge case: the code only checks `if (a0 > lp.amount0In && up.token0 != lp.denomination)` before decoding `swapParams1`. If `a0 > lp.amount0In` is false (vault used exactly what the user provided for token0), the swap block is skipped. But `lp.maxBorrowAmount` has already been borrowed from the lending pool (line 135). Any borrowed amount that isn't used in swaps is then "repaid" via `denomBalance` (line 172). However, if the user supplies empty/garbage `swapParams1` when `a0 > lp.amount0In` is true and `token0 != denomination`, `abi.decode` will attempt to decode the garbage bytes and revert with a confusing error, making the operation fail silently. This is minor but the user-facing error is unclear. The more interesting concern is that `lp.vault0In` and `lp.vault1In` are fully user-controlled with no upper-bound validation — a user can set enormous `vault0In`/`vault1In` which causes the contract to `pullFunds` far beyond what they provide, effectively pulling a huge flash loan that must all be returned. The constraint is that `pushFunds` must be called for the same amounts — so it is self-limiting and not exploitable without a way to avoid `pushFunds`.

collectFees() uses mainPosition.tickUpper instead of vestPosition.tickUpper when collecting fees for the vesting position. This causes fee collection to target a Uniswap position that does not exist (wrong ticks), so vesting position fees are never actually collected and the vested position's tokens are permanently inaccessible via the normal fee path. The wrong position (vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper) will simply return 0 from Uniswap if no position exists there, or could inadvertently touch another position's state.

_withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() uses an incorrect denominator in the vesting rate formula. It divides by (vp.endTs - vp.startTs) — the full vest duration — but the numerator is (lastValid - vp.lastUpdate) — the time since the LAST update, not since start. This means each successive call to collectFees vests a progressively smaller fraction of remaining liquidity, causing permanent under-vesting. Liquidity that should be fully vested by endTs will not be (remainingLiquidity > 0 when the schedule ends), causing depositors to lose entitled vesting rewards.

_setSecondaryPositionsTicks() can create an invalid (zero-width or inverted) secondary position when modulo == 0. When tick is exactly on a tick spacing boundary, modulo=0, and the code sets secondaryPosition.tickUpper = tick - 0 = tick for the token1-heavy branch, while mainPosition.tickLower may also equal tick. This results in tickLower == tickUpper, which Uniswap V3 will reject with a revert on the subsequent mint, causing rebalance() to permanently revert when the spot price lands exactly on a tick spacing multiple.

balances() does not account for the vesting position's liquidity. When there is an ongoing vesting position, the strategy holds LP liquidity on behalf of the vesting schedule in addition to the main and secondary positions, but balances() only sums idle + main + secondary. This means the vault's share-price calculation (in Vault.deposit/withdraw) uses an understated total value, allowing new depositors to buy shares at below-fair-value prices (diluting existing depositors) whenever a vesting position is active.

changePositionWidth() has no onlyRebalancer modifier; it only gains rebalancer access indirectly because it calls rebalance() internally, which has onlyRebalancer. However, changePositionWidth() itself is external with no modifier, so anyone can call it. While rebalance() will revert if not called by rebalancer, there is a subtle issue: positionWidth is updated BEFORE rebalance() is called. An unauthorized caller can set positionWidth to an arbitrary value (satisfying the divisibility check) and the require inside rebalance() will then revert — but positionWidth has already been permanently changed. This allows any address to brick the strategy by setting an undesirable positionWidth.

withdrawPartial() calculates the user's share of idle balances BEFORE subtracting protocol fees that were just distributed in the preceding collectFees() call. However, in the normal withdraw flow (Vault calls collectFees then withdrawPartial), the protocol fee tokens have already left the strategy to feeRecipient, so idleBalances() correctly reflects post-fee balances. But there is an edge case: if collectFees() is NOT called prior to withdrawPartial (the onlyVault modifier means Vault controls this), and Vault.withdraw does call collectFees first, this ordering is safe. The real issue is that withdrawPartial doesn't include the vesting position in its calculation, meaning users withdrawing while a vesting position is active will receive LESS than their fair share (the unvested portion is excluded from their withdrawal). This is a permanent value leak: even if the user deposited before the vesting position was created, they cannot withdraw their proportional claim on it.

Both deposit() and withdraw() rely on Strategy.balances(), which uses slot0() sqrtPriceX96 to compute how much token0 and token1 are locked in mainPosition and secondaryPosition via LiquidityAmounts.getAmountsForLiquidity(). This spot price can be manipulated via a flash loan within the same transaction. An attacker can: (1) Flash-borrow large amount of token0 from another protocol (2) Swap token0 → token1 in the Uniswap pool to push price up (3) Call vault.deposit() — balances() now over-values token1 relative to token0
    The min(cross0, cross1) logic in _calcDeposit picks the smaller cross product,
    which now forces victim depositor's proportion to be measured at the manipulated price
(4) Repay flash loan This can cause a depositor to receive fewer shares than deserved (price pushed one way makes one token appear worth more, shrinking the cross product for the other direction).

Strategy.balances() (called by Vault.deposit and Vault.withdraw) does NOT account for the vesting position's remaining locked liquidity. The vesting position tokens are locked in Uniswap but balances() only sums idle + mainPosition + secondaryPosition (lines 502-521). This means the total value tracked by the vault is artificially low when a vesting position is active. New depositors who deposit DURING an active vesting position get shares priced on a lower total value (excluding vesting locked liquidity), so they receive MORE shares than they should. When the vesting position eventually unlocks (via collectFees → _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition), the tokens flow into idle and suddenly appear in balances(), diluting ALL current shareholders — but the new depositors (who bought in cheap) benefit disproportionately. This is an economic invariant: vault total assets should always be correctly accounted.

In Vault.deposit(), the first-deposit share formula at line 133 is: `shares = (amount0 > amount1 ? amount0 : amount1) - 1000` This uses raw token amounts WITHOUT normalizing for token decimals. WBTC has 8 decimals and USDC has 6 decimals. If a first depositor deposits 1e8 WBTC and 100_000e6 USDC, shares = max(1e8, 100_000e6) - 1000 = 100_000e6 - 1000 ≈ 1e11. If instead they deposit 1e8 WBTC and 1e6 USDC, shares = max(1e8, 1e6) - 1000 = 1e8 - 1000. The shares minted to the first depositor depend entirely on the raw numeric magnitude of whichever token amount is larger — this has no economic meaning and creates an artificial dependency between the share scale and the token decimals. A first depositor who provides an imbalanced deposit (e.g., only USDC) sets the share scale based on USDC magnitude, affecting all future depositors' precision. Additionally, the 1000-share BURN mint has different economic significance depending on which token dominates the first deposit: if shares ≈ 1e11 (USDC-dominant), 1000 shares is negligible; if shares ≈ 1e8 (WBTC-dominant), 1000 shares is 1/100000 of supply which could be material at low deposit sizes.

Vault.withdraw() computes withdrawAmount0/1 as `totalBalance * shares / totalSupply` (line 91-92), then checks if idle balances are sufficient (line 96). If idle IS sufficient, it directly calls safeTransferFrom(strategy, msg.sender, withdrawAmount0/1) WITHOUT calling withdrawPartial(). This fast path works only if the Strategy has approved the Vault for token transfers. Strategy constructor grants `IERC20(token0).forceApprove(vault, type(uint256).max)` at lines 96-97. This is the "arbitrary from in transferFrom" flagged by Slither. While the Strategy intentionally approves the Vault, any bug in the Vault's access control (e.g., if an attacker could become msg.sender inside withdraw()) could drain Strategy's tokens. More concretely: the withdrawAmount0 is computed using spot-price-based balances(), but the actual transfer comes from idle balances. If balances() over-estimates idle-equivalent value (due to spot price manipulation), withdrawAmount0 > actual idle0, causing the idle check `idle0 < withdrawAmount0` to be TRUE, forcing the withdrawPartial() path. But if spot price was UNDER-estimated (opposite manipulation), idle0 >= withdrawAmount0 when it shouldn't be, the fast path sends more idle tokens than the user's fair share from perspective of the total vault, leaving less for remaining shareholders.

In collectFees(), the vesting position's fees are collected using vestPosition.tickLower but mainPosition.tickUpper instead of vestPosition.tickUpper (line 167). After any rebalance, the main position is moved to new ticks so mainPosition.tickUpper != vestPosition.tickUpper. As a result the wrong Uniswap position is targeted: the burn+collect call silently targets a non-existent or different position, meaning (a) vesting position fees are never collected, and (b) a 0-liquidity burn is issued on the wrong tick range, which is a no-op but wastes gas and produces incorrect accounting. Any protocol fees computed on afterBal - preBal will be zero for the vesting position even when fees have accrued, permanently locking those fees inside the pool position.

_withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() computes liquidityToRemove using vp.initialLiquidity instead of vp.remainingLiquidity for the proportional (non-final) withdrawal case (line 467). Over the vesting period the function is called multiple times. Each call removes initialLiquidity * elapsed / totalDuration, but since initialLiquidity never decreases, consecutive calls can remove more total liquidity than was ever deposited. Specifically, if the function is called N times with equal intervals, it removes N * (initialLiquidity / N) = initialLiquidity per interval, so after the Nth call the total removed exceeds initialLiquidity. When the pool position has insufficient liquidity the Uniswap burn will revert or return less than requested, causing remainingLiquidity to underflow (uint128 subtraction of too-large a value).

balances() (lines 502-521) omits the vesting position entirely. It sums idle balances, main position amounts, and secondary position amounts, but never adds the vesting position's liquidity value. The vault uses strategy.balances() to compute the total assets backing shares (for deposit/withdraw pro-rata). While the vesting position is meant to accrue to depositors over time, the portion already removed from Uniswap (unlocked principal) does appear in idle balances. However, the locked portion — the liquidity still in vestPosition — is permanently excluded. This means the vault undervalues total assets, causing depositors to receive fewer shares than warranted, and withdrawers to receive less than their fair portion. The vested-but-unlocked amount IS in idle balances (after _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition), but the still-locked vesting liquidity is not counted, creating a systematic undercount that benefits late depositors over early ones.

collectFees() takes a protocol fee cut on all fee income before calling _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() (line 179). But when the vesting position fees are collected on line 167 (which targets wrong ticks per FH-001, but assume it were correct), those fees pass through the preBal/afterBal delta calculation and have protocol fee deducted. This means the protocol extracts a fee from vesting position income that was meant entirely for depositors. Even if FH-001 is fixed, the ordering means vesting position fees always have protocol fee taken before being distributed. Additionally, when _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition eventually unlocks principal liquidity (not fees), that principal lands in idleBalances and is correctly distributed — but any fees earned by the vesting position during its lifetime are partially siphoned to the fee recipient.

changePositionWidth() (lines 395-399) is declared external with no access control modifier. It calls rebalance() which has onlyRebalancer, so a non-rebalancer caller will be rejected inside rebalance(). However, the positionWidth state variable is updated BEFORE calling rebalance() on line 397. If somehow rebalance() were ever made non-reverting for non-rebalancers (e.g., due to an upgrade), any caller could permanently alter positionWidth. More concretely and immediately: the rebalanceInterval check inside rebalance() enforces a time delay, but changePositionWidth has no separate cooldown. A rebalancer can call changePositionWidth at any time to force a rebalance that bypasses the rebalanceInterval check, since changePositionWidth never checks block.timestamp - lastRebalance. This allows the rebalancer to rebalance more frequently than the intended interval by using changePositionWidth with a cosmetically-different width.

_setSecondaryPositionsTicks() (lines 366-382) uses the spot price from price() — which reads slot0 directly — to decide whether surplus token is token0 or token1 after the main position mint (line 370-372). This decision happens AFTER _requirePriceWithinRange() in rebalance() checks that spot vs TWAP deviation is within bounds, but the spot price read for the balance comparison occurs separately and can differ from the slot0 read in _requirePriceWithinRange(). More importantly, the secondary position direction (OOR above or below current price) is determined by which token has more idle balance in value terms. If a sandwicher manipulates the spot price between the main-position mint and this check (within the same block/transaction context is not possible in Uniswap V3 due to callback ordering, but across blocks an adversary can push price to influence the secondary position direction). This is a low-severity manipulation: the secondary position ends up on the wrong side, locking the wrong token OOR, which reduces LP efficiency but does not cause direct fund loss.

feeRecipient is declared as a public state variable (line 47) but is NEVER initialized in the constructor and there is NO setter function. It defaults to address(0). When liquidatePosition collects a protocol fee (pf0/pf1 > 0), the tokens are transferred to address(0) — permanently burned — instead of the intended protocol treasury. This is both a loss-of-protocol-funds bug and indicates an incomplete implementation.

In liquidatePosition (line 318), borrowedValue is calculated as:
  borrowedValue = owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()
The call `.decimals()` returns the raw uint8 decimal count (e.g., 6 for USDC, 8 for WBTC), NOT 10**decimals. The divisor should be 10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals() (e.g., 1e6 for USDC). Using 6 instead of 1e6 inflates borrowedValue by a factor of ~166,666x for USDC. As a result, totalValueUSD > borrowedValue is almost always FALSE, meaning the protocol fee branch is never entered — the protocol collects no fee. Additionally, if this comparisons were used in a different branch to gate liquidation logic, it could block legitimate liquidations.

In the withdraw function, the branch handling repayment when borrowed == up.token1 (lines 231-235) contains a copy-paste error: it uses amountOut0 instead of amountOut1 for repayFromWithdraw:
  repayFromWithdraw = amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount;
When amountOut1 < owedAmount (the common case when needing to repay), repayFromWithdraw is set to amountOut0 (token0 amount) instead of amountOut1 (token1 amount). This causes: 1. owedAmount is decremented by amountOut0 (wrong token's amount). 2. amountOut1 is decremented by the wrong value. 3. The repayment accounting is broken: the user may underpay or overpay debt,
   and the contract may attempt to transfer negative amounts (underflow if
   amountOut0 > amountOut1, leading to revert or incorrect state).

The withdraw function checks _isApprovedOrOwner (line 211), which allows NFT-approved operators to call withdraw on someone else's position. This means any address approved via ERC721.approve() or setApprovalForAll() can withdraw collateral from the position and receive the tokens themselves (IERC20.safeTransfer(msg.sender, ...)). This creates an implicit trust: if a user approves an address to transfer the NFT, that address also gains full withdrawal rights including receiving the underlying collateral funds. A user approving a marketplace contract (e.g., OpenSea) to transfer their NFT could have their position drained by a malicious marketplace operator.

The pricefeed state variable (line 41) defaults to address(0) and is only set by the owner via setPriceFeed(). If openLeveragedPosition, isLiquidateable, or liquidatePosition are called before setPriceFeed() is called (e.g., due to deployment race or admin error), all calls to IPriceFeed(pricefeed).getPrice() and IPriceFeed(pricefeed).hasPriceFeed() will call address(0), returning 0 (which in Solidity is a successful staticcall to address(0) returning empty data that decodes to 0). This can cause positions to be opened with zero collateral value, or liquidated at incorrect prices, or liquidated when they shouldn't be.

In withdraw(), when the borrowed token is token1, the repayFromWithdraw variable is computed using amountOut0 instead of amountOut1. Line 232 reads `amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount` — the condition correctly tests amountOut1 but the true branch returns amountOut0 (the wrong token's amount). This means the contract subtracts from amountOut1 a value derived from amountOut0, leading to underflow (revert) or incorrect accounting: the user gets more token1 back than they should and the protocol under-repays the lending pool.

In liquidatePosition(), line 318 computes `borrowedValue = owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()`. ERC20.decimals() returns a uint8 (e.g. 18 for WETH, 6 for USDC), NOT 10**decimals. The correct denominator (as used everywhere else in the contract, e.g. line 131, 401, 447) is `10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()`. Using the raw decimals value (18 or 6) instead of the proper scaling factor (1e18 or 1e6) inflates borrowedValue by roughly 55,555x for WETH or 166,666x for USDC. This makes `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` almost always false, so the protocol fee block (lines 324-331) is never triggered. Liquidators receive no bounty subtraction and the fee accounting is completely broken.

The state variable `feeRecipient` (line 47) is never initialized in the constructor or any setter function. It defaults to address(0). In liquidatePosition(), lines 328-329 transfer protocol fees to `feeRecipient`. If LH-02 is fixed and fees are correctly computed, all protocol fees from liquidations would be permanently burned (sent to address(0)). This is confirmed by the Slither prepass signal.

In withdraw(), the denomination-token direct repayment block (lines 227-235) uses `if...else if` structure, so only ONE of token0 or token1 is directly repaid even if the denomination somehow equals neither. But more importantly: the block uses a local `amountToRepay` snapshot (line 224) taken BEFORE `owedAmount` is modified, and then repays exactly `amountToRepay` via the lending pool (line 265). However `owedAmount` is modified in place as repayment source tracking. If `hasToSwap == true`, the swap outputs (denomination token) are NOT added back to `owedAmount` before the `if (owedAmount > 0)` pull (line 263). If the user swaps token0 -> denomination (token1), the resulting denomination tokens accumulate in the contract but `owedAmount` was already reduced by the direct token1 pull — meaning the user can receive the swapped tokens as profit while also having the full `amountToRepay` taken from them. Asymmetric double-accounting.

In openLeveragedPosition(), the vault flashloan repayment (lines 168-169) pushes back exactly `delta0` and `delta1` — the amounts originally flash-borrowed from the lending pool. However, the actual amounts deposited in the vault (a0, a1) may differ from `lp.vault0In` / `lp.vault1In` due to vault rounding or slippage. If the vault deposits less than requested, the delta is not recalculated — the contract tries to push back more tokens than it has, causing a revert. Conversely if MORE tokens are returned from the vault (impossible here, but worth noting), the extra stays in the contract and is swept to msg.sender via _sweepTokens, potentially enriching the user at the expense of the lending pool.

In _calculateTokenValues(), when only token0 has a price feed (chPrice1 == 0), the formula to convert token1 to USD is: `amount1 * PRECISION / price * chPrice0 / decimals0` (line 447). The TWAP `price` from IVault.twapPrice() is expressed as token1 per token0 scaled by PRECISION (1e30). To convert token1 → token0 equivalent, you need `amount1 * PRECISION / price` — this is correct dimensionally only if price = token1/token0 * PRECISION. But if price = token0/token1 * PRECISION (the opposite convention), then this formula gives the inverse and yields wrong USD values. The exact convention must be verified against the Vault's twapPrice() implementation. This asymmetry between the two branches (lines 444-448) should be checked for consistency.

feeRecipient is never initialized (address(0)). In liquidatePosition(), when totalValueUSD > borrowedValue, the contract calls IERC20.safeTransfer(feeRecipient, pf0/pf1). Most ERC-20 implementations (including WBTC/USDC/WETH via OpenZeppelin SafeERC20) revert on transfer to address(0). This permanently blocks ALL profitable liquidations — i.e., any position where collateral > debt. Only underwater positions (where fees would be 0) can be liquidated. The protocol accumulates bad debt as healthy-but-liquidatable positions cannot be closed.

In Leverager.withdraw(), line 232 has a copy-paste bug: when token1 == denomination, the repayFromWithdraw calculation incorrectly uses amountOut0 instead of amountOut1. Specifically: `uint256 repayFromWithdraw = amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount` When amountOut1 < owedAmount (common case), repayFromWithdraw = amountOut0 (wrong token amount). Then `amountOut1 -= repayFromWithdraw` at line 234 subtracts amountOut0 from amountOut1. If amountOut0 > amountOut1, this underflows (Solidity 0.8 revert) — permanently blocking withdrawal for any position where token1 is the denomination token and amountOut0 > amountOut1.

In liquidatePosition() at line 318, the borrowedValue calculation uses `ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` (returns e.g. 6 for USDC) instead of `10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` (= 1e6). This divides by 6 instead of 1e6, making borrowedValue ~166,666x too large. As a result, totalValueUSD > borrowedValue is almost never true for any realistic position, so the fee logic is skipped entirely. More critically, the downstream repay logic proceeds using owedAmount computed from the correct bIndex/borrowedAmount — but the fee distribution is completely broken. Indirect DoS: legitimate liquidators receive no profit incentive (the fee branch never executes correctly), reducing liquidation incentive and potentially causing bad debt.

LendingPool has an emergencyPauseAll() function callable by owner. When paused, borrow() is blocked by the notPaused modifier. Since openLeveragedPosition() calls ILendingPool(lendingPool).borrow(), any pause of the LendingPool permanently blocks ALL new leveraged position openings. Additionally, pullFunds() does NOT have the notPaused modifier, creating an asymmetry: flashloan-style pulling of funds is allowed while borrowing is not. This means the protocol is in a broken intermediate state during pause — existing positions can still be liquidated (liquidatePosition calls withdraw then repay, both of which work when paused), but no new positions can open. This is semi-DoS on new position creation.

In Leverager.withdraw() at line 232, the repayFromWithdraw variable uses amountOut0 (token0 amount) when the code intends to repay from token1 (the denomination token). Specifically: `uint256 repayFromWithdraw = amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount` The ternary condition is `amountOut1 < owedAmount` (checking token1 availability), but the true branch returns `amountOut0` (token0 amount) instead of `amountOut1`. This means when token1 is denomination and token1 balance is insufficient to cover debt, we subtract the token0 amount from token1 tracking — which causes an arithmetic underflow (Solidity 0.8) whenever token0 raw units > token1 raw units (very common: WBTC=1e8, USDC=1e6). Result: withdraw() permanently reverts for any position using USDC as denomination, when amountOut0 (WBTC wei) > amountOut1 (USDC wei). This is a near-certain DoS for the entire WBTC/USDC leveraged position ecosystem.

Path.skipToken() returns a new bytes slice but the caller in _getTokenIn() does not capture the return value. The loop `while (path.hasMultiplePools()) { path.skipToken(); }` never advances `path` because the return value is discarded — `path` stays the same bytes reference forever. For any multi-hop exactOutput swap path, `hasMultiplePools` is always true, causing an infinite loop / out-of-gas revert whenever a multi-hop path is used. This means openLeveragedPosition will always revert for multi-pool routes, and the fix-up call to _getTokenIn also cannot validate the correct tokenIn, creating a denial-of-service.

In Leverager.withdraw(), the branch `else if (borrowed == up.token1)` computes `repayFromWithdraw` using `amountOut0` instead of `amountOut1`. This means when the borrowed token is token1 (e.g., USDC), the code reads the token0 balance (WBTC) to determine how much of the debt to reduce, even though the debt is in token1. Whenever amountOut0 < owedAmount, the function will under-reduce owedAmount (using the WBTC amount, which is smaller in raw units when token0 is WBTC with 8 decimals vs token1 USDC with 6 decimals), leaving owedAmount too large, so the contract will over-pull denomination tokens from msg.sender.

In Leverager.liquidatePosition(), line 318 calculates borrowedValue as:
  `uint256 borrowedValue = owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals();`
The divisor uses `.decimals()` directly (returns uint8, e.g. 6 for USDC or 8 for WBTC) instead of `10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` (which would be 1e6 or 1e8). This means borrowedValue is inflated by 1e6/6 ≈ 166,666x for USDC, making `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` almost always FALSE, causing every liquidation to send zero protocol fees to feeRecipient, and — more critically — the solvency check `if (totalValueUSD > borrowedValue)` fails improperly. Positions that should yield a surplus (liquidator profit) appear insolvent. The direct impact is that the protocol fee calculation (pf0, pf1) is never triggered for USDC-denominated positions.

The state variable `Leverager.feeRecipient` (line 47) is declared but never initialized in the constructor or initVault(). The prepass signal confirms this. In liquidatePosition(), when the position is solvent (totalValueUSD > borrowedValue), protocol fees (pf0, pf1) are transferred to `feeRecipient`. With feeRecipient = address(0), the tokens are sent to the zero address and permanently lost. Note that this interacts with LIB-03: if borrowedValue calculation is fixed, feeRecipient=0 becomes the primary loss vector. Even with the LIB-03 bug active (borrowedValue inflated), if denomination is a non-USDC token with larger decimals or the position is deeply solvent, the fee transfer to address(0) will occur.

In Leverager.withdraw(), when the borrowed token is token1, the code calculates repayFromWithdraw as `amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount`. It uses amountOut0 (token0 amount) instead of amountOut1 (token1 amount) for the ternary-false branch. This means the contract takes min(amountOut1, owedAmount) as the condition but when amountOut1 >= owedAmount it STILL uses amountOut0 — which could be much larger than amountOut1 and larger than the owedAmount, meaning owedAmount is reduced by the wrong amount (potentially 0 if amountOut0 > owedAmount but the condition was amountOut0 > owedAmount). The user can under-repay while receiving full collateral back, creating bad debt. In the worst case, if amountOut0 >> owedAmount but amountOut1 < owedAmount, repayFromWithdraw = amountOut0, owedAmount -= amountOut0 underflows and reverts. But if amountOut1 >= owedAmount, repayFromWithdraw = amountOut0 which could be > owedAmount causing underflow in owedAmount -= repayFromWithdraw, OR if amountOut0 < owedAmount the user can avoid full repay of their token1 debt while still getting amountOut0 worth of debt forgiven.

In Leverager.liquidatePosition(), the borrowedValue calculation divides by `ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` instead of `10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()`. For USDC (6 decimals), this divides by 6 instead of 1,000,000. For WBTC (8 decimals), divides by 8 instead of 100,000,000. This makes borrowedValue astronomically larger than it should be. Specifically: borrowedValue = owedAmount * bPrice / 6 (USDC) instead of owedAmount * bPrice / 1e6. The result is ~166,666x inflated for USDC. Consequence: `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` is almost NEVER true (borrowedValue is huge), so the protocol fee is skipped. More critically, the liquidator is checked against an inflated debt amount, potentially causing liquidations to revert or compute incorrect amounts. The `owedAmount` in denomination token units is compared against an inflated USD value, which breaks all liquidation profit/loss accounting.

Leverager.feeRecipient (line 47) is declared as `address public feeRecipient` but is never initialized and there is no setter function. It defaults to address(0). In liquidatePosition(), when a profitable liquidation occurs, protocol fees (pf0, pf1) are transferred to feeRecipient (address(0)). This permanently destroys protocol revenue. Additionally, if the ERC20 token implementation reverts on transfer to address(0) (some do), profitable liquidations would be completely bricked.

In Leverager.withdraw(), when hasToSwap=true, the code sets:
  amountOut0 -= swapParams.amountIn  (line 249)
  amountOut1 -= swapParams.amountIn  (line 259)
These deductions happen unconditionally AFTER the swap executes. However, the swap is an exactInput swap — the user specifies how much goes in. The swapParams.amountIn could be set to an amount larger than the actual amountOut0 or amountOut1. There is NO check that `swapParams.amountIn <= amountOut0` before the subtraction. If amountOut0 < swapParams.amountIn, this underflows (unchecked arithmetic in pre-0.8 but here Solidity 0.8 catches it). However, the approve is done unconditionally:
  IERC20(up.token0).forceApprove(swapRouter, swapParams.amountIn)
If swapParams.amountIn > amountOut0, the router gets approval for more than available, and the swap could drain the contract of other users' tokens. This is acknowledged in a comment ("might be good here to set amountIn to the lower"), confirming the dev knew.

In initVault(), the parameter `_maxCumulativeBorrowUSD` is described as "denominated in USD" and stored in vaultParams.maxCumulativeBorrowedUSD. In the Setup.sol, it's initialized as `1e27` (1e27 USD? That's 1 octillion USD, effectively uncapped). However, currBorrowedUSD is accumulated with `up.initBorrowedUsd` which is computed as:
  up.initBorrowedUsd = up.borrowedAmount * bPrice / (10 ** ERC20(lp.denomination).decimals())
The result should be in USD scaled to 1e18. But `maxCumulativeBorrowedUSD = 1e27` in setup while initBorrowedUsd uses 1e18 scaling. This means the cap is set 1000x higher than intended (1e27 / 1e18 = 1e9 = $1 billion when bPrice is 1e18 and denomination has 18 decimals). If the denomination is USDC (6 decimals), initBorrowedUsd = amount * 1e18 / 1e6 = amount * 1e12, so to hit cap of 1e27 requires 1e15 USDC = $1 quadrillion. The check is effectively useless/broken. Additionally, `_checkWithinlimits` compares `up.initBorrowedUsd` against `vp.maxUsdLeverage` — same unit inconsistency if operator confuses 1e18 and 1e27.

After openLeveragedPosition(), _sweepTokens() is called which transfers the ENTIRE balance of token0 and token1 held by Leverager to msg.sender. While normally the Leverager should hold 0 tokens between transactions, if any tokens are "stuck" (e.g., from a failed previous transaction that left tokens behind, or from a token that rebases/airdrop to the contract), those tokens are sent to the position opener — not their rightful owner. The comment in the code acknowledges this: "if for some reason there have previously been a large amount of tokens stuck, this could fail". Additionally, the denomination token balance is repaid to the pool but any non-denomination tokens (token0 or token1) from other positions' partial swaps can be swept by the next opener.

In openLeveragedPosition(), swaps only execute if `a0 > lp.amount0In` and token0 != denomination, OR `a1 > lp.amount1In` and token1 != denomination. There is no check that `lp.denomination` is one of (token0, token1). If denomination is a third token (e.g., WETH when vault is WBTC/USDC), the Leverager borrows WETH (enableTokenAsBorrowed must have been called), performs no swaps (since neither token0 nor token1 equals WETH surplus), then repays WETH balance. But the position's denomination = WETH, so the user has a leveraged position "backed" by WBTC/USDC collateral but denominated in WETH. The borrowedAmount accounting would work, but `initCollateralValue` is converted to WETH units using WETH price, while the collateral is in WBTC/USDC. If WETH price moves relative to WBTC/USDC, the leverage ratio is incorrectly computed. More critically, since denomination != token0 and denomination != token1, the withdraw() will always `transferFrom(msg.sender, this, owedAmount)` of the denomination (WETH), requiring the user to always bring WETH to repay, which is a valid but unusual design. The real issue is no validation of denomination being in {token0, token1}.

In _calculateTokenValues(), the logic is:
  if hasPriceFeed(token0): usdValue += amount0 * chPrice0 / decimals0; chPrice0 set
  if hasPriceFeed(token1): usdValue += amount1 * chPrice1 / decimals1; chPrice1 set
  if chPrice0 == 0: use TWAP to convert token0 to token1 units, then apply chPrice1
  elif chPrice1 == 0: use TWAP to convert token1 to token0 units, then apply chPrice0
When BOTH tokens have pricefeeds, chPrice0 and chPrice1 are both non-zero, so neither fallback branch executes. This is correct. However, if hasPriceFeed(token0) = true but getPrice(token0) returns 0 (edge case: oracle returns 0 price), then chPrice0 == 0 even though token0 has a pricefeed. In that case, the fallback branch executes:
  usdValue += (amount0 * price / PRECISION) * chPrice1 / decimals1
This ADDS to usdValue which already accumulated `amount1 * chPrice1 / decimals1`. So token1's value is correctly counted, but now we also add a TWAP-derived estimate for token0 using chPrice1. This is the intended behavior. BUT: the second `elif chPrice1 == 0` branch also executes if token1 oracle returns 0. If both return 0, neither branch has complete price info → usdValue = 0 → silently returns 0, making any position appear worthless (immediately liquidateable).

En liquidatePosition (línea ~318):
  uint256 borrowedValue = owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals();

ERC20.decimals() devuelve uint8 (6 para USDC, 8 para WBTC, 18 para WETH).
El divisor correcto es 10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals().

Inflación por denominación:
  USDC (6 dec):  borrowedValue ×166,667
  WBTC (8 dec):  borrowedValue ×12,500,000
  WETH (18 dec): borrowedValue ×5,555,555,555,555,555

Consecuencias directas:
1. totalValueUSD > borrowedValue es casi siempre FALSE → rama de protocol fee NUNCA se ejecuta.
2. El protocolo jamás cobra comisiones de liquidación independientemente del valor de liquidationFee.
3. Los liquidadores reciben SIEMPRE el surplus completo.
4. Si este bug se corrige sin corregir DD-DDH-02 (feeRecipient=address(0)),
   todas las liquidaciones con surplus revertirán (safeTransfer a address(0)).

La variable pública `feeRecipient` (Leverager.sol:47) permanece en address(0) porque:
1. El constructor NO la inicializa.
2. Ninguna función del contrato permite cambiarla (no existe setFeeRecipient()).

  - El protocolo simplemente no cobra fees.

Escenario tras parchar DD-DDH-01 + setLiquidationFee(X > 0):

  - TODAS las liquidaciones de posiciones con surplus revertirán
  - Las posiciones underwater no se pueden liquidar → bad debt sistémico

El protocolo no puede recuperarse sin upgrade del contrato.

En withdraw() (Leverager.sol:~231-235):

      uint256 repayFromWithdraw = amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount; // BUG
      owedAmount -= repayFromWithdraw;
      amountOut1 -= repayFromWithdraw;  // BUG

Debería ser: `amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut1 : owedAmount`

CASO B (amountOut1 < owedAmount): ternario = amountOut0 (token erróneo)

  - amountOut1 = USDC (valor bajo en USD, muchas unidades base)

withdraw() valida:

Cualquier dirección aprobada (via approve() o setApprovalForAll()) puede:
1. Llamar withdraw() con pctWithdraw=1e18 (100%)
2. Recibir TODO el colateral en su propia wallet
3. El propietario del NFT pierde sus fondos sin consentimiento

Vectores de explotación prácticos:

  El marketplace (o un operador malicioso con acceso) drena el colateral antes de vender el NFT.
- Phishing de approvals: contrato malicioso solicita setApprovalForAll para "gestionar posiciones".
- Protocolo composable: cualquier integrador con aprobación puede operar en nombre del usuario.

La diferencia con el modelo ERC721 estándar es crítica: normalmente, la aprobación
permite TRANSFERIR el NFT, no LIQUIDAR el activo subyacente. Aquí la aprobación
concede control total sobre el colateral.

  → Hace que totalValueUSD > borrowedValue sea siempre FALSE

  → Si la rama de fees se ejecuta, safeTransfer(address(0)) revierte

Interacción: Bug A "oculta" Bug B. Si un auditor parcha solo Bug A:

  2. totalValueUSD > borrowedValue = TRUE para posiciones con surplus
  3. pf0 o pf1 > 0 (fee no trivial)
  4. safeTransfer(address(0), pf0) → REVERT
  5. TODAS las liquidaciones de posiciones solventes fallan
  6. Solo se pueden liquidar posiciones ya underwater (sin surplus)
  7. Las posiciones borderline que se vuelven insolventes acumulan bad debt

currBorrowedUSD es un tracker acumulativo que se incrementa en openLeveragedPosition
y se decrementa en withdraw (full y partial) y liquidatePosition.

La invariante de conservación requiere que en todo momento:
  vaultParams[vault].currBorrowedUSD == Σ(positions[id].initBorrowedUsd) para todas
  las posiciones abiertas del vault.

Puntos donde la invariante puede romperse:
1. El bug DD-DDH-03 (amountOut0 vs amountOut1) puede causar reverts parciales
   que dejan el estado inconsistente si hay un patrón try/catch externo.
2. Partial withdraw reduce initBorrowedUsd y currBorrowedUSD proporcionalmente,
   pero el truncado por división entera puede acumular discrepancias.
3. Reentrancia (DD-DDH-04) podría causar doble decremento de currBorrowedUSD.

Esta es una propiedad de alto valor para el fuzzer — cualquier ruptura indica
un bug de contabilidad grave.

En withdraw(), la rama `borrowed == up.token1` usa `amountOut0` en lugar de `amountOut1` para calcular cuánto se repaga directamente desde el retiro. Esto hace que el protocolo calcule mal cuánto debe el usuario, pudiendo resultar en repago insuficiente (saldo de deuda incorrecto) o underflow si amountOut0 > owedAmount y amountOut1 era menor.

En liquidatePosition() línea 318, el cálculo de borrowedValue divide por `ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` (que devuelve un uint8, por ej. 6 para USDC) en lugar de `10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()`. Esto hace que borrowedValue sea masivamente sobreestimado (multiplicado por ~10^20 extra), haciendo que casi ninguna posición parezca liquidable desde el punto de vista del cálculo del profit, y que el feeRecipient no reciba fees en liquidaciones normales.

`feeRecipient` es declarado pero nunca inicializado en el constructor ni en ninguna función de setup. Permanece como address(0). En liquidatePosition(), si hay profit, los tokens de fee se transfieren a address(0) (quemados / stuck). Esto es una pérdida directa de fondos del protocolo en cada liquidación con profit.

En openLeveragedPosition() y withdraw(), el swap router es un address mutable controlado por el owner. El Leverager otorga allowance ilimitada (`forceApprove(swapRouter, amountInMaximum)`) al router antes de cada swap y luego resetea a 0 después. Sin embargo, si el owner cambia swapRouter por una dirección maliciosa, puede drenar cualquier token que esté temporalmente en el contrato durante una transacción, incluyendo tokens flashloaneados del lending pool. Adicionalmente, el swapRouter no es validado (podría ser cualquier dirección).

En openLeveragedPosition(), `_sweepTokens` envía al msg.sender TODOS los balances de token0 y token1 del contrato al final de la función. Si un usuario malicioso puede hacer que tokens de otro usuario queden en el contrato (por ejemplo, via una transacción fallida parcial o un ataque de sandwich), puede robar dichos tokens llamando a openLeveragedPosition() con amount0In=0, amount1In=0 justo después. La función también carece de cualquier chequeo de que vault0In >= amount0In y vault1In >= amount1In (si vault0In < amount0In, el cálculo `delta0 = lp.vault0In - lp.amount0In` hace underflow, revertiendo — pero esto es seguro).

En openLeveragedPosition(), el vault es un parámetro del usuario (`lp.vault`). Solo se verifica que `vaultParams[lp.vault].leverageEnabled == true`. Un vault malicioso podría: 1) En deposit(): retornar shares=0 o amounts inflados → bypass de límites de leverage. 2) En twapPrice(): retornar precio manipulado para afectar los cálculos de colateral. 3) En token0()/token1(): retornar tokens maliciosos que tienen hooks (ERC-777). La condición `leverageEnabled` la setea el owner, así que vaults no autorizados no pueden pasar, pero el análisis de qué pasa con un vault legítimo comprometido/hackeado es relevante.

En withdraw(), cuando `wp.hasToSwap == true`, el usuario provee swapParams con `swapParams.amountIn` como parámetro libre. El código verifica que `tokenIn == up.token0` (o token1), pero no verifica que `swapParams.amountIn <= amountOut0` (o amountOut1). Si un usuario proporciona `amountIn > amountOut0`, la línea `amountOut0 -= swapParams.amountIn` hará underflow (revertirá en Solidity ^0.8). Pero más grave: el código en línea 245 ejecuta `forceApprove(swapRouter, swapParams.amountIn)` y llama al router ANTES de verificar que tiene suficientes tokens. El router puede ejecutarse con tokens que no tiene el contrato pero que estaban aprobados previamente (allowance residual). Sin embargo, dado que forceApprove setea exactamente amountIn, el router no puede tomar más de amountIn. El underflow en línea 249 sí revierte, así que el swap real no puede exceder amountOut0. MÁS IMPORTANTE: en línea 248-249, el código hace `amountOut0 -= swapParams.amountIn` DESPUÉS del swap, pero NO verifica cuánto se recibió del swap. Si el swap devuelve menos tokens de lo esperado (amountOutMinimum=0 en el ejemplo del Setup), el usuario recibe menos dinero pero el protocolo repaga la deuda completa. Esto es pérdida para el usuario, no para el protocolo. Pero si se configura recipient=leverager en el swap y amountOutMinimum=0, el atacante puede recibir 0 tokens del swap y el contrato gastará los tokens de token0 del usuario sin compensación.

In liquidatePosition(), `borrowedValue` is computed as `owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()`. `ERC20.decimals()` returns a raw uint8 (e.g. 6 for USDC, 18 for WETH), NOT 10**decimals. This divides by 6 or 18 instead of 1e6 or 1e18, making borrowedValue astronomically larger than totalValueUSD. As a result, the `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` check almost always fails, so the protocol fee calculation is skipped and the liquidator receives no profit accounting — but more critically, the `repayAmount` is computed from `owedAmount` (correct), while the fee subtraction logic is bypassed because the inflated `borrowedValue` always exceeds totalValueUSD. This breaks liquidation economics entirely.

In withdraw(), the branch handling `borrowed == up.token1` (line 232) incorrectly references `amountOut0` instead of `amountOut1` when computing `repayFromWithdraw`. The correct logic should compute how much of token1 (the denomination) can be used to repay. Using amountOut0 (token0 amount) instead means: - If amountOut0 > amountOut1: repayFromWithdraw is too large → amountOut1 underflows
  on the subsequent subtraction, OR more debt is "repaid" from the wrong bucket.
- If amountOut0 < amountOut1: user underpays the debt; the shortfall is incorrectly
  charged from the user's wallet at the wrong amount.
In both cases, `amountOut1` is subtracted by an incorrect amount, corrupting the remaining collateral returned to the user and the debt tracking.

In `_calculateTokenValues()`, the no-pricefeed-for-token1 branch (line 447) computes:
  `amount1 * PRECISION / price * chPrice0 / decimals0`
This performs division before multiplication: first divides by `price` (which can be large, e.g. 1e30 for the TWAP in Q30 format), then multiplies by `chPrice0`. When `price` is large relative to `amount1 * PRECISION`, the intermediate `amount1 * PRECISION / price` truncates to 0, producing a 0 USD value for token1. This causes the collateral to be undervalued, which can make a healthy position appear liquidatable, or make an undercollateralized position appear healthy. The correct order is: `amount1 * PRECISION * chPrice0 / price / decimals0` or equivalently: `amount1 * chPrice0 * PRECISION / price / decimals0`. PRECISION = 1e30. price is in Q1e30 format (token0/token1 scaled by 1e30).

In `isLiquidateable()` (line 408), the calculation:
  `uint256 base = owedAmount * 1e18 / (vp.maxTimesLeverage - 1e18)`
will revert with division-by-zero if `maxTimesLeverage == 1e18` (representing 1x leverage). Furthermore, if `maxTimesLeverage` is set to any value <= 1e18 (which the admin can do via `changeVaultMaxLeverage`), the subtraction underflows (panic) in checked arithmetic. Even at values slightly above 1e18 (e.g. 1.001e18 = 1.001x leverage), the denominator is tiny (1e15), causing `base` to be astronomically large, disabling liquidations (base >> initCollateralValue always, so the min() always returns initCollateralValue, which is working correctly — but the overflow risk remains). There is no validation in `changeVaultMaxLeverage` that prevents setting values <= 1e18.

In `openLeveragedPosition()` (line 131), `initCollateralValue` is computed as:
  `up.initCollateralUsd * (10 ** ERC20(lp.denomination).decimals()) / bPrice`
where `bPrice` comes from `IPriceFeed(pricefeed).getPrice(lp.denomination)`, which calls `_getChainlinkPrice()` returning the raw Chainlink answer (uint256). Chainlink price feeds for USD pairs return prices with 8 decimals (e.g. USDC/USD = 1e8, ETH/USD = ~3000e8). However, `initCollateralUsd` is scaled in 1e18 (USD value in 18 dec). The formula: `initCollateralUsd_1e18 * 10^decimals / chainlinkPrice_8dec` For USDC (6 dec): result = value_1e18 * 1e6 / 1e8 = value * 1e16 For WETH (18 dec): result = value_1e18 * 1e18 / chainlinkPrice_8dec The intended unit of `initCollateralValue` is "denomination tokens" (e.g. USDC with 6 dec). With USDC denomination: correct formula = initCollateralUsd_1e18 * 1e6 / 1e18 (price in 1e18) or = initCollateralUsd_1e18 * 1e6 / (chainlinkPrice * 1e10) for 8-dec feeds. Since `bPrice` is raw 8-dec Chainlink and not scaled to 1e18, `initCollateralValue` is off by a factor of 1e10 for USDC denomination. This affects leverage limit checks.

In `liquidatePosition()` (line 318), `borrowedValue` is used to determine whether there is a profit on liquidation (i.e., whether `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue`). Due to MATH-01 (using `.decimals()` instead of `10**decimals()`), `borrowedValue` is always massively inflated. This means `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` is always false, so the `protocolFeePct` calculation block is never entered. Consequence 1: the fee recipient NEVER receives liquidation fees. Consequence 2: more critically, `amount0` and `amount1` are not reduced by fees, so the liquidator receives the full position value — but the fee accounting in the contract is still wrong regardless. Consequence 3: if the protocol later changes `borrowedValue` formula correctly, the fee accounting logic `(totalValueUSD - borrowedValue) / totalValueUSD` would divide by totalValueUSD (which is in 1e18 USD), but this value is already used inconsistently with borrowedValue's current scale.

In `_calculateTokenValues()` (line 445), the branch for token0 without a pricefeed:
  `usdValue += (amount0 * price / PRECISION) * chPrice1 / decimals1`
This is division-before-multiplication in the outer expression: First: `amount0 * price / PRECISION` → truncated intermediate value Then: `* chPrice1 / decimals1` For small amounts of token0 (e.g. 1 WBTC in 8 decimals = 1e8 wei), and price = twapPrice in Q1e30 format: 1e8 * price_1e30 / 1e30 = 1e8 (if price = 1, i.e. equal token values) This is actually fine for typical amounts. But for sub-unit amounts (1 wei), and high prices (e.g. WBTC/USDC ~ 100_000 * 1e6/1e8 * 1e30): 1 * 1e36 / 1e30 = 1e6 → ok. However when price is small (e.g. <1e30), amount0 * price can underflow to 0 before division. The PRECISION = 1e30 is the Leverager constant (not PRECISION from libraries). This path is lower severity — typically amounts are large enough.

In `_getTokenIn`, `path.skipToken()` is called but its return value is discarded — `path` is never reassigned. For multi-hop exactOutput swap paths, the function always decodes the FIRST pool segment (returns second address = token at position 43 bytes), never advancing to the actual tokenIn at the end of the path. As a result, the `require` checks in `openLeveragedPosition` ("token should be denomination") can be bypassed by crafting a multi-hop path where the second token of the FIRST segment equals `denomination`, but the actual tokenIn (last segment) is an arbitrary token — including vault share tokens. This allows an attacker to drain vault share tokens via an approved swap router call.

In `liquidatePosition`, `borrowedValue` is computed as: `owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` (line 318). The code calls `.decimals()` directly (returns e.g. 6 for USDC) instead of `10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` (which returns 1e6). This means the denominator is off by a factor of ~166666x for USDC (6 vs 1e6) and ~333333x for WETH (18 vs 1e18). The resulting `borrowedValue` is massively inflated — making it appear the collateral always covers the debt — so `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` is almost always false, meaning the `protocolFeePct` branch is almost never entered and fee accounting is broken. More critically, positions that should yield a liquidation profit appear not to, preventing fee distribution and potentially disrupting the liquidation incentive math.

In `withdraw`, the branch handling token1 as denomination (line 232) uses `amountOut0` instead of `amountOut1` in the ternary operator: `uint256 repayFromWithdraw = amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount;` When `amountOut1 < owedAmount` is true, repayFromWithdraw is set to `amountOut0` (wrong token), which is then subtracted from both `owedAmount` and `amountOut1`. If `amountOut0 > amountOut1`, this results in `amountOut1` underflowing (reverts) or `owedAmount` being incorrectly reduced. When `amountOut0 < amountOut1`, it under-repays the debt. In either case the accounting is broken: users are over- or under-charged, and the protocol may under-repay the lending pool.

`feeRecipient` is declared as a public state variable (line 47) but is NEVER initialized (confirmed by Slither prepass signal). It defaults to `address(0)`. Any liquidation that collects a protocol fee (pf0 > 0 or pf1 > 0) will call `IERC20.safeTransfer(address(0), ...)`. SafeERC20's safeTransfer calls the ERC20's `transfer(address(0), amount)`. For most ERC20 tokens (including WBTC, USDC), transfer to address(0) reverts — causing ALL liquidations that would collect a fee to revert. For tokens that don't revert on transfer to address(0), the fee is permanently burned. Either outcome is harmful: DoS on profitable liquidations or permanent fund loss.

In liquidatePosition(), borrowedValue is computed as `owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` instead of `owedAmount * bPrice / (10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals())`. ERC20.decimals() returns a uint8 (e.g., 6 for USDC, 8 for WBTC). Using the raw integer 6 or 8 as the denominator instead of 1e6 or 1e8 inflates borrowedValue by a factor of ~166,667x (USDC) or ~12,500,000x (WBTC). As a result, `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` is almost never true, and the protocol fee branch is effectively dead — liquidators receive 100% of the position's profit that should have been split with the protocol.

In withdraw(), when the borrowed token is token1, the repayFromWithdraw calculation incorrectly uses `amountOut0` instead of `amountOut1`:
  `uint256 repayFromWithdraw = amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount;`
When `amountOut1 < owedAmount` (the common case when a leveraged position cannot fully self-repay from withdrawals), the code assigns `amountOut0` (the token0 withdrawal amount) to repayFromWithdraw. This means: - `owedAmount` is decremented by token0's amount (wrong token, wrong magnitude) - `amountOut1` is decremented by the same value, potentially underflowing - The actual debt repayment logic is corrupted: the user under-repays their token1 debt The severity depends on relative magnitudes: if token0 amount > token1 owedAmount, the position over-repays from the wrong amount; if token0 >> owedAmount, user's amountOut1 is reduced by more than owedAmount causing amountOut1 to go negative (underflow revert), or the debt tracking becomes inconsistent.

In openLeveragedPosition(), the `_sweepTokens` function (line 198) sweeps ALL remaining token0 and token1 balances to msg.sender after the position is opened. The function borrows `lp.maxBorrowAmount` from the lending pool, swaps what is needed, then repays all remaining denomination balance. However, if the denomination token is token0 or token1, and the repay (line 172) rounds down via LendingPool.repay() (which caps at totalBorrows), any residual denomination tokens remaining in the contract would be swept to msg.sender — effectively letting the user receive borrowed tokens for free. Specifically: `ILendingPool(lendingPool).repay(lp.denomination, denomBalance)` where denomBalance = ALL denomination tokens in contract. But `repay()` internally caps the repay to `reserve.totalBorrows` (line 192 of LendingPool.sol). If `denomBalance > totalBorrows`, the excess is returned via `safeTransferFrom` from msg.sender (Leverager) to yTokenAddress — but then the remaining balance after repay is 0 (the whole balance was sent). So the sweep would send 0. Actually: after repay, the denomination tokens transferred are min(denomBalance, totalBorrows). The remaining denomination tokens (denomBalance - amountRepaid) stay in Leverager and are swept to msg.sender. This allows the user to extract borrowed tokens that exceeded the reserve's totalBorrows — effectively stealing idle tokens sitting in the Leverager.

In isLiquidateable(), the health factor denominator calculation uses `(vp.maxTimesLeverage - 1e18)` at line 408. If maxTimesLeverage is exactly 1e18 (1x leverage — effectively no leverage), this causes a division by zero revert. More importantly, if maxTimesLeverage is set to a value <= 1e18 by the owner (via changeVaultMaxLeverage), all calls to isLiquidateable() for that vault will revert, making positions permanently un-liquidatable. This creates a DoS on liquidation, allowing bad debt to accumulate in the lending pool.

In withdraw(), when `wp.pctWithdraw < 1e18` (partial withdrawal), the function does NOT check isLiquidateable() after modifying the position. While the comment at line 207 says "We do not check whether position is liquidateable as we remove collateral and repay debt in the same ratio", this is only safe if the collateral and debt are perfectly proportional. However, due to the FLW-02 bug (wrong token in repayFromWithdraw), the actual repayment may be incorrect, leaving the position with a different collateral-to-debt ratio than intended. Combined with FLW-02, a user could withdraw collateral without fully repaying debt, creating an undercollateralized position that bypasses the liquidation check.

PriceFeed._getChainlinkPrice has the staleness check commented out. The heartbeat parameter is stored but never enforced (line 60: `// require(block.timestamp - updatedAt <= heartbeat);`). A Chainlink feed that has not updated in hours or days will return an arbitrarily stale price without any revert. This stale price flows into every call to Leverager that reads `pricefeed.getPrice()`: openLeveragedPosition (collateral USD value, borrowed USD value), isLiquidateable (total denom value, owed denom), and liquidatePosition (borrowedValue, protocolFeePct).

In liquidatePosition (line 318), `borrowedValue` is computed as `owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` instead of `owedAmount * bPrice / (10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals())`. For USDC (6 decimals), this divides by 6 instead of 1e6, making `borrowedValue` ~166,666x larger than the correct value. For WBTC (8 decimals), it divides by 8 instead of 1e8. This causes `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` to be false almost always, meaning the protocol fee branch is never entered, and the liquidator receives all collateral surplus without protocol fee deduction. More critically, the `borrowedValue` used to compute `protocolFeePct` is wrong by many orders of magnitude.

The Uniswap V3 TWAP window used for all leveraged position pricing is only 5 minutes (twap = 300 seconds, set in Strategy constructor line 100). openLeveragedPosition calls IVault(lp.vault).twapPrice() and also checkPoolActivity(), but checkPoolActivity only blocks opening when consecutive observations show > maxObservationDeviation (100 ticks, ~1%) deviation. A well-funded attacker can manipulate the TWAP within a single 5-minute window by maintaining a skewed pool price, then open a leveraged position at an inflated collateral value or trigger false liquidations.

PriceFeed._getChainlinkPrice returns the raw Chainlink answer (line 61: `return uint256(answer)`) without normalizing to a consistent decimal precision. Chainlink price feeds return values in 8 decimals for most crypto/USD pairs (e.g., WBTC/USD answer = 10000000000000 for $100,000). However, Leverager._calculateTokenValues uses `bPrice` (from pricefeed.getPrice) to compute USD values assuming 1e18 scaling (line 131: `up.initCollateralValue = up.initCollateralUsd * (10 ** ERC20(lp.denomination).decimals()) / bPrice`). If bPrice is in 8 decimals (e.g., 1e8 for USDC) instead of 1e18, the collateral value is off by 1e10, making positions appear to have 10,000,000,000x more or less collateral than they actually have. NOTE: Setup.sol uses MockOracle which returns PRICE_WBTC = 100_000e18, so in the test environment this is 1e18-scaled. But in production with real Chainlink feeds returning 8-decimal prices, this would be a critical decimal mismatch.

_calculateTokenValues uses Chainlink prices for tokens that have a feed, and falls back to the Uniswap V3 TWAP price for tokens without a feed. If BOTH tokens have a Chainlink feed (the common case: WBTC and USDC both have feeds), the `price` parameter (TWAP) is completely ignored. The function then double-counts: it adds `amount0 * chPrice0 / decimals0` AND `amount1 * chPrice1 / decimals1`, which is correct when both tokens have feeds. However, if for any reason one token's pricefeed is removed or misconfigured (hasPriceFeed returns false for one), the fallback silently uses the TWAP price — creating an inconsistency between the two pricing sources. More critically: the fallback path at lines 444-447 computes: `amount0 * price / PRECISION * chPrice1 / decimals1` where `price` is token0/token1 in 1e30 precision. If chPrice1 is also in 1e30 precision instead of 1e18, this double-scales.

isLiquidateable() calls IPriceFeed(pricefeed).getPrice(pos.denomination) without any circuit breaker for zero or extremely low prices. PriceFeed._getChainlinkPrice only checks `require(answer > 0)` but does not enforce a minimum reasonable price or a maximum change from the previous round. If a Chainlink oracle returns a near-zero price (e.g., due to a flash crash in the feed, misconfigured aggregator, or oracle attack that pushes the answer to 1), then: - `totalDenom = totalValueUSD * (10 ** decimals) / bPrice` becomes
  astronomically large (near max uint256 with bPrice=1).
- `owedAmount > totalDenom` is false. - `totalDenom - owedAmount` is enormous → position is never liquidatable. - Protocol accrues bad debt silently as real collateral erodes.

In withdraw(), when denomination == token1, the ternary expression uses `amountOut0` instead of `amountOut1` to determine how much can be repaid directly from withdrawn funds. This means: if amountOut1 < owedAmount, repayFromWithdraw = amountOut0 (the wrong token amount), and amountOut1 is reduced by that (potentially larger) value, causing an underflow revert OR letting the user avoid transferring their owed denomination token while the lending pool is short-changed. In the non-reverting path (amountOut0 >= owedAmount) the ternary evaluates to `owedAmount`, so behaviour is correct — the bug manifests only when amountOut1 < owedAmount, making it a selective denial-of-service and potential fund drain in edge conditions.

In liquidatePosition(), the denominator used to convert owedAmount to USD is `ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` (which returns uint8, e.g. 8 for WBTC, 6 for USDC, 18 for WETH) instead of `10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` (which should be e.g. 1e8 for WBTC). For WBTC with 8 decimals, this divides by 8 instead of by 1e8, inflating borrowedValue by a factor of 12,500,000. This makes every WBTC-denominated position appear massively over-collateralised (borrowedValue is ~12.5M× too large), so `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` is almost always false, meaning the protocol fee branch is never entered AND the liquidator receives no surplus — the position can only be liquidated at a massive apparent loss, leading to underwater positions and bad debt.

`feeRecipient` is never set anywhere in the contract. It is declared as a public address state variable (line 47) but has no initializer and no setter function. It defaults to address(0). When liquidationFee > 0 (set via setLiquidationFee()), the liquidation code attempts `IERC20(up.token0).safeTransfer(feeRecipient, pf0)` which transfers to address(0). With OpenZeppelin's SafeERC20 and standard ERC20 tokens, safeTransfer to address(0) reverts. This means any non-zero liquidation fee permanently blocks ALL liquidations, creating bad debt accumulation.

In withdraw(), when hasToSwap is true, the contract reduces amountOut0 by swapParams.amountIn BEFORE confirming the actual swap output. If the user specifies amountIn > amountOut0 (after denomination deduction), the subtraction `amountOut0 -= swapParams.amountIn` underflows (Solidity ≥0.8 reverts). There is no upper bound check: the comment says "might be good here to set amountIn to the lower of swapParams.amountIn and amountOut0" but it's never implemented. This creates a DoS vector: a malicious operator (who has approval over the NFT) can pass crafted swapParams with amountIn > available to permanently brick a position.

The `_checkWithinlimits` function computes positionLeverage as `(initCollateralValue + borrowedAmount) * 1e18 / initCollateralValue`. Both `initCollateralValue` and `borrowedAmount` are in denomination token units (not USD), which is correct in theory. However `initCollateralValue` is computed in line 131 as `initCollateralUsd * (10 ** decimals) / bPrice` — a USD value scaled down to denomination units. `borrowedAmount` is the raw token amount borrowed (line 177). If the denomination token has very low decimals (WBTC = 8) and bPrice is large (100_000e18), the division `initCollateralUsd / bPrice` results in a tiny number, and small rounding errors can make positionLeverage compute incorrectly. More critically, there is no check that `initCollateralValue > 0` before the division — if initCollateralUsd rounds to 0 during calculation, a division-by-zero reverts, bricking position opening for small deposits.

In isLiquidateable(), the calculation on line 408:
  `uint256 base = owedAmount * 1e18 / (vp.maxTimesLeverage - 1e18)`
will revert (division by zero) if maxTimesLeverage == 1e18. More critically, if maxTimesLeverage < 1e18, the subtraction underflows (Solidity ≥0.8 panic). Owner can set maxTimesLeverage to any value via changeVaultMaxLeverage(). If this is set to a value <= 1e18, every call to isLiquidateable() reverts, which DoS's liquidatePosition (which calls isLiquidateable) and also the final check in openLeveragedPosition (line 195: `require(!isLiquidateable(_id))`), bricking the entire protocol for that vault.

En la función withdraw, cuando denomination == token1 y amountOut1 < owedAmount, se usa amountOut0 (en lugar de amountOut1) como repayFromWithdraw. Esto corrompe el accounting: owedAmount se reduce por el valor equivocado, y amountOut1 se reduce por ese mismo valor incorrecto, potencialmente causando underflow o enviando al usuario más token1 del que le corresponde y dejando la deuda sin cubrir correctamente.

En liquidatePosition, el calculo de borrowedValue usa ERC20(up.denomination).decimals() (que retorna el numero crudo, ej: 6 para USDC) en lugar de 10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals() (ej: 1e6). Esto divide por 6 en lugar de 1e6, inflando borrowedValue por un factor de ~166,666x para USDC. Como resultado, el chequeo de si hay profit (totalValueUSD > borrowedValue) casi siempre falla, privando al protocolo de sus fees de liquidacion. Ademas, el calculo de profit para el liquidador es fundamentalmente incorrecto.

La variable feeRecipient en Leverager nunca es inicializada (empieza en address(0)) y no hay ninguna funcion setter para cambiarla. Segun el prepass de Slither, se usa en liquidatePosition para transferir fees. Cualquier fee de liquidacion se enviaria a address(0) (quemandola). Ademas, el bug WC-02 hace que esto raramente ocurra. Pero si se corrige WC-02, todos los fees de liquidacion se perderan permanentemente hasta que el owner establezca feeRecipient.

En la funcion withdraw, cuando hasToSwap = true, el codigo substrae swapParams.amountIn de amountOut0/amountOut1 ANTES de verificar que el contrato realmente tiene esa cantidad disponible. Si el usuario proporciona un swapParams.amountIn mayor que amountOut0 (despues de la reduccion por repayFromWithdraw), la substraccion hace underflow (el codigo usa aritmetica default de Solidity ^0.8.x que revierte en underflow, pero el check es inapropiado). Ademas, no se verifica que el output del swap cubra el owedAmount restante.

En openLeveragedPosition, la funcion _sweepTokens envia al msg.sender TODOS los balances de token0 y token1 en el contrato Leverager al final de la transaccion. Si otra transaccion deja fondos en el contrato (por ejemplo, tokens atrapados de una tx anterior fallida o tokens enviados directamente), cualquier usuario que abra una posicion puede robar esos tokens. Esto es semi-documentado como "by design" pero representa un riesgo real de perdida de fondos para cualquiera que transfiera tokens directamente al contrato.

En _calculateTokenValues, cuando chPrice1 == 0 (token1 no tiene pricefeed), el calculo usa:
  usdValue += amount1 * PRECISION / price * chPrice0 / decimals0
La division por `price` ocurre antes de la multiplicacion por `chPrice0`, lo que puede causar perdida de precision severa. Si `price` es grande (PRECISION = 1e30, y price puede ser menor que eso), la division intermedia puede truncar a 0. Esto subvalua el colateral del usuario, potencialmente haciendolo liquidatable de forma injusta.

collectFees() calls collectPositionFees with vestPosition.tickLower but mainPosition.tickUpper instead of vestPosition.tickUpper. This burns and collects fees for the wrong tick range, potentially operating on a position that does not exist (different tickUpper than the vesting position's actual tickUpper). The vesting position's fees are never collected from the correct range, and a non-existent position range is passed to the pool burn/collect, which either silently no-ops or reverts depending on pool state. This also means the vesting position accumulates uncollectable fees.

_withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() uses initialLiquidity in the pro-rata vesting formula instead of accounting for the time elapsed correctly. The formula is: liquidityToRemove = initialLiquidity * (lastValid - lastUpdate) / (endTs - startTs). While mathematically correct for distributing the full initial liquidity over the full duration, it fails when the vesting position's remaining liquidity diverges from what the formula expects. Specifically, if a previous iteration removed more or less than expected (due to rounding), subsequent calls still use initialLiquidity as the numerator, meaning the sum of all removals can exceed remainingLiquidity. However since the final check uses remainingLiquidity at endTs, the worst case is accumulated rounding under-payment to users.

_setSecondaryPositionsTicks() can produce a secondary position where tickLower >= tickUpper when the current tick is at or near a tick spacing boundary in the "above current price" branch. When bal0in1 >= bal1 (token0 is the excess), the code sets tickLower = tick - modulo + tickSpacing and tickUpper = mainPosition.tickUpper. If tick is already near or above the main position's upper tick (which can happen during extreme price moves between the main tick setting and secondary tick setting), tickLower can equal or exceed tickUpper. Uniswap V3 requires tickLower < tickUpper, so the subsequent mint call in _addLiquidityToSecondaryPosition will revert, causing the entire rebalance to fail.

In collectFees(), when the vesting position fees are collected (line 167), the code mistakenly passes mainPosition.tickUpper instead of vestPosition.tickUpper. After a rebalance, mainPosition.tickUpper may have changed. The call collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper) burns 0 liquidity from (vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper [new]) — a tick range where the strategy has NO POSITION. This causes IUniswapV3Pool.burn() to silently no-op (the position at that range has 0 liquidity), and collect() returns 0 tokens. The REAL vesting position at (vestPosition.tickLower, vestPosition.tickUpper) accumulates fees that are NEVER collected and NEVER charged the protocol fee. This also means that when _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition removes the vesting liquidity, it gets back principal + accrued fees, but those fees bypass the protocol fee mechanism entirely — the protocol loses revenue and all vesting fees go directly to the vault depositors without the protocol cut.

`feeRecipient` is declared as a public state variable (line 47) but is NEVER initialized and there is NO owner-only setter for it anywhere in Leverager.sol. It therefore permanently equals address(0). When `liquidatePosition` sends protocol fees via `IERC20(up.token0).safeTransfer(feeRecipient, pf0)` (lines 328-329), those tokens are sent to address(0) — permanently destroyed. This also means ANY non-zero `liquidationFee` setting is useless because the fee always burns tokens rather than reaching the protocol treasury.

In `liquidatePosition` at line 318, `borrowedValue` is computed as:
  `owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()`
`ERC20.decimals()` returns the raw decimal count (e.g., 6 for USDC, 8 for WBTC, 18 for WETH) — NOT 10**decimals. The correct divisor should be `10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()`. This causes `borrowedValue` to be orders of magnitude too large (e.g., for WBTC with 8 decimals, it divides by 8 instead of 1e8 — a factor of 12.5 million error). Because `borrowedValue` is astronomically larger than `totalValueUSD`, the condition `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` is almost always false, so protocol fees are NEVER collected even when there is profit. More critically, this incorrect calculation is used for nothing except the fee logic — the actual repayment is unaffected — but it means all liquidation fee revenue is permanently suppressed.

In `withdraw` at line 232, when `borrowed == up.token1`, the code reads:
  `uint256 repayFromWithdraw = amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount;`
The ternary's true-branch uses `amountOut0` instead of `amountOut1`. When `amountOut1 < owedAmount`, `repayFromWithdraw` is set to `amountOut0` (the amount of token0 withdrawn, an unrelated value). This means `owedAmount` is reduced by the WRONG amount, and `amountOut1` is reduced by a value that might be greater than `amountOut1`, causing an underflow. Alternatively, if `amountOut0` is much smaller than `amountOut1`, the position owner underpays the debt. This is a copy-paste error from the `token0` branch (line 228) that was not updated for token1.

`_sweepTokens` (lines 484-490) sends all token0 and token1 balances held by the Leverager contract to `msg.sender`. This is called at the end of `openLeveragedPosition`. If any previous transaction left tokens stranded in the contract (e.g., due to rounding, failed positions, or deliberate donation), any user who opens a new position — even with minimal collateral — receives those leftover tokens as a free bonus. The comment on line 175 even acknowledges this: "anyone could sweep them". There is no owner-only sweep function, and non-owners can always collect leftovers by opening a position.

In `isLiquidateable` at line 408:
  `uint256 base = owedAmount * 1e18 / (vp.maxTimesLeverage - 1e18);`
If `vp.maxTimesLeverage` is set to exactly `1e18` (1x leverage) or any value less than `1e18`, this subtraction underflows (reverts in Solidity ^0.8) or produces division by zero. The owner can set `maxTimesLeverage` to any value via `changeVaultMaxLeverage` — there is no lower-bound check. If `maxTimesLeverage <= 1e18`, every call to `isLiquidateable` reverts, which also blocks `liquidatePosition` (which calls `isLiquidateable`). This creates a permanent DoS on liquidations for that vault.

`liquidationFee` (line 51) is declared private (no visibility modifier defaults to internal in Solidity, but the naming implies it's intended to be set). There IS a `setLiquidationFee` function (line 512), so the fee itself can be configured. However, `feeRecipient` (the destination of those fees) has NO setter whatsoever.
