_withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() computes liquidityToRemove using:
  uint128(vp.initialLiquidity * (lastValid - vp.lastUpdate) / (vp.endTs - vp.startTs))
This uses initialLiquidity (the original amount) rather than remainingLiquidity, making the released amount proportional to total duration elapsed since startTs, not since lastUpdate. However the formula divides by (endTs - startTs) and multiplies by (lastValid - lastUpdate), which IS the incremental amount for this period — that part is correct. BUT: the formula can accumulate rounding errors over time. More importantly, if collectFees is called very frequently (many tiny intervals), the integer division `vp.initialLiquidity * (lastValid - vp.lastUpdate) / (vp.endTs - vp.startTs)` rounds down each time, causing the sum of released liquidity to be LESS than initialLiquidity at endTs. When lastValid == vp.endTs the code correctly uses remainingLiquidity instead, so the final call is accurate. The bug is subtle: during the vesting period, slightly less liquidity is released per period due to integer truncation, with the deficit accumulating in remainingLiquidity until the final call.

collectFees() charges protocol fees on ALL new idle balance increases, including the incremental vesting position withdrawal that happens AFTER the protocol fee is charged. However, the comment says "doing that now, otherwise we'd charge protocol fee for the vested position." So protocol fees are intentionally not charged on the vested tokens. The issue is that the fee is computed BEFORE _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition is called, based on (afterBal0 - preBal0) which includes Uniswap fees from main and secondary positions but NOT the vesting withdrawal. However, if collectPositionFees for the vesting position (line 167) uses the WRONG ticks (SH-001), the vesting position fees are NOT collected in the afterBal snapshot — they're essentially lost. This compounds the SH-001 bug: not only are vesting fees collected from the wrong range, but the protocol fee calculation is also based on incomplete data.

checkPoolActivity() uses `observationCardinality` as both the loop bound and the modular divisor for the index calculation. The correct index calculation in a Uniswap V3 circular buffer should use `observationCardinalityNext` for the buffer size, or more precisely the actual cardinality. The loop index calculation `(observationCardinality + currentIndex - i) % observationCardinality` is correct for a fully initialized buffer. However, the loop iterates from i=1 to i=observationCardinality (inclusive). Since observations are 0-indexed and currentIndex is the most recent, index i=1 is the previous one, up to i=observationCardinality-1 covers all unique positions. The i=observationCardinality iteration wraps back to currentIndex itself, reading the same observation twice (the most recent one). The timestamp check `if (timestamp == 0) { revert("timestamp 0"); }` prevents reading uninitialized slots. But reading currentIndex twice could compute a zero-time delta, causing division by zero in `int56(uint56(nextTimestamp - timestamp))`.

checkPoolActivity() reverts with "timestamp 0" if any observation slot in the ring buffer has not been initialized (timestamp == 0). Uniswap V3 pools only populate observation slots as blocks pass — slots beyond the originally initialized count are zero until populated. If anyone calls increaseObservationCardinalityNext() to grow the cardinality, the new slots remain zero until a transaction occurs in that block. The loop in checkPoolActivity() iterates ALL slots up to observationCardinality and reverts immediately on any zero-timestamp slot. Since collectFees() calls checkPoolActivity() indirectly through rebalance/compound, and deposit()/withdraw() call collectFees() directly, this revert will brick ALL vault operations: deposit, withdraw, rebalance, and compound are all permanently DoS'd until the pool fills every observation slot.

checkPoolActivity() returns false — blocking rebalance() and compound() — whenever the loop exhausts all observationCardinality entries without finding any observation with timestamp < lookAgo (i.e., older than `twap` seconds ago). This happens on new pools or pools with high cardinality but short history: if the oldest filled observation is still more recent than `block.timestamp - twap`, the function returns false (line 341). Because _priceWithinRange() returns false in this case, both rebalance() and compound() permanently revert with "price out of range". The vault accumulates fees but cannot compound them, and positions cannot be rebalanced even when price moves out of range.

checkPoolActivity() has an off-by-one error in its loop bounds: the loop runs `for (uint16 i = 1; i <= observationCardinality; i++)` where the last iteration at i == observationCardinality computes index as `(observationCardinality + currentIndex - observationCardinality) % observationCardinality = currentIndex`. This is the SAME index as the very first slot read before the loop (nextTimestamp, nextCumulativeTick). So the last iteration computes a tick delta between the most recent observation and itself — producing a zero time delta. The division `(nextCumulativeTick - tickCumulative) / int56(uint56(nextTimestamp - timestamp))` at line 326 will DIVIDE BY ZERO when `nextTimestamp == timestamp` (both are the most recent observation). This causes a revert on the last iteration of any fully-initialized ring buffer, permanently bricking all vault operations that call collectFees().

Vault.withdraw() calls IStrategy(strategy).collectFees() at the start (line 84), which in turn calls IUniswapV3Pool(pool).burn() and collect() for each active position. The collectFees() function in Strategy (line 167) passes wrong tick ranges for the vesting position: `collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper)` instead of `collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, vestPosition.tickUpper)`. After a rebalance, mainPosition.tickUpper changes but vestPosition.tickUpper does not. The pool's burn(0) call on a non-existent position silently creates a new zero-liquidity position at that tick range. This does not revert, but subsequent calls to withdraw or collect fees will include fees from both the real vesting position AND spurious zero-liquidity positions, potentially causing _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() to undercount available liquidity. More critically, if vestPosition.tickLower == mainPosition.tickUpper (degenerate tick range), the pool's burn call will revert with "TLU" (tick lower must be less than tick upper), permanently bricking collectFees() and thus all vault operations.

Vault.withdraw() uses `safeTransferFrom(strategy, msg.sender, withdrawAmount0/1)` (lines 103-104). This requires the strategy to have approved the vault to transfer tokens on its behalf. The strategy sets `forceApprove(vault, type(uint256).max)` in the constructor (lines 96-97), which works correctly for standard ERC20 tokens. However, if `withdrawAmount0` or `withdrawAmount1` exceeds the strategy's actual token balance (due to a rounding error or accounting bug in `withdrawPartial`), the safeTransferFrom will revert, permanently blocking the withdrawal for that user. This can happen because `withdrawPartial` returns calculated amounts that may slightly exceed actual balances due to integer arithmetic in the liquidity-to-token conversion in LiquidityAmounts. A user could be left unable to withdraw their full position.

In `withdraw()`, when `borrowed == up.token1`, the ternary condition for computing `repayFromWithdraw` uses `amountOut0` instead of `amountOut1` in the true branch. The code reads: `uint256 repayFromWithdraw = amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount;` When `amountOut1 < owedAmount`, the repayment is taken as `amountOut0` (token0 amount) instead of `amountOut1` (token1 amount). This causes `amountOut1 -= repayFromWithdraw` to underflow (panic revert) when `amountOut0 > amountOut1`, or to under-deduct, allowing the user to receive more token1 than they should while the lending pool is under-repaid.

In `liquidatePosition()`, line 318, the borrowed value in USD is computed as: `uint256 borrowedValue = owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals();` The divisor uses `.decimals()` directly (e.g. 6 for USDC, 8 for WBTC) instead of `10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` (e.g. 1e6, 1e8). This makes `borrowedValue` orders of magnitude larger than the actual USD value (e.g. dividing by 6 instead of 1e6 inflates by 166,666x for USDC). Consequently `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` is almost always false — the fee collection block is never entered, and the liquidation fee is never charged, meaning the protocol always receives zero liquidation fees on profitable liquidations.

`feeRecipient` is declared as `address public feeRecipient` at line 47 but is NEVER initialized in the constructor or any owner function. Its value is permanently `address(0)`. In `liquidatePosition()`, liquidation fees collected (pf0, pf1) are transferred to `feeRecipient` (address(0)), permanently burning them. The protocol can never collect fees even if TBH-LEV-02 is fixed. There is no `setFeeRecipient` function.

The `collectFees` modifier on `liquidatePosition` executes BEFORE the `nonReentrant` modifier lock is acquired (Solidity modifiers are applied right-to-left in execution order but the function signature is `collectFees(liqParams.id) nonReentrant`). Actually, with Solidity, modifiers are stacked left-to-right in declaration order, so `collectFees` runs first, then `nonReentrant`. The `collectFees` modifier calls `IStrategy(strat).collectFees()` on an external contract BEFORE the reentrancy lock is set. If the strategy's `collectFees` were malicious or upgradeable, it could reenter `liquidatePosition`. Additionally, the modifier reads `positions[_id]` before it is known whether the ID is valid — a call with a nonexistent `_id` leads to `up.vault = address(0)`, causing `IVault(address(0)).strategy()` to succeed (returns address(0) since it's an empty external call), then `IStrategy(address(0)).collectFees()` also silently returns, so no revert, but execution continues with invalid state data.

In `withdraw()`, when `borrowed == up.token1` and the branch enters the true branch of the ternary (amountOut1 < owedAmount), `repayFromWithdraw = amountOut0`. Then `amountOut1 -= repayFromWithdraw` executes. If `amountOut0 > amountOut1` this panics with underflow. But even when it doesn't underflow (amountOut0 <= amountOut1), the semantics are wrong: `amountOut1` is reduced by `amountOut0` (a token0 quantity), not by the actual amount of token1 used for repayment. The user then receives the wrong amount of token1, and the lending pool receives the wrong repayment quantity. This is the same root cause as TBH-LEV-01 but the secondary effect is worth independently tracking: the repaid amount sent to the lending pool is `amountToRepay` (= original owedAmount), which is correct, BUT the tokens taken from the user via `safeTransferFrom` are reduced by `repayFromWithdraw = amountOut0` instead of `amountOut1`, meaning the user is under-charged by the difference.

pullFunds() transfers underlying tokens out of the yToken contract but does NOT decrement reserve.underlyingBalance. This causes the pool's internal accounting to permanently diverge from the actual token balance held by the yToken contract. After pullFunds(asset, X), reserve.underlyingBalance is X higher than the real token balance. Since availableLiquidity() returns reserve.underlyingBalance, all subsequent checks (redeem liquidity gate, borrow liquidity gate) operate on a stale inflated number. A depositor can redeem tokens that no longer exist in the yToken contract, causing the safeTransfer inside yToken.burn() to revert — but only for later redeemers. Earlier redeemers drain the pool, and the last redeemers are stuck.

pushFunds() receives tokens into the yToken contract but does NOT increment reserve.underlyingBalance. This is the mirror bug to TBH-LP-001. After pushFunds(asset, X), the actual token balance in yToken is X higher than reserve.underlyingBalance reflects. The donated X tokens become permanently inaccessible accounting-wise: they inflate the real balance but the reserve's underlyingBalance never captures them. As interest accrues, borrowedLiquidity grows but underlyingBalance stays stale-low. Eventually totalLiquidityAndBorrows will reflect less than what is actually held, so lenders earn less yield than they should and the extra tokens are stranded.

_deposit() calls safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, yTokenAddress, amount) and then unconditionally sets reserve.underlyingBalance += amount. For fee-on-transfer tokens, the actual amount received by yToken is less than `amount`. The inflated underlyingBalance causes the exchange rate to be miscalculated (higher than real), so subsequent depositors receive fewer yTokens than they deserve, and early redeemers can drain more underlying than their share, leaving later redeemers stuck with insufficient actual balance.

pullFunds() does not call reserve.updateState() before moving tokens. The borrow() function calls reserve.updateState() before any accounting change, ensuring interest accrues up to the current block before modifying state. pullFunds() skips this step entirely. If pullFunds is followed by pushFunds in the same transaction, no interest window is missed; but if time passes between pullFunds and pushFunds (intended flash-loan pattern or multi-block leverager use), the interest that should have accrued on the outstanding borrows during that window will be computed from a stale borrowingIndex when the next updateState() runs. Additionally, since pullFunds reads a memory copy (DataTypes.ReserveData memory) the getReserve check is skipped (no active-state verification for memory copy path vs storage path).

The combination of pullFunds() not decrementing underlyingBalance and pushFunds() not incrementing it creates a situation where the total liquidity as seen by the protocol (reserve.underlyingBalance + accrued borrows) diverges from the true economic value. Specifically: after a pull-push cycle, the reserve's underlyingBalance is stale. If pushFunds is called with MORE tokens than were pulled (e.g. leverager returns principal + profit), the extra tokens are silently absorbed into the yToken contract balance with no accounting update. This means lenders never see the yield from the leverager's profits — the exchange rate (yTokenToReserveExchangeRate) does not improve because underlyingBalance did not increase. The tokens are locked in yToken forever (they can only be recovered if someone calls repay() or deposit() to trigger underlyingBalance updates, but those paths don't credit the stranded balance).

pullFunds() reads the reserve with `DataTypes.ReserveData memory reserve = getReserve(asset)` (memory copy), while pushFunds() does the same. Since the reserve is read into memory, any state mutations would not persist — but neither function mutates reserve fields anyway (which is the actual bug: they SHOULD be mutating underlyingBalance). However there is a subtler issue: getReserve() internally returns a storage reference. The caller casts it to memory. In Solidity, assigning a storage struct to a memory variable creates a copy. This is correct for reads but means if future code were added to update the memory struct, it would silently not persist. The divergence between pullFunds/pushFunds using memory and borrow/repay using storage is a maintenance landmine. Additionally, the active-reserve check in getReserve() uses `reserve.getActive()` on the storage reference — this still works for the check itself, but the memory copy returned from getReserve (which is a storage ref in the function body) means the pattern is inconsistent and confusing.

In liquidatePosition(), borrowedValue is computed as `owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()` (line 318). The denominator is `ERC20.decimals()` which returns the raw uint8 (e.g. 8 for WBTC, 6 for USDC), NOT `10 ** decimals`. The correct denominator is `10 ** decimals` (e.g. 1e8). Using 8 instead of 1e8 inflates `borrowedValue` by a factor of 1e8/8 = 12.5M for WBTC and 1e6/6 = 166k for USDC, making `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` almost never true. Consequently the entire fee collection block (lines 320-332) is never entered, so the protocol never collects liquidation fees. Furthermore, the profit-vs-loss determination used to decide whether liquidators get leftover collateral is completely wrong: a genuinely profitable liquidation (collateral > debt) appears as a loss, breaking the economic accounting of the liquidation flow.

In withdraw(), when the denomination is token1, the code on line 232 reads: `uint256 repayFromWithdraw = amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount;` The ternary true-branch returns `amountOut0` (the token0 amount) instead of `amountOut1`. This means: when amountOut1 < owedAmount (i.e. vault returned less token1 than owed), the contract caps repayment at `amountOut0` (the token0 amount) rather than `amountOut1` (the available token1). The subsequent `amountOut1 -= repayFromWithdraw` will subtract the token0 amount from token1's balance — leading to either underflow (revert in safe arithmetic), or incorrect accounting where more/less denomination is credited toward repayment than actually available. When amountOut0 > amountOut1, this causes an underflow revert, bricking withdrawals for token1-denominated positions whenever the vault returns less token1 than owed.

In liquidatePosition(), line 318: `uint256 borrowedValue = owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals();` This is a secondary consequence of MATH-01: the function uses `.decimals()` (returns uint8 e.g. 8) instead of `10 ** .decimals()` (returns 1e8). But there's an additional implication for the profitability check: `if (totalValueUSD > borrowedValue)` — since borrowedValue is inflated by ~12.5M×, this condition is almost NEVER true. However when it IS true (i.e. when owedAmount is extremely small), the liquidation fee calculation on line 324: `uint256 protocolFeePct = 1e18 * liquidationFee * (totalValueUSD - borrowedValue) / (totalValueUSD * 10_000)` would compute a fee based on a massive `(totalValueUSD - borrowedValue)` that is wrong. In addition, the `feeRecipient` is uninitialized (address(0) by default, confirmed by Slither signal). Transfer to address(0) may revert for some ERC20 tokens (OpenZeppelin SafeERC20 does NOT prevent transfer to 0, but some tokens do). Even if it doesn't revert, the fee is lost to the zero address.

In collectFees() at line 167, the fee-collection call for the ongoing vesting position
passes mainPosition.tickUpper as the upper tick instead of vestPosition.tickUpper:

    collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper)  // BUG

The vesting position is minted at (vestPosition.tickLower, vestPosition.tickUpper), where
vestPosition.tickUpper is set to mainPosition.tickUpper AT CREATION TIME and stored in the
VestingPosition struct. After any rebalance(), _setMainTicks() updates mainPosition.tickUpper
to a new value based on the current tick, while vestPosition.tickUpper retains the
creation-time value.

Post-rebalance, collectFees() calls:
    IUniswapV3Pool.burn(vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper_NEW, 0)

This targets a position key that either: (a) does not exist — Uniswap V3 creates a phantom
zero-liquidity entry and returns 0 fees, or (b) is the new main position (same ticks) —
causing fees to be double-counted from the main position key rather than the vesting position.

The correct vesting position at (vestPosition.tickLower, vestPosition.tickUpper_OLD) never
has its fee accumulation triggered via burn(0). Its owed fees are only materialized when
_withdrawPartOfVestingPosition eventually calls _removeFromPosition (burn + collect), which
bypasses the preBal/afterBal delta used for protocol fee calculation.

Effect chain:
  1. collectPositionFees on wrong ticks → no-op / wrong position
  2. vestingPosition fees not included in afterBal - preBal delta
  3. Protocol fee not charged on vesting position yield (revenue loss)
  4. Vesting fees are eventually recovered via _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition but without
     protocol fee deduction, violating the protocol's economic model
  5. After a rebalance + endTs reached, ongoingVestingPosition = false but accumulated
     fees from the entire vesting period escaped protocol fee entirely

changePositionWidth() (line 395) lacks any access-control modifier:

    function changePositionWidth(uint24 _newWidth) external {
        require((_newWidth / 2) % uint24(tickSpacing) == 0, ...);
        positionWidth = _newWidth;
        rebalance();       // onlyRebalancer guard lives here
    }

The comment "Access control is performed within rebalance" is misleading: rebalance() uses
onlyRebalancer, NOT onlyOwner. This means the REBALANCER (an operational role) can:
  1. Call changePositionWidth(_newWidth)
  2. positionWidth is mutated BEFORE rebalance() is called
  3. rebalance() succeeds because msg.sender == rebalancer

Every other parameter-setting function in the contract uses onlyOwner:
  setTwap, setTickTwapDeviation, setMaxObservationDeviation, setRebalanceInterval,
  setProtocolFee, changeFeeRecipient, changeRebalancer — all onlyOwner.

positionWidth governs the width of the main liquidity position, directly controlling:
  - Capital efficiency vs IL exposure trade-off
  - How much of each token is deployed per unit of liquidity
  - Rebalance frequency requirements

A compromised or malicious rebalancer can set positionWidth to minimum (2 * tickSpacing)
to concentrate risk dangerously, or to maximum to dilute fee earnings. This bypasses the
protocol governance model where the owner controls strategy parameters.

_setSecondaryPositionsTicks() can produce an invalid tick range (tickLower >= tickUpper),
causing getLiquidityForAmounts to divide by zero (sqrtRatioB - sqrtRatioA = 0) and reverting.

TOKEN0-HEAVY BRANCH (bal0in1 >= bal1):
    secondaryPosition.tickLower = tick - modulo + tickSpacing
    secondaryPosition.tickUpper = mainPosition.tickUpper

When tick is near mainPosition.tickUpper — specifically when:
    tick - modulo + tickSpacing >= mainPosition.tickUpper
e.g. tick = mainPosition.tickUpper - tickSpacing + 1, modulo = 1:
    tickLower = (mainPosition.tickUpper - tickSpacing + 1) - 1 + tickSpacing = mainPosition.tickUpper
    tickUpper = mainPosition.tickUpper
    → tickLower == tickUpper → INVALID

TOKEN1-HEAVY BRANCH (bal0in1 < bal1):
    secondaryPosition.tickLower = mainPosition.tickLower
    secondaryPosition.tickUpper = tick - modulo

When tick is near mainPosition.tickLower — specifically when:
    tick - modulo <= mainPosition.tickLower
e.g. tick = mainPosition.tickLower + 1, modulo = 1:
    tickUpper = mainPosition.tickLower + 1 - 1 = mainPosition.tickLower
    tickLower = mainPosition.tickLower
    → tickLower == tickUpper → INVALID

In both cases, _addLiquidityToSecondaryPosition calls getLiquidityForAmounts with a
zero-width range. When sqrtRatioA == sqrtRatioB, the function divides by
(sqrtRatioBX96 - sqrtRatioAX96) = 0, causing an arithmetic revert.

Additionally, _setSecondaryPositionsTicks does NOT apply the negative-modulo correction
that _setMainTicks explicitly performs:
    _setMainTicks: `if (modulo < 0) modulo += tickSpacing;`
    _setSecondaryPositionsTicks: NO correction
For negative ticks, this causes the secondary tick boundary to be off by tickSpacing.

In checkPoolActivity() (line 322-324):

    if (timestamp == 0) {
        revert("timestamp 0");
    }

When the Uniswap pool's observation cardinality has been increased (via
increaseObservationCardinalityNext) but not all new slots have been filled by swaps,
some slots remain at timestamp=0. The function reverts instead of returning false.

Correct behavior (consistent with the `return false` at loop end) should be:
    if (timestamp == 0) return false; // not enough history yet

Since checkPoolActivity() is called by _priceWithinRange() → _requirePriceWithinRange(),
both rebalance() and compound() will revert whenever any observation in the ring buffer
is uninitialized. This window can last indefinitely if swap activity is low.

Secondary issue: when observationCardinality == 1 and i == 1:
    index = (1 + currentIndex - 1) % 1 = 0 = currentIndex
This compares the current observation against itself, computing:
    int56(uint56(nextTimestamp - timestamp)) == int56(0) → division by zero → revert

A pool with freshly-increased cardinality (a common operational task to enable TWAP)
creates an attack surface: any actor who calls increaseObservationCardinalityNext on
the pool can trigger this DoS on the strategy.

collectFees() (line 159) has no access-control modifier and is callable by any address.
When ongoingVestingPosition == true, every collectFees() call triggers
_withdrawPartOfVestingPosition(), which:
  1. Removes liquidity proportional to elapsed time from the vesting position
  2. Adds freed tokens to the strategy's idle balance
  3. Increases the effective token balances tracked by balances() / vault.balances()

An attacker can exploit this before a large deposit:
  1. Attacker calls collectFees() just before victim deposits
  2. _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition releases vested liquidity → idle balance increases
  3. vault.balances() increases → shares are minted at a higher price per share
  4. Depositor receives fewer shares for the same tokens → value extracted

Additionally, high-frequency collectFees() calls fragment vesting into tiny increments,
each with integer division truncation of liquidityToRemove. This can cause cumulative
under-vesting (less total liquidity removed than expected) since:
    liquidityToRemove = initialLiquidity * (lastValid - lastUpdate) / (endTs - startTs)
Each call truncates down, and many small calls may remove less total liquidity than one
call at the same end timestamp.

The protocol fee calculation (afterBal - preBal delta) can also be sandwiched: an attacker
calls collectFees() around large swaps to capture extra fee income in the delta calculation.

_setSecondaryPositionsTicks() has two distinct logic errors:

ERROR A — Always-else when both balances are zero:
    uint256 bal0in1 = bal0 * _price / PRECISION;
    if (bal0in1 < bal1) { /* lower-sided secondary */ }
    else                { /* upper-sided secondary */ }

When both bal0 == 0 and bal1 == 0 (constructor call, before any deposits):
    bal0in1 = 0 * _price / PRECISION = 0
    condition: 0 < 0 → false → always takes the ELSE branch
Secondary position is unconditionally placed on the upper side (token0-heavy) at
construction regardless of actual pool balance or initial deposit split.

This stale secondary position persists until the first rebalance(). During this window,
user deposits find the secondary position incorrectly configured: it expects a token0
surplus but the initial deposit is typically 50/50.

ERROR B — Missing negative modulo correction:
    _setMainTicks has:  `if (modulo < 0) modulo += tickSpacing;`
    _setSecondaryPositionsTicks: NO such correction

For negative ticks (pools where token0 is worth more than token1), Solidity's % operator
returns a negative modulo. Without correction:
    tick = -105, tickSpacing = 10
    modulo = -5 (uncorrected)
    tick - modulo = -100  (rounds TOWARD ZERO = ceiling division)

With correction (as in _setMainTicks), modulo = 5, tick - modulo = -110 (floor division).
The secondary position boundary is off by one tickSpacing for all negative-tick pools,
creating a misalignment between the main and secondary position boundaries.

In _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() (line 467), each partial withdrawal computes:

    uint128 liquidityToRemove = uint128(
        vp.initialLiquidity * (lastValid - vp.lastUpdate) / (vp.endTs - vp.startTs)
    );

Each call truncates down. If collectFees() is called N times during the vesting window,
the total liquidity removed by time T is:

    sum_i [ initialLiquidity * dt_i / totalDuration ]

where sum(dt_i) = T - startTs, but each term is individually floor-divided. The sum of
floor-divided terms is <= floor of the sum, meaning:

    sum_i <= initialLiquidity * (T - startTs) / totalDuration

The shortfall is bounded by N (number of partial calls), since each truncates by at most 1.

However, since collectFees() is publicly callable by anyone (Bug 5), an attacker can call
it N times per second, maximizing N and thus maximizing cumulative truncation. For large N:
    remainingLiquidity after time T ≈ initialLiquidity - (initialLiquidity * (T-startTs)/totalDuration) + N

At endTs, the `lastValid == vp.endTs` branch is triggered and remainingLiquidity is burned
in full (correct), but the ACCUMULATED EFFECT is that the intermediate state of
remainingLiquidity is always HIGHER than expected — meaning at any point in time,
more liquidity than intended remains vesting in the pool.

For a high-frequency attacker scenario: 1000 calls with 1-second spacing each lose 1 unit of
liquidity to truncation, causing ~1000 units of liquidity to remain in the pool at endTs when
they should have vested earlier. This delays value delivery to depositors.

collectFees() in Strategy.sol calls collectPositionFees() with vestPosition.tickLower but mainPosition.tickUpper instead of vestPosition.tickUpper. After any rebalance that changes mainPosition ticks, vestPosition and mainPosition diverge. The burn/collect call to the Uniswap pool uses a tick range that does not match the real vesting position, so vesting position fees are never collected from the pool. The protocol fee is then calculated on a delta that includes zero vesting fees (or wrong range fees), causing accumulated vesting position fees to be permanently stranded in the pool.

Strategy.balances() does not include the vesting position's liquidity value in its total. It sums idle balances + main position + secondary position, but entirely omits the vestPosition liquidity. Since Vault._calcDeposit and Vault.withdraw both use IStrategy.balances() to calculate fair share of tokens per LP share, the vesting position value is invisible to the accounting. New depositors get shares priced against a pool that does not include the vesting position's real value, meaning when the vesting position eventually vests (adding tokens to idle), those tokens dilute existing shareholders unfairly. Conversely, users who deposit AFTER a vesting position is added benefit when it vests — they paid less per share than the true vault value.

In Vault._calcDeposit(), when bal0 > 0 and bal1 > 0, both amount0 and amount1 are rounded UP (ceiling division): amount0 = (cross-1)/bal1 + 1 and amount1 = (cross-1)/bal0 + 1. However, the shares calculation uses floor division: shares = cross * totalSupply / bal0 / bal1. The result is that new depositors are systematically charged slightly MORE tokens than their fair share, while receiving shares based on the un-rounded (floor) cross product. Each deposit donates a small amount of token0 and token1 to existing shareholders. While the individual effect is small, it is structurally incorrect: the protocol over-charges depositors in both tokens simultaneously when only one should be rounded up.

withdrawPartial() in Strategy.sol does not remove any liquidity from the vesting position when a user withdraws. It proportionally removes from mainPosition and secondaryPosition only. However, since balances() also omits the vesting position, the withdrawing user never gets their proportional share of the vesting position value. This creates a systematic loss for withdrawing users during any period when an ongoing vesting position exists. Users who withdraw early forfeit their share of the vesting position entirely, which is redistributed to remaining users and eventually to whoever is in the vault when the position finishes vesting.

pullFunds() and pushFunds() never update reserve.underlyingBalance. The availableLiquidity() function returns reserve.underlyingBalance directly (ReserveLogic.sol line 37). After a pullFunds() call, actual tokens are transferred out of the yToken contract but underlyingBalance is not decremented. This inflates the reported available liquidity and allows the leverager to call borrow() afterward and pass the "amount <= availableLiquidity()" check even when the yToken contract does not actually hold those tokens. The borrow() call will then fail on the underlying ERC20 transfer (insufficient balance), but the state-view mismatch is a real accounting integrity bug. More critically, the inflated underlyingBalance also inflates totalLiquidity used for exchange rate calculations: depositors get fewer yTokens than they deserve (reserveToYTokenExchangeRate returns a higher value), and redeemers can withdraw more underlying than proportionally correct (yTokenToReserveExchangeRate returns a higher value).

pushFunds() never updates reserve.underlyingBalance. When the leverager pushes tokens back via pushFunds(), underlyingBalance is not incremented. This means the pool's recorded underlyingBalance progressively diverges from reality with each pull/push cycle. If pullFunds is called N times (each balanced by a pushFunds), the underlyingBalance remains at its initial value (neither decremented nor incremented), while the actual yToken balance stays correct. However if pullFunds and pushFunds are called asymmetrically (pull without push, or push without pull via a different path), the divergence compounds. In the push-without-pull scenario (e.g., a generous deposit by the leverager directly), the underlyingBalance remains low while the real balance is higher, causing lenders to receive MORE yTokens than fair value on subsequent deposits (since reserveToYTokenExchangeRate uses stale underlyingBalance).

pullFunds() lacks the notPaused modifier. When the LendingPool is paused via emergencyPauseAll(), deposits and borrows are blocked (notPaused modifier). However pullFunds() has no such guard. This means the leverager can continue pulling raw underlying tokens out of the yToken contract even during an emergency pause. The intent of pausing is to freeze the system in a safe state; allowing fund extraction during a pause undermines the safety mechanism. Combined with the missing underlyingBalance update (AH-001), this creates a window where the leverager can extract all available liquidity from the pool while it is supposed to be frozen.

freezeReserve() and unFreezeReserve() both carry the notPaused modifier. This means that when the contract is in emergency pause, the owner cannot freeze individual reserves either. This is a defensive capability gap: the owner may want to freeze a specific reserve while the contract is paused (e.g., to mark it permanently frozen before unpausing), but the notPaused modifier on freezeReserve prevents this. The result is that the only recovery path after a pause is to unpause the entire contract before being able to freeze individual reserves, which temporarily opens the system to deposits and borrows again.

The leverager address can never be changed once set (setLeverager enforces a one-time set). If the leverager contract is found to have a critical bug or is compromised, the owner has no way to update the leverager to a patched version. All borrow/repay/pullFunds/pushFunds access is permanently granted to the original leverager address. Additionally, since the Leverager contract has no upgrade mechanism (not upgradeable proxy), a compromised leverager means all pooled funds are permanently at risk with no owner remedy. This is an access control design flaw: the permanent grant with no revocation path violates least-privilege principles.

The underlyingBalance accounting is broken by the pullFunds/pushFunds path. The core invariant should be: reserve.underlyingBalance == yToken.balanceOf(underlying). borrow() correctly decrements underlyingBalance and repay() correctly increments it. But pullFunds() extracts tokens without decrementing, and pushFunds() injects tokens without incrementing. A sequence of pullFunds(X) followed by borrow(X) will cause the borrow to decrement underlyingBalance below the actual yToken balance (underlyingBalance goes negative relative to reality), or in the worst case below zero causing a revert on the underflow. This means the leverager effectively holds a double claim on X tokens. The combination breaks the invariant used by all liquidity checks, exchange rates, and utilization rate calculations.

In `withdraw`, when the borrowed denomination is token1, the repayment cap calculation uses `amountOut0` instead of `amountOut1`. Concretely, `repayFromWithdraw` is set to `amountOut0 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount` when it should use `amountOut1`. This means: if amountOut0 < owedAmount the cap is taken from the wrong variable, but then `amountOut1` is still decremented by that amount. When token0 balance is 0 but token1 balance is sufficient, `repayFromWithdraw` becomes 0 (since amountOut0 = 0 < owedAmount), so the contract fails to deduct any amount from amountOut1 and forces the user to pay the full owedAmount from their wallet — effectively double-counting. Conversely, when token0 is large, repayFromWithdraw exceeds the real token1 available and can underflow or create an inflated debt repayment from user.

In `liquidatePosition`, the `borrowedValue` used to determine whether there is profit (and hence whether a liquidation fee should be collected) is computed as `owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()`. The denominator is the raw return of `decimals()` (e.g. 8 for WBTC, 6 for USDC) instead of `10 ** decimals()` (1e8 or 1e6). This causes `borrowedValue` to be inflated by a factor of `10**decimals / decimals` — for WBTC (8 decimals) that is 1e8/8 = 12_500_000x overstatement. The result: `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` is almost always false, so the protocol fee branch is never entered and the fee recipient receives nothing from liquidations. Beyond the fee loss, the incorrect `borrowedValue` is only used for the fee calculation branch, so liquidation still proceeds correctly (owed repayment uses `owedAmount` directly), but the fee mechanism is permanently broken.

`feeRecipient` is declared as a public state variable (`address public feeRecipient`) but is never initialized in the constructor or any setter function. It defaults to `address(0)`. In `liquidatePosition`, when the fee condition is met, tokens are transferred to `address(0)` via `IERC20.safeTransfer`, which for most ERC-20 tokens will succeed (burning the tokens). There is no owner function to set `feeRecipient`. All protocol liquidation fees are permanently burned/lost. Combined with SIG-LEV-02, the fee branch is doubly broken: even if the arithmetic were fixed, fees would go to the zero address.

In `withdraw`, when `borrowed == up.token1`, after correctly computing `repayFromWithdraw` (assuming SIG-LEV-01 were fixed to use amountOut1), the code decrements `amountOut1` by `repayFromWithdraw`. But the repay call uses `amountToRepay` (= full owedAmount for the period), not the adjusted `owedAmount`. This means even after deducting the withdrawal proceeds from `owedAmount`, the contract repays the full `amountToRepay` to the lending pool. If the user also had to send `owedAmount` from their wallet, that means the lending pool is repaid for the full amount AND gets the user wallet transfer too — overpaying by the amount covered by the withdrawn tokens. More precisely, `amountToRepay` is set before any deduction and is always `totalOwedAmount * pctWithdraw / 1e18`, while only the residual `owedAmount` (after deducting vault proceeds) is pulled from the user. The repayment of `amountToRepay` (full) with funds sourced from vault withdrawal + user wallet is the correct accounting. However, when token1 is denomination and amountOut1 covers all of owedAmount, the user should not need to transfer anything — yet the stack of deductions from amountOut1 means `if (owedAmount > 0)` fires incorrectly due to the SIG-LEV-01 copy-paste bug, showing SIG-LEV-01 is the root cause. This hypothesis captures the resulting accounting invariant that should hold.

In `isLiquidateable`, the denominator used in the `base` calculation is `(vp.maxTimesLeverage - 1e18)`. If `maxTimesLeverage` is set exactly to `1e18` (1x leverage), this denominator becomes zero and the function reverts with a division-by-zero panic. While `initVault` does not explicitly prevent `_maxTimesLeverage = 1e18`, a value of 1e18 means no leverage is allowed. Any attempt to call `isLiquidateable` for any position under such a vault (or after the governance sets maxTimesLeverage to 1e18 via `changeVaultMaxLeverage`) would permanently revert, preventing liquidations and locking positions. Similarly, if `maxTimesLeverage` is less than 1e18 (which is accepted by `changeVaultMaxLeverage`), the subtraction itself underflows (in unchecked Solidity 0.8 it would panic), also bricking the liquidation path.

The `_sweepTokens` function in `openLeveragedPosition` sends the entire balance of token0 and token1 held by the Leverager contract to `msg.sender`. The natspec explicitly acknowledges that tokens can be "stuck" in the contract due to prior failed transactions or MEV activity. Any user who calls `openLeveragedPosition` can sweep any previously-stuck token0/token1 balances from the Leverager contract as a bonus, even if those tokens belong to the protocol or are residuals from other users' operations. While the protocol dismisses this as acceptable (comment on line 174-176), if the amounts are non-trivial this constitutes theft of funds from the contract.

In `openLeveragedPosition`, the `borrowedAmount` is calculated as `lp.maxBorrowAmount - denomBalance` where `denomBalance` is the remaining denomination token balance after swaps and flashloan repayments. The comment explicitly notes this can fail if there are previously stuck tokens (line 174-176). More critically: if the user passes a `maxBorrowAmount` that is less than or equal to the flashloan delta for the denomination token (delta0 or delta1), the arithmetic `lp.maxBorrowAmount - denomBalance` will underflow because `denomBalance` (which includes repaid flashloan amounts) exceeds `maxBorrowAmount`. This would panic-revert in Solidity 0.8, but only at the end of the function after the vault deposit has already occurred, wasting gas and leaving the user's collateral temporarily in limbo (recovered by revert). The check `require(!isLiquidateable(_id))` also happens after the `_id` is assigned but before the NFT is minted, and borrowedAmount is stored. The underflow would revert before storage writes, so no state corruption — but this is a DoS vector if maxBorrowAmount is misconfigured.

In Leverager.withdraw(), when the borrowed denomination is token1, the code calculates repayFromWithdraw using amountOut0 (token0 balance) instead of amountOut1 (token1 balance). This means:
  - If amountOut1 < owedAmount: repayFromWithdraw = amountOut0 (wrong token amount!)
  - owedAmount is reduced by amountOut0 instead of the actual token1 proceeds
  - amountOut1 is reduced by repayFromWithdraw (which equals amountOut0)
Result: The position owner may receive extra token1 that should have been used for repayment, and `amountOut1` may underflow if amountOut0 > amountOut1. Alternatively, a user can withdraw a position denominated in token1 and receive significantly more token1 than entitled, under-repaying the debt.

In Leverager.liquidatePosition(), the borrowedValue calculation uses ERC20(up.denomination).decimals() (which returns a uint8, e.g. 18 for WETH or 6 for USDC) instead of 10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals() (i.e. 1e18 or 1e6). For WETH (18 decimals): the divisor is 18 instead of 1e18, making borrowedValue ~5.5e16x too large. For USDC (6 decimals): divisor is 6 instead of 1e6, making borrowedValue ~166_666x too large.
Consequence: borrowedValue will almost always exceed totalValueUSD, causing the condition `if (totalValueUSD > borrowedValue)` to be false. The protocol fee branch is skipped, meaning feeRecipient receives nothing on liquidations. More critically, the liquidation profit math is completely broken — positions that are very profitable to liquidate will appear unprofitable.

In Leverager.withdraw(), after a partial withdrawal (pctWithdraw < 1e18), positions[wp.id].borrowedAmount is set to `totalOwedAmount - amountToRepay` (i.e., the interest-accrued remaining debt), but `positions[wp.id].borrowedIndex` is set to the CURRENT bIndex. This is the correct behavior for updating the position's debt.
However, `positions[wp.id].initBorrowedUsd` is reduced proportionally from the ORIGINAL initBorrowedUsd (not recomputed at current price). Over time, as prices change, `initBorrowedUsd` diverges from true USD value of `borrowedAmount`. `currBorrowedUSD` in vaultParams is also maintained using these stale values.
More critically: if a user does many small partial withdraws (say 1% each), the minBorrow check at line 280 uses the stale `up.initBorrowedUsd` (loaded from storage at the start of the function). Since `up` is a MEMORY copy loaded before updates, the check `up.initBorrowedUsd * (1e18 - wp.pctWithdraw) / 1e18 > minBorrow` uses the value BEFORE this withdrawal's update — which is fine for a single call. But note: the check does NOT recompute borrowedAmount * current_price to check the real USD value of remaining debt against minBorrow. A user could repeatedly withdraw 99% each time, always satisfying the proportion check but eventually leaving dust-level real debt (if denomination price crashed).

In Leverager.liquidatePosition(), the `collectFees` modifier executes IStrategy(strat).collectFees() BEFORE the nonReentrant guard is applied. The modifier order in the function signature is:
  `external collectFees(liqParams.id) nonReentrant`
Solidity applies modifiers left-to-right, so collectFees runs first, then nonReentrant sets the lock.
The collectFees modifier reads `positions[liqParams.id]` to get the vault/strategy. If an attacker could manipulate the position state between the collectFees call and the actual liquidation body (via reentrancy through collectFees), they might be able to exploit stale state. However, Strategy.collectFees() calls Uniswap and the ERC-20 token transfers — these do not call back into Leverager.
The more practical issue: the nonReentrant guard should protect the FULL operation including fee collection. If collectFees is called outside the lock, a cross-function reentrancy via ERC-777 or similar hooks could potentially re-enter a non-guarded function (like withdraw) while collectFees is executing. Since token0/token1 are WBTC/USDC (no hooks), the practical risk is low, but the design is architecturally unsound.

In Leverager.withdraw(), when borrowed == up.token1 and a swap is also requested (wp.hasToSwap == true), there is a double-reduction on amountOut1.
First, at line 232-235, amountOut1 is reduced by repayFromWithdraw. Then at lines 252-260, if swapParams2 specifies amountIn for token1, amountOut1 is AGAIN reduced by swapParams.amountIn.
The problem: after the first reduction, amountOut1 already reflects the amount sent to repayment. If swapParams2 then also tries to swap from amountOut1, the user is effectively double-spending from amountOut1. The swap could consume tokens already "allocated" to repayment. The repayment still uses `amountToRepay` (unchanged), so LendingPool.repay() is called for the full owed amount regardless. If there's a shortfall, `owedAmount` (remaining after token subtraction) triggers safeTransferFrom(msg.sender) at line 263 to cover it.
However, the amount transferred FROM msg.sender could be miscalculated if the swap outputs go to the user (as the comment suggests: "recipient should be user"). The swap outputs are NOT tracked back into amountOut0/amountOut1 — so after the swap, the leverager may not have enough token1 to cover amountToRepay, requiring msg.sender to provide extra funds that shouldn't be needed.

The `feeRecipient` state variable (line 47) is declared but never initialized in the constructor or in any initializer function. It defaults to address(0).
In liquidatePosition(), if the protocol fee branch executes (requires fixing FH-LEV-02 first), `pf0` and `pf1` amounts are transferred to address(0) via safeTransfer. Since WBTC and USDC do NOT revert on transfer to address(0) (they are standard ERC-20s), these funds would be permanently burned.
Additionally, a separate setter `setFeeRecipient` function does not appear to exist in the contract — the owner has no way to set feeRecipient without a setter function. This is a missing function that means the protocol can never collect liquidation fees even after the FH-LEV-02 decimals bug is fixed.

In Leverager._calculateTokenValues(), when both token0 and token1 have price feeds (both chPrice0 > 0 and chPrice1 > 0), neither of the fallback branches at lines 444-448 execute, which is correct.
However, when only token0 has a price feed (chPrice1 == 0), the formula used is: `amount1 * PRECISION / price * chPrice0 / decimals0`
The TWAP `price` is defined in PRECISION (1e30) units as token0/token1 ratio. To convert amount1 of token1 to token0 equivalent:
  token0_equiv = amount1 * PRECISION / price  (PRECISION/price gives token0 per token1)
Then convert to USD: token0_equiv * chPrice0 / decimals0
This is mathematically correct ONLY if price = token0 per token1 expressed in PRECISION units. But looking at the TWAP computation in Strategy.sol (not read here), the price units may be inverted or differently scaled. If price = token1 per token0 (i.e. how much token1 per token0), then converting amount1→token0 would need: amount1 * price / PRECISION (not divide).
Depending on price directionality, the USD value of LP positions could be computed with inverted exchange rates, causing all collateral valuations and liquidation thresholds to be wrong.

Strategy.balances() computes the vault's token0 and token1 totals using slot0().sqrtPriceX96 (the Uniswap V3 spot price) to convert liquidity into token amounts via LiquidityAmounts.getAmountsForLiquidity. This spot price is fully manipulable within a single transaction via a large swap (no flash-loan even needed for a well-capitalised attacker). Vault.deposit() calls IStrategy(strategy).balances() to compute totalBalance0 / totalBalance1 before minting shares. Vault.withdraw() does the same before computing withdrawAmount0 / withdrawAmount1. An attacker can:
  1. Push the pool price far in one direction with a large swap.
  2. Call vault.deposit() — the distorted balances make shares cheap (over-mint).
  3. Restore the price (swap back).
  4. Call vault.withdraw() — now shares redeem at the fair price, extracting value from existing LPs.
The TWAP guard (_requirePriceWithinRange) is only checked inside rebalance() and compound(), NOT inside deposit() or withdraw(). No oracle protection exists on the share-issuance path.

Strategy.price() (line 127-129) returns the spot price derived from slot0().sqrtPriceX96. This function is called inside _setSecondaryPositionsTicks() (line 370) to determine which token is in excess after adding liquidity to the main position. The direction of the secondary position (below or above the current tick) is chosen based on whether bal0 * spot_price / PRECISION < bal1. If an attacker manipulates the spot price before a rebalance, they can cause the secondary position to be placed on the wrong side, locking one token into an OOR position that will never become in-range until price crosses that range. This wastes idle capital and can result in permanently stranded funds in a position that cannot be exited (would require price to reach those extreme ticks).

Vault.deposit() calls IStrategy(strategy).balances() to get totalBalance0/totalBalance1 which drives share calculation via _calcDeposit. Strategy.balances() uses slot0().sqrtPriceX96 (spot) to convert the Uniswap V3 liquidity positions into token amounts. As a result, natural price movement between two deposit transactions can cause the second depositor to receive more or fewer shares than expected, independently of any malicious intent. More importantly, the vault's invariant that shares represent a proportional claim on real underlying assets is violated when the sqrtPrice used to compute balances differs from the sqrtPrice at which liquidity is actually settled on withdrawal. This creates a rounding error that systematically disadvantages late depositors during periods of high volatility.

The TWAP interval is initialized to 300 seconds (5 minutes) and can be set as low as 31 seconds via setTwap() (only requires _twap > 30). The _priceWithinRange() guard compares spot tick vs TWAP tick with a 200-tick tolerance. A 5-minute TWAP window is generally considered too short for manipulation-resistance in DeFi protocols handling significant TVL. An attacker with sufficient capital can move the pool price for 5 minutes (e.g., using a series of smaller swaps to avoid detection), then rebalance occurs at the manipulated price. The TWAP will reflect the manipulated price after 5 minutes, allowing the attacker to pass the _requirePriceWithinRange() check while both TWAP and spot are at the manipulated level. This is especially dangerous for the WBTC/USDC pool which has moderate liquidity depth.

checkPoolActivity() (Strategy.sol line 310-342) iterates through all stored pool observations (up to observationCardinality entries). At line 322-324, if any observation has timestamp == 0 (uninitialized), the function reverts with "timestamp 0". This function is called inside:
  - _requirePriceWithinRange() → rebalance() and compound()
  - collectFees() → called by deposit() and withdraw()
If the Uniswap V3 pool has insufficient observation cardinality (few initialized slots with zeros interspersed), every call to deposit(), withdraw(), rebalance(), and compound() will revert. A pool with observation cardinality of 1 (the minimum, which is the default before expansion) will have only index 0 initialized. When checkPoolActivity loops with i from 1 to observationCardinality, it accesses index (cardinality + currentIndex - i) % cardinality. For cardinality=1, i=1, this is index 0 (initialized). This edge case may be safe, but for pools with expanded-but-sparse cardinality, intermediate uninitialized observations cause permanent DoS of the entire vault.

In rebalance() (line 207-213), the current tick is read from slot0() and used to set both main and secondary position ticks. Per the OracleHunter methodology: slot0.tick is floor(log1.0001(price)), and when price moves leftward past a tick boundary, Uniswap stores currentTick - 1 (the tick BELOW the current price) rather than the actual tick. This means _setMainTicks(tick) and _setSecondaryPositionsTicks(tick) can center positions one tick off from the true price. Since main position width is 4 * tickSpacing (= 240 ticks for the WBTC/USDC 0.3% pool with tickSpacing=60), being off by 1 tick (or even by tickSpacing) causes an asymmetric range: the position is not truly centered on the current price. This means liquidity is not optimally deployed, and users experience suboptimal fee capture. Combined with the TWAP-based protection allowing 200 ticks of deviation, the actual position center can be up to 201 ticks away from the TWAP center.

`changePositionWidth` has no access control modifier. Any caller can invoke it. The function sets `positionWidth` and then calls `rebalance()` which has `onlyRebalancer`. However the state mutation `positionWidth = _newWidth` occurs BEFORE the call to `rebalance()`. Because the entire transaction reverts if the caller is not the rebalancer (due to `rebalance()`'s `onlyRebalancer` check), a non-rebalancer cannot persist the change. BUT the rebalancer can call `changePositionWidth` directly — bypassing the `onlyOwner` protection that all other parameter-setter functions have. The rebalancer (a less-trusted role) can arbitrarily change `positionWidth`, which governs the width of the main liquidity position and directly affects capital efficiency, impermanent loss exposure, and the tick range of deployed liquidity.

`collectFees()` is a `public` function with no access control modifier. Any external caller — including attackers — can trigger fee collection at will. This function: (1) collects accumulated Uniswap fees from all positions, (2) computes and immediately transfers `protocolFee` percentage to `feeRecipient`, (3) if an ongoing vesting position exists, withdraws the vested portion. An attacker can sandwich the fee collection (call it right before or after large swaps) to influence when and how fees are recognized, or grief the protocol by collecting at suboptimal times. More critically, it can be used to force premature vesting position withdrawal at attacker-chosen timestamps.

In `collectFees()`, when collecting fees for the vesting position, the code uses `vestPosition.tickLower` for the lower tick but `mainPosition.tickUpper` for the upper tick instead of `vestPosition.tickUpper`. Since the vesting position's ticks are set to `mainPosition.tickLower` and `mainPosition.tickUpper` at creation time (lines 433-434 in `addVestingPosition`), this may coincidentally work if the main position hasn't changed. HOWEVER, after a rebalance, `mainPosition.tickUpper` changes but `vestPosition.tickUpper` retains the old value. After a rebalance, `collectFees` will call `burn(vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper_NEW, 0)` on the WRONG position — a position that either doesn't exist or is a different position belonging to this contract. This causes incorrect fee collection and can corrupt position accounting.

In `_withdrawPartOfVestingPosition()`, the liquidity calculation for a partial withdrawal uses `(vp.endTs - vp.startTs)` as the denominator (total vesting duration) but `(lastValid - vp.lastUpdate)` as the numerator (time elapsed since last update). This is WRONG: the denominator should reflect the REMAINING duration from the start of the vesting period, not the total duration. As a result, each partial call withdraws LESS than the correctly vested amount (the denominator is always the full original duration rather than decaying as vesting progresses). This effectively means vesting is stretched beyond the intended `endTs`, because later calls cover smaller fractions than expected. While not a direct access control bypass, this is a core accounting invariant: vested liquidity by time T should equal `initialLiquidity * (T - startTs) / (endTs - startTs)`, but repeated partial calls give a different (lower) result.

`collectFees()` is public and calls `_withdrawPartOfVestingPosition()` when `ongoingVestingPosition` is true. This means any external caller can force-advance the vesting position's `lastUpdate` timestamp. By repeatedly calling `collectFees`, an attacker can fragment the vesting releases into many small calls, each of which charges a gas overhead but causes the vesting position to advance `lastUpdate`. Combined with the accounting bug in ACCESS-04, an attacker could maximize the divergence between intended and actual vesting release amounts by calling `collectFees` at high frequency. Additionally, an attacker can call `collectFees` immediately before a large deposit to force a vesting unlock that increases `balances()`, inflating the share price and diluting incoming depositors.

The `Strategy` constructor sets initial positions by reading the current pool tick from `slot0()` (spot price, not TWAP). This means if a constructor is called when the pool's spot price is significantly different from the TWAP — for example during a sandwich attack on deployment — the initial main and secondary positions will be set to manipulated ticks. Furthermore, `_setSecondaryPositionsTicks` in the constructor is called with `bal0 = 0` and `bal1 = 0` (no funds yet), so `bal0in1 = 0 < bal1 = 0` is false and the secondary position incorrectly branches to the else case (bal0in1 >= bal1 when both are 0), always setting secondary to the upper-sided position regardless of actual token distribution. The first rebalance corrects this, but during initial deposits before the first rebalance, the secondary position tick is set based on this degenerate comparison.

`changePositionWidth` has no `onlyOwner` modifier, unlike ALL other parameter-setting functions in the contract (`setTwap`, `setTickTwapDeviation`, `setMaxObservationDeviation`, `setRebalanceInterval`, `setProtocolFee`, `changeFeeRecipient`, `changeRebalancer` all use `onlyOwner`). The comment says "Access control is performed within rebalance" but this is incorrect — `rebalance()` only has `onlyRebalancer`, not `onlyOwner`. This means the REBALANCER (a different, less-trusted role than the owner) can call `changePositionWidth` and successfully change `positionWidth` along with triggering a rebalance. This breaks the intended separation between the owner role (controls parameters) and rebalancer role (controls timing of rebalances/compounds). A malicious or compromised rebalancer can set extremely narrow (single tick-spacing) positions to concentrate risk, or extremely wide positions to reduce fee earnings.

pullFunds does not decrement reserve.underlyingBalance. When the leverager calls pullFunds(asset, amount), real ERC20 tokens leave the yToken contract via transferUnderlyingTo, but reserve.underlyingBalance is never decremented. This inflates the recorded available liquidity permanently until pushFunds is called. availableLiquidity() returns reserve.underlyingBalance, so every downstream calculation (exchange rate, utilization rate, capacity checks) operates on a phantom balance. A malicious or buggy leverager that calls pullFunds and omits pushFunds leaves the pool in a state where depositors see inflated NAV but actual redeems will revert because the yToken contract has insufficient ERC20 balance for the inflated amount.

pushFunds does not increment reserve.underlyingBalance. The mirror of AH-LP-001. When the leverager calls pushFunds(asset, amount) to return tokens to the yToken contract, the ERC20 tokens arrive but reserve.underlyingBalance is never incremented. This deflates the recorded available liquidity. The consequence is that after a legitimate pullFunds + pushFunds cycle, underlyingBalance ends up equal to what it was before (no net change), which is correct ONLY if pullFunds also didn't update it (they cancel out). However, when interacting with repay(), borrow(), or deposit() in between, the intermediate phantom state causes incorrect interest rate calculations and incorrect exchange rates. More critically: pushFunds alone (without prior pullFunds) INCREASES the real ERC20 balance in yToken but does NOT increase underlyingBalance. This means depositing tokens for free into the yToken, which increases lenders' actual claim without affecting the accounting NAV — effectively a donation that benefits existing yToken holders but breaks the invariant that underlyingBalance == yToken ERC20 balance (when no borrows are outstanding).

The first-deposit anti-inflation guard is checked AFTER the exchange rate is computed and AFTER the mint amount is calculated, using the TOTAL supply check. A race condition exists: if totalSupply() == MINIMUM_YTOKEN_AMOUNT (i.e., exactly the dead address amount), the check `if (IyToken(reserve.yTokenAddress).totalSupply() == 0)` evaluates to false and the MINIMUM_YTOKEN_AMOUNT is NOT burned from the second deposit's yTokenAmount. But more critically, the guard uses `>` (strict), so a depositor receiving exactly MINIMUM_YTOKEN_AMOUNT yTokens has their deposit silently reverted with "deposit is dust amount", while a deposit yielding MINIMUM_YTOKEN_AMOUNT + 1 succeeds but returns only 1 yToken to the first real depositor (MINIMUM_YTOKEN_AMOUNT burned). This 1-wei share is exploitable: attacker deposits minimum viable amount to get 1 yToken share, then watches for the next large depositor and front-runs with a donation to inflate the exchange rate, making the large depositor get 0 yTokens (they only get dust), while attacker redeems at the inflated rate.

The invariant that reserve.underlyingBalance equals the actual ERC20 balance of the yToken contract (adjusted for borrowed-out amounts) is broken by pullFunds and pushFunds. The accounting variable underlyingBalance is updated by deposit (+amount), redeem (-amount), borrow (-amount), and repay (+amount). But pullFunds and pushFunds move real tokens in/out without touching underlyingBalance. This means the critical liquidity check in _redeem:
  require(underlyingTokenAmount <= reserve.availableLiquidity())
uses a stale/wrong value after any pullFunds that is not matched by an exactly equal pushFunds. An attacker who controls the leverager role can exploit this to either: (a) Cause all redemptions to fail (DoS) by pulling funds and not pushing back. (b) Allow redemptions to pass the check but fail on actual transfer (same DoS outcome). (c) If pushFunds is called with MORE than pullFunds (net positive), underlyingBalance is
    deflated relative to reality, and the exchange rate is deflated, so depositing after
    a net-positive push gives MORE yTokens, which can later be redeemed for more value.

The borrowing rate is computed from utilizationRate which is computed from totalLiquidityAndBorrows(). The totalBorrows component uses latestBorrowingIndex() which compounds interest from lastUpdateTimestamp. An attacker who is the leverager can manipulate the utilization rate by calling borrow() to push utilization to 100%, then waiting for interest to accrue at the max rate (150% APR), then calling repay() to bring utilization back to 0% — all in a coordinated sequence over time. Since updateState() is only called at transaction time (not continuously), large time gaps allow disproportionate interest accrual. However the real exploit is: borrow() increments totalBorrows but decrements underlyingBalance. After borrow, the utilization rate jumps. If an attacker can flash-borrow (borrow + repay in same block), the interest rate recorded (currentBorrowingRate) between those two txs is at 100% utilization. The currentBorrowingRate is stored as-is. If another tx happens BEFORE repay (impossible in same block, but possible across blocks), the high rate accrues for longer. More critically: flash-borrowing (borrow in tx1, repay in tx2 same block but different call) does not accrue extra interest because lastUpdateTimestamp check prevents double-counting. The true risk is over multiple blocks with near-100% utilization.

The yToken-to-underlying exchange rate (yTokenToReserveExchangeRate) is:
  totalLiquidity * PRECISION / totalYTokens
where totalLiquidity = underlyingBalance + (borrowingIndex/borrowingIndex * totalBorrows). After any interest accrual, totalLiquidity increases (via borrowedLiquidity growing) while totalYTokens stays constant. This correctly increases the exchange rate for lenders — they earn interest. HOWEVER: the exchange rate monotonicity invariant can be broken if underlyingBalance is decremented more than it should be (e.g., via a borrow without proper accrual), or if a series of deposit + redeem cycles at different exchange rates creates rounding artifacts that reduce underlyingBalance below what it should be. Specifically: in _redeem, underlyingTokenAmount = yTokenToReserveExchangeRate() * yAssetAmount / PRECISION. This rounds DOWN. The user gets fewer tokens, but underlyingBalance is decremented by the rounded-down amount. Over many redeem cycles, the rounding accumulates in the protocol's favor. In _deposit, yTokenAmount = amount * reserveToYTokenExchangeRate() / PRECISION. This also rounds DOWN, so the user gets fewer yTokens. The asymmetry means the protocol consistently benefits from rounding, which is acceptable — but the exchange rate should be monotonically non-decreasing for lenders.

The repay() function caps amount at reserve.totalBorrows before decrementing:
  if (amount > reserve.totalBorrows) { amount = reserve.totalBorrows; }
This means if a leverager tries to repay more than owed, only totalBorrows is taken. However, this cap is applied AFTER updateState() but BEFORE the transfer. The actual transfer amount is the capped value. The accounting update is:
  reserve.totalBorrows -= amount;  (amount = capped value)
  reserve.underlyingBalance += amount;
This is correct. BUT: there is a subtle issue with interest accrual in updateState() vs what the leverager tracks. The Leverager tracks borrowedAmount at position open time. When the Leverager computes how much to repay, it uses getCurrentBorrowingIndex() to scale the original borrow. If the Leverager passes a slightly under-calculated amount (due to rounding in index calculation), totalBorrows never reaches 0. The residual dust in totalBorrows continues to accrue interest forever, and the utilization rate is never truly 0. This is a known acknowledged comment in the code:
  "@dev Due to rounding down, totalBorrows might be a few wei less than what the Leverager tries to repay."
The comment acknowledges the rounding direction is favorable to the protocol (Leverager overpays or exact), but in practice the Leverager might underpay due to index rounding.

The deposit function includes a capacity check via checkCapacity() which verifies:
  totalLiquidity + depositAmount <= reserveCapacity
Since reserveCapacity is initialized to type(uint256).max and can only be set by the owner, this check is initially benign. However, after interest accrual (via updateState()), the totalLiquidity value returned by totalLiquidityAndBorrows() includes accrued interest on borrows. This means that even with reserveCapacity = type(uint256).max, an extreme interest accrual scenario could theoretically cause totalLiquidity to approach type(uint256).max, making deposits fail. In practice, with 150% max APR and realistic amounts this takes centuries. The real DoS vector is that the owner can set reserveCapacity to 0 (or any value below current totalLiquidity), which would permanently brick all new deposits. Since this is an admin action, it's a centralization risk rather than an exploit. More relevant: the checkCapacity() check in `_deposit` reads `totalLiquidityAndBorrows()` which calls `borrowedLiquidity()` which calls `latestBorrowingIndex()`. Since `updateState()` was already called, `lastUpdateTimestamp == block.timestamp`, so `latestBorrowingIndex()` returns the already-updated `reserve.borrowingIndex`. This double-update does not occur, which is correct. No bug here for the DoS angle, but confirming the flow.

`price()` returns the manipulable Uniswap V3 spot sqrtPriceX96 and is used in `_setSecondaryPositionsTicks()` to decide which side (token0-only or token1-only) the secondary position goes on. An attacker can flash-loan/sandwich to make the spot price appear to favour one side, causing the secondary position to be placed on the wrong side immediately after a rebalance. Because `_requirePriceWithinRange()` only checks that spot is within `tickTwapDeviation` of TWAP (default 200 ticks ≈ 2%), and `price()` is called AFTER the range check, the attacker has up to 200 ticks of room to tilt the spot price and flip the secondary-position side decision while still passing the guard.

In `collectFees()`, when there is an ongoing vesting position, the code calls `collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper)` (line 167) instead of `collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, vestPosition.tickUpper)`. It uses `mainPosition.tickUpper` as the upper tick of the vesting position. These are equal right after `addVestingPosition` (which copies ticks from mainPosition), but after a rebalance the main position ticks change while the vesting position ticks do not. After the first rebalance following `addVestingPosition`, fee collection for the vesting position will reference a position that does not exist in the pool (wrong tick pair), causing the burn+collect call to either revert or silently collect from the wrong position, permanently locking vesting position fees.

The TWAP window defaults to 300 seconds (5 minutes) and the owner can set it as low as 31 seconds (`setTwap` requires only `_twap > 30`). A 5-minute TWAP on a low-liquidity pool can be manipulated for the full window duration using a sustained price push, at a cost proportional to pool depth. For the WBTC/USDC 0.3% pool the liquidity depth is substantial, but if the owner lowers the window to 31 seconds, manipulation becomes trivially cheap. In either case, once the TWAP is manipulated, `_requirePriceWithinRange()` passes at the manipulated price and all subsequent oracle-dependent logic (tick selection, liquidity split) operates on wrong data.

`changePositionWidth()` has no access-control modifier. Any external caller can invoke it with any `_newWidth` that satisfies the divisibility requirement, which then calls `rebalance()`. Since `rebalance()` checks `block.timestamp - lastRebalance >= rebalanceInterval`, an unauthorized caller cannot force a rebalance before the interval elapses. However, once the interval elapses, ANY address can call `changePositionWidth()` to set an arbitrary position width and trigger a rebalance — including setting an extremely narrow (e.g., 2 * tickSpacing) or extremely wide (unbounded) position width that is harmful to depositors. An attacker can front-run the legitimate rebalancer, rebalancing with a width chosen to maximise their MEV extraction.

`checkPoolActivity()` iterates pool observations and returns `false` (price out of range) if it cannot reach an observation older than `twap` seconds ago. If the pool has low observation cardinality (few observations recorded), the loop exhausts all observations without reaching `lookAgo` and returns `false`, causing `_requirePriceWithinRange()` to revert. This is a DOS vector: on a fresh pool or after pool reinitialization, legitimate rebalances and compounds are permanently blocked. Additionally, the loop uses `observationCardinality` (not `observationCardinalityNext`) which means newly grown cardinality is not considered, potentially reading uninitialized slots.

In `rebalance()` (line 207), `slot0()` is called once and returns both `sqrtPriceX96` and `tick`. The `tick` is used in `_setMainTicks()` and `_setSecondaryPositionsTicks()`, while `sqrtPriceX96` is passed to `_addLiquidityToMainPosition()` and `_addLiquidityToSecondaryPosition()`. Per Uniswap V3 spec, `slot0.tick` is `floor(log_1.0001(sqrtPrice^2))`, meaning when the price crosses a tick boundary leftward, `slot0.tick` stores `currentTick - 1` while sqrtPriceX96 reflects the exact price. Using `tick` (possibly off by 1) to compute position boundaries and `sqrtPriceX96` to compute liquidity creates an asymmetry: the range is centered on `tick` (which may be 1 below the true price), so the main position might be slightly asymmetric, and the secondary position side may be decided based on a stale tick.

pullFunds() does not decrease reserve.underlyingBalance. After the leverager calls pullFunds(asset, X), the yToken's actual ERC20 balance decreases by X, but reserve.underlyingBalance is unchanged. All subsequent calls to availableLiquidity(), totalLiquidityAndBorrows(), utilizationRate(), reserveToYTokenExchangeRate(), and yTokenToReserveExchangeRate() now return inflated values (they include X tokens that no longer physically exist in the yToken contract). A deposit made between pullFunds and pushFunds mints fewer yTokens than correct (rate is computed against phantom liquidity), effectively stealing yield from that depositor. Similarly, checkCapacity passes even when the pool is effectively full, enabling deposits that exceed the real capacity.

Because pullFunds does not update underlyingBalance, the yToken-to-reserve exchange rate (yTokenToReserveExchangeRate) is artificially inflated while funds are pulled. A user who redeems yTokens during this window receives more underlying tokens than their fair share, because the rate formula returns totalLiquidity/totalYTokens and totalLiquidity is overstated. This lets an attacker drain liquidity that rightfully belongs to other depositors if the leverager contract has a publicly callable pullFunds-equivalent path, or if the leverager itself is exploited.

The borrowing rate is computed from utilizationRate(), which uses totalLiquidityAndBorrows(). totalLiquidityAndBorrows() sums availableLiquidity() (= underlyingBalance) and borrowedLiquidity(). After pullFunds() without updating underlyingBalance, the utilization rate is artificially depressed: the denominator (total liquidity) is overstated while borrows are unchanged. This causes currentBorrowingRate to be set too low in updateInterestRates(), under-accruing interest for lenders. The stored currentBorrowingRate persists until the next updateState() call, meaning every block between pullFunds and pushFunds uses a wrong rate.

reserve.underlyingBalance can become permanently desynchronized from the actual token balance held by the yToken contract if pushFunds is called with an amount different from what pullFunds pulled, or if tokens are sent directly to the yToken contract (donation). There is no check in pushFunds or pullFunds enforcing that the balance is restored exactly. The leverager can push more than it pulled (increasing underlyingBalance beyond reality via the += in repay... wait — pushFunds has no += either). Actually, pushFunds does safeTransferFrom but does NOT update underlyingBalance at all. So any pushFunds call increases the real yToken token balance without increasing underlyingBalance, making underlyingBalance UNDERSTATE reality after pushFunds, and the effect compounds with time.

In _updateIndexes (ReserveLogic.sol), newTotalBorrows is computed as newBorrowingIndex * reserve.totalBorrows / reserve.borrowingIndex. This is a truncating integer division. Each call to updateState() permanently loses the fractional wei of accrued interest. Over many compounding periods, the accumulated rounding error means lenders receive systematically less interest than the rate implies. This is a well-known precision loss in lending protocols, but the magnitude here is bounded per-block so it is a low-severity informational finding unless block intervals are very short (e.g., L2 with sub-second blocks).

latestBorrowingIndex() (ReserveLogic.sol line 109-118) returns a freshly computed index using reserve.currentBorrowingRate — the rate stored at the LAST updateInterestRates() call. Between two updateState() calls, currentBorrowingRate is fixed even though the actual utilization rate may have changed dramatically (e.g., large borrow or repay happened but updateState was already called in that block). However, the critical issue is that currentBorrowingRate is set inside updateInterestRates() which is called AFTER state changes in deposit/redeem/borrow/repay. When borrow() is called: (1) updateState uses the OLD rate to accrue, (2) totalBorrows increases, (3) updateInterestRates sets NEW higher rate. The new rate applies starting from the CURRENT timestamp. So the accrual at the new (higher) rate starts immediately. This is correct behavior. No oracle staleness bug here in the interest path. BUT: the currentBorrowingRate used in latestBorrowingIndex is the rate stored AFTER the last state-changing tx. If no state-changing tx happens for a long time (e.g., 7 days), currentBorrowingRate remains the last-set value. A large borrow made in that period would cause: updateState accrues 7 days at the old (low) rate, then sets the new high rate. The interest gap is: (high_rate - low_rate) * 7_days.
