(b) it was removed but the modifier was left behind.

If (a), there may be missing admin functionality (e.g., emergency fund recovery).

All other admin/provider functions in Oracle.sol have both nonReentrant
and whenNotPaused modifiers. But pause() (line 460) and unpause() (line 465)
only have onlyRole(DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE) — missing nonReentrant.

While reentrancy on pause/unpause is extremely unlikely (they don't make
external calls), this is a modifier inconsistency.

Oracle.createPool() (line 359) is callable by PROVIDER_ROLE. It passes
feePaidBy and feeAmount to factory.createPool(), which does:
usdcAddress.transferFrom(feePaidBy, feeRequestor, feeAmount).

The feeRequestor is msg.sender (the provider, line 375).
The feePaidBy is an arbitrary address provided by the provider.

A malicious provider can set feePaidBy = victim_address (any address that
has approved USDC to the factory), feeAmount = their full allowance, and
extract USDC from any user who has approved the factory contract.

This is the severe consequence of VAR-AC-02. The removeProvider() function
has require(numProviders > 1) to prevent removing the last provider.
revokeRole() override also has this check. But renounceRole() bypasses both.

Scenario: Single provider system (numProviders = 1). The provider calls
renounceRole(PROVIDER_ROLE, self). The role is removed but numProviders
stays at 1. Now there are ZERO providers but numProviders says 1.

Result: No one can call any PROVIDER_ROLE function. All fund movements
(deposits, withdrawals, settlements, fee collection) are permanently frozen
until admin manually calls addProvider().

Oracle.grantRole() calls super.grantRole() FIRST (line 439), which grants the role, then checks hasRole on line 442. Since super already granted it, hasRole returns true and the require("Provider already added") ALWAYS reverts. This means grantRole() for PROVIDER_ROLE is permanently broken — only addProvider() works. If admin code or external tooling calls the standard AccessControl.grantRole() (which is the OpenZeppelin standard path), it will always revert. This is a logic bug but may be Low since addProvider() exists as an alternative.

Oracle.createPool writes to BOTH Oracle.pools[poolUuid] (line 379) AND Factory.getPool[poolUuid] (via Factory.createPool, line 96). These are the ONLY write paths for both mappings. Functions use different lookups: withdrawUSDC/depositUSDC/atomicDeposit use Oracle.getPool() (Oracle.pools), while collectFees/batchAtomicDeposit/processTreasuryManagement* use factory.getPool(). If setSettlementPoolFactory() is called (line 392-398) to point to a NEW factory, the new factory has EMPTY getPool mappings. All functions using factory.getPool() would fail, while functions using Oracle.pools would still work. This creates an inconsistent state where some operations work and others don't.

In SettlementPool.batchDepositUSDCAtomic (line 122-157), the loop iterates over items and for EACH item where creatorPartyAmountRequested > 0, it calls _depositUSDCOnBehalf with creatorPartyAmountRequested (line 131-136). This means the creator is charged creatorPartyAmountRequested ONCE PER ITEM, not once total. If there are 10 items, the creator pays 10x. The first item uses parentQuoteUuid for replay protection, but after that, transferUuid is reset to 0 (line 140), so items 2-10 have no replay protection AND each pulls the full creatorPartyAmountRequested from the creator.

Oracle.transferFromOLPToPool (line 267-285) accepts both poolUuid and poolAddress as parameters but NEVER validates that poolAddress actually corresponds to poolUuid. The poolAddress is used for the actual USDC transfer (line 282), while poolUuid is only used in the event emission (line 284). A provider could pass a mismatched poolAddress (any address, including their own) and the USDC would be sent there, while the event logs a different poolUuid.
Descripción corta del invariante

Oracle.grantRole() override for PROVIDER_ROLE always reverts due to ordering bug. Line 439 calls super.grantRole() FIRST (which grants the role via _grantRole internally), then line 442 checks require(!hasRole(PROVIDER_ROLE, account)) — but the role is ALREADY granted, so hasRole returns true, !hasRole is false, and the require reverts. This means grantRole(PROVIDER_ROLE, addr) is a dead code path. Only addProvider() works (it calls _grantRole directly, bypassing the override). While the immediate impact is that grantRole reverts (so no state change occurs), the real concern is that the developer INTENDED this to keep numProviders in sync — the broken logic reveals the counter is fragile and depends on all callers using addProvider/removeProvider exclusively. See ORC-W-02 for the actual exploit.

Oracle overrides grantRole and revokeRole to track numProviders, but does NOT override renounceRole(). OpenZeppelin's AccessControl.renounceRole() calls _revokeRole() directly, which bypasses the numProviders decrement in the revokeRole override. A provider can call renounceRole(PROVIDER_ROLE, self) to remove their own provider role WITHOUT decrementing numProviders. If the last provider does this: 1. numProviders remains 1 (stale) 2. Zero actual providers exist 3. All PROVIDER_ROLE functions (deposit, withdraw, createPool, etc.) are permanently
   inaccessible — no one has the role to call them
4. Admin can addProvider(newAddr) — numProviders goes to 2 (should be 1) 5. Now removeProvider has numProviders=2, so it can remove this provider — numProviders
   goes to 1, but there are again 0 real providers
6. The "Cannot remove the only provider" guard is permanently broken

Oracle.transferFromOLPToPool() (line 267-285) transfers USDC to a pool address via direct ERC20 transfer (usdc.transfer(poolAddress, amount)) WITHOUT calling any pool deposit function. The pool's internal accounting (transfers_processed mapping, events) is not updated. The USDC just lands in the pool's balance but is untracked. This means the pool's _totalBalance() (which reads balanceOf) includes these funds, but no deposit event was emitted and no transferUuid was recorded. If the pool uses internal balance tracking for anything, this creates an accounting discrepancy. Furthermore: the poolAddress parameter is passed directly by the provider — it does NOT validate that the address corresponds to the given poolUuid. A malicious provider could route OLP funds to any address.

Factory.setOracleAddress(newOracle) (line 103) updates the oracle reference. All existing pools derive their oracle via factory.oracle(). So changing the oracle immediately changes access control for ALL existing pools. The new oracle can call all onlyOracle functions on existing pools (withdraw, deposit, addOtherParty). The old oracle loses access instantly. Combined with Oracle.pools[] mapping: the OLD Oracle has pool addresses cached in its pools[] mapping, but calling getPool then operating on those pools will fail because the pools now check msg.sender against the NEW oracle. If the new oracle is malicious or misconfigured, it can drain all pools.

SettlementPoolFactory inherits Ownable but does NOT override renounceOwnership(). If the factory owner calls renounceOwnership(), the owner becomes address(0) permanently. Effects: (1) createPool requires msg.sender == owner() || msg.sender == address(oracle) — owner path dies, only oracle can create pools. (2) setOracleAddress is onlyOwner — permanently impossible to change oracle. If the current oracle becomes compromised or needs upgrade, there's no recovery path. (3) The SettlementPool.onlyFactoryOwner modifier checks factory.getOwner() — this returns address(0), so no address passes that check.

SettlementPool.sol line 11 imports forge-std console.sol: import {console} from "../lib/forge-std/src/console.sol"; This is a development/testing dependency that should NOT be in production code. While console.log calls are no-ops when deployed (they call a non-existent address), the import itself increases deployment bytecode size and signals code quality issues. The console.sol import may also cause compilation issues if forge-std is not present in the production build environment.

In Oracle.atomicDeposit() lines 298-308: when partyOneAmountRequested > 0 and partyTwoAmountRequested == 0, the function transfers USDC from partyOne to the pool. It checks atomic_deposits_processed[parentQuoteUuid] == false for replay protection. But line 305: if (parentQuoteUuid != 0) { atomic_deposits_processed[parentQuoteUuid] = true; } This means if parentQuoteUuid IS 0, the replay protection flag is NEVER set. A provider could call atomicDeposit with parentQuoteUuid=0 multiple times, each time pulling USDC from partyOne (as long as they have allowance and balance). Similarly in _depositUSDCOnBehalf (SettlementPool line 106-108): transfers_processed is only set when transferUuid != 0. With transferUuid=0, the same deposit can be replayed.

In SettlementPool.batchDepositUSDCAtomic() (line 122-157), the function loops over items[] and for EACH item, if creatorPartyAmountRequested > 0, it deposits that amount from the creator. This means if there are N items, the creator deposits creatorPartyAmountRequested * N total USDC (not creatorPartyAmountRequested once).
Looking at line 130-141: for each iteration, if creatorPartyAmountRequested > 0, it calls _depositUSDCOnBehalf(creatorPartyAddress, creatorPartyAmountRequested, transferUuid, false).
BUT: transferUuid = items[i].parentQuoteUuid for each item. After the first deposit, transferUuid is set to 0 (line 140). For the SECOND item, transferUuid = items[1].parentQuoteUuid (NOT 0 — it's re-assigned on line 129). So each item gets its OWN parentQuoteUuid as the transferUuid.
Actually re-reading: the transferUuid=0 reset on line 140 is LOCAL to each loop iteration. Line 129 assigns transferUuid = items[i].parentQuoteUuid at the START of each iteration. So the reset on line 140 only affects the SAME iteration's second deposit (the other party).
This means: for N items in the batch, the creator deposits creatorPartyAmountRequested N times (once per item). The transfers_processed check uses each item's parentQuoteUuid, so they're all unique. The creator loses N * creatorPartyAmountRequested USDC.
This may be INTENTIONAL (batch = multiple atomic deposits) or a bug (creator amount should be deposited once for the whole batch, not per-item).

Oracle.pause() (line 460) pauses all provider operations. While paused: depositUSDC, withdrawUSDC, createPool, atomicDeposit, collectFees ALL revert (whenNotPaused modifier). However, SettlementPool functions only check onlyOracle (msg.sender == oracle address). The pause is on the ORACLE, not on the pools. If the admin pauses the oracle, all funds in pools are trapped — no one can withdraw. The parties themselves can still call depositUSDC(amount, transferUuid) directly on the pool (onlyParties modifier), but there is NO party-callable withdrawal function. ALL withdrawal paths go through the Oracle.
So: pause = all pool funds frozen. If admin key is lost while paused, funds are permanently frozen.

_removeLiquidity usa checkApproval(params.from, msgSender()) donde msgSender() es _getLocker() (el caller original de modifyLiquidities). Verificar que NO existe un path donde el locker se fija a una dirección y luego otro usuario puede ejecutar acciones con ese locker como identidad. En particular, modifyLiquiditiesWithoutLock NO adquiere vault lock — ¿podría un actor malicioso usar esto para burn tokens de otro usuario?

multicall usa delegatecall a sí mismo — permite batch de llamadas en una sola tx. Dentro de delegatecall, msg.sender se preserva. Pero el locker se almacena en transient storage (tstore/tload). Si multicall llama modifyLiquidities y luego otra función, el locker se resetea a address(0) al final de modifyLiquidities (isNotLocked modifier limpia). ¿Es posible que multicall permita re-entrada al combinar modifyLiquidities con permit o sweep de manera que el locker context se corrompa?

BinFungibleToken.batchTransferFrom tiene onlyIfVaultUnlocked modifier — las transferencias ERC1155 solo funcionan cuando el vault NO tiene un locker activo (vault.getLocker() == address(0)). Esto impide transferencias de LP tokens DURANTE operaciones de pool. Pero approveForAll NO tiene este modifier — las aprobaciones se pueden dar en cualquier momento. Verificar que no hay un race condition donde alguien aprovecha el timing de lock/unlock.

La función _pay usa permit2.transferFrom(payer, vault, amount, token) cuando payer != address(this). El payer se determina por _mapPayer(payerIsUser) donde payerIsUser viene de los calldata params. Si un atacante construye calldata con payerIsUser=true, el payer será msgSender() = _getLocker() = msg.sender del atacante mismo. Verificar que NO hay un path donde payerIsUser=true pero permit2 transfiere de un payer diferente al locker.

TAKE action permite enviar tokens a un recipient arbitrario (no necesariamente el caller). Si un usuario tiene crédito positivo en el vault (delta > 0), puede dirigir los tokens a CUALQUIER dirección via el param recipient. Verificar que un atacante NO puede take los créditos que pertenecen a otra operación del mismo contrato.
idSlippage check has underflow risk when activeIdDesired < idSlippage
ERC1155 LP token totalSupply conservation: sum of all balances must equal totalSupply for every tokenId
initializePool silently swallows all errors — pool can appear initialized when it's not
removeLiquidity burns ERC1155 tokens but never cleans up _positions mapping — stale position metadata persists

Oracle (PROVIDER_ROLE) can drain entire pool balance via withdrawFees() with arbitrary requestor and arbitrary amountRequested — no check that requestor is a pool party, no cap on amount relative to fees actually owed. The PROVIDER_ROLE trust status is UNCLEAR in Immunefi scope. If a provider key is compromised or a malicious provider is added, they can steal all USDC from every pool.

Oracle (PROVIDER_ROLE) can withdraw USDC to ANY address via withdrawUSDC/withdrawUSDCNoEvent, including addresses that are NOT parties of the pool. The _withdrawUSDCOnBehalf check requires requestor to be creatorAddress or otherAddresses, BUT the Oracle.processTreasuryManagementWithdrawals() passes an arbitrary `requestor` parameter controlled by the PROVIDER_ROLE caller. If provider specifies a requestor that IS a pool party, funds go to that party regardless of whether the party requested the withdrawal. Provider can forcibly move funds between parties.

USDC blocklist can permanently freeze pool funds. USDC has a blocklist — if either the pool address or a party address gets blocklisted, all transfers involving that address will revert. Since SettlementPool uses try/catch for transfers, a blocklisted requestor in withdrawFees causes the catch block to revert the entire transaction. In batchDepositUSDCAtomic, if the creatorPartyAddress is blocklisted, ALL deposits in the batch fail (entire tx reverts since _depositUSDCOnBehalf reverts in catch). No fallback mechanism exists.

Factory owner can swap Oracle address at any time via setOracleAddress(), instantly changing who has full control over all settlement pools. The SettlementPool resolves oracle dynamically via _oracle() -> factory.oracle(). A new oracle address gains immediate power to: withdraw all funds, add parties, deposit on behalf of anyone. There is no timelock or migration mechanism.

transferUuid=0 bypass in _depositUSDCOnBehalf allows duplicate deposits to be processed. When transferUuid is 0, the duplicate check (transfers_processed[transferUuid]) is evaluated against key 0, but the result is never stored (line 106: `if (transferUuid != 0)`). In batchDepositUSDCAtomic and depositUSDCAtomic, after the first deposit in an atomic pair, transferUuid is intentionally reset to 0 for the second deposit. This means the second deposit has NO replay protection at all. A malicious oracle could replay the same atomic deposit multiple times by using different parentQuoteUuids for the first leg.

No mechanism to remove a party from a pool. addOtherParty() exists but there is no removeOtherParty(). Once an address is added as a party, it permanently has depositUSDC access via onlyParties modifier. If a party's key is compromised, they can still deposit (potentially griefing with dust deposits to consume transferUuids). More critically, if the compromised party address is used in oracle-mediated withdrawals, there's no way to revoke their party status.

Oracle.grantRole() for PROVIDER_ROLE has a logic bug — the require(!hasRole) check on L442 runs AFTER super.grantRole() on L439 has already granted the role. The require will always revert because hasRole is now true. This means grantRole(PROVIDER_ROLE, account) always reverts for new providers, but addProvider() still works. However, if admin uses the standard AccessControl.grantRole interface (e.g., from a multisig or governance contract that calls grantRole directly), it will always fail for PROVIDER_ROLE. The numProviders counter becomes desynchronized if someone uses renounceRole() (inherited from AccessControl, not overridden).

batchDepositUSDCAtomic charges creatorPartyAmountRequested ONCE PER ITEM in the batch loop, but the event emits it as a single amount — Oracle/off-chain may believe only one deposit of creatorPartyAmountRequested was taken, while N*creatorPartyAmountRequested was actually transferred from the creator wallet. This is a logic discrepancy: the loop calls _depositUSDCOnBehalf for creatorPartyAmountRequested on EVERY iteration, draining the creator N times.

transferUuid=0 bypasses transfers_processed replay protection in _depositUSDCOnBehalf. When transferUuid is 0, the function skips both the duplicate check (line 97 checks transfers_processed[0] which is shared/global) AND skips marking it as processed (line 106-107: if transferUuid != 0). This means deposits with transferUuid=0 have NO replay protection whatsoever.

withdrawFees has no balance check — Oracle can withdraw more USDC than the pool holds, causing subsequent legitimate withdrawals to fail (griefing/fund theft). The function relies on USDC.transfer reverting on insufficient balance, but the try/catch catches this and reverts with a generic message. More critically, there is no accounting: the pool has no internal tracking of how much belongs to fees vs party deposits, so the Oracle can extract party funds as "fees".

depositUSDCAtomic emits DepositedAtomic event and returns early when partyOneAmountRequested > 0 && partyTwoAmountRequested == 0, WITHOUT actually performing any deposit or transfer. The comment says "we already completed the single party transfer in the calling function" — this refers to Oracle.atomicDeposit which does a direct transferFrom to the pool address. But crucially, this path SKIPS the transfers_processed[parentQuoteUuid] check in _depositUSDCOnBehalf, relying instead on atomic_deposits_processed in Oracle. If the Oracle path is called directly (not through Oracle.atomicDeposit), the event is emitted without any transfer happening, creating a phantom deposit event.

Oracle.grantRole override has an inverted check: it calls super.grantRole FIRST (which grants the role), then checks require(!hasRole(PROVIDER_ROLE, account)) — but by this point hasRole returns TRUE because super.grantRole already granted it. This means grantRole for PROVIDER_ROLE ALWAYS reverts, making it impossible to add providers via the standard AccessControl grantRole path.

renounceRole is inherited from AccessControl and NOT overridden in Oracle. A provider can call renounceRole(PROVIDER_ROLE, self) to remove their own role WITHOUT decrementing numProviders. This desyncs the counter. After enough renouncements, numProviders could be >1 while only 1 (or 0) real providers exist. The removeProvider function requires numProviders > 1, so with a desynced counter, even the last real provider could be removed, bricking the Oracle.

Si srcToken == destToken, el balance-before-after pattern produce resultados incorrectos. srcInitial y destInitial son el MISMO balance. Después del swap (que en realidad no cambia nada si Augustus no hace nada útil), srcFinal == destFinal. Entonces srcAmount = srcInitial - srcFinal y destAmount = destFinal - destInitial. Si Augustus toma N tokens y devuelve M tokens del MISMO tipo: srcFinal = destFinal = srcInitial - N + M. Entonces srcAmount = N - M (si N>M) y destAmount = M - N (si M>N). Pero si N>M, destAmount underflows (Solidity 0.8 reverts). Si M>N, srcAmount underflows. Uno de los dos SIEMPRE hace underflow si N != M, así que el swap revierte. Si N == M, srcAmount = 0, destAmount = 0, y minDestAmount != 0 check falla. Resultado: srcToken == destToken SIEMPRE revierte. Esto no es un bug per se (no hay pérdida de fondos), pero es un DoS path si alguien construye un bundle con srcToken == destToken.

sell() y buy() son funciones external SIN el modifier onlyBundler3. Solo swap() (internal) tiene onlyBundler3. Esto significa que sell() y buy() pueden ser llamadas por CUALQUIERA directamente en el adapter. Sin embargo, sell() y buy() llaman a swap() que SÍ tiene onlyBundler3, así que en la práctica SOLO Bundler3 puede llamar exitosamente. PERO el finding de Solodit referenciado ("Lack of onlyBundler modifier inside functions of ParaswapAdapter adapter allows stealing funds") sugiere que hubo/hay un vector. Analizar: ¿puede sell() hacer algo ANTES de llegar a swap()? Sí: sell() con sellEntireBalance=true llama updateAmounts() que modifica callData en MEMORY. Pero callData es un parámetro memory local. No hay side effects observables antes de swap(). Conclusión: el finding de Solodit fue válido para una versión anterior donde sell/buy hacían algo más antes del swap internal, o es un finding de defensa en profundidad.

modifyLiquiditiesWithoutLock has NO deadline check, unlike modifyLiquidities. A transaction calling modifyLiquiditiesWithoutLock can be held in the mempool indefinitely and executed at an arbitrarily later time when pool conditions (price, liquidity, fees) have changed drastically. This is especially dangerous for mint/increase actions where the user may add liquidity at a very different price than intended, or for decrease/burn where the returned amounts reflect stale expectations.

_sweep transfers the entire contract balance of a currency to a specified recipient with no access control beyond being part of a modifyLiquidities action batch. Any caller can sweep any tokens sitting in the contract. If tokens are accidentally sent to the contract (direct transfer, not via the action system), any user can sweep them.

transferFrom is overridden (line 488-491) to auto-unsubscribe when a position NFT is transferred, but ONLY calls unsubscribe via the internal _unsubscribe (not the external unsubscribe which requires onlyIfApproved). The unsubscribe uses try/catch for notifyUnsubscribe, so a malicious subscriber cannot block the transfer. However, the onlyIfVaultUnlocked modifier IS applied to transferFrom. This means position NFTs CANNOT be transferred while the vault is locked (during a vault.lock callback). This could block legitimate operations where a composing contract needs to transfer a position NFT as part of an atomic operation within a vault lock.

Oracle.grantRole() for PROVIDER_ROLE has a dead-code duplicate check. Line 442: require(!hasRole(PROVIDER_ROLE, account), ...) executes AFTER super.grantRole() on line 439 which already granted the role. So the require on L442 will ALWAYS revert if the account didn't already have the role (because super.grantRole just granted it, so hasRole returns true), and will never revert if the account already had the role (because super.grantRole is a no-op for existing holders, hasRole returns true, and the require reverts).
Wait — re-analyzing: super.grantRole() calls _grantRole() which sets the role. So after super.grantRole(PROVIDER_ROLE, account): - If account DID NOT have role before: now has it → hasRole = true → !hasRole = false → REVERTS - If account DID have role before: still has it → hasRole = true → !hasRole = false → REVERTS
This means grantRole(PROVIDER_ROLE, ...) ALWAYS REVERTS. numProviders can never be incremented via grantRole. The only way to add a provider is via addProvider() which uses _grantRole (internal, no override).
Impact: grantRole for PROVIDER_ROLE is permanently broken. Admin must use addProvider() instead. The OZ AccessControl grantRole path is dead code. This is a LOW severity design inconsistency — the intended path (addProvider) works correctly.

Oracle.revokeRole() for PROVIDER_ROLE: the logic is correct but the ordering is fragile. Lines 450-456: it checks hasRole and numProviders > 1 BEFORE calling super.revokeRole on L456. This is actually correct — the checks happen before the state change. However, note the asymmetry with grantRole (which is broken). revokeRole works correctly.
BUT: there's a subtle issue. If someone calls revokeRole for a non-PROVIDER_ROLE, it bypasses the PROVIDER_ROLE checks and goes straight to super.revokeRole. This is correct behavior. No bug here upon deeper analysis.

Oracle.transferFromOLPToPool (L267-285): Provider specifies poolAddress as a raw address parameter. There is NO validation that poolAddress is a legitimate pool created by the factory. The function: 1. Calls usdc.transferFrom(olpWallet, address(this), amount) — needs OLP approval 2. Calls usdc.transfer(poolAddress, amount) — sends to ANY address
If PROVIDER_ROLE is NOT trusted, a rogue provider can redirect OLP funds to any arbitrary address by setting poolAddress to their own wallet.
Contrast with other functions like withdrawUSDC which use getPool(poolUuid) to validate the pool address. transferFromOLPToPool bypasses this entirely.

Oracle.collectFees (L28-43): Calls pool.withdrawFees(msg.sender, amount, batchId). The requestor is hardcoded as msg.sender — i.e., the provider themselves. So fees are sent directly to the provider's address.
SettlementPool.withdrawFees (L247-260): NO check that requestor is a pool party. It just does usdc.transfer(requestor, amountRequested). Any amount can be withdrawn as "fees" as long as the pool has balance and batchId hasn't been processed.
If provider is NOT trusted: provider can drain ALL pool balances by calling collectFees with arbitrary amounts. The pool has no concept of "fee balance" vs "party balance" — it's just USDC balance.

SettlementPoolFactory.setOracleAddress (L103-106): Factory owner can change the oracle address at any time. ALL existing pools use factory.oracle() for their onlyOracle modifier (SettlementPool._oracle() at L82-84). So a new oracle instantly controls ALL existing pools' deposits, withdrawals, and fees.
This is a centralization risk. Factory owner is stated as trusted by Immunefi, so this is likely by design. But the trust chain is: factory owner → sets oracle → oracle controls all pool funds.

Oracle.addOtherParty (L382-390): Provider can add ANY address as a party to any pool. Once added, that address can: - Call depositUSDC directly (as onlyParties) - Receive withdrawals (passes _withdrawUSDCOnBehalf party check)
Combined with TB-04 (collectFees) or TB-06 (provider-controlled withdrawal): Provider adds their own address as otherParty → can now receive withdrawals from the pool as a "legitimate" party.
Alternatively: provider adds attacker-controlled address → attacker calls depositUSDC (with their own funds, which is harmless) → but now attacker is an authorized party for events/integrations.

Oracle.setSettlementPoolFactory (L392-398): Admin can change the factory. Oracle maintains its OWN pool mapping (mapping pools at L21) AND uses factory.getPool() for some functions. After factory change:
- Oracle.getPool(uuid) → uses Oracle.pools[uuid] (OLD pools still accessible) - Functions using factory.getPool(uuid) → uses NEW factory mapping (different pools)
Functions using Oracle.pools (via getPool): - withdrawUSDC (L258: getPool) - atomicDeposit (L296: getPool) - depositUSDC (L350: getPool)
Functions using factory.getPool: - collectFees (L103: factory.getPool) - processTreasuryManagementDeposits (L154: factory.getPool) - processTreasuryManagementWithdrawals (L203: factory.getPool) - batchAtomicDeposit (L330: factory.getPool) - addOtherParty (L386: factory.getPool)
After factory swap, the same poolUuid may resolve to DIFFERENT addresses depending on which function is called. This is a split-brain state.

_checkInfiClPositionManagerCall usa denylist en vez de allowlist: bloquea CL_INCREASE_LIQUIDITY (0x00), CL_DECREASE_LIQUIDITY (0x01) y CL_BURN_POSITION (0x03), pero NO bloquea CL_INCREASE_LIQUIDITY_FROM_DELTAS (0x04). El comentario dice "we only allow Actions.MINT" pero el código permite pasar 0x04 (increase from deltas). Si un usuario aprobó el UniversalRouter para su posición, un atacante puede usar CL_INCREASE_LIQUIDITY_FROM_DELTAS para alterar su posición inyectando liquidez con parámetros controlados por el atacante.

_checkInfiBinPositionManagerCall solo bloquea BIN_REMOVE_LIQUIDITY (0x1a) pero NO bloquea BIN_DONATE (0x20). El comentario dice "we only allow BIN_ADD_LIQUIDITY" pero BIN_DONATE pasa el check. Un atacante podría donar tokens a un bin pool usando fondos del router si hay tokens residuales.

_checkInfiClPositionManagerCall NO bloquea acciones de swap (CL_SWAP_EXACT_IN_SINGLE 0x06, CL_SWAP_EXACT_IN 0x07, CL_SWAP_EXACT_OUT_SINGLE 0x08, CL_SWAP_EXACT_OUT 0x09) ni acciones de settling/taking (SETTLE, TAKE, etc.). Aunque estas acciones son ejecutadas vía modifyLiquidities, pueden permitir a un atacante hacer swaps o settle/take con fondos del router, dado que INFI_CL_POSITION_CALL envía address(this).balance como value.

transferUuid=0 completely bypasses duplicate transfer protection in _depositUSDCOnBehalf. Line 97 checks transfers_processed[transferUuid] == false, which passes for 0 since mapping defaults to false. Line 106: if (transferUuid != 0) — so transferUuid=0 is NEVER marked as processed. depositUSDCNoEvent (L285-296) does NOT require transferUuid != 0, unlike depositUSDC (L224) and depositUSDCOnBehalfOfParty (L238). The oracle can call depositUSDCNoEvent with transferUuid=0 unlimited times for the same logical transfer.

Allowance check in _depositUSDCOnBehalf (L98-102) is redundant and can be stale. The function checks allowance >= amount, then calls transferFrom which also checks allowance internally. Between the allowance check (L98) and the transferFrom (L105), the allowance can change (e.g., another contract spends it). This is not a direct vulnerability but wastes gas and the error message is misleading when the real failure is different. More importantly: for USDC which has a separate allowance mechanism (permit), the allowance() check may not reflect permit-based approvals correctly in all implementations.
INFI_CL_POSITION_CALL y INFI_BIN_POSITION_CALL envían address(this).balance completo — un comando anterior puede depositar ETH que será reenviado a un position manager sin control del usuario

morphoRepay con shares == type(uint256).max Y assets == type(uint256).max simultáneamente puede crear un escenario donde se repaga más de lo debido. El código procesa primero assets = balanceOf(adapter), luego shares = borrowShares(onBehalf). Morpho.repay() requiere que "either assets or shares should be zero" pero no enforcea esto — el adapter tampoco. Si ambos son non-zero, Morpho usará uno de los dos (probablemente el mínimo para proteger al borrower), pero el adapter puede haber cargado más tokens de los necesarios, dejando residuales o causando un repay incorrecto.

ERC4626 slippage check es post-hoc y puede ser sandwiched. El flujo es: 1) forceApprove vault max, 2) vault.deposit(assets), 3) forceApprove vault 0, 4) check slippage. Entre paso 2 (operación real) y paso 4 (check), la operación ya ocurrió. Si el vault es legítimo pero el share price fue manipulado ANTES del deposit (via sandwich), el slippage check revierte la TX completa. Esto es el comportamiento correcto — el slippage check PROTEGE al usuario. No es un bypass de slippage sino su implementación estándar.

morphoFlashLoan deja approval permanente de MORPHO sobre el token flashloaned. El comentario dice "Morpho's allowance is not reset as it is trusted." Esto es by design porque MORPHO es immutable. PERO: si el token tiene un comportamiento no estándar donde approval de max permite algo más que transferFrom (e.g., algunos tokens raros), esto podría ser un vector. Para tokens estándar ERC20, esto es seguro. Morpho Blue solo usa el approval para pullback del flashloan repayment.

erc4626Withdraw y erc4626Redeem permiten owner == initiator(). Esto significa que el adapter llama vault.withdraw(assets, receiver, initiator) o vault.redeem(shares, receiver, initiator). Para que esto funcione, el initiator debe haber aprobado el adapter para gastar sus vault shares. Si un vault malicioso es pasado como parámetro, el adapter NO aprueba nada (a diferencia de deposit/mint) — solo llama withdraw/redeem. El vault malicioso podría intentar manipular el return value (shares/assets) para hacer pasar el slippage check, pero no puede drenar tokens del adapter porque no hay approval en withdraw/redeem direction.

morphoSupply con onBehalf != initiator permite que el usuario supply tokens a la posición de CUALQUIER dirección (excepto address(this)). Esto es by design en Morpho Blue — cualquiera puede supply on behalf of anyone. No es un bug, pero verificar que el adapter no permite que un callback dentro de morphoSupply redirija fondos. El callback (onMorphoSupply) llama reenterBundler3(data) donde data es arbitrario pero controlado por el initiator (viene del bundle original).

withdrawFees() no verifica que el requestor sea una party del pool. A diferencia de _withdrawUSDCOnBehalf() (L270-272 que requiere requestor == creatorAddress || otherAddresses[requestor]), withdrawFees() en L273-286 solo chequea onlyOracle y permite enviar USDC a CUALQUIER dirección arbitraria. Un oracle comprometido o malicioso puede drenar todo el pool a una dirección externa que no es party del pool.

En batchDepositUSDCAtomic() L122-157, el creatorPartyAmountRequested se cobra N veces (una por cada item) al creatorPartyAddress, pero el transferUuid se resetea a 0 después del primer depósito del creator en cada iteración. Esto significa que para items[1..N-1], el depósito del creator pasa transferUuid=0 a _depositUSDCOnBehalf, y en L106 el check `if (transferUuid != 0)` es false, así que NO marca transfers_processed[0] = true. El creator es cargado N veces por creatorPartyAmountRequested pero la protección de duplicados NO aplica a los depósitos subsiguientes del creator.

La protección de replay via transfers_processed[transferUuid] tiene un bypass deliberado cuando transferUuid == 0. En _depositUSDCOnBehalf() L97 el require `transfers_processed[transferUuid] == false` pasa para transferUuid=0 la primera vez, pero en L106 el `if (transferUuid != 0)` previene que se marque como procesado. Esto significa que transferUuid=0 NUNCA se marca como procesado y puede usarse infinitamente. Las funciones depositUSDCNoEvent (L285-296) y las atomic deposits usan transferUuid=0 intencionalmente, pero cualquier path que pase transferUuid=0 a _depositUSDCOnBehalf permite depósitos repetidos sin replay protection.

La función depositUSDCAtomic() L169-180 tiene un path donde partyOneAmountRequested > 0 y partyTwoAmountRequested == 0, y el parentQuoteUuid NO se valida como != 0 en este path (el require en L181 está DESPUÉS del early return en L180). Tampoco se marca transfers_processed[parentQuoteUuid]. Esto significa que el mismo parentQuoteUuid puede reutilizarse infinitamente para este path específico, emitiendo eventos DepositedAtomic falsos cada vez sin ningún cambio de estado.

Overlapping offsets in sell()/buy() corrupt callData — if exactAmount offset == limitAmount offset, updateAmounts() first writes exactAmount, then reads it back as the "old" limitAmount, computing limitAmount as newExact^2/oldExact instead of the correct proportional value. This corrupts the slippage protection: minDestAmount (sell) or maxSrcAmount (buy) becomes wrong.

srcToken == destToken in swap() makes balance accounting degenerate. srcAmount and destAmount measure the same token balance changes. If Augustus routes through a path that temporarily decreases then increases the balance (net positive), both srcAmount (loss) and destAmount (gain) reflect the same underlying balance changes but measured against the same initial value. The srcAmount = srcInitial - srcFinal could underflow if Augustus returns MORE srcToken than it took (e.g., via a rebasing token or a fee-on-transfer token that has negative fees on certain routes).

swap() transfers only destAmount = destFinal - destInitial to receiver, not the full destFinal balance. If the adapter held pre-existing destToken from a previous operation in the same bundle, those tokens are STRANDED. They can only be recovered via a separate erc20Transfer call. If the bundle doesn't include this cleanup step, tokens are left in the adapter and can be stolen by anyone who calls erc20Transfer in the next bundle.

autoCompound() line 440:
  if (state.amount0 < config.autoCompoundMin0 || state.amount1 < config.autoCompoundMin1)
      revert NotEnoughReward();
The OR condition means: if EITHER token is below its minimum, the whole compound reverts.
For out-of-range positions: - Position below range: only token1 fees accumulate → amount0 = 0 - Position above range: only token0 fees accumulate → amount1 = 0
If config.autoCompoundMin0 > 0 AND position is below range (amount0 = 0):
  → 0 < autoCompoundMin0 → condition TRUE → revert NotEnoughReward()

Result: out-of-range positions with one-sided fees NEVER compound. This is a permanent DoS for a common and legitimate use case. The correct condition should be AND: compound only if BOTH tokens below threshold (i.e., not enough total value to be worth compounding).
Impact: position owner's fees sit idle, earning nothing while in-range positions compound. Depending on position value, this could be thousands of dollars in lost compounding returns.

autoCompound() swaps either token0→token1 or token1→token0 to balance amounts for addLiquidity. The swap direction is determined by which token is in excess. For out-of-range positions, one token is zero. After swap, the resulting split must match the pool's current price ratio for addLiquidity to use both tokens. If the position is far out of range, addLiquidity might only accept one token anyway (since the price is outside the range), making the swap wasteful. Wasted swap = swap fees paid unnecessarily + slippage exposure.
solidity: // INV-ARC-D-03: no swap if position would only accept one token anyway

description: sell() y buy() sin onlyBundler3 explícito — verificar que swap() interno bloquea llamadas directas
Augustus malicioso podría drenar tokens durante la ventana de approval type(uint256).max
receiver puede ser cualquier dirección — ¿permite redirección de fondos del initiator?
callData offsets arbitrarios — el caller puede apuntar a cualquier posición del calldata
buyMorphoDebt() no valida que onBehalf tenga relación con el initiator
Residual approval si augustus.call revierte — forceApprove(0) nunca se ejecuta

autoCompound() line 470: _poolSwap(pool, zeroForOne, amountIn, 0) The 4th parameter is amountOutMin = 0. NO slippage protection. Contrast: execute() calls _validateSwap() which computes amountOutMin based on TWAP price and maxPriceDiffX64. autoCompound's ONLY protection is the TWAP tick difference check at line 425:
  _hasMaxTWAPTickDifference() — blocks if |currentTick - TWAP tick| > MAX_TWAP_TICK_DIFFERENCE
  MAX_TWAP_TICK_DIFFERENCE = 200 ticks ≈ 2% price difference
Attack window: MEV bot can sandwich the autoCompound swap within the 2% window. For a $100K fee compound with 1% swap, attacker extracts up to 2% = $2000. Over many positions and many compounds, this represents systematic value extraction.

execute() has BOTH: TWAP check AND _validateSwap() amountOutMin protection. autoCompound() has ONLY: TWAP check (no amountOutMin protection). The execute() function was written with better protection because it moves more value (whole position rerange). autoCompound() handles only fee compounding. BUT: autoCompound() is called FAR MORE FREQUENTLY (every fee cycle vs. every rerange). The cumulative extraction from autoCompound MEV dwarfs the occasional execute() risk. Design inconsistency: more frequent operation has WEAKER protection.
solidity: // INV-ARC-O-04: autoCompound should use _validateSwap(), not raw _poolSwap()

description: V2 swap usa spot price (getReserves) para calcular amountOut, sin TWAP ni oracle externo. El Dispatcher despacha a V2SwapRouter que lee reserves instantaneas (linea 28-30 de V2SwapRouter). Esto es manipulable via flash loan: flash loan → deposit en el pair → manipular reserves → ejecutar swap via router → restaurar.

onERC721Received() checks `from != address(vault) && from != tokenIdToGauge[tokenId]`. When a tokenId has never been staked, tokenIdToGauge[tokenId] == address(0). This means the check becomes: `from != address(vault) && from != address(0)`. Any address that is NOT the vault can send an NFT to GaugeManager as long as the `from` field equals address(0) — which is impossible for real ERC721 transfers since the zero address cannot own tokens. However: the `from` argument in onERC721Received is the PREVIOUS OWNER passed by the NFT contract, and in Solidity ERC721 safeTransferFrom, `from` is whatever is passed in, NOT necessarily validated by the NPM. The NPM will set `from` to the actual previous owner. But here's the real bug: ANY address can call NPM.safeTransferFrom(gaugeManager, ..., tokenId) if they own that NFT — the `msg.sender` check `if (msg.sender != address(nonfungiblePositionManager))` is correct and blocks direct calls. The `from` parameter is msg.sender in the NPM transfer, so it will be the actual token owner. There is no bypass here. HOWEVER: if tokenIdToGauge[tokenId] is address(0) for a NEW tokenId (never staked), and someone sends a DIFFERENT (unrelated) NFT tokenId where tokenIdToGauge[that_tokenId] == address(0), the condition `from == address(vault)` must be true. So unrelated NFTs can only come in via the vault. This seems safe.

compoundRewards() is callable DIRECTLY by the position owner (not just by the vault). When the owner calls it directly, the function performs: claimRewards → withdraw from gauge → swap AERO → addLiquidity → re-deposit to gauge. The position NFT is inside the gauge during the entire call. The vault's health check for the loan only runs when the vault calls _requireLoanIsHealthy (after transform). If the owner calls compoundRewards() directly on GaugeManager (bypassing vault.transform()), the vault does NOT re-check health. The compound operation increases liquidity, which should IMPROVE health. BUT: during the compound, the NFT is briefly withdrawn from the gauge and re-deposited. The vault tracks whether a position is staked via its own stakeStatus mapping. If vault.stakePosition was used to send the NFT to GaugeManager, and GaugeManager internally calls gauge.withdraw/deposit during compound, the vault is UNAWARE. The vault only knows the NFT left its custody (it's in GaugeManager or gauge), not the sub-steps. The health check bypass is the key concern.

claimRewards() accepts an arbitrary `recipient` address when called by the vault. The function _requireVaultOrOwner() returns the owner of the tokenId from vault.ownerOf(). If msg.sender == vault, the check passes. Then `recipient` is used as-is if non-zero. The vault can therefore redirect ALL AERO rewards for any position to any address — including address(0xdead), the vault contract itself, or any attacker-controlled address. Under the current vault code (transformWithRewardCompound and _unstakePosition in vault), the vault always passes the actual owner as recipient. But if a malicious vault-registered transformer calls vault.transform() and inside the transform callback somehow causes the vault to call claimRewards with a different recipient, rewards could be stolen. More directly: in _unstakePosition (vault-internal), the vault calls gaugeManager.unstakeIfStaked() which calls _claimAndSendRewardsBestEffort internally — it always sends to vault.ownerOf(tokenId). So rewards during unstake go to the correct owner. But claimRewards() is a SEPARATE external function that CAN be called by msg.sender == vault with arbitrary recipient. The vault calls claimRewards only through transformWithRewardCompound indirectly via compoundRewards, not claimRewards directly. The direct attack vector is: can a transformer call vault -> then invoke something that triggers claimRewards with a bad recipient? Not in current code, but the function signature allows it.

setCompoundReward() enforces that `_totalRewardX64 <= totalRewardX64` (can only DECREASE the fee). This is a one-way ratchet — once lowered, the owner can never raise it back (MAX_REWARD_X64 = 2%). This is almost certainly intentional (anti-rug protection). However: setWithdrawer() allows the owner to change the withdrawer to any non-zero address, including the owner themselves. If the owner sets withdrawer = owner, then the owner can call withdrawBalances() for all protocol fees. This is expected behavior, but it means if the owner key is compromised, the attacker can both: (a) change the withdrawer to themselves (via setWithdrawer) and (b) drain all token balances in the contract (rewardAmount0, rewardAmount1 accumulated). The owner cannot raise the reward fee, but they CAN drain all accumulated fees instantly by updating the withdrawer. This is a privilege escalation path via key compromise, not an on-chain bug.

_requireVaultOrOwner() calls vault.ownerOf(tokenId) which returns tokenOwner[tokenId] from the vault's storage. During vault.transform() execution, transformedTokenId is set to the tokenId being transformed, but the ownership record (tokenOwner[tokenId]) is NOT changed — the original owner is still the owner. So during a transform, _requireVaultOrOwner returns the original owner. The concern: if a malicious transformer is executing inside vault.transform(), and inside that execution it calls GaugeManager.compoundRewards() or claimRewards(), the vault IS msg.sender (because vault.transform calls transformer.call(), and the transformer could call gaugeManager directly as msg.sender == transformer, NOT vault). So the transformer can only pass _requireVaultOrOwner if the transformer IS the vault or the transformer IS vault.ownerOf(tokenId). If a transformerAllowList[transformer] is true, and that transformer calls GaugeManager directly, it would fail _requireVaultOrOwner unless it's the owner. This is safe. BUT: what if an allowed transformer IS the same address as a position owner? Unlikely by design.

setGauge() validates that pool.gauge() == gauge address via a staticcall, but does NOT validate that the gauge contract is a legitimate Aerodrome CLGauge. Any contract that implements a gauge() function returning a specific address could be used as the `pool` argument. The real concern is whether a malicious or misconfigured gauge could be registered. Once registered, that gauge receives NFT custody (via IGauge.deposit) and can refuse to return it (IGauge.withdraw could revert). If the gauge is malicious and IGauge.withdraw reverts, _unstakePosition reverts, which would block vault liquidation and unstaking. The try/catch in _claimAndSendRewardsBestEffort does NOT protect the withdraw() call — only the getReward() call is wrapped in try/catch.

modifyLiquiditiesWithoutLock no tiene checkDeadline — las transacciones no tienen protección contra stale execution. A diferencia de modifyLiquidities que tiene checkDeadline(deadline), modifyLiquiditiesWithoutLock no exige un deadline. Un atacante podría retener la transacción en el mempool y ejecutarla cuando las condiciones de mercado sean desfavorables para el usuario.

SWEEP amountMin truncado silenciosamente de uint256 a uint160 — el comentario dice abi.decode(inputs, (address, address, uint256)) pero el código declara uint160 amountMin. Si el usuario envía un amountMin > type(uint160).max, los bits superiores se pierden y el check de mínimo se debilita drásticamente (e.g., 2^161 se convierte en 0).

INFI_CL_POSITION_CALL e INFI_BIN_POSITION_CALL envían address(this).balance completo como value. En un batch de múltiples comandos, si un usuario anterior dejó ETH en el router (o ETH de otros comandos del mismo batch), todo ese ETH se envía al position manager. El ETH no está particionado por usuario/comando.

leverageDown computes collectParams.amount0Max as SafeCast.toUint128(amount0 + params.feeAmount0). If amount0 (uint256 from decreaseLiquidity) + params.feeAmount0 (uint128) exceeds type(uint128).max, SafeCast.toUint128 reverts. This permanently DoSes deleverage for positions with very large liquidity amounts combined with non-zero feeAmount params. Workaround: use feeAmount = type(uint128).max.
distributionX/Y are passed as uint256[] but silently truncated to uint64 in LiquidityConfigurations.encodeParams — values > 2^64 lose upper bits, causing incorrect liquidity distribution across bins
Round-trip add-then-remove liquidity in a single bin should not be profitable — user should receive <= what they deposited (rounding favors the pool/protocol)
Maximize round-trip profit: deposit into a bin and immediately withdraw, measuring net token gain across various amount/bin combinations
modifyLiquiditiesWithoutLock has no deadline check — actions can be executed at any time after signing, enabling stale-state exploitation
LP token totalSupply must equal sum of all user balances for every tokenId — _mint and _burn use unchecked arithmetic that could desync if overflow/underflow occurs

Oracle.grantRole (line 438-446) overrides AccessControl.grantRole. It calls
super.grantRole(role, account) FIRST, which grants the role. Then it checks
require(!hasRole(PROVIDER_ROLE, account)) — but since the role was JUST granted,
hasRole returns true, and the require ALWAYS reverts.

This means grantRole() for PROVIDER_ROLE is a dead function — it always reverts.
The transaction reverts entirely (including the super.grantRole), so no state change
occurs. The intended path addProvider() uses _grantRole() directly and works fine.

However, if an admin uses the standard AccessControl.grantRole path (which is the
standard OZ interface), it silently fails. More critically: if someone discovers
the bug and uses _grantRole via another path, numProviders goes out of sync.

Multiple functions accept unbounded arrays:
- Oracle.collectFees: requests.length unbounded (line 102 loop)
- Oracle.processTreasuryManagementDeposits: deposits.length unbounded (line 153)
- Oracle.processTreasuryManagementWithdrawals: withdrawals.length unbounded (line 202)
- Oracle.batchAtomicDeposit: items.length unbounded (line 334)
- SettlementPool.batchDepositUSDCAtomic: items.length unbounded (line 127)
- SettlementPoolFactory.createPool: otherAddresses with O(n^2) dedup loop (line 50-64)

Each iteration does external calls (transferFrom/transfer) which cost ~25K+ gas.
A batch with 200+ items could exceed the Arbitrum block gas limit.

The factory's createPool has O(n^2) duplicate checking for otherAddresses (line 59-64)
which is especially gas-intensive for large arrays.

Oracle does NOT override renounceRole from AccessControl. A provider can call
renounceRole(PROVIDER_ROLE, self) to remove their own role. This does NOT
decrement numProviders. If the last 2 providers each renounce their role,
numProviders stays at 2 but there are actually 0 providers.

More critically: removeProvider requires numProviders > 1. If providers renounce
instead of being removed, numProviders is inflated. The admin can never call
removeProvider to clean up because the removed providers no longer have the role
(hasRole check fails on line 426-428).

Conversely, if one provider renounces and numProviders drops to what the admin
thinks is 1, calling removeProvider on the remaining provider fails because
numProviders is still 2 (not decremented by renounce), so the check passes but...
actually the numProviders > 1 check on line 429 would pass, and the removal would
succeed, leaving numProviders=1 but 0 actual providers. No one can call provider
functions anymore.
Position metadata for binId=0 is never stored — _positions[tokenId].binId == 0 used as 'empty' sentinel collides with actual bin 0
idSlippage underflow — if activeIdDesired < idSlippage, the subtraction activeIdDesired - idSlippage wraps to a huge uint256, making the check always pass
ERC1155 transferBatch requires vault to be unlocked (onlyIfVaultUnlocked) — transfers are blocked during lock callback, preventing composable position transfers

INFI_CL_POSITION_CALL denylist incompleta: _checkInfiClPositionManagerCall NO bloquea CL_INCREASE_LIQUIDITY_FROM_DELTAS (0x04). Si un usuario aprueba el UniversalRouter para su posicion (necesario para mint), un atacante podria construir un EXECUTE_SUB_PLAN que incluya CL_INCREASE_LIQUIDITY_FROM_DELTAS para modificar la posicion del usuario sin su consentimiento, ya que el check solo bloquea CL_INCREASE_LIQUIDITY (0x00), CL_DECREASE_LIQUIDITY (0x01) y CL_BURN_POSITION (0x03), pero no el variante FROM_DELTAS.

autoCompound() collects fees (amount0, amount1), then optionally swaps. The compoundFees are deducted from the collected amounts BEFORE adding liquidity. If the fee deduction makes amount0 or amount1 go negative (impossible in Solidity 0.8 checked arithmetic), revert. But if the fee is calculated as % of collected and the % rounds up, the deduction could exceed the collected amount. Root cause: fee = totalFees * COMPOUND_FEE_X64 / 2^64. Division rounds down, so compoundFees <= collected is always guaranteed. Invariant holds.
solidity:
// INV-ARC-M-01: compoundFees0 <= amount0 && compoundFees1 <= amount1
// Holds by design: compoundFee = amount * COMPOUND_FEE_X64 / Q64 ≤ amount

description: execute() line 245: baseTick = currentTick - (((currentTick % tickSpacing) + tickSpacing) % tickSpacing) Line 262: SafeCast.toInt24(baseTick + config.lowerTickDelta) — if lowerTickDelta is large negative and baseTick is near MIN_TICK, sum could underflow int256 or exceed int24 range. Similarly for upperTickDelta near MAX_TICK. Attack: position configured with extreme deltas triggers permanent revert in execute(). configToken() doesn't validate that baseTick + delta stays within int24 bounds. This is a DoS finding — operator-set config can permanently block range adjustment.

Fund conservation invariant: amounts collected from fees = amounts added as liquidity + compoundFees + leftover. If there's a discrepancy, tokens are either lost or duplicated. Swap path: collected → swap some → addLiquidity with swapped amounts → compound fees → leftover to owner. The leftover is sent to params.rewardConversion or position owner. Verify: amount0_collected = amount0_added_to_liq + compoundFee0 + leftover0.

Line 245: baseTick = currentTick - (((currentTick % tickSpacing) + tickSpacing) % tickSpacing) For negative currentTick, Solidity's % operator returns negative results. Example: currentTick = -100, tickSpacing = 60
  currentTick % tickSpacing = -100 % 60 = -40 (Solidity rounds toward zero)
  (-40 + 60) % 60 = 20 % 60 = 20
  baseTick = -100 - 20 = -120 ✓ (correct floor)
The arithmetic handles negative ticks correctly. Lower risk than initially suspected. But: if tickSpacing = 0 (edge case, shouldn't happen), division by zero. tickSpacing comes from pool.tickSpacing() — should always be > 0 for valid pools.
solidity:
// INV-ARC-M-05: baseTick is always a valid tick floor
// Correctly handles negative ticks via modular arithmetic

description: En _swapAeroForPosition, el positionPool es usado en ambas llamadas a _swapAeroToTarget: una vez en sentido otherToken→targetToken (para token0) y otra en sentido opuesto (para token1). Cada llamada lee el slot0 del positionPool por separado. Si en el path two-hop para token0 se usa el directPool para token1 (o viceversa), se mezclan paths que usan distintos pools, y el precio del positionPool se lee en un estado que puede haber cambiado entre los dos swaps (si los swaps modifican el positionPool en el mismo bloque — lo cual ocurre en el two-hop de token1). Específicamente: si el two-hop de token0 hace swap en positionPool (USDC→WETH), el precio del positionPool cambia. Luego el two-hop de token1 valida su slippage contra el precio YA MODIFICADO del positionPool (desde el primer swap). El TWAP check del segundo hop usa el precio post-primer-swap como referencia.

El cálculo de leftoverAero en _sendLeftoversAndRewards asume state.spentAero <= state.aeroAmount. Si por cualquier razón spentAero > aeroAmount, la substracción `state.aeroAmount - state.spentAero` wrappea (underflow en unchecked o revert). En el código actual esto parece imposible porque spentAero = spentAero0 + spentAero1, y cada uno es exactamente amountIn (o 0 si amountIn = 0). Pero si el shortcut `targetToken == address(aeroToken)` se activa para AMBOS tokens (token0 == aeroToken y token1 == aeroToken), spentAero = requestedAero0 + requestedAero1 = aeroAmount — correcto. Sin embargo, si aeroToken es token0 Y hay two-hop para token1 que falla silenciosamente, spentAero podría ser != amountIn esperado. No es un bug activo pero es un invariante que vale fuzzear para confirmar que el accounting de AERO nunca se corrompe.

_validateSwap con REWARD_TWAP_SECONDS = 60 en Aerodrome Slipstream (Base, bloques 2s): el TWAP cubre exactamente 30 bloques. En Uniswap V3 clásico esto sería muy manipulable, pero Aerodrome Slipstream tiene una cardinality mínima efectiva por su diseño. Sin embargo, si el pool acaba de ser creado o reiniciado y tiene < 30 observaciones, la llamada a pool.observe(secondsAgos) puede revertir con OLD, haciendo que _getTWAPTick devuelva twapOk = false. En ese caso, _hasMaxTWAPTickDifference retorna false y _validateSwap lanza TWAPCheckFailed(). Esto bloquearía todos los compoundRewards para posiciones en ese pool. No es un bug de seguridad sino un DoS de disponibilidad, pero merece documentación. Si un nuevo pool se añade a rewardBasePools y tiene < 60s de historia TWAP, compoundRewards falla silenciosamente (o revierte) para todos los tokens que usen ese pool.

autoCompound() has `nonReentrant` modifier (line 416). execute() does NOT have `nonReentrant` modifier (line 162). Both functions: - Call external contracts (npm.decreaseLiquidity, npm.collect, npm.mint, npm.addLiquidity) - Transfer NFTs (npm.safeTransferFrom) - Interact with V3Vault via transform mode The NFT transfer in execute() (line ~340: npm.safeTransferFrom to vault) triggers V3Vault.onERC721Received. That function updates loan state and calls _cleanupLoan. If onERC721Received re-enters execute() before the first call completes, the positionConfigs for the new tokenId may not yet be set (config set at line ~350, AFTER the transfer at ~340). Attack: malicious vault or manipulated onERC721Received re-enters execute() between NFT transfer and config setup.
solidity: // INV-ARC-A-01: execute() should have nonReentrant by symmetry with autoCompound()

description: configToken() stores positionConfigs without validating tick relationship. If lowerTickDelta >= upperTickDelta (same tick or inverted), execute() would create a position with invalid tick range (lower >= upper). npm.mint() with tickLower >= tickUpper reverts in Uniswap V3. This means misconfigured positions permanently revert on execute() — DoS. A legitimate user can misconfigure their own position, leading to stuck range adjustment.

execute() flow for vault strategy: 1. mint newTokenId (line ~265) 2. Transfer newTokenId to vault (line ~340): npm.safeTransferFrom(this, vault, newTokenId) 3. Set positionConfigs[newTokenId] (line ~350) Between steps 2 and 3, newTokenId exists in vault but has NO config in AutoRangeAndCompound. If anyone calls autoCompound(newTokenId) in this window (impossible in single tx, but MEV bots could call in next block before the config tx lands), it would proceed with empty config (zeros for all fields). With empty config, autoCompoundMin0=0, autoCompoundMin1=0 → always passes threshold. compoundFeesX64=0 → no keeper fee. rewardX64=0 → no reward. Not exploitable, just incorrect.
solidity: // INV-ARC-A-03: positionConfigs[tokenId].isActive implies config was set

description: COMPOUND_FEE_X64 is a fee that goes to the protocol/keeper. If set to Q64 (100%), all collected fees go to the compound fee recipient. Position owner receives nothing from the autoCompound. This is operator abuse (requires owner/deployer to set), but worth validating the maximum fee bounds.
solidity: // INV-ARC-A-06: COMPOUND_FEE_X64 <= MAX_COMPOUND_FEE (should be capped)

description: rDivUp rounding direction consistency: en todas las funciones donde el usuario PAGA (erc4626Mint, erc4626Deposit, morphoSupply, morphoRepay), el slippage check usa rDivUp(assets, shares) <= maxSharePriceE27. rDivUp redondea ARRIBA el precio, lo cual es conservador para el usuario (exige que incluso el peor-caso redondeado no exceda su maximo). Verificar que ningun path usa rDivDown donde deberia usar rDivUp.

Division by zero en rDivUp/rDivDown cuando shares=0. Si un vault ERC4626 retorna 0 shares para un deposit, o Morpho retorna 0 suppliedShares, la division por cero causa revert. Verificar que todos los paths previenen shares=0 ANTES del calculo, o que el revert natural es aceptable como proteccion.

Overflow en x * RAY dentro de rDivUp/rDivDown. RAY = 1e27. Si x > type(uint256).max / 1e27 (aprox 1.15e50), la multiplicacion causa overflow y revert en Solidity 0.8.28. Para tokens con 18 decimales, esto equivale a ~1.15e32 tokens — un valor astronomico que ningun protocolo real manejaria. Pero un vault ERC4626 malicioso podria retornar valores artificialmente altos.

SafeCast160 truncation en permit2TransferFrom. La funcion usa amount.toUint160() despues de resolver type(uint256).max a balanceOf(initiator). Si el balance real excede type(uint160).max (~1.46e48), el cast revertira. Verificar que no hay truncacion silenciosa.

maxSharePriceE27 slippage bypass con valor type(uint256).max. Si el usuario pasa maxSharePriceE27 = type(uint256).max, el slippage check rDivUp(assets, shares) <= max SIEMPRE pasa. Esto es by-design (usuario opta por no tener proteccion de slippage). PERO: si un frontend/integrador por defecto pasa type(uint256).max, el usuario queda sin proteccion contra sandwich attacks o manipulacion de precio del vault.

minSharePriceE27 = 0 desactiva proteccion de slippage en withdrawals. En erc4626Withdraw, erc4626Redeem, morphoBorrow, morphoWithdraw, el check es rDivDown(assets, shares) >= minSharePriceE27. Si minSharePriceE27 = 0, el check SIEMPRE pasa (rDivDown retorna >= 0 para inputs no negativos).

erc4626Deposit: si un vault ERC4626 inflado via donation attack retorna shares=0 para un deposit de assets>0, la transaccion revierte en el slippage check (division por cero). PERO el deposito real ya ocurrio dentro de vault.deposit() — sin embargo como todo esta en la misma transaccion, el revert deshace todo. Verificar que no hay un path donde el vault consume assets sin mintear shares Y la tx no revierte.
morphoRepay con shares=type(uint256).max resuelve a borrowShares del onBehalf (no del initiator). Verificar que la correccion del bug conocido (Solodit finding) esta implementada correctamente.

compoundV2RedeemErc20 calcula received = wMulDown(exchangeRateCurrent, amount) ANTES del redeem. Si Compound V2 internamente redondea de forma distinta a wMulDown (mulDivDown(x, y, 1e18)), el adapter puede intentar transferir MAS tokens de los que realmente recibio del redeem, causando revert o robo de tokens residuales de otros usuarios en el adapter.

compoundV2RedeemEth tiene el mismo problema que CV2-01 pero con ETH. received = wMulDown(exchangeRateCurrent, amount) puede diferir del ETH realmente recibido del redeem de cETH. sendValue transfiere received, no el ETH real recibido.
Despues de compoundV2RedeemErc20, no deberia quedar underlying stuck en el adapter (asumiendo receiver != adapter). Todo el `received` calculado debe llegar al receiver.

erc20WrapperWithdrawTo L58 hace safeTransferFrom(initiator, adapter, amount). Esto requiere que el initiator haya aprobado al adapter para el wrapped token. Si el initiator no aprobo, la tx revierte. Esto podria ser un DoS si el usuario no sabe que necesita aprobar.

erc20WrapperDepositFor: si underlying.balanceOf(adapter) == 0 cuando amount == type(uint256).max, el require(amount != 0) revierte. Esto es correcto pero puede causar confusion si el usuario espera un no-op.
Rounding direction en updateAmounts: sell() Ceil vs buy() Floor — ¿favorece al usuario o al protocolo?
sell(sellEntireBalance=true) con balance > type(uint160).max: ¿SafeCast truncation?
solidity: // No aplica — no hay truncación en el contrato

description: updateAmounts escala limitAmount proporcionalmente, pero el swap real puede tener slippage no lineal

Burn de posición con liquidity=0 pierde fees acumuladas: _burn() solo llama modifyLiquidity si liquidity > 0, pero fees pueden acumularse en el pool manager para posiciones con 0 liquidity (por actividad de otros LPs en el mismo tick range). Esos fees se pierden para siempre.

Multicall + msg.value re-use: un usuario que envía ETH con multicall puede reutilizar msg.value en múltiples sub-llamadas (modifyLiquidities, initializePool, subscribe) porque delegatecall preserva msg.value a lo largo de todo el loop del multicall

initializePool silently swallows ALL errors incluyendo errores críticos — un usuario que cree que su pool fue inicializada puede hacer mint/increase en una pool inicializada por otro con parámetros distintos
modifyLiquiditiesWithoutLock NO tiene checkDeadline — acciones ejecutadas sin lock pueden ser incluidas en bloques arbitrariamente futuros sin protección de deadline

Subscriber deadlock completo: si notifyModifyLiquidity revierte, el usuario NO puede decrease liquidity, y si notifyBurn revierte, NO puede burn. El único escape es transferFrom (que auto-unsubscribes con try-catch). Pero si el vault está locked durante la operación, transferFrom también revierte.

In leverageUp when token==token0:
  amount0 = borrowAmount (borrow in token0)
  If amountIn1 > 0: swap token1 → token0, amount0 += amountOut
  If amountIn0 > 0: swap token0 → token1, amount0 -= amountIn0
The subtraction `amount0 -= amountIn0` can underflow if amountIn0 > (borrowAmount + swapOut1). Solidity 0.8 reverts on underflow. But the issue is: the user can accidentally craft params where amountIn0 > borrowAmount (intending to leverage using more token0 than borrowed). The tx reverts silently without clear error message, leaving user confused. More critically: if there's a code path where overflow/underflow check is bypassed (e.g., unchecked block), this becomes a real accounting bug.

leverageDown sequence: (1) nft.decreaseLiquidity() → reduces liquidity, credits token amounts to position. (2) nft.collect() → transfers credited amounts to LeverageTransformer. Between steps 1 and 2, another transaction could interact with the position (if the vault allows concurrent transforms, which it doesn't due to transformedTokenId). However if called directly by owner (not via vault.transform()), the transformedTokenId is not set, so concurrent vault operations might be possible in theory.

_routerSwap() in Swapper.sol validates amountOutDelta >= amountOutMin. If params.swapData encodes amountOutMin=0 (or the swap type doesn't pass amountOutMin to the router), there's no slippage protection on the swap. In leverageUp, borrowed tokens are swapped to the other token for addLiquidity. Zero slippage means a sandwicher can extract the borrow proceeds. The vault's health check at the end is the only protection — if sandwich causes < expected liquidity added, health check fails → revert. But: sandwich extract value WITHIN the health check boundary (extract just enough that health check still passes). Sophisticated attack vector.

Overlapping offsets: si exactAmount y limitAmount apuntan al mismo offset en callData, el segundo set() sobrescribe el primero en updateAmounts(). En sell(), esto causa que maxSrcAmount (leído de exactAmount offset) tenga el valor del limitAmount escalado, NO el exactAmount original. El check srcAmount <= maxSrcAmount usa un valor corrupto.

updateAmounts con oldExactAmount = 0 causa division by zero en mulDiv. Si el callData original tiene 0 en la posición de exactAmount, la llamada a mulDiv(limitAmount, exactAmount=newValue, oldExactAmount=0) revierte. En sell() con sellEntireBalance y balance > 0, esto es un DoS si el callData mal-formado tiene exactAmount = 0.

_addLiquidity skips increaseLiquidity entirely when BOTH maxAddAmount0 == 0 AND maxAddAmount1 == 0. This happens when amount0Out == 0 AND amount1Out == 0, which occurs when aeroSplitBps == 0 AND token1 == aeroToken (the passthrough returns (amountIn, amountIn) = (aeroAmount, aeroAmount) for amount0Out=0 because requestedAero0=0, and amount1Out = aeroAmount as passthrough), OR when all swaps produced zero output.
ACTUALLY: Let's trace aeroSplitBps=0 precisely: - requestedAero0 = 0, requestedAero1 = aeroAmount - _swapAeroToTarget(positionPool, token0, token1, 0) → returns (0, 0) [amountIn=0 early return] - _swapAeroToTarget(positionPool, token1, token0, aeroAmount) → swaps aeroAmount for amount1Out - state.amount0Out = 0, state.amount1Out = amount1Out - maxAddAmount0 = 0 * Q64 / ... = 0 - maxAddAmount1 = amount1Out * Q64 / (reward + Q64) > 0 - Condition: maxAddAmount0 != 0 || maxAddAmount1 != 0 → TRUE (maxAddAmount1 > 0) - So addLiquidity IS called with amount0Desired=0, amount1Desired=maxAddAmount1 - NPM handles this correctly (adds only token1 liquidity if position favors it)
The TRUE skip case is when amount0Out=0 AND amount1Out=0, which requires: aeroSplitBps=0 AND token1 has a configured base pool BUT the swap produced zero output (e.g., price is at a limit and amountOutMin > 0 causes SlippageError before reaching zero). Actually if swap reverts, compoundRewards reverts — the skip case is unreachable normally.
REAL EDGE CASE: position is fully out of range on BOTH sides. increaseLiquidity is called with amount0Desired > 0 and amount1Desired > 0 but the NPM returns amountAdded0=0 and amountAdded1=0 (position at a tick boundary where both are zero). Then: rewardAmount0 = 0, rewardAmount1 = 0. leftover0 = amount0Out - 0 - 0 = amount0Out (ALL sent to owner as leftover). leftover1 = amount1Out - 0 - 0 = amount1Out (ALL sent to owner as leftover). Protocol earns ZERO fee. Position gets ZERO added liquidity. The compound "succeeds" but adds nothing. Owner gets everything back as leftovers. minAeroReward only protects the AERO claim threshold, not the position outcome.

_swapAeroToTarget intermediate routing asymmetry: when called for the token0 leg, the "other token" is token1. When called for the token1 leg, the "other token" is token0. If NEITHER rewardBasePools[token0] NOR rewardBasePools[token1] is set, both legs revert. If ONLY rewardBasePools[token0] is set: - token0 leg: direct AERO→token0 via rewardBasePools[token0]. OK. - token1 leg: no direct pool, uses intermediate = rewardBasePools[token0] (otherToken=token0).
  Does AERO→token0 via rewardBasePools[token0], then token0→token1 via positionPool.

This means for the token1 leg using the two-hop path, the positionPool is used for token0→token1 swap. SIMULTANEOUSLY, for the token0 leg (if it uses direct route), no positionPool usage. So only the token1 leg uses the positionPool.
BUT: if the pool between AERO and token0 (rewardBasePools[token0]) has low liquidity, both legs hammering it in the same transaction create high slippage: - token0 leg: buys token0 with X aero → moves price - token1 leg: buys token0 with Y aero (for intermediate) → moves price MORE
The token1 leg's TWAP check (for the AERO→token0 pool) is done at call time for that specific _swapThroughPool invocation, but the TWAP (60-second time-weighted average) doesn't change within the same block. Both calls use the same TWAP but different current prices (second call is post-first-swap). The 200-tick tolerance means a ~2% move doesn't fail the check, but both calls hitting the same low-liquidity pool can cause the second call to exceed the tolerance if the first already moved it significantly.

NOVEL HIGH-VALUE FINDING: compoundRewards adds liquidity with amount0Min=0 and amount1Min=0 in the increaseLiquidity call (line 491). This means the position owner accepts ANY outcome from addLiquidity, including being given zero liquidity even when tokens are provided.
The attack scenario from AccessHunter GM-A-03 identified the 0 slippage issue. This hypothesis extends it: specifically, the SEQUENCE of operations creates a sandwich window.
Timeline of compoundRewards: 1. gauge.withdraw(tokenId) — NFT leaves gauge, goes to GM 2. _swapAeroForPosition — N swaps happen with TWAP protection (good) 3. _addLiquidity:
   a. safeIncreaseAllowance(NPM, maxAdd0/1) — GM approves NPM
   b. NPM.increaseLiquidity(tokenId, maxAdd0, maxAdd1, 0, 0, deadline) — adds at current price
   c. safeApprove(NPM, 0) — allowance reset
4. gauge.deposit(tokenId) — NFT back to gauge
The sandwich window is step 3b: after the swap protections in step 2, but before the liquidity add. An MEV bot can: a. Let step 2 (swap) complete — can't front-run the whole tx atomically in Solidity b. Observe the pending tx, front-run step 3b specifically by executing between blocks — but this is impossible since steps 2 and 3 are in the same transaction.
HOWEVER: the positionPool used in two-hop routing IS the same pool that addLiquidity uses. The two-hop swap at step 2 MOVES the positionPool price. Then addLiquidity at step 3 uses the NEW (post-swap) price. If the two-hop swap moved the price out of the position's tick range, addLiquidity adds 0 of one token (as noted in GM-W-02). No sandwich needed. The position pool self-interference creates the slippage without any external attacker.
THE REAL NOVEL FINDING: The `deadline` parameter in compoundRewards controls ONLY the increaseLiquidity deadline, NOT the swaps. The swaps in _swapThroughPool use sqrtPriceLimitX96 = MIN/MAX_SQRT_RATIO ± 1 (no price limit on the swap itself). The TWAP check happens BEFORE the swap in _validateSwap. But if the block timestamp advances past the deadline BETWEEN the TWAP check and the increaseLiquidity call, the liquidity add reverts but the swaps have already executed — AERO was already spent on token0/token1, the NFT is withdrawn from gauge but not re-deposited.
Wait — the revert propagates and undoes everything (EVM atomicity). So deadline expiry still reverts the whole transaction. The deadline only affects the final state of increaseLiquidity, and since it all reverts, the position is safe.
BUT: if deadline == block.timestamp and a slow block includes the tx AFTER the deadline, the whole compound reverts with expired deadline. The position remains staked (all reverted), but the user passed a deadline they thought was valid. This is standard deadline behavior.

transferFromOLPToPool (Oracle:267-285) accepts a raw `poolAddress` parameter and sends USDC directly to it via `usdc.transfer(poolAddress, amount)` WITHOUT validating that poolAddress == factory.getPool(poolUuid). A malicious/compromised provider can route OLP funds to ANY arbitrary address. This is the ONLY function in Oracle that takes poolAddress as a direct parameter — all other functions resolve poolAddress from poolUuid via getPool() or factory.getPool().

Oracle.grantRole() (line 438-446) calls super.grantRole(role, account) BEFORE checking require(!hasRole(PROVIDER_ROLE, account)). Since super.grantRole() already grants the role, hasRole() returns true at the require check, making !hasRole() always false. The require ALWAYS reverts for PROVIDER_ROLE, making the standard OZ grantRole() path permanently broken. The addProvider() function still works as an alternative path.

withdrawFees (SettlementPool:247-260) does the USDC transfer BEFORE setting transfers_processed[fees_batch_id] = true (line 256). The transfer is inside a try/catch, and the state update happens in the try success block. This is technically an Interaction-before-Effect pattern. However, USDC on Arbitrum is a standard ERC20 with no callbacks (not ERC777), and the function has nonReentrant. Additionally, the Oracle calling this function also has nonReentrant, so there are TWO mutex locks active.

Oracle maintains its OWN pool registry (mapping pools, line 21) AND the factory also maintains a pool registry (getPool mapping). Oracle.createPool() (line 359-380) writes to BOTH: factory.createPool() writes to factory.getPool, and then line 379 writes to Oracle.pools[poolUuid]. Some Oracle functions use Oracle.getPool() (which reads Oracle.pools) while others use factory.getPool(). If these ever diverge, fund routing could break.
Functions using Oracle.pools (via getPool): withdrawUSDC (258), atomicDeposit (296), depositUSDC (350).
Functions using factory.getPool: collectFees (103), processTreasuryManagementDeposits (154), processTreasuryManagementWithdrawals (203), batchAtomicDeposit (330), addOtherParty (386).
transferFromOLPToPool: uses NEITHER — takes poolAddress as raw parameter.

batchAtomicDeposit (Oracle:324-342) calls pool.batchDepositUSDCAtomic() which uses the item's parentQuoteUuid as the transferUuid for _depositUSDCOnBehalf. The dupe check in _depositUSDCOnBehalf (line 97) uses Pool.transfers_processed. BUT: for the first item with creatorPartyAmountRequested > 0, after the creator deposit, transferUuid is reset to 0 (line 140). When transferUuid == 0, _depositUSDCOnBehalf still checks transfers_processed[0], but transferUuid 0 is never set to true (line 106-108: only set if transferUuid != 0). This means ALL second-party deposits with transferUuid=0 BYPASS the dupe check. If provider submits the same batch twice, the creator deposits will be caught by the dupe check (parentQuoteUuid is real), but the other party deposits with transferUuid=0 will succeed again.

removeLiquidity burns ERC1155 tokens from params.from but the vault delta (tokens owed to the user) is not explicitly directed to params.from — the tokens go wherever the caller routes them via TAKE/TAKE_PAIR/CLOSE actions. An approved operator can burn someone's position and route the underlying tokens to themselves.

activeIdDesired underflow in slippage check — if activeIdDesired < idSlippage, the subtraction `activeIdDesired - idSlippage` underflows (both are uint256), producing a very large number that will always be > activeId, causing a revert. This means users cannot add liquidity to very low bin IDs with any slippage tolerance.
initializePool swallows ALL errors including legitimate ones, returning type(int24).max as a silent failure indicator
_mintFromDeltas and _increaseFromDeltas use spot sqrtPriceX96 for liquidity calculation — manipulable via sandwich
Asymmetry: _burn clears positionInfo BEFORE modifyLiquidity call, allowing hook to read stale/zero position data during the burn callback

setGauge() can update poolToGauge[pool] to a new gauge address for an existing pool, but tokenIdToGauge[tokenId] entries for already-staked positions in the OLD gauge are NOT migrated. They continue to point to the old gauge. All subsequent operations (claimRewards, unstakePosition, compoundRewards) will use the old gauge address. If the old gauge is deprecated/killed by Aerodrome governance (or its rewards stop), positions are permanently stuck staked to a dead gauge.
