Fee-on-transfer tokens causan revert sistemático en _routeTokens. SpendPermissionManager transfiere `value` tokens desde el account al SpendRouter (como spender), pero si el token cobra fee-on-transfer, SpendRouter recibe menos que `value`. Luego _routeTokens intenta transferir exactamente `value` al recipient → revert por saldo insuficiente. Cualquier permission creada con un FoT token queda permanentemente inutilizable via SpendRouter.

SpendRouter no tiene mecanismo de rescue para tokens ERC-20 enviados accidentalmente al contrato. Si un token es transferido directamente al SpendRouter (no via el flujo normal de spend), esos tokens quedan permanentemente bloqueados. Para ETH, el receive() solo acepta de PERMISSION_MANAGER, así que ETH accidental de otras fuentes revierte. Pero ERC-20 tokens pueden enviarse libremente al contrato sin restricción.
El balance de ETH y ERC20 del SpendRouter debe ser 0 antes y despues de cada transaccion completa. El SpendRouter es un pass-through — nunca debe retener fondos.
Los fondos del _routeTokens() SIEMPRE deben llegar al recipient decodificado del extraData, nunca a otra direccion. La cantidad routeada debe ser exactamente `value`.
Solo el executor codificado en extraData puede triggerar spendAndRoute y variantes. Ningun otro msg.sender debe poder ejecutar la routing de una permission.

Multicallable permite batching de calls al SpendRouter. Si un executor batchea spendAndRoute + spendAndRoute con la misma permission, no debe poder exceder el allowance del periodo. El total acumulado via multicall debe respetar el limite.

revokeAsSpender() NO valida que recipient != address(0), a diferencia de _validateAndDecodeExtraData(). Esto significa que una permission con executor valido pero recipient = address(0) puede ser revocada por el executor pero NO puede ser ejecutada (spendAndRoute revierte en el check de recipient). El invariante: si una permission puede ser revocada via revokeAsSpender, el hash debe coincidir con el que se revoca en SpendPermissionManager.

Callback abuse via ERC20 tokens con hooks (ERC-777, ERC-677): cuando _routeTokens() ejecuta SafeTransferLib.safeTransfer(token, recipient, value), si el token es ERC-777 y el recipient tiene un tokensReceived hook registrado en ERC-1820, el hook se ejecuta DESPUES del transfer. Desde ese callback, el recipient podria re-entrar al SpendRouter.

Multicallable + spendAndRouteWithSignature: si un executor batchea una approveWithSignature y un spendAndRoute en un multicall, la permission se aprueba Y ejecuta atomicamente. Verificar que la firma no pueda ser re-usada en otro contexto (replay cross-chain, cross-permission-manager).

decodeExtraData() valida length == 64 pero no valida que los addresses decodificados sean validos (non-zero). Solo encodeExtraData() y _validateAndDecodeExtraData() tienen zero-checks. Un extraData de 64 bytes con executor = address(0) pasaria decodeExtraData() sin revertir.
Allowance fija en SpendPermission no se ajusta por precio de token — un período con allowance alta puede ser drenado completamente en un momento de precio bajo
No existe oracle de precio en SpendRouter ni SpendPermissionManager — todas las cantidades son nominales en tokens, no en USD
El vault no tiene name ni symbol (ERC20('', '')) — las vault shares son indistinguibles en block explorers y wallets, aumentando el riesgo de phishing

En borrowedLiquidity() línea 62: `liquidity = latestBorrowingIndex(reserve) * reserve.totalBorrows / reserve.borrowingIndex` El orden de operaciones es: multiplicar latestBorrowingIndex * totalBorrows, LUEGO dividir. Esto evita truncación prematura. PERO: si latestBorrowingIndex * totalBorrows excede uint256 (overflow), la operación revertiría por Solidity >=0.8 checked arithmetic. Análisis de overflow: latestBorrowingIndex <= type(uint128).max (enforced en _updateIndexes línea 174), totalBorrows es uint256 sin cap explícito. Si totalBorrows acumula el monto total del protocolo y el índice se acumula durante años a tasas altas: max(latestBorrowingIndex) = 2^128 - 1 ≈ 3.4e38 Para que el producto overflow uint256 (2^256 ≈ 1.15e77): necesitaría totalBorrows > 1.15e77 / 3.4e38 ≈ 3.4e38. Prácticamente imposible. PERO: hay una truncación de rounding que sí importa. En _updateIndexes línea 172: `newTotalBorrows = newBorrowingIndex * reserve.totalBorrows / reserve.borrowingIndex` Esto se hace en cada update. Cada división trunca hacia abajo → totalBorrows decrece artificialmente por rounding en cada accrual. A largo plazo, totalBorrows puede ser menor de lo correcto, permitiendo que prestatarios paguen menos de lo que deben.

collectFees() calls collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper) instead of collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, vestPosition.tickUpper). The vesting position was created with its own tickUpper (copied from mainPosition at creation time), but after a subsequent rebalance the mainPosition ticks shift. From that point on, collectFees() attempts to burn/collect fees from a position range that does not match the actual vesting position, causing the call to touch the wrong Uniswap V3 position (or a nonexistent one), so vesting-position fees are never properly collected and protocol-fee accounting on those fees is also wrong.

_setSecondaryPositionsTicks() uses price() (spot price from slot0) to decide which direction the secondary position should be placed. price() reads sqrtPriceX96 from IUniswapV3Pool(pool).slot0() which is the instantaneous, manipulable spot price. If an attacker manipulates spot price at the time of rebalance (within the tickTwapDeviation tolerance), the secondary position ticks can be forced into the wrong direction, causing the secondary position to hold the wrong token and disrupting the intended 50:50 + OOR strategy.

_withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() calculates the amount of liquidity to remove as `vp.initialLiquidity * (lastValid - vp.lastUpdate) / (vp.endTs - vp.startTs)`. The denominator is the TOTAL vesting duration (endTs - startTs), not the remaining duration. However, the numerator uses `lastValid - vp.lastUpdate` which is only the elapsed time since last update. This means on each call, only a proportional slice of initialLiquidity is removed. The concern is that due to integer division truncation, the sum of all partial removals can be slightly less than initialLiquidity, leaving dust liquidity permanently locked in the vesting position even after endTs passes. The final call sets `lastValid == vp.endTs` and uses `vp.remainingLiquidity` which should catch the remainder — but only if the condition check on line 476 fires correctly. Line 476 reads `vestPosition.endTs` after `vestPosition = vp`, so it checks the just-written value, which is correct. However, if `vp.remainingLiquidity` went to 0 through rounding before endTs, the vesting flag is never cleared because `ongoingVestingPosition = false` is only set when `lastValid == vestPosition.endTs`.

pullFunds (line 209-214) and pushFunds (line 217-222) transfer tokens to/from the
yToken contract WITHOUT updating underlyingBalance, totalBorrows, or any state.

These functions read reserve as MEMORY (line 212, 219), not storage. No state changes
are persisted. The functions exist for the leverager to temporarily move funds for
operations like swap/rebalance.

CRITICAL FLOW:
pullFunds(asset, X) -> tokens leave yToken, underlyingBalance unchanged
... leverager does work ...
pushFunds(asset, X) -> tokens return to yToken, underlyingBalance unchanged

If pushFunds amount != pullFunds amount:
- push > pull: extra tokens stranded in yToken (not reflected in accounting)
- pull > push: actual balance < underlyingBalance -> redeems may fail

There is NO enforcement that pull and push amounts match. The leverager is
fully trusted to maintain this invariant.

Flow analysis:
1. Alice deposits 1000 tokens -> gets yTokens based on exchange rate
2. Leverager borrows 800 tokens -> totalBorrows += 800, underlyingBalance -= 800
3. Time passes -> interest accrues on totalBorrows
4. After accrual: totalBorrows = 800 + interest, totalLiquidity = 200 + (800 + interest)
5. Alice's yTokens are now worth more than 1000 (she earns interest)
6. Alice redeems -> gets 1000 + her share of interest

This is the correct flow. But what if leverager never repays?
7. underlyingBalance = 200 (only 200 available)
8. Alice tries to redeem all yTokens worth 1000+interest
9. Redeem fails: underlyingTokenAmount > availableLiquidity (200)
10. Alice can only redeem up to 200 tokens worth of yTokens

The exchange rate is "correct" accounting-wise (includes accrued borrows) but
the actual redeemable amount is limited by available liquidity. This is standard
but creates a bank-run scenario.

Every state-changing function follows the pattern:
1. updateState() - accrue interest, update indexes
2. Perform action (change balances, mint/burn)
3. updateInterestRates() - set new rate based on new state

If this ordering is violated, interest is calculated on wrong state. Verification:
- _deposit: updateState (108) -> transfer+mint+updateBalance (115-129) -> updateRates (131) OK
- _redeem: updateState (138) -> calculate+burn+updateBalance (141-150) -> updateRates (151) OK
- borrow: updateState (168) -> updateBorrows+updateBalance (172-173) -> transfer (176) -> updateRates (178) OK
- repay: updateState (190) -> updateBorrows+updateBalance (196-197) -> transfer (200) -> updateRates (202) OK

All four functions maintain correct ordering. No vulnerability found.

_sweepTokens() envia el balance COMPLETO del contrato a msg.sender sin restriccion de rol. Cualquier llamante de openLeveragedPosition() puede barrer tokens ajenos que hayan quedado "stuck" en el contrato (residuos de posiciones anteriores, tokens enviados directamente, diferencias de redondeo de vault deposits).

withdraw() verifica _isApprovedOrOwner pero envia los fondos a msg.sender, NO al owner del NFT. Un spender aprobado puede retirar los fondos del owner para SI MISMO, no para el owner. Esto viola el principio de que la aprobacion ERC721 solo deberia dar el derecho de transferir el NFT, no extraer el colateral subyacente.

En withdraw(), cuando borrowed == up.token1 (L289), el calculo de repayFromWithdraw usa amountOut0 en lugar de amountOut1. Esto permite que el deudor repague menos deuda de la correcta cuando token1 es el denomination, potencialmente dejando al protocolo con deuda no repagada o transfiriendo tokens incorrectos.

initVault() otorga forceApprove(type(uint256).max) al vault y al lendingPool para los tokens devueltos por IVault(vault).token0() y token1(). No hay validacion de que el vault sea un contrato legitimo. Un owner malicioso (o comprometido) puede llamar initVault con un vault malicioso que devuelva tokens arbitrarios, obteniendo aprobacion maxima para drenar cualquier token del contrato Leverager.

withdraw() acepta swapParams con recipient arbitrario (IMainnetRouter.ExactInputParams contiene un campo `recipient`). Si el usuario configura recipient=user (no el contrato), el swap envia tokens FUERA del contrato. El codigo luego hace `amountOut0 -= swapParams.amountIn` asumiendo que los tokens del swap regresaron al contrato, pero si el recipient es externo, el contrato no tiene esos tokens. Resultado: el contrato intenta transferir tokens que no tiene, o peor, la contabilidad de amountOut es incorrecta permitiendo que el usuario retire mas de lo que le corresponde.

Ownership del contrato Leverager usa Ownable de OpenZeppelin con transferOwnership en un solo paso (single-step). Si el owner hace transferOwnership a una direccion incorrecta por error tipografico, el control del protocolo se pierde permanentemente. Funciones criticas bloqueadas: initVault, toggleVaultLeverage, setSwapRouter, setPriceFeed, setLiquidationFee, setMinBorrow, enableTokenAsBorrowed.

liquidatePosition() computes `borrowedValue` at line 318 as `owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()`. The function `ERC20.decimals()` returns a raw uint8 (e.g. 8 for WBTC, 6 for USDC), NOT the power-of-ten scale factor. The correct divisor should be `10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()`. With WBTC (8 decimals) as denomination, the divisor is 8 instead of 1e8 — making `borrowedValue` 12,500,000x too large. Since `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` is almost always false, the `if` branch for protocol fee collection is NEVER entered. The protocol permanently loses all liquidation fee revenue. Additionally, `borrowedValue` is used to compare against `totalValueUSD` for the fee percent calculation — with a wrong scale, the comparison is meaningless.

`feeRecipient` is declared as a public state variable at line 47 but is NEVER set anywhere in the contract. There is no `setFeeRecipient()` function, no constructor parameter, and no initialization. The variable defaults to `address(0)`. In `liquidatePosition()`, if `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` (even with the L-11 bug, this might occur for tokens with 0-1 decimals), fees are sent to `address(0)` via `IERC20.safeTransfer(feeRecipient, pf0)`. Sending ERC20 tokens to `address(0)` burns them permanently (assuming the token follows the standard). This is both a permanent loss of protocol revenue and a missing admin function that the interface (`ILeverager.feeRecipient()`) already declares.

collectFees() collects fees for the vesting position using the wrong upper tick. Line 167 reads: collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper) instead of collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, vestPosition.tickUpper). The vesting position is minted at (vestPosition.tickLower, vestPosition.tickUpper), which equals mainPosition ticks AT CREATION TIME. But mainPosition.tickUpper changes on every rebalance. After the first rebalance post-vesting-creation, collectFees() burns/collects a DIFFERENT position than the actual vesting position. The actual vesting position accumulates fees that are never swept to feeRecipient. When _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() later burns and collects the real position, all its accrued fees transfer to the Strategy as idle balance with no protocol fee deducted.

checkPoolActivity() reverts with "timestamp 0" if any observation slot in the pool's circular buffer has an uninitialized zero timestamp. In Uniswap V3 pools, observations slots beyond the current write index may be uninitialized (timestamp=0). The function iterates ALL observationCardinality slots and explicitly reverts on zero timestamps rather than treating them as "not enough history" and returning false gracefully. Since _requirePriceWithinRange() calls checkPoolActivity(), any rebalance(), compound(), or addVestingPosition() permanently reverts until the pool's observation buffer is fully populated with real observations. An attacker can sustain this DoS cheaply by calling pool.increaseObservationCardinalityNext() to expand the buffer faster than swaps can fill it.

collectFees() is public, has no reentrancy guard, and transfers tokens to feeRecipient (line 175-176) BEFORE calling _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() (line 179). If token0 or token1 is an ERC-777 token, the feeRecipient's tokensReceived hook fires during safeTransfer, allowing reentry into collectFees(). In the reentrant call, the snapshot preBal is taken AFTER the outer call already transferred fees out, so protocolFees=0 in the inner call. But critically, _withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() is called in the INNER call: it updates vestPosition.lastUpdate = block.timestamp. When the outer call resumes and reaches line 179, the guard `if (vestPosition.lastUpdate == block.timestamp) return;` fires — the vesting position withdrawal is silently skipped for the outer call, effectively freezing vesting progress for that entire block interval.

addVestingPosition() sets ongoingVestingPosition = true AFTER calling IUniswapV3Pool(pool).mint() (line 448 vs line 452). This violates Checks-Effects-Interactions. During the uniswapV3MintCallback, the state variable ongoingVestingPosition is still false. If the pool (or token with ERC-777 hooks) triggers a reentrant call to addVestingPosition() during the callback: - require(!ongoingVestingPosition) passes because it is still false - A second mint is executed, creating a second vesting position in Uniswap - The second call completes: sets ongoingVestingPosition=true, vestPosition=second - The first call completes: sets ongoingVestingPosition=true, vestPosition is
  immediately overwritten or remains as the second vesting entry
The first position's liquidity is orphaned in the Uniswap pool with no way to burn it.

_setSecondaryPositionsTicks() uses price() which reads spot price from slot0() to decide which side of the current tick the secondary (out-of-range) position should be placed. The spot price is not TWAP-validated at this point — the TWAP check runs at the top of rebalance(), but _setSecondaryPositionsTicks() is called AFTER collectFees() and _addLiquidityToMainPosition(), reading a FRESH slot0() that may differ from the one checked. An attacker who can move the spot price within the allowed tickTwapDeviation range (±200 ticks) can flip the direction decision, placing the secondary position on the wrong side of the tick. This creates an in-range secondary position (consuming both tokens) instead of an out-of-range one (consuming only one token), wasting capital and misaligning the strategy's intended single-sided exposure.

If token0 or token1 (USDC, USDT, or any blocklist-capable ERC-20) adds the Strategy contract address to its blocklist, ALL core operations that transfer tokens are permanently bricked with no recovery path. Specifically: collectFees() reverts (transfer to feeRecipient), and since collectFees() is called at the start of rebalance(), compound(), and setProtocolFee(), all of those functions also revert. Vault.withdraw() calls IStrategy.collectFees() then safeTransferFrom(strategy, user, ...) — both fail. There is no emergency-exit function, no owner sweep, and no way to migrate liquidity to a new strategy address. All depositor funds are permanently locked.

The FullMath library contains a bug on line 87: `uint256 inv = (3 * denominator) ^ 2`. In Solidity, `^` is the bitwise XOR operator, NOT exponentiation. The correct Newton-Raphson seed for the modular inverse of `denominator` mod 2^4 is `(3 * denominator) XOR 2` which happens to equal `3*d ^ 2` only when 3*d is odd (denominator is odd, which is enforced upstream). Bitwise XOR with 2 flips bit 1 of (3*denominator). For odd denominator d, 3*d is always odd, so 3*d ends in binary ...1. XOR 2 = ...1 XOR 10 = ...11 in the lower bits. This gives a value that satisfies d*inv ≡ 1 (mod 2^4) for all odd d because the Newton-Raphson starting seed just needs denominator * inv ≡ 1 (mod 16), and by coincidence `3*d XOR 2` achieves this. The Slither report flagged this as incorrect-exp but the existing XOR behavior is actually correct for this algorithm. However, the code is confusing and any future modification risk introducing a real bug. This is marked as a false positive / informational.

_withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() computes liquidityToRemove as:
  initialLiquidity * (lastValid - vp.lastUpdate) / (vp.endTs - vp.startTs)
This formula uses (lastValid - lastUpdate) as the numerator but (endTs - startTs) as the denominator. For the first call, this is correct proportionally. For subsequent calls, the fraction represents "what proportion of the TOTAL duration elapsed since last update" rather than "what proportion of REMAINING liquidity should be released." As a result: if collectFees() is called infrequently, each call correctly releases a proportional slice. But if called very frequently in small intervals, integer division truncation causes each call to release 0 or 1 liquidity unit, while cumulative releases over the full period sum to LESS than initialLiquidity. The endTs catch-all (release all remainingLiquidity) would eventually correct this, but users who hold shares between creation and endTs receive less vested liquidity per unit time than promised.

In withdraw(), when the borrowed denomination equals token1, the code computes `repayFromWithdraw = amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount`. It uses `amountOut0` (the token0 output) as the ternary true-branch value instead of `amountOut1`. This is a copy-paste error from the token0 branch above. When denomination==token1 and amountOut1 < owedAmount, the code deducts amountOut0 (potentially a much larger or smaller number) from owedAmount and then subtracts it from amountOut1, causing an underflow (if amountOut0 > amountOut1) or an under-repayment to the lending pool while the user retains more tokens than they should.

In liquidatePosition(), the borrowed value in USD is computed as:
  `uint256 borrowedValue = owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals();`
This calls `.decimals()` (which returns e.g. 8 for WBTC, 6 for USDC) and divides by that raw integer, NOT by `10 ** decimals`. The correct formula would be `owedAmount * bPrice / (10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals())`. Dividing by 8 instead of 1e8 inflates `borrowedValue` by a factor of 1e7 for WBTC, making every solvent position appear massively undercollateralized. This means `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` is almost never true, so the protocol fee is never charged and the fee recipient receives nothing. More critically, it breaks the profitability calculation — liquidations always skip the fee path, transferring all residual value to the liquidator without the protocol's cut.

`feeRecipient` is declared as `address public feeRecipient` (line 47) but is never initialized in the constructor and there is no setter function for it. It remains `address(0)` permanently. In `liquidatePosition()`, any protocol fee (pf0, pf1) is transferred to `address(0)`, effectively burning those tokens. This was flagged by Slither as an uninitialized-state variable.

In withdraw(), when denomination==token1 and the vault returns enough token1 to cover the full owed amount, the repayFromWithdraw branch correctly takes from amountOut1. However the `owedAmount -= repayFromWithdraw` path is only followed when `amountOut1 >= owedAmount` (the else branch sets repayFromWithdraw=owedAmount). The deeper bug is in the true-branch: `amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount`. This results in `repayFromWithdraw = amountOut0` (token0 amount) being subtracted from `amountOut1`. Since `amountOut0` is denominated in WBTC (8 decimals) and `amountOut1` in USDC (6 decimals), even numerically small amountOut0 values can cause `amountOut1 -= repayFromWithdraw` to underflow in checked arithmetic (Solidity 0.8+), causing the transaction to revert. Users cannot partially withdraw when denomination==token1 and vault doesn't return enough token1.

In `openLeveragedPosition()`, after the vault deposit and swaps, the contract repays denomination tokens via:
  `uint256 denomBalance = IERC20(lp.denomination).balanceOf(address(this));`
  `ILendingPool(lendingPool).repay(lp.denomination, denomBalance);`
  `up.borrowedAmount = lp.maxBorrowAmount - denomBalance;`
The issue is that `denomBalance` includes ANY pre-existing denomination tokens stuck in the Leverager contract from previous operations (e.g., leftover from `_sweepTokens` that failed, or from a direct token transfer). If there are any stuck tokens, `denomBalance` will be higher than the true leftover from this operation, causing `up.borrowedAmount` to be LOWER than the actual net borrowed amount (it could even underflow if denomBalance > lp.maxBorrowAmount). The comment in the code acknowledges this risk but dismisses it. The real issue: `borrowedAmount` is used for liquidation threshold calculations — an understated borrowedAmount makes a position appear less leveraged than it truly is, potentially blocking legitimate liquidations.

In `isLiquidateable()`, the collateral percentage check uses:
  `uint256 base = owedAmount * 1e18 / (vp.maxTimesLeverage - 1e18);`
  `base = base < pos.initCollateralValue ? base : pos.initCollateralValue;`
  `if (owedAmount > totalDenom || totalDenom - owedAmount < vp.minCollateralPct * base / 1e18)`
The `base` is capped at `pos.initCollateralValue`, which is the collateral at position OPEN time (never updated during partial withdrawals via `withdraw()`). After partial withdrawals, `initCollateralValue` is reduced proportionally, but it still reflects the original opening value (scaled down). This means as a user makes partial withdrawals, the `base` could shrink, making the threshold easier to breach (potentially becoming liquidatable even when the current leverage is fine). However this is likely intentional design (conservative liquidation). The more concrete issue: `vp.maxTimesLeverage - 1e18` could underflow if `maxTimesLeverage < 1e18`, i.e., if admin sets leverage below 1x (which would be < 100% meaning no borrowing), causing a panic revert in `isLiquidateable()` — permanently DOSing liquidations for that vault.

_deposit (line 115): safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, yToken, amount)
Then line 129: reserve.underlyingBalance += amount

If the token has transfer fees (e.g., USDT-like tokens, deflationary tokens),
the actual amount received by yToken is less than `amount`. But underlyingBalance
increases by the full `amount`. This creates a permanent accounting discrepancy:
underlyingBalance > actual yToken balance.

Same issue in repay (line 200): safeTransferFrom transfers amount but fee-on-transfer
means yToken receives less. underlyingBalance += amount at line 197 is too high.

borrow (line 176): transferUnderlyingTo sends amount. If token has fee, recipient
gets less but underlyingBalance -= amount. This actually favors the pool (borrower
gets less but owes full amount).

CRITICAL: If the token has fees, the protocol becomes increasingly insolvent with
each deposit and repay, as accounting exceeds actual balance.

_deposit (line 120): require(yTokenAmount > MINIMUM_YTOKEN_AMOUNT, "deposit is dust amount")

This check only applies when yTokenAmount <= 1000. As the exchange rate diverges from 1:1
(due to interest accrual), the minimum deposit in underlying terms changes:
- If 1 yToken = 2 underlying: min deposit = 1001 * 2 = 2002 underlying
- If 1 yToken = 0.5 underlying: min deposit = 1001 * 0.5 = 500.5 underlying

The dust check is on yToken amount, not underlying amount. This means the effective
minimum deposit in underlying terms fluctuates with the exchange rate. At high exchange
rates (after significant interest accrual), the minimum deposit becomes large.

This could prevent small depositors from participating if exchange rate grows significantly.
Not a security issue but a UX concern.

En _updateIndexes() linea 174: `require(newBorrowingIndex <= type(uint128).max)` Si el indice supera 2^128 - 1, esta linea revierte. updateState() llama _updateIndexes(). Si el LendingPool llama updateState() al inicio de cada operacion (deposito, retiro, prestamo, repago), un require revertente aqui bloquea TODAS las operaciones del protocolo para esa reserva.
Cuando puede ocurrir: el indice crece con el interes compuesto acumulado. borrowingIndex inicial (tipicamente 1e27 = PRECISION). Si la tasa de interes es del 100% anual compuesto y el tiempo es largo: newBorrowingIndex = 1e27 * e^(1 * T) Para que newBorrowingIndex > 2^128 ≈ 3.4e38: 1e27 * e^T > 3.4e38 --> e^T > 3.4e11 --> T > ln(3.4e11) ≈ 26.3 anios a 100% anual. Con tasa 1000% anual: T ≈ 2.6 anios. Con tasa 10000% anual: T ≈ 3 meses.
Si InterestRateUtils no tiene cap de tasa maxima, o si el cap es muy alto (>1000%), y el protocolo lleva suficiente tiempo sin que nadie llame updateState(), el indice puede superar el uint128 max y el protocolo queda bloqueado PERMANENTEMENTE.
El bloqueo es PERMANENTE porque para updatear el indice necesitas llamar updateState(), y updateState() revierte. No hay forma de avanzar sin reducir el indice o el tiempo.

Como documentado en RL-W-02 (WildcardHunter), si borrowingIndex == 0: borrowedLiquidity() linea 62: `latestBorrowingIndex(reserve) * reserve.totalBorrows / reserve.borrowingIndex` Con borrowingIndex == 0 -> division por cero -> REVERT. Esta funcion es llamada por totalLiquidityAndBorrows() -> checkCapacity() -> deposit(). Tambien es llamada por utilizationRate() -> updateInterestRates() y borrowingRate(). Un borrowingIndex == 0 bloquea: depositos, calculo de tasas, y exchange rates.
Es un DoS de inicializacion, no de ataque. Pero si el LendingPool no valida que borrowingIndex > 0 antes de activar la reserva, la reserva queda bloqueada.

checkCapacity() linea 136-140: `require(totalLiquidity + depositAmount <= reserve.reserveCapacity)` Si la reserva esta casi al limite de capacidad y un depositor A envia una tx, un atacante puede front-runear con un deposito que lleva la capacidad al maximo. La tx de A revierte ("capacidad insuficiente"), aunque A hubiera llegado primero en condiciones normales.
Tambien: si el protocolo acumula interes que incrementa borrowedLiquidity() hasta llegar a reserveCapacity, TODOS los depositos nuevos son bloqueados automaticamente (checkCapacity revierte). Los prestamistas existentes pueden retirar pero no se pueden anadir nuevos.
Front-run grief: atacante puede grief sistematicamente a depositores de alto valor depositando un monto minimo para llenar el cap y luego retirando.

Con el tiempo, el interes acumulado incrementa borrowedLiquidity(): totalLiquidity = underlyingBalance + borrowedLiquidity (crece con interes) Si totalLiquidity > reserveCapacity (por interes acumulado, no por depositos nuevos), checkCapacity() revierte para CUALQUIER depositAmount > 0: `totalLiquidity + 0 <= reserveCapacity` --> FALSE. Esto bloquea efectivamente todos los depositos nuevos de forma automatica, sin accion del atacante.
Esto puede ser by design (el cap tambien aplica al interes acumulado), pero es importante documentarlo como un posible DoS de prestamistas que quieren reinvertir.

withdraw() uses amountOut0 instead of amountOut1 when computing repayFromWithdraw for the case where borrowed == token1 (line 232). The ternary reads:
  repayFromWithdraw = amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount
When amountOut1 < owedAmount (common: vault does not hold enough denomination to cover the debt), the true branch picks amountOut0 (the OTHER token's raw amount). Then line 234 subtracts: amountOut1 -= repayFromWithdraw. In a WBTC/USDC vault with denomination=USDC, amountOut0 is in WBTC units (1e8 precision) and amountOut1 is in USDC units (1e6 precision). If amountOut0 > amountOut1 (very likely after a rebalance), the subtraction underflows → panic revert. This permanently bricks withdraw() for ALL USDC-denominated positions whenever the vault holds more WBTC value than USDC value by raw integer comparison.

feeRecipient is declared on line 47 but is NEVER initialized. No constructor assignment and no setter function exists in Leverager. It permanently remains address(0). In liquidatePosition(), when a liquidation is profitable (totalValueUSD > borrowedValue), the contract calls:
  IERC20(up.token0).safeTransfer(feeRecipient, pf0)  -- safeTransfer to address(0)
  IERC20(up.token1).safeTransfer(feeRecipient, pf1)
Tokens that revert on transfer to address(0) (e.g., OZ ERC-20 with zero-address check) will cause ALL profitable liquidations to permanently revert. Even if WBTC/USDC don't revert, all liquidation fee revenue is burned forever. The Slither prepass flagged this explicitly.

withdraw() line 232-234: when borrowed == token1 and amountOut1 < owedAmount, repayFromWithdraw is set to amountOut0 (wrong token), then owedAmount is decremented by amountOut0, not amountOut1. Even in non-reverting cases (when amountOut0 <= amountOut1), owedAmount ends up underestimated by a cross-token unit error. The actual repay call on line 265 uses amountToRepay (the original owedAmount, correctly saved before the buggy branch). But positions[wp.id].borrowedAmount on line 289 is set to `totalOwedAmount - amountToRepay`, meaning the remaining debt stored is wrong. Over successive partial withdrawals, the stored borrowedAmount diverges from reality, allowing users to extract more collateral than they should or causing phantom debt that blocks future withdrawals.

The collectFees modifier (line 494-498) is applied to liquidatePosition() and calls IStrategy(strat).collectFees() BEFORE the isLiquidateable check. If the Strategy contract reverts on collectFees() for any reason (e.g., Uniswap position is out-of-range and collectFees has a require, or the vault's strategy has been changed to a broken address by the vault owner), ALL liquidations for that vault are permanently blocked. The Vault owner can exploit this: by updating vault.strategy() to a contract that always reverts on collectFees(), they make their leveraged position immune to liquidation regardless of collateral ratio.

In withdraw() with hasToSwap=true, lines 249 and 259 subtract swapParams.amountIn from amountOut0/amountOut1 WITHOUT verifying that amountOut >= swapParams.amountIn. The dev's own comment on line 247 acknowledges this: "might be good here to set amountIn to the lower of swapParams.amountIn and amountOut0". If the vault rebalances between position opening and withdrawal (concentrating liquidity toward one token), amountOut0 on withdrawal may be less than the swapParams.amountIn the user specified based on the old ratio. Result: amountOut0 -= swapParams.amountIn underflows → panic revert → user cannot withdraw. Same issue exists for amountOut1 on line 259.

setMinBorrow() can be called by the owner at any time to increase the minimum borrow threshold. withdraw() line 279-282 checks:
  require(up.initBorrowedUsd * (1e18 - wp.pctWithdraw) / 1e18 > minBorrow, ...)
using the CURRENT minBorrow, not the value at position open time. If the owner raises minBorrow after a position is opened, partial withdrawals may become permanently impossible. A user with initBorrowedUsd = 25e18 (opened when minBorrow=20e18) cannot do ANY partial withdraw if minBorrow is raised to 30e18, because any pctWithdraw < 1e18 leaves remaining < 30e18. They are forced to fully close (pctWithdraw == 1e18) even if they only want to reduce exposure.

isLiquidateable() calls IPriceFeed(pricefeed).getPrice(pos.denomination) (line 400). liquidatePosition() calls it again at line 317. PriceFeed uses Chainlink with a staleness check (heartbeat). During high-volatility periods — exactly when liquidations are most needed — Chainlink sequencers or heartbeat windows may fail. Any revert from getPrice() propagates up through isLiquidateable() → liquidatePosition() cannot proceed. There is no fallback oracle or circuit breaker. Additionally, setPriceFeed(address(0)) by the owner would set pricefeed to address(0), making every call to getPrice() revert (call to zero address).

reserveToYTokenExchangeRate() y yTokenToReserveExchangeRate() calculan el exchange rate basándose en totalLiquidityAndBorrows(), que llama borrowedLiquidity(), que llama latestBorrowingIndex() — esto SÍ usa el índice actualizado al timestamp actual.
Sin embargo, la función NO llama updateState() primero (no actualiza reserve.borrowingIndex ni reserve.totalBorrows en storage). Esto significa que el valor de exchange rate calculado es CORRECTO (usa latestBorrowingIndex que proyecta al tiempo actual), pero el valor en storage (reserve.totalBorrows, reserve.borrowingIndex) puede estar desactualizado.
El bug real: si el LendingPool calcula el exchange rate y LUEGO llama updateState() en la misma transacción, el exchange rate calculado reflejará el interés correcto. PERO si el LendingPool usa el exchange rate PARA calcular cuántos yTokens mintear, y updateState() no ha sido llamado todavía, el totalBorrows en storage es stale y el exchange rate real es diferente del calculado.
Caso concreto: un depósito entre el bloque N y N+1 sin llamar updateState() primero usa el exchange rate de bloque N → el depositante recibe más yTokens de lo que debería (el interés acumulado entre N y N+1 no se refleja en la deuda, entonces totalLiquidity parece más alto → exchange rate reserveToYToken más bajo → depositante recibe más yTokens).

CONVERGENCE: RL-M-01 + RL-D-02 + YLD-LP-M2 all touch repay/totalBorrows but none analyzed
the full accounting cycle with index normalization.

The critical insight: totalBorrows is updated in TWO different ways:
1. In _updateIndexes (line 156): newTotalBorrows = newBorrowingIndex * totalBorrows / borrowingIndex
   This REBASES totalBorrows to current index units.
2. In borrow (line 172): totalBorrows += amount (raw token amount)
3. In repay (line 196): totalBorrows -= amount (raw token amount)

After _updateIndexes, totalBorrows is in "current index" units. When borrow adds a raw
amount, it's adding tokens to an index-adjusted total. This is CORRECT because the protocol
only has one borrower (leverager) and tracks absolute debt, not per-user normalized debt.

BUT: the repay caps at totalBorrows (line 192-194). After updateState(), totalBorrows includes
accrued interest. If leverager calls repay(type(uint256).max), it repays totalBorrows exactly.
The leverager transfers totalBorrows tokens to yToken. underlyingBalance increases by totalBorrows.

THE BUG: If the leverager calls repay() in the same block as borrow() (same timestamp),
updateState() is a no-op (lastUpdateTimestamp == block.timestamp). totalBorrows is the value
from the last cross-block updateState. Interest accrued between the last updateState and now
is NOT reflected in storage totalBorrows, BUT it IS reflected in borrowedLiquidity() via
latestBorrowingIndex(). So:
- repay(type(uint256).max) repays storage totalBorrows (excluding intra-block interest)
- After repay, totalBorrows = 0
- BUT latestBorrowingIndex was calculated AFTER updateState which set lastUpdateTimestamp = now
- So borrowedLiquidity = latestIdx * 0 / borrowingIndex = 0. Correct.

Actually wait — updateState() at line 190 DOES update totalBorrows to include interest
(via _updateIndexes). So after updateState, totalBorrows IS the full debt including interest.
repay(type(uint256).max) caps at this updated value. The leverager transfers this exact amount.
underlyingBalance increases by the full amount. This is CORRECT.

REAL ISSUE: The rounding in _updateIndexes line 156:
newTotalBorrows = newBorrowingIndex * totalBorrows / borrowingIndex
This truncates. Over many updateState() calls (every tx), the cumulative rounding error
means totalBorrows is LESS than the mathematically correct value.
Lenders receive LESS interest than they should.

Quantification: With PRECISION=1e27, each truncation loses at most 1 unit of borrowingIndex.
The loss per update is at most totalBorrows / borrowingIndex² (negligible for large indices).
Over 10,000 updates with 1M USDC borrowed: total loss ≈ 10000 * 1e6 * 1e6 / (1e27)² ≈ 0.
This is dust. NOT exploitable.

CONVERGENCE: YLD-LP-F1 + YLD-LP-TB2 both identify pullFunds as dangerous.
DeepDive goes further: analyzing the INTERACTION between pullFunds and redeem.

pullFunds (line 209-214):
1. Only checks msg.sender == leverager
2. Reads reserve as MEMORY (no state changes)
3. Calls yToken.transferUnderlyingTo(leverager, amount)
4. NO check: amount <= reserve.underlyingBalance
5. NO check: amount <= yToken.actualBalance
6. NO update to underlyingBalance

The yToken.transferUnderlyingTo does a safeTransfer, so it reverts if yToken doesn't have
enough tokens. This is the ONLY protection.

ATTACK SCENARIO (requires leverager bug or compromise):
1. Lenders deposit 1000 USDC → yToken holds 1000 USDC, underlyingBalance = 1000
2. Leverager borrows 500 USDC → yToken holds 500, underlyingBalance = 500, totalBorrows = 500
3. Leverager calls pullFunds(USDC, 500)
4. yToken now holds 0 USDC, but underlyingBalance STILL = 500
5. Lender tries to redeem → _redeem checks underlyingBalance (500) ≥ redemption amount
6. _redeem calls yToken.burn which does safeTransfer of underlying
7. safeTransfer REVERTS — yToken has 0 tokens but tries to send
8. ALL REDEEMS FAIL until leverager pushes funds back

The protocol comment says "Should always push the same amount of tokens back, at the end
of the transaction." But this is NOT enforced on-chain. There is no callback, no check,
no require that pullFunds and pushFunds happen atomically.

If the leverager contract has ANY code path where pullFunds succeeds but pushFunds fails
(or pushes a different amount), lender funds are trapped.

WORSE: between pullFunds and pushFunds (even within the same tx), if there's ANY external
call that could fail or reenter, the funds are at risk. The leverager is NOT behind
the same nonReentrant guard as LendingPool.

CONVERGENCE: RL-M-04 identified utilizationRate > PRECISION as possible.
DeepDive proves the exact mechanism and downstream impact.

The chain:
1. borrowedLiquidity() = latestBorrowingIndex * totalBorrows / borrowingIndex
   This grows with compound interest (latestBorrowingIndex increases every second).
2. availableLiquidity() = underlyingBalance (static, only changes on deposit/redeem/borrow/repay)
3. totalLiquidity = underlyingBalance + borrowedLiquidity()
4. utilizationRate = borrowedLiquidity / totalLiquidity

After a long time without updateState() (or even with it, as interest compounds):
borrowedLiquidity grows WITHOUT underlyingBalance growing.

Example: underlyingBalance = 200, initial totalBorrows = 800. utilization = 80%.
After 1 year at 50% APY: borrowedLiquidity ≈ 800 * 1.5 = 1200.
totalLiquidity = 200 + 1200 = 1400. utilization = 1200/1400 = 85.7%. Still < 100%.

Can utilization exceed 100%? NO mathematically:
utilization = borrows / (available + borrows). This is always < 100% as long as available > 0.
If available = 0: utilization = borrows / borrows = 100% exactly.

BUT WAIT: _updateIndexes line 156 updates totalBorrows:
newTotalBorrows = newBorrowingIndex * totalBorrows / borrowingIndex
This INCREASES totalBorrows. But underlyingBalance doesn't change.
So totalLiquidity = underlyingBalance + newTotalBorrows.
utilizationRate = newTotalBorrows / (underlyingBalance + newTotalBorrows).

With underlyingBalance = 0 (all borrowed): utilizationRate = totalBorrows / totalBorrows = PRECISION.
With underlyingBalance > 0: utilizationRate < PRECISION.

HOWEVER: there's a view function path. If totalLiquidityAndBorrows() is called WITHOUT
updateState() first, borrowedLiquidity uses latestBorrowingIndex (which projects interest),
but totalBorrows in storage hasn't been updated. The view function uses:
borrowedLiquidity = latestBorrowingIndex * storedTotalBorrows / storedBorrowingIndex

The stored values are stale, but latestBorrowingIndex is fresh. The computation is still:
borrows = latest * stored_borrows / stored_index
total = underlyingBalance + borrows
util = borrows / total

This is still mathematically bounded by 100% as long as underlyingBalance >= 0.
underlyingBalance is uint256, so it's always >= 0.

CONCLUSION: utilizationRate CANNOT exceed PRECISION (100%).
RL-M-04 was a FALSE POSITIVE for the >100% case.

BUT: the interest rate at 100% utilization is maxBorrowingRate (default 150% = 15000 bps).
This is the ACTUAL config from initReserve line 236:
(8000, 2000, 9000, 5000, 15000) = (80% util → 20% rate, 90% → 50%, 100% → 150%)

At 150% APY, calculateCompoundedInterest Taylor approximation diverges from true exponential.
After 1 year without update at 150% rate:
True: e^1.5 ≈ 4.4817
Taylor 3rd order: 1 + 1.5 + 1.5²*0.5 = 1 + 1.5 + 1.125 + 0.5625 = 4.1875
Error: ~6.6% UNDERPAYMENT to lenders at extreme rates with infrequent updates.
This is a known approximation but the magnitude at max rate is significant.

CONVERGENCE: YLD-LP-DOS2 partially identifies this. DeepDive proves the full value extraction.

Scenario:
1. First depositor deposits 10,000 USDC. Gets 10,000 - 1000 = 9,000 yTokens.
   Dead address gets 1,000 yTokens. underlyingBalance = 10,000.
2. Leverager borrows 8,000. underlyingBalance = 2,000. totalBorrows = 8,000.
3. Time passes. Interest accrues. totalBorrows grows to 10,000 (25% interest).
4. totalLiquidity = 2,000 + 10,000 = 12,000.
5. yTokenToReserve rate = 12,000 * PRECISION / 10,000 = 1.2 * PRECISION.
6. First depositor redeems all 9,000 yTokens.
   underlyingTokenAmount = 1.2 * 9,000 = 10,800.
   But availableLiquidity = 2,000. FAILS: 10,800 > 2,000.
7. First depositor can only redeem up to 2,000 USDC worth of yTokens.
   yTokensToRedeem = 2,000 / 1.2 = 1,666 yTokens. Gets 2,000 USDC.
8. Now: yToken supply = 10,000 - 1,666 = 8,334. underlyingBalance = 0. totalBorrows = 10,000.
9. Leverager repays full 10,000 USDC. underlyingBalance = 10,000. totalBorrows = 0.
10. Depositor redeems remaining 7,334 yTokens.
    Exchange rate = 10,000 / 8,334 = 1.2. Gets 7,334 * 1.2 = 8,800.
11. Total received: 2,000 + 8,800 = 10,800. Deposited 10,000. Earned 800 interest. Correct.
12. Dead shares (1,000) still hold: 1,000 * 1.2 = 1,200 USDC of value.

Now the problematic scenario:
13. ALL live holders fully redeem. Only dead shares (1,000) remain.
14. underlyingBalance has the dead shares' value (1,200 USDC).
15. New depositor deposits 100 USDC.
    Exchange rate reserveToYToken = 1,000 * PRECISION / 1,200 = 0.833 * PRECISION
    yTokens minted = 100 * 0.833 = 83 yTokens.
16. New depositor owns 83 / (1000 + 83) = 7.7% of total yTokens.
17. totalLiquidity = 1,200 + 100 = 1,300. New depositor's share = 7.7% * 1,300 = 100.
18. This is CORRECT — the new depositor gets exactly their value back.

HOWEVER: the 1,200 USDC "belonging" to dead shares is permanently locked.
No one can ever redeem those tokens. They are LOST PROTOCOL VALUE.

The loss comes from: dead shares were minted at 1:1 rate but accumulated interest.
The 200 USDC of interest earned by dead shares (1000 shares * 0.2 interest) is
effectively removed from circulation forever.

MAGNITUDE: dead shares earn proportional interest. With 1000 dead shares out of 10,000 total,
dead shares capture 10% of all interest. This is a PERMANENT 10% tax on interest earned.
As the total supply grows (more depositors), the dead share proportion shrinks.
With 1M total supply, dead shares are 0.1% — negligible.

CRITICAL FOR SMALL POOLS: In a pool with only a few depositors and small amounts,
the dead share interest capture is significant (up to 10% of first depositor's interest).

CONVERGENCE: RL-D-04 identified this asymmetry. DeepDive verifies and quantifies.

checkCapacity (ReserveLogic line 120-124) is called ONLY in _deposit (line 111).
borrow() (line 159-179) does NOT call checkCapacity.
repay() does NOT call checkCapacity.

The capacity check ensures: totalLiquidity + depositAmount <= reserveCapacity.
But totalLiquidity = underlyingBalance + borrowedLiquidity().
borrowedLiquidity grows with interest compounding.

Scenario:
1. reserveCapacity = 1,000,000 USDC.
2. Deposits fill pool to 1,000,000 USDC. No more deposits accepted.
3. Leverager borrows 800,000. underlyingBalance = 200,000. totalBorrows = 800,000.
4. After 1 year at 50% rate: borrowedLiquidity ≈ 1,200,000.
5. totalLiquidity = 200,000 + 1,200,000 = 1,400,000.
6. 1,400,000 > reserveCapacity (1,000,000).
7. checkCapacity fails for ANY new deposit (even 1 wei):
   1,400,000 + 1 > 1,000,000. REVERT.
8. New deposits are PERMANENTLY blocked until admin increases reserveCapacity
   OR until enough interest is repaid to bring totalLiquidity below cap.

This is a SOFT DoS: existing lenders can still redeem, leverager can repay.
But no new liquidity can enter the pool. This could prevent:
- Lenders from re-depositing after partial redeems
- New lenders from providing liquidity during high-demand periods
- The protocol from growing organically

The admin must actively monitor and adjust reserveCapacity.
If reserveCapacity was set to type(uint256).max (the default in initReserve line 63),
this is not an issue. But if admin sets a specific cap, it WILL be exceeded by interest.

CONVERGENCE: YLD-LP-D3 + YLD-LP-M3 + YLD-LP-F2 all touch this. DeepDive proves the
exact mechanics and shows why this is worse than standard lending protocols.

In Aave/Compound: bad debt is socialized via a reserve factor or insurance module.
When a borrower defaults, the protocol can:
1. Write off the bad debt (reduce totalBorrows)
2. Use the safety module to cover lender losses
3. Socialize losses across all depositors proportionally

In Yieldoor: NONE of these mechanisms exist.
- No reserve factor (0% protocol fee)
- No safety module or insurance fund
- No bad debt write-off function
- No socialized loss mechanism

CONVERGENCE: YLD-LP-M1 identifies deposit rounding. DeepDive analyzes the full round-trip.

Deposit (line 118): yTokenAmount = amount * exchangeRate / PRECISION
where exchangeRate = totalYTokens * PRECISION / totalLiquidity (reserveToYToken)
→ yTokenAmount = amount * totalYTokens / totalLiquidity (rounds DOWN → user gets fewer yTokens)

Redeem (line 141): underlyingTokenAmount = yTokenToReserveRate * yAssetAmount / PRECISION
where yTokenToReserveRate = totalLiquidity * PRECISION / totalYTokens
→ underlyingTokenAmount = yAssetAmount * totalLiquidity / totalYTokens (rounds DOWN → user gets fewer underlying)

BOTH operations round DOWN against the user. This means:
- Depositor gets fewer yTokens than their deposit is worth
- Redeemer gets fewer underlying than their yTokens are worth

A full round-trip (deposit X → immediately redeem all yTokens) loses up to 2 rounding units.
The "lost" value goes to the pool (benefiting remaining yToken holders and dead shares).

This is the CORRECT and SAFE rounding direction for the protocol. If either operation
rounded UP (in favor of user), it would enable value extraction:
- Deposit rounding UP: user gets more yTokens → steals from existing holders
- Redeem rounding UP: user gets more underlying → steals from remaining holders

ASSESSMENT: Rounding is correct. Both directions favor the protocol/remaining holders.
The per-operation loss is at most 1 wei equivalent. NOT a vulnerability.

Path.skipToken() return value is ignored in Leverager._getTokenIn(). The function Path.skipToken() is a pure function that returns a NEW bytes slice — it does NOT mutate the input bytes in place. In _getTokenIn(), the loop calls `path.skipToken()` but discards the return value, so `path` never advances. For multi-hop paths, hasMultiplePools() never becomes false, causing an infinite loop (gas exhaustion) or — if the compiler loop limit is hit — getting the wrong tokenIn (always the first pool's tokenB instead of the last pool's tokenIn). This means the `require(tokenIn == lp.denomination, ...)` check can be bypassed by constructing a multi-hop path where the denomination appears somewhere in the middle while an arbitrary tokenIn is last.

In Leverager.liquidatePosition() (line 318), the borrowed value in USD is calculated as:
  `uint256 borrowedValue = owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals();`
This uses the raw return of `.decimals()` (e.g., 8 for WBTC, 6 for USDC) as the divisor instead of `10 ** ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()`. For WBTC (8 decimals), the divisor should be 1e8 but is instead 8, making borrowedValue approximately 12,500,000x too large. This causes `totalValueUSD > borrowedValue` to be almost always FALSE, so the protocol never collects liquidation fees (the fee branch is skipped). More critically, it means the position's owed amount appears far larger than the collateral in the fee calculation, preventing fee distribution to feeRecipient.

In Leverager.withdraw() (line 232), the token1 repayment branch contains a copy-paste bug:
  `uint256 repayFromWithdraw = amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount;`
When `borrowed == up.token1`, the code should use `amountOut1` in the ternary true branch but instead uses `amountOut0`. If `amountOut1 < owedAmount`, the function subtracts `amountOut0` from `owedAmount` instead of `amountOut1`, and then also subtracts `repayFromWithdraw` from `amountOut1`. This means: 1) The owed amount is reduced by the wrong value (token0 amount instead of token1 amount) 2) `amountOut1` is decremented by `amountOut0`, which can underflow if amountOut0 > amountOut1. The result: wrong repayment amount is computed, potentially leaving the lending pool under-repaid or causing a revert on underflow.

In FullMath.mulDiv() (line 87), the Newton-Raphson seed for the modular inverse is:
  `uint256 inv = (3 * denominator) ^ 2;`
The `^` operator in Solidity is bitwise XOR, NOT exponentiation. The mathematically correct seed formula should be `(3 * denominator) ** 2` which gives the initial approximation for the modular inverse (correct for 4 bits). Instead, `^ 2` flips only bit 1 of `(3 * denominator)`. The Newton-Raphson iteration `inv *= 2 - denominator * inv` requires the seed to satisfy `denominator * inv = 1 mod 2^4`. With the XOR seed, this condition may not hold for most denominators, producing a wrong modular inverse and thus a wrong quotient from mulDiv. Since FullMath.mulDiv is used extensively in LiquidityAmounts (getLiquidityForAmount0/1, getAmountsForLiquidity), incorrect liquidity computations propagate to vault deposits and withdrawals.

Leverager.feeRecipient is declared as a public state variable (line 47) but is never initialized — neither in the constructor nor via any setter function. The prepass signal confirms this. In liquidatePosition(), when a liquidation is profitable (totalValueUSD > borrowedValue), the protocol fee is sent to feeRecipient (lines 328-329):
  `if (pf0 > 0) IERC20(up.token0).safeTransfer(feeRecipient, pf0);`
  `if (pf1 > 0) IERC20(up.token1).safeTransfer(feeRecipient, pf1);`
Since feeRecipient == address(0), all protocol fees are burned (sent to the zero address). Note: with LIB-02 also present, borrowedValue computation is wrong so the profitable branch is rarely entered anyway — but both bugs must be fixed independently.

For USDC (decimals=6): divisor is 6 instead of 1e6 — inflates borrowedValue by ~166,666x. For WBTC (decimals=8): divisor is 8 instead of 1e8 — inflates by ~12,500,000x. For WETH (decimals=18): divisor is 18 instead of 1e18 — inflates by ~5.5e16x. Since borrowedValue >> totalValueUSD in every realistic case, the condition `if (totalValueUSD > borrowedValue)` is ALWAYS false — the protocol fee block is never entered, feeRecipient receives 0 fees from ALL liquidations forever. Compare with correct usage on line 131 and line 178 of the same file which use `(10 ** ERC20(lp.denomination).decimals())` correctly.

Leverager.feeRecipient is declared as `address public feeRecipient` (line 47) but is never initialized in the constructor, and there is no owner-callable setFeeRecipient() function in the contract. Its value is permanently address(0). The prepass (Slither) flagged this. If the decimals bug (DH-02) is ever fixed, all liquidation fees would be sent to address(0), permanently burning them. This is a separate protocol invariant violation: the protocol claims to charge a liquidation fee for its own economic sustainability, but the fee recipient is address(0).

In Leverager.isLiquidateable() (line 408), the formula:
  uint256 base = owedAmount * 1e18 / (vp.maxTimesLeverage - 1e18)
will revert with division-by-zero if vp.maxTimesLeverage == 1e18, and with arithmetic underflow (Solidity 0.8+) if vp.maxTimesLeverage < 1e18. Neither initVault() nor changeVaultMaxLeverage() enforce that maxTimesLeverage > 1e18. If an owner sets maxTimesLeverage = 1e18 (intending to mean "1x leverage max"), the isLiquidateable() function reverts for ALL positions in that vault. Since liquidatePosition() calls isLiquidateable() (line 302), liquidations become permanently impossible for that vault. Existing undercollateralised positions cannot be cleared; the lending pool accumulates irrecoverable bad debt.

In Leverager.openLeveragedPosition() (line 198), _sweepTokens(token0, token1) sends the ENTIRE balance of token0 and token1 held by the Leverager contract to msg.sender. This is a necessary cleanup for the caller's own excess tokens. However, this creates a cross-position contamination risk: if any prior failed transaction, griefing donation, or rounding residual left token0 or token1 in the Leverager, ALL of it is swept to the current caller — including tokens that belong to the lending pool (e.g. flashloan dust) or were stuck from previous users. More importantly: the sweep sends all of token0 AND token1. If denomination == token0, token1 residuals (e.g. unused swap output) are sent to the caller gratis. If denomination is a third token (e.g. WETH), both token0 and token1 residuals from swaps are swept. The lending pool's pullFunds/pushFunds pair should balance exactly, but any rounding in exactOutput swap (amountIn slightly less than amortised), combined with sweeping the full balance, means the caller profits from any dust at the lending pool's expense.

In Leverager.withdraw() (line 247-249), when hasToSwap=true, the code decrements amountOut0 by swapParams.amountIn WITHOUT first verifying that swapParams.amountIn <= amountOut0. The developer acknowledges this in a comment at line 247:
  "// might be good here to set amountIn to the lower of swapParams.amountIn and amountOut0"
This is a known-but-unimplemented safety check. If swapParams.amountIn > amountOut0, the subtraction at line 249 underflows (Solidity 0.8+ checked arithmetic), causing a revert that permanently locks the user's position — they cannot withdraw because their own swap parameters cause the function to revert, and they may not be able to correct this if the vault's balance has shifted since they constructed the params. The same issue exists for amountOut1 at line 259.

In Leverager._calculateTokenValues() (line 447), when chPrice1 == 0 (token1 has no pricefeed), the token1 USD value is computed as:
  usdValue += amount1 * PRECISION / price * chPrice0 / decimals0
The order of operations is: ((amount1 * PRECISION / price) * chPrice0) / decimals0. For small amount1 values relative to PRECISION/price, the intermediate expression `amount1 * PRECISION / price` truncates to 0 before the second multiplication. This causes token1's contribution to the USD value to be silently set to zero, understating the collateral value of LP positions that hold mostly token1. Compare with the chPrice0==0 branch (line 445) which correctly multiplies first:
  usdValue += (amount0 * price / PRECISION) * chPrice1 / decimals1
The asymmetry between the two branches can cause healthy positions to appear undercollateralised and be incorrectly flagged as liquidatable.

collectFees() (Strategy.sol line 167) calls
  collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper)
instead of
  collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, vestPosition.tickUpper).
The vesting position is created with its ticks matching mainPosition at creation time.  After any rebalance the main ticks shift while vestPosition ticks are frozen. collectFees() then targets a non-existent Uniswap position (wrong tickUpper), so the burn(0)/collect call silently collects zero fees from the vesting position — or reverts with Uniswap's "NP" error if the mixed-tick range is completely invalid — permanently DoS-ing collectFees, rebalance, and compound.

Strategy constructor (lines 96-97) grants type(uint256).max approval on both token0 and token1 to the vault address via forceApprove().  No function exists to reduce or revoke this approval.  If the vault is ever upgraded to a malicious implementation (if it is a proxy) or if a re-entrancy bug is discovered in the vault, the vault can call IERC20.transferFrom(strategy, attacker, balance) and drain all idle tokens held by the Strategy without any further authorization from the Strategy contract.

changePositionWidth() (Strategy.sol line 395) is external with no access control modifier of its own.  It delegates access control to the internal call to rebalance(), which carries onlyRebalancer.  The Solidity transaction atomicity means non-rebalancer callers are effectively blocked (the entire tx reverts). However the design creates an asymmetry: the rebalancer can unilaterally change positionWidth (a protocol-wide configuration parameter) without any approval from the owner.  A compromised or malicious rebalancer can set positionWidth to an extreme value (including 0, which passes the `(_newWidth/2) % tickSpacing == 0` validation since `0 % N == 0`) and immediately trigger a rebalance. Setting positionWidth=0 yields tickLower == tickUpper — an invalid Uniswap position that causes every subsequent mint to revert with "TLU", permanently DoS-ing the vault.

_withdrawPartOfVestingPosition() (Strategy.sol lines 465-467) computes the incremental liquidity to remove using:

  liquidityToRemove = vp.initialLiquidity * (lastValid - vp.lastUpdate)
                      / (vp.endTs - vp.startTs)

The numerator base is initialLiquidity (the ORIGINAL full amount) but the time window (lastValid - vp.lastUpdate) is only the incremental elapsed interval since the last update, not the full elapsed time from startTs.  This formula is the correct linear-vesting formula ONLY if called exactly once.  When called multiple times (as collectFees() is public and called on every rebalance), the formula distributes a fraction of initialLiquidity per interval, with rounding truncation on each step.  Because truncation always rounds down, the SUM of all intermediate removals is slightly LESS than initialLiquidity, leaving unremovable dust in remainingLiquidity.  However, in the worst case with very small initialLiquidity (e.g., 1 unit) and very long duration, every intermediate call computes liquidityToRemove = 0 (integer division floor), and the vesting position never vests incrementally — the entire amount only releases at endTs.

collectFees() is a public function callable by ANY address with no access control. It collects all outstanding Uniswap fees and immediately transfers the protocol's share (protocolFee bps) to feeRecipient.  setProtocolFee() calls collectFees() internally to "snapshot" fees at the current rate before changing to the new rate. However, this frontrun protection only works if the owner's setProtocolFee() tx executes BEFORE any external collectFees() call.  An attacker watching the mempool can front-run setProtocolFee(lower_rate) with a collectFees() call, causing all accumulated fees to be collected at the OLD (higher) rate.

Exhaustive scan of Strategy.sol confirms ZERO cryptographic signature mechanisms. No ecrecover, ECDSA.recover, EIP-712 domain separator, nonces, permit(), ERC-2612, Permit2, meta-transactions, or ERC-2771 _msgSender() anywhere in the contract or its libraries (FullMath, TickMath, LiquidityAmounts). All access control uses direct msg.sender comparisons:
  - onlyVault:      msg.sender == vault
  - onlyRebalancer: msg.sender == rebalancer
  - onlyOwner:      Ownable (msg.sender == owner())
This is the primary SignatureHunter checklist result — negative finding.
withdraw() reverts con minAmounts > 0 cuando el pool esta OOR — usuarios no pueden salir si el precio se mueve
collectFees() revert bloquea TODOS los deposits y withdrawals — punto unico de fallo

In withdraw() at line 232, the else-if branch for borrowed == up.token1 contains a copy-paste bug: the ternary expression returns amountOut0 instead of amountOut1. The correct line for token0 (line 228) reads:
  repayFromWithdraw = amountOut0 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount
But the token1 branch (line 232) reads:
  repayFromWithdraw = amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount
The condition checks amountOut1 but returns amountOut0 in the true branch. This causes two failure modes: (A) if amountOut0 > amountOut1, then amountOut1 -= repayFromWithdraw underflows (checked arithmetic revert), permanently DoS-ing withdraw for any token1-denominated position. (B) if amountOut0 < amountOut1, the repayment is undercounted (owedAmount is reduced by amountOut0 units instead of amountOut1 units), allowing the user to underpay their debt.

In liquidatePosition() at line 318, borrowedValue is computed as:
  borrowedValue = owedAmount * bPrice / ERC20(up.denomination).decimals()
This uses the raw return of decimals() (e.g., 6 for USDC, 8 for WBTC, 18 for WETH) as the divisor instead of 10 ** decimals() (i.e., 1e6, 1e8, 1e18). For WBTC (8 decimals): divisor is 8 instead of 100_000_000, inflating borrowedValue by a factor of 12,500,000x. For USDC (6 decimals): inflated by ~166,667x. Compare with the correct pattern used elsewhere in the same file:
  - Line 131: * (10 ** ERC20(lp.denomination).decimals())
  - Line 401: * (10 ** ERC20(pos.denomination).decimals())
The inflation makes totalValueUSD > borrowedValue virtually always false, so the protocol fee block is never executed. The protocol earns zero liquidation fees. Additionally, since borrowedValue is used nowhere else in the function (only in the fee calculation), this specific bug has no impact on whether a position can be liquidated or how much the liquidator receives — only the protocol fee is affected.

The state variable feeRecipient (line 47) is declared public but never initialized and has no setter function anywhere in the contract. It permanently remains address(0). Any liquidation fee tokens computed in liquidatePosition() that pass the totalValueUSD > borrowedValue check are sent via safeTransfer(feeRecipient, pf0/pf1) to address(0), permanently burning them. Slither flagged this as uninitialized-state. Combined with HYP-TB-02 (where the check is almost always skipped due to the decimals bug), this means that even if HYP-TB-02 is fixed, fees would still be burned. The interface ILeverager.feeRecipient() exists and is callable, confirming external parties expect a valid address.

In withdraw() at line 249, amountOut0 is decremented by swapParams.amountIn AFTER the exactInput swap executes, but there is no validation that swapParams.amountIn does not exceed the actual amountOut0 available. The code comment at line 247 explicitly acknowledges this: "might be good here to set amountIn to the lower of swapParams.amountIn and amountOut0". If the user (or a front-runner who manipulates vault balances) causes amountOut0 to be smaller than swapParams.amountIn, the subtraction at line 249 underflows under checked arithmetic, reverting the withdraw. More critically, the swap on line 248 executes BEFORE the underflow check — meaning the router could consume tokens from the contract's balance (including stuck tokens from other users) before the tx reverts. If the tx does NOT revert (because the contract has extra tokens covering the difference), the user has used more than their entitled vault withdrawal to pay for swaps.

The collectFees modifier in liquidatePosition() (line 494-498) executes BEFORE the nonReentrant modifier in the function signature:
  function liquidatePosition(LiquidateParams calldata liqParams)
    external collectFees(liqParams.id) nonReentrant
In Solidity, modifiers execute in declaration order. Therefore IStrategy.collectFees() is called before the ReentrancyGuard mutex is set. If the strategy uses an ERC-777 tokensReceived hook or any other callback mechanism, that callback fires before the reentrancy lock is active. An attacker controlling a malicious strategy (or exploiting a strategy with ERC-777 tokens in its fee sweep) could re-enter liquidatePosition() for the same position ID. The inner call would succeed (position still exists, mutex not set), burning the NFT and sending tokens to the re-entrant caller. The outer call then sees a deleted position, and isLiquidateable() would return false (denominator in base calculation would be 0 → revert). This constitutes a double-liquidation attempt where only the inner succeeds, but could enable theft of liquidation proceeds.

Fee-on-transfer (FoT) tokens break the repayment invariant in both withdraw() and liquidatePosition(). In withdraw() at line 263:
  IERC20(up.denomination).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), owedAmount)
If denomination is a FoT token, the contract receives owedAmount * (1 - fee%) < owedAmount. Then at line 265: ILendingPool(lendingPool).repay(borrowed, amountToRepay) is called with the original amountToRepay (not the actually-received amount). The LendingPool repay() does a safeTransferFrom(msg.sender=leverager, yTokenAddress, amount), and since Leverager doesn't have enough balance, the tx reverts. This permanently prevents closing any position denominated in a FoT token via withdraw(). The same pattern exists in liquidatePosition() at line 369-371. Additionally, in openLeveragedPosition() at lines 116-117, safeTransferFrom from the user deposits less than lp.amount0In/lp.amount1In into the Leverager, but the vault deposit at line 127 uses the original vault0In/vault1In values (already accounting for flash loan), so the accounting still works — but the user effectively paid more (the FoT fee) without getting commensurate vault shares.

In isLiquidateable() at line 408, the formula computes:
  base = owedAmount * 1e18 / (vp.maxTimesLeverage - 1e18)
If vp.maxTimesLeverage equals exactly 1e18 (1x leverage, meaning zero borrowing is allowed), the denominator is zero → division by zero revert. If maxTimesLeverage is less than 1e18 (which changeVaultMaxLeverage() allows since there is no lower-bound validation), the subtraction underflows under checked arithmetic → revert. Both cases permanently block isLiquidateable() and transitively liquidatePosition() for all positions in that vault. The owner function changeVaultMaxLeverage() (line 524-527) accepts any uint256 value with no validation, making this misconfiguration trivially possible. The owner could call it with 0, 1, or 1e18 and brick all liquidations.

borrow (line 159-179) only checks:

2. reserve not frozen
3. borrowing enabled

There is NO check against:

pullFunds (line 209-214):

- Calls yToken.transferUnderlyingTo with arbitrary amount
- No check against available liquidity

initReserve (line 49-64) checks lastUpdateTimestamp == 0 to prevent re-initialization.

timestamp, not at yTokenAddress or other fields. If somehow lastUpdateTimestamp were

In withdraw() at lines 231-235, the token1-denomination branch has a copy-paste bug:
  } else if (borrowed == up.token1) {
      uint256 repayFromWithdraw = amountOut1 < owedAmount ? amountOut0 : owedAmount; // BUG
      owedAmount -= repayFromWithdraw;
      amountOut1 -= repayFromWithdraw; // then subtracts the wrong amount from amountOut1
  }
When amountOut1 < owedAmount (common case: partial repayment), repayFromWithdraw = amountOut0 instead of amountOut1. With token0=WBTC (1e8 scale) and token1=USDC (1e6 scale):
  - amountOut0 could be ~1e7 (0.1 WBTC)
  - owedAmount could be ~500e6 (500 USDC)
  - amountOut0 (1e7) < owedAmount (500e6) → repayFromWithdraw = amountOut0 = 1e7
  - owedAmount -= 1e7 → 500e6 - 1e7 = 490e6 (under-subtracts, user pays more)
  - amountOut1 -= 1e7 → but amountOut1 might be < 1e7 in some configurations → REVERT
With token0=WETH (1e18 scale):
  - amountOut0 = 1e18 (1 WETH), owedAmount = 1000e6 (1000 USDC)
  - amountOut1 (1000e6 = 1e9) < owedAmount (1000e6) depends on exact amounts
  - If amountOut1 < owedAmount: repayFromWithdraw = amountOut0 = 1e18
  - owedAmount (1000e6) -= 1e18 → UNDERFLOW → revert
This permanently blocks withdrawals for positions where denomination=token1 and amountOut1 < owedAmount (the most common partial repayment scenario).

In _calculateTokenValues() two fallback paths perform division before multiplication: Line 445: (amount0 * price / PRECISION) * chPrice1 / decimals1 Line 447: amount1 * PRECISION / price * chPrice0 / decimals0 In both cases, the first division (by PRECISION=1e30 or by price) happens before multiplication by chPrice0/chPrice1. Correct order: amount0 * price * chPrice1 / PRECISION / decimals1
               amount1 * PRECISION * chPrice0 / price / decimals0
Precision loss analysis for line 447 (token1 has no pricefeed):
  - amount1=1e6 (1 USDC), price=2e30 (2 token0 per token1 in 1e30 scale)
  - Step1: amount1 * PRECISION / price = 1e6 * 1e30 / 2e30 = 5e5 (OK)
  - But for small amount1 and large price: amount1=100, price=3e30
  - Step1: 100 * 1e30 / 3e30 = 33 (lost 1 wei due to truncation)
  - Step2: 33 * chPrice0 / decimals0 — already lost precision
  - Correct: 100 * 1e30 * chPrice0 / 3e30 / decimals0 = higher precision
This causes systematic under-valuation of collateral in positions where one token lacks a pricefeed and the TWAP fallback is used. Under-valued collateral leads to positions appearing liquidatable when they are not (false liquidations).

Line 167: `collectPositionFees(vestPosition.tickLower, mainPosition.tickUpper)`.
The vesting position is created at addVestingPosition() with mainPosition.tickLower/tickUpper
(lines 433-434). However, after a rebalance(), mainPosition ticks change via _setMainTicks().
At that point, collectFees() calls burn(0) + collect on a tick range that does NOT match the
actual vesting position in the Uniswap pool. This results in:
1. Fees from the real vesting position are NEVER collected (permanent loss)
2. If the mixed tick range happens to match another existing position, fees from that
   position are incorrectly collected
Call path: rebalance() changes mainPosition ticks → any subsequent collectFees() →
line 167 uses vestPosition.tickLower (old mainPosition.tickLower) + mainPosition.tickUpper (NEW) →
Uniswap burn(0) on non-existent position → collect returns 0 → vesting fees permanently locked.
This is clearly a copy-paste bug. Should be vestPosition.tickLower + vestPosition.tickUpper.

Line 467: `uint128(vp.initialLiquidity * (lastValid - vp.lastUpdate) / (vp.endTs - vp.startTs))`
This calculates liquidity to remove based on initialLiquidity, not remainingLiquidity.
After multiple partial withdrawals, remainingLiquidity < initialLiquidity.
Example: initialLiquidity=1000, vesting over 100 seconds.
- t=50: withdraws 1000*50/100 = 500. remaining=500. Correct so far.
- t=75: withdraws 1000*(75-50)/100 = 250. remaining=250. Still OK.
- t=90: withdraws 1000*(90-75)/100 = 150. remaining=100. OK.
- t=95: withdraws 1000*(95-90)/100 = 50. remaining=50. OK.
The issue is that rounding in integer division means the partial chunks may NOT
sum exactly to initialLiquidity. If chunks round UP cumulatively, the final
`vp.remainingLiquidity -= liquidityToRemove` underflows.
More critically: if collectFees is NOT called regularly, a single large chunk
can try to remove more than remainingLiquidity. E.g., if first call is at t=80:
removes 1000*80/100=800. remaining=200. Then at endTs: takes remainingLiquidity=200.
But if rounding accumulates: 800+201 > 1000 → underflow revert on line 471.
This would permanently brick the vesting position and lock fees.

Lines 502-521: balances() sums mainPosition + secondaryPosition + idle.
It completely ignores the vesting position's liquidity. This is used by Vault.deposit()
(line 54: `IStrategy(strategy).balances()`) to calculate shares.
When a vesting position is active with significant liquidity, balances() under-reports TVL.
Result: new depositors receive MORE shares than they should (TVL appears lower),
diluting existing holders. When vesting completes and that liquidity becomes "visible",
existing depositors are diluted.
Attack: 1) Owner adds large vesting position. 2) Attacker deposits right after →
gets inflated shares because balances() doesn't count vesting liquidity.
3) After vesting completes or after collectFees unlocks the liquidity, attacker
withdraws more than they deposited.
Impact scales with vesting position size relative to total vault TVL.

Line 375: `secondaryPosition.tickUpper = tick - modulo`. When tick is exactly at a
tickSpacing multiple, modulo=0, so tickUpper = tick. Meanwhile tickLower =
mainPosition.tickLower. If tick equals mainPosition.tickLower (possible when tick is
at the lower border of the main range), then tickLower == tickUpper → zero-width range.

Line 377: `secondaryPosition.tickLower = tick - modulo + tickSpacing`. Similarly,
if this equals mainPosition.tickUpper, zero width.

Additionally, _setSecondaryPositionsTicks uses spot price() at line 370 which reads
slot0 — manipulable via flash loan. An attacker can skew the bal0in1 vs bal1
comparison (line 373) to force the wrong branch, potentially creating a suboptimal
or inverted secondary position. Combined with the tickSpacing edge case, this can
cause rebalance() to revert (Uniswap rejects tickLower >= tickUpper).

Lines 134-155: withdrawPartial() only removes proportional liquidity from
mainPosition and secondaryPosition, plus idle balances. The vesting position
liquidity is completely ignored.

When a user withdraws during active vesting:
1. Vault.withdraw() calls balances() which under-reports (DD-S-03)
2. If idle < needed, calls withdrawPartial() which skips vesting liquidity
3. User gets less than their fair share

Combined with DD-S-03: the under-reported balances mean the user's share
calculation (Vault line 91-92) already under-counts. Then withdrawPartial
also doesn't touch vesting liquidity. Double loss for withdrawers.

Remaining users benefit: when vesting completes, the liquidity that should
have been partially owned by the exited user stays in the vault.

Lines 319-341: The loop runs for i=1..observationCardinality. In the final iteration
(i == observationCardinality), `index = (N + currentIndex - N) % N = currentIndex`,
which wraps back to the MOST RECENT observation.

At this point, `nextTimestamp` has been updated by the previous (N-1) iterations to
the OLDEST observation's timestamp. The final `timestamp` is `observations[currentIndex].timestamp`
= the MOST RECENT observation ≈ block.timestamp.

The expression `nextTimestamp - timestamp` computes
`oldest_observation.timestamp - newest_observation.timestamp` as a uint32 subtraction.
Since oldest < newest, this UNDERFLOWS → Solidity 0.8 reverts with ArithmeticError.

This only triggers when ALL N observations have timestamps >= lookAgo (all within
the TWAP window, none older than `twap` seconds). This can happen when:
1. Pool is newly deployed and has fewer blocks of history than the TWAP window.
2. Pool cardinality was recently increased to N, and N observations have not yet
   spanned > twap seconds.
3. A high-cardinality pool (e.g. N=25) with 12-second blocks: 25 * 12 = 300 seconds
   = exactly the default TWAP. If ALL 25 observations are within the last 300 seconds,
   the loop exhaust ALL slots without finding one older than lookAgo, and crashes.

Note: This is DISTINCT from DD-S-07 (premature single-observation return, design
weakness) and from the "timestamp 0" revert (uninitialized slots). This is a
hard arithmetic crash on a fully-initialized pool that simply lacks sufficient history.

Impact: `_requirePriceWithinRange()` propagates the revert, permanently blocking
`rebalance()`, `compound()`, and `addVestingPosition()` until the pool accumulates
enough history or cardinality is reduced (impossible to decrease in Uniswap V3).

call_stack:
  rebalance() → _requirePriceWithinRange() → _priceWithinRange() → checkPoolActivity()
  → iteration i=N → uint32(oldest.ts - newest.ts) → ArithmeticError REVERT

In `_setSecondaryPositionsTicks()` the ELSE branch (bal0in1 >= bal1, token0 excess):

  secondaryPosition.tickLower = tick - modulo + tickSpacing;   // nearest initializable tick ABOVE current
  secondaryPosition.tickUpper = mainPosition.tickUpper;        // = tickBorder + halfWidth

When `isLowerSided == true` (tick's modulo < tickSpacing/2):
  - tickBorder = tick - modulo (lower-sided border)
  - mainPosition.tickUpper = (tick - modulo) + halfWidth

If halfWidth == tickSpacing (i.e. positionWidth == 2 * tickSpacing):
  - secondaryPosition.tickLower  = tick - modulo + tickSpacing
  - secondaryPosition.tickUpper  = (tick - modulo) + tickSpacing  ← SAME VALUE
  => tickLower == tickUpper → zero-width range
