Nearly every function in V3Vault calls _updateGlobalInterest() or _calculateGlobalInterest()
which calls interestRateModel.getRatesPerSecondX64(). If IRM reverts, the following
functions ALL revert: deposit, mint, withdraw, redeem, borrow, repay, liquidate,
create (onERC721Received), transform, decreaseLiquidityAndCollect, remove (indirectly),
stakePosition (via loanInfo), and ALL view functions.

The IRM is immutable (set in constructor), so it cannot be replaced.

A bricked IRM = entire vault frozen permanently with no recovery path.

An attacker can exhaust dailyDebtIncreaseLimitLeft by borrowing and immediately repaying
in a loop. Repay adds back to dailyDebtIncreaseLimitLeft (line 1081), but borrow subtracts
from it (line 658). However, the check is `assets > dailyDebtIncreaseLimitLeft` (line 655),
so net-zero borrow+repay should not drain. BUT: if exchange rate changes between borrow and
repay (same block = no change, different block = change), the repay may return fewer assets
than borrowed (rounding), slowly draining the limit.

More directly: an attacker with enough collateral just borrows the entire limit legitimately,
blocking all other users from borrowing for the rest of the day.

The daily limit resets based on `block.timestamp / 1 days` (line 1389-1390).

repay() at line 1088-1092 checks that if partial repay leaves remaining debt < minLoanSize,
it reverts with MinLoanSize(). This means a borrower whose debt is between minLoanSize and
2*minLoanSize CANNOT partially repay -- they must fully repay in one tx.

If the borrower does not have enough assets for full repay, they are stuck:
- Cannot partial repay (MinLoanSize revert)
- Cannot full repay (insufficient funds)
- Position accrues interest and eventually gets liquidated

This is especially problematic if minLoanSize is set high by emergencyAdmin.

_withdraw() at line 1033-1035 checks `balance < assets` and reverts InsufficientLiquidity.
When utilization is ~100% (all assets are borrowed), lenders CANNOT withdraw.

The protocol relies on interest rate increases to incentivize repayment, but:
- If borrowers are insolvent, they won't repay
- If oracle is down, liquidation is blocked
- There is NO emergency withdrawal that bypasses liquidity check
- There is NO withdrawal queue mechanism

Lender funds can be locked indefinitely when utilization hits 100%.

_transform() at lines 617-620: if the position was staked before transform, it re-stakes
after transform via _stake(). If _stake() fails (GaugeManager revert, gauge removed,
NFT approval issue), the entire transform reverts.

This means a user with a staked position CANNOT use any transformer (AutoRange,
LeverageTransformer, etc.) if GaugeManager staking is broken.

Combined with the one-time GaugeManager lock, this is permanent.

stakePosition() at line 1391 checks loan health AFTER staking. Staking changes the
valuation model: _checkLoanIsHealthy() passes ignoreFees=true for staked positions
(line 1429), meaning fee value is EXCLUDED from collateral.

If a position's health depends on accumulated fees, staking it immediately makes it
unhealthy. The stakePosition function reverts with CollateralFail.

But the deeper issue: what if someone ELSE calls a path that stakes the position
(e.g., transform with wasStaked=true re-stakes at line 619), and the position was
healthy before but unhealthy after staking due to fee exclusion?
The transform would revert even though the user didn't explicitly request staking.

An attacker can front-run a large deposit by depositing the remaining dailyLendIncreaseLimitLeft
themselves, causing the victim's deposit to revert with DailyLendIncreaseLimit.

The attacker can then withdraw immediately (withdrawal adds back to the limit at line 1043),
but the victim's tx already reverted.

Cost to attacker: only gas fees (deposit + withdraw in same block = no interest cost).
The limit resets daily at block.timestamp / 1 days boundary.

_updateAndCheckCollateral() updates tokenConfigs[token].totalDebtShares on both borrow
AND repay. On repay (line 1083-1085), oldShares > newShares, so the difference is
SUBTRACTED from totalDebtShares. The collateral limit check only triggers when
newShares > oldShares (increasing debt).

However, consider: repay calls _updateAndCheckCollateral with
(loanDebtShares + shares, loanDebtShares) where shares was already subtracted.
Wait -- line 1083: oldShares = loanDebtShares + shares (before repay), newShares = loanDebtShares (after).
So oldShares > newShares -> subtraction path, no limit check. This is correct.

BUT: if SafeCast.toUint192 overflows (debtShares difference > type(uint192).max),
the subtraction at line 1346 reverts. This would block repay if totalDebtShares
somehow got into an inconsistent state. Unlikely but worth checking.

remove() at line 853 calls nonfungiblePositionManager.safeTransferFrom() to return
the NFT to the user. If the recipient is a contract that reverts in onERC721Received(),
or if the NFT manager is paused/upgraded, the remove() call fails.

Additionally, remove() first calls _unstakeIfNeeded() (line 850). If the position
is staked and GaugeManager.unstakeIfStaked() reverts, the user cannot remove their
position even after fully repaying debt.

Combined: fully repaid user with staked position + broken GaugeManager = NFT stuck forever.

_transform() at line 586 uses a low-level call:
  (bool success,) = transformer.call(data);

The transformer is from transformerAllowList (set by owner), so it's trusted.
However, if a transformer is compromised or has a bug, it could return a huge
amount of data (returnbomb). The low-level call copies ALL return data to memory,
consuming gas proportional to return data size.

With (bool success,) pattern, Solidity still copies return data to memory before
discarding it. A malicious transformer could return 2MB+ of data, consuming all
remaining gas and causing the transform to fail.

Mitigation: transformers are admin-curated, so this requires compromised transformer.
Solvency invariant: vault balance + outstanding debt >= total lent amount (lender claims)
Debt exchange rate monotonicity: debtExchangeRateX96 must never decrease (only exception: zero debt)
Lend exchange rate monotonicity with socialization exception: lendExchangeRateX96 must never decrease except during reserve socialization (bad debt haircut)
Token ownership consistency: every tokenId in ownedTokens has correct tokenOwner mapping and vice versa
No position can have debt without being tracked in vault ownership (orphan debt prevention)
Liquidation only possible for unhealthy positions: collateralValue < debt
ERC4626 roundtrip safety: redeem(deposit(X)) <= X for any X (no value extraction via deposit-then-redeem)
Collateral value limit tracking: totalDebtShares per token config must equal sum of debtShares for positions using that token
Transform mode isolation: transformedTokenId must be 0 outside of an active transform() call
Daily limit replenishment symmetry: borrow replenishes on repay, deposit replenishes on withdraw
Reserve protection: withdrawReserves cannot drain below protected amount (reserveProtectionFactorX32 * lentAmount)
Symmetric pair: borrow/repay must conserve debtSharesTotal (borrow adds X shares, repay removes at most X shares for same asset amount)
Liquidation penalty bounds: liquidation penalty must be between MIN_LIQUIDATION_PENALTY_X32 (2%) and MAX_LIQUIDATION_PENALTY_X32 (10%)
NFT custody invariant: for every tracked position, the NFT must be owned by either the vault or the gaugeManager (if staked)
Only the vault-recorded owner of a tokenId can call borrow() outside transform mode
Only the vault-recorded owner can call decreaseLiquidityAndCollect for their tokenId
transformedTokenId sentinel must be 0 outside of an active transform call -- no stuck transform mode
Transform approval auto-migration: when tokenId changes during transform, old approvals are correctly transferred and old ones deleted
setGaugeManager can only be called once -- subsequent calls must revert
Liquidation is blocked during transform mode (transformedTokenId != 0)
emergencyAdmin can call setLimits but NOT other admin functions (withdrawReserves, setTransformer, setTokenConfig, setReserveFactor)
Only tokens from nonfungiblePositionManager are accepted via onERC721Received -- other NFT contracts must be rejected
setTransformer cannot set dangerous addresses (address(0), vault itself, asset, NPM) as transformers
Token ownership count (loanCount) must match the actual number of tokens stored for each owner
unstakePosition can only be called by token owner or during active transform for that token

registerOperatorWithFeeDestination() does NOT validate that _feeDestination != address(0).
If an operator calls registerOperatorWithFeeDestination(address(0)), their feeDestination
is set to address(0). The operatorIsRegistered modifier checks
feeDestinations[_intent.operator] != address(0), so ALL subsequent transfer intents
signed by this operator will revert with OperatorNotRegistered.
This is inconsistent with registerOperator() which safely uses msg.sender as destination,
and with Sweepable.setSweeper which HAS a notZero check.

An operator can call unregisterOperator() at any time, instantly invalidating ALL
pending transfer intents they signed. There is no grace period or cooldown.
If a payer has already submitted a transaction to the mempool with a valid intent,
the operator can front-run with unregisterOperator(), causing the payer's tx to revert.
The payer loses gas fees and the payment fails.

subsidizedTransferToken uses _signatureTransferData.owner as the sender (not msg.sender).
The validIntent modifier is called with _signatureTransferData.owner as sender, meaning
the intent signature binds the owner address but NOT the relayer. Any address can call
this function and relay the payment on behalf of the owner.

The EIP-2612 permit call sets allowance for address(this) from owner. If the permit
signature is a one-time nonce-based permit, a malicious relayer could front-run the
legitimate relayer, causing the legitimate relayer's tx to revert (nonce consumed).

More critically: if the owner also planned to call transferTokenPreApproved directly
(without a relayer), the relayer could front-run by calling subsidizedTransferToken,
consuming the permit signature and executing the transfer before the owner intended.

The owner can set ANY address as sweeper via setSweeper(). The sweeper can then
immediately call sweepETH/sweepToken to drain ALL funds from the contract.
There is no timelock, no multisig requirement, no delay. If the owner key is
compromised, an attacker can set sweeper and drain everything in one block.

While the contract shouldn't hold funds long-term (it's a pass-through), during
swap operations (swapAndTransfer*) there is a brief window where tokens are held
by the contract before being forwarded to Uniswap. Additionally, any stuck funds
(from failed transfers or accumulated dust) are sweepable.

feeDestinations mapping is mutable — an operator can call registerOperatorWithFeeDestination()
multiple times, overwriting their feeDestination. The TransferIntent struct includes the
operator address, and the intent signature binds the operator. But the feeDestination is
looked up from storage at execution time, NOT from the intent.

This means: operator signs intent with feeDestination=A in mind, then changes feeDestination
to B before the payer executes. The fees go to B, not A. If the operator and merchant
agreed on a specific fee destination, the operator can redirect fees.

More critically: if the operator's key is compromised, the attacker can change the
feeDestination to their own address and collect all fees from ALL pending intents.

The contract owner (Coinbase) has NO ability to block or blacklist operators.
registerOperator() is fully permissionless. If a malicious operator signs intents
with harmful parameters (e.g., extremely high feeAmount relative to recipientAmount),
the owner cannot prevent those intents from being executed.

However, the operator must sign the intent which includes all amounts, and the payer
must consent by submitting the transaction. So the practical attack surface is limited
to social engineering scenarios.

processedTransferIntents is keyed as mapping(operator => mapping(id => bool)).
The same intent ID (bytes16) can be used by different operators without conflict.
This is by design but worth documenting: if a merchant works with multiple operators
and uses the same payment ID for tracking, the ID will NOT be marked as processed
across operators. However, since the signature includes the operator address, the
same intent cannot be replayed with a different operator — this is safe.

When recipientAmount = 0 and feeAmount = 0, neededAmount = 0. All transfer functions
(transferNative L160, transferToken L189, transferTokenPreApproved L247, wrapAndTransfer L281,
unwrapAndTransfer L315, etc.) skip the actual transfer logic with `if (neededAmount > 0)` or
`if (msg.value > 0)` guards, but STILL call `succeedPayment()` at L753 which sets
`processedTransferIntents[operator][id] = true` and emits `Transferred`.
This means an operator can sign a zero-amount intent, anyone executes it, and the intent ID
is permanently marked as processed. If the system later tries to process a real payment with
that same intent ID, it reverts with AlreadyProcessed.
Attack: operator signs intent with id=X, amount=0. Attacker front-runs the real payment by
submitting the zero-amount intent first. Real payment with same id=X fails.

The operator registration system is permissionless: anyone calls registerOperator() (L788)
and unregisterOperator() (L794). The operatorIsRegistered modifier (L128-132) checks
feeDestinations[operator] != address(0) at transaction execution time.
An operator can sign a valid intent, the payer submits the tx, and between signing and
execution the operator calls unregisterOperator(). The payer's tx reverts with
OperatorNotRegistered. The payer has wasted gas and the payment is blocked.
More critically: in the subsidizedTransferToken flow (L505-559), a relayer pays gas on behalf
of the payer. The operator can grief the relayer by repeatedly signing intents then
unregistering before execution, causing relayer gas losses.

In swapTokens() L592-699, the return value calculation at L699 is:
`(payerBalanceBefore + routerBalanceBefore) - (payerBalanceAfter + routerBalanceAfter)`
This accounts for tokens the router already held (L603/L627). The SWEEP command in the
Uniswap execution sends leftover input tokens back to the payer.
If an attacker donates tokenIn to the Uniswap router before the swap tx, routerBalanceBefore
increases. After execution, SWEEP sends all leftover (including donated tokens) to the payer.
payerBalanceAfter increases by the donated amount, routerBalanceAfter decreases by the same.
Net effect on the formula: (pBefore + rBefore + donation) - (pAfter + donation + rAfter - donation)
Wait -- let's recalculate: rBefore includes the donation. After SWEEP, rAfter = 0 (swept),
pAfter = pOriginalAfter + donation. So:
(pBefore + rBefore+donation) - (pAfter+donation + 0) = (pBefore + rBefore+donation) - pAfter - donation
= pBefore + rBefore - pAfter. The donation cancels out.
The developers explicitly accounted for this in the comment at L684-687. Safe.

In wrapAndTransfer (L266-290):
1. msg.value is wrapped: wrappedNativeCurrency.deposit{value: msg.value}() — L283
2. transferFundsToDestinations(_intent) is called — L286
3. Inside transferFundsToDestinations (L720-737): since _intent.recipientCurrency is address(wrappedNativeCurrency)
   (checked at L277), it takes the ELSE branch (L728-736), doing safeTransfer of the ERC20 token.

This is correct — the contract wraps ETH to WETH, then sends WETH to recipient and feeDestination.

BUT: succeedPayment emits spentCurrency=NATIVE_CURRENCY (L289), not the actual wrappedNativeCurrency
that was delivered. This is a logging inconsistency, not a fund loss bug.

The actual flow is sound: exactValueSent ensures msg.value == recipientAmount + feeAmount,
deposit wraps ALL of it, then safeTransfer sends exact amounts. No funds stuck.

In unwrapAndTransfer (L295-337):
1. permit2.permitTransferFrom transfers WETH from payer to contract (L325-330)
2. unwrapAndTransferFundsToDestinations is called directly (L333)
3. NO revertIfInexactTransfer check between step 1 and step 2

Compare with transferToken (L169-217) which DOES call revertIfInexactTransfer after
the permit2 transfer (L210).

For WETH specifically this is NOT exploitable because WETH is not a fee-on-transfer token.
But the code pattern is inconsistent — if wrappedNativeCurrency were ever set to a
non-standard wrapped token with fees, the unwrap would fail or send wrong amounts.

The contract is immutable (wrappedNativeCurrency set in constructor), so this is only
relevant if deployed with a non-standard wrapped token.

unwrapAndTransferPreApproved (L342-377) has the same missing check.

In sendNative (L757-766), native ETH is sent via:
  payable(destination).call{value: amount}("")

This triggers the receive()/fallback() function on the destination address. While the
contract uses nonReentrant on ALL external functions, the callback can still:

1. Call OTHER contracts that read Transfers state (read-only reentrancy is not blocked)
2. Execute arbitrary logic with up to 63/64 of remaining gas

In transferFundsToDestinations (L720-737), the order is:
  - First: send recipientAmount to recipient (L723)
  - Second: send feeAmount to feeDestination (L726)

If recipient is a malicious contract, its receive() callback executes BETWEEN the two
sends. At that point:
  - processedTransferIntents is NOT yet set (set in succeedPayment, which runs AFTER)
  - The contract's ETH balance still holds feeAmount

However, nonReentrant prevents re-entering any external function. The only concern is
if the recipient's callback interacts with other protocols that depend on the Transfers
contract's balance or state during the callback.

For the Coinbase Commerce use case, recipient addresses are merchant-controlled, so
the recipient is trusted. BUT feeDestination is operator-controlled (L34), and any
address can register as operator (L781-792). A malicious operator could set feeDestination
to a contract that does something unexpected during receive().

Net assessment: nonReentrant is sufficient protection. The callback cannot re-enter
Transfers. Cross-contract read-only reentrancy is theoretically possible but requires
a specific vulnerable external protocol.

In ALL transfer functions, there is a pattern:
  if (neededAmount > 0) { ... transferFundsToDestinations ... }
  succeedPayment(...)  // ALWAYS called regardless of neededAmount

When recipientAmount=0 AND feeAmount=0:
  - neededAmount = 0
  - No funds are transferred
  - But succeedPayment sets processedTransferIntents[operator][id] = true
  - Event Transferred is emitted with spentAmount=0

This means an operator can sign a zero-value intent and the payer can "process" it,
permanently burning that intent ID. This could be used to:
  1. Front-run a real intent: if operator signs intent with ID=X for $100, attacker
     signs a DIFFERENT zero-value intent with same ID... BUT the signature includes
     the amounts, so attacker can't forge this. The operator would need to sign both.
  2. Operator intentionally signs zero-value intent to "cancel" an existing ID on-chain.

For transferNative with exactValueSent: msg.value must equal 0 (neededAmount=0), so
the payer sends 0 ETH. This is a no-op that wastes gas.

For transferToken/transferTokenPreApproved: similar no-op.

The operator controls the signature, so they can only "waste" their own intent IDs.
Not a security issue — more of a gas waste / design observation.

HOWEVER: in subsidizedTransferToken (L505-559), the msg.sender (relayer) pays gas but
the intent is for _signatureTransferData.owner. A zero-value subsidized transfer wastes
relayer gas. The relayer should check off-chain, but no on-chain protection.

swapAndTransferUniswapV3Native (L384-410) does NOT use the exactValueSent modifier.
The payer sends msg.value as the maximum they're willing to pay for the swap.

The Uniswap UniversalRouter flow:
1. WRAP_ETH: wraps msg.value into WETH at the router
2. V3_SWAP_EXACT_OUT: swaps for exactly neededAmount of tokenOut
3. TRANSFER x2: sends recipientAmount to recipient, feeAmount to feeDestination
4. UNWRAP_WETH: unwraps leftover WETH at the router
5. SWEEP ETH: sends leftover ETH back to _msgSender()

The SWEEP (L622) uses amount=0, meaning it sweeps the ENTIRE remaining balance of ETH
from the router to the payer. This should return any excess.

BUT: if the Uniswap router already had a pre-existing ETH or WETH balance (from a
previous failed tx or donation), that balance gets swept to the CURRENT payer too.
The contract accounts for this in L602-603 and L699:
  payerBalanceBefore = _msgSender().balance + msg.value
  routerBalanceBefore = address(uniswap).balance + WETH.balanceOf(address(uniswap))
  return (payerBalanceBefore + routerBalanceBefore) - (payerBalanceAfter + routerBalanceAfter)

This calculation returns the NET amount consumed by the swap, correctly excluding any
pre-existing router balance that got swept to the payer. The return value (amountSwapped)
is used in the Transferred event.

The actual fund flow is safe — excess returns to payer via SWEEP. However, the event
may report amountSwapped differently than what the user "really" spent if the router
had pre-existing balance.

In subsidizedTransferToken (L505-559):
- validIntent uses _signatureTransferData.owner as the sender (not _msgSender())
- The EIP-2612 permit is called with the owner's signature
- Then safeTransferFrom transfers from owner to contract

The key insight: the PERMIT signature (EIP-2612) is a separate signature from the
operator's TransferIntent signature. The permit signature authorizes THIS contract
to spend owner's tokens.

Attack scenario:
1. Owner signs EIP-2612 permit for Transfers contract, amount=neededAmount
2. Owner shares both the TransferIntent and the EIP-2612 signature with a relayer
3. A different relayer (or anyone watching mempool) sees the tx and front-runs it
4. Front-runner calls subsidizedTransferToken with the SAME data
5. The permit executes, the transfer happens, intent is processed

BUT: who benefits? The funds still go to _intent.recipient and _intent.feeDestination.
The front-runner gains nothing — they just pay gas. The original relayer's tx then
reverts with AlreadyProcessed.

The only "attack" is: the original relayer wastes gas on the reverted tx. This is
standard permit front-running and is a known limitation of EIP-2612.

HOWEVER: there's a subtler issue. The permit (L530-536) sets allowance to neededAmount
with deadline=_intent.deadline. If the permit is front-run and the allowance is consumed,
any future permit with the SAME nonce will fail (EIP-2612 nonce is consumed). The owner
cannot reuse that permit signature. But the intent is already processed, so this is fine.

In swapAndTransferUniswapV3Token (L413-455):
1. maxWillingToPay = _signatureTransferData.transferDetails.requestedAmount (L431)
2. permit2 transfers maxWillingToPay tokens from payer to contract (L439-444)
3. swapTokens is called with maxWillingToPay as the amountIn cap (L450)
4. Inside swapTokens, tokens are sent to uniswap router (L663)
5. SWEEP returns leftover tokenIn to payer (L643/L659)

There is NO check that maxWillingToPay >= neededAmount. The swap is V3_SWAP_EXACT_OUT
which tries to get exactly neededAmount of tokenOut. If maxWillingToPay is insufficient
for the swap, Uniswap will revert with V3TooMuchRequested.

BUT: the payer sets maxWillingToPay themselves (it's in their permit2 signature). If
they set it too low, the tx just reverts. No fund loss — just UX issue.

The more interesting case: what if maxWillingToPay is MUCH higher than needed? After the
exact-out swap, the router SWEEPs leftover tokenIn back to payer. This works correctly.

ACTUAL CONCERN: In the token-to-token swap path (L644-660), the SWEEP at L659 sends
leftover tokenIn to _msgSender() with amount=0 (sweep all). But this sweep is executed
by the Uniswap router. If the router has pre-existing tokenIn balance from another tx
in the same block, that balance gets swept to the current payer. This is a known
Uniswap router behavior (MEV opportunity, not a Transfers bug).

In EVERY transfer function, neededAmount is calculated as:
  uint256 neededAmount = _intent.recipientAmount + _intent.feeAmount;

Both are uint256 values from the calldata. If recipientAmount + feeAmount > type(uint256).max,
this overflows... BUT Solidity ^0.8.17 has built-in overflow checks. The addition would
revert with a panic.

The operator signs these values, so only the operator can create an intent with values
that sum to overflow. When the payer tries to execute it, the tx reverts. The intent
is effectively unusable — the operator would be sabotaging their own intents.

Additionally, the exactValueSent modifier (used in transferNative, wrapAndTransfer) also
computes this sum. The overflow would revert there too.

Not a vulnerability — Solidity 0.8 overflow protection handles this.

The Transfers contract inherits Sweepable. The _sweeper variable is never set in the
Transfers constructor (L54-75). It defaults to address(0).

Sweepable.setSweeper (L36) requires onlyOwner and notZero. So the owner CAN set a sweeper
after deployment. But if the owner never does, or if ownership is renounced:
  - Any tokens accidentally sent to the contract are stuck forever
  - ETH sent via selfdestruct/coinbase is stuck forever
  - Leftover dust from swap rounding is stuck forever

The sweep functions (sweepETH, sweepToken, etc) all require onlySweeper modifier,
which checks sweeper() == _msgSender(). If _sweeper == address(0), nobody can call sweep.

This is a deployment configuration issue, not a code bug. But worth noting that the
contract has NO mechanism to handle "accidentally received" funds without a sweeper.

The receive() function (L811-813) only accepts ETH from wrappedNativeCurrency, so
random ETH sends are rejected. But selfdestruct can force ETH into the contract.

In unwrapAndTransferFundsToDestinations (L739-745):
1. wrappedNativeCurrency.withdraw(amountToWithdraw) — unwraps WETH to ETH
2. transferFundsToDestinations(_intent) — sends ETH to recipient and feeDestination

transferFundsToDestinations uses sendNative (L757-766) which does:
  payable(destination).call{value: amount}("")

If _intent.recipient is a contract that does NOT have receive()/fallback(), or reverts
in receive(), the call fails → sendNative reverts with NativeTransferFailed → entire
tx reverts → intent stays UNPROCESSED.

The payer has valid WETH, the operator signed a valid intent, but the payment CANNOT be
completed because the recipient cannot accept ETH. There is NO fallback mechanism to
send WETH instead or to allow the recipient to claim later.

The intent is now permanently blocked (assuming recipient won't change their contract).
The payer's WETH is never transferred (tx reverted), so no fund loss. But the intent ID
is "reserved" — it can never be used because the same issue will recur.

Same issue applies if feeDestination is a contract that rejects ETH.

Impact: DoS on specific intents where recipient/feeDestination cannot accept native ETH.
The operator should validate recipient addresses off-chain before signing, but there's
no on-chain protection.

In transferNative (L147-166):
- exactValueSent: neededAmount = 0 + 0 = 0. msg.value must be 0. Passes.
- if (msg.value > 0) — FALSE, so transferFundsToDestinations is skipped
- succeedPayment runs: sets processedTransferIntents = true, emits event

A zero-value native transfer succeeds. This "burns" an intent ID.

The operator must sign this (recipientAmount=0, feeAmount=0), so only the operator can
create such an intent. It's effectively a no-op that permanently marks an intent ID
as processed.

Potential use: operator could intentionally create zero-value intents to "cancel" them
on-chain (prevent future use of that ID). This is a feature, not a bug.

In validIntent (L96-103):
If _intent.prefix.length > 0, the signed hash becomes:
  keccak256(abi.encodePacked(_intent.prefix, hash))
instead of the standard:
  ECDSA.toEthSignedMessageHash(hash) → keccak256("\x19Ethereum Signed Message:\n32", hash)

The custom prefix allows the operator to use alternative signature schemes. However:

1. If the prefix is chosen poorly (e.g., empty or short), it could collide with signatures
   from other protocols that use the same private key.
2. abi.encodePacked with a bytes prefix and a bytes32 hash is unambiguous (fixed-length hash),
   so length-extension attacks don't apply.
3. The hash includes address(this) and block.chainid, providing replay protection across
   contracts and chains.

The real risk: if the operator reuses their signing key across protocols and another protocol
also uses a custom prefix scheme, a signature from protocol A could be replayed on protocol B
if the message structures collide. The inclusion of address(this) in the hash prevents this
for Transfers specifically.

Net: the custom prefix is flexible but safe given the inclusion of address(this) and chainid.

neededAmount = _intent.recipientAmount + _intent.feeAmount is used across all
transfer functions. In Solidity 0.8.17, this addition is checked and will revert
on overflow. However, if both values are 0, neededAmount=0 and the `if (neededAmount > 0)`
guard skips all transfers, but succeedPayment still marks the intent as processed.
An operator could sign a zero-value intent, and it would be marked processed without
any actual transfer — the event still emits spentAmount=0.

registerOperatorWithFeeDestination allows any address to register as an operator
with ANY feeDestination, including address(this) (the Transfers contract itself).
When a payment is processed, feeAmount is sent to the contract itself. For ERC20,
these funds accumulate in the contract and can only be retrieved by the sweeper.
For native currency, the receive() function only allows msg.sender == wrappedNativeCurrency,
so native fees to address(this) would revert.

An operator can call unregisterOperator() which deletes feeDestinations[operator].
However, if there are pending signed intents from this operator that haven't been
processed yet, they will now revert with OperatorNotRegistered. The operator can
then re-register with a DIFFERENT feeDestination and the old intents become
processable again but with fees routed to the new destination.

subsidizedTransferToken uses _signatureTransferData.owner as the payer (not
msg.sender). The validIntent modifier receives owner as the sender parameter.
This means anyone can submit the transaction on behalf of the owner (gasless/meta-tx).
The EIP-2612 permit signature authorizes the contract to spend owner's tokens.
If the permit signature is intercepted from the mempool, a front-runner can
execute the payment before the intended relayer.

The core payment invariant. For every successful payment (non-swap path),
the recipient must receive exactly recipientAmount and the feeDestination must
receive exactly feeAmount. Fee-on-transfer tokens are explicitly rejected via
revertIfInexactTransfer. For swap paths, the Uniswap V3_SWAP_EXACT_OUT ensures
exact output. This invariant should hold across all 10 transfer functions.

Comparing permit2-based and pre-approved paths reveals an asymmetry.
transferToken (permit2, L199-210) checks fee-on-transfer via revertIfInexactTransfer.
transferTokenPreApproved (L248-255) also checks fee-on-transfer.
unwrapAndTransfer (permit2, L315-333) does NOT check fee-on-transfer — it skips
revertIfInexactTransfer after permit2.permitTransferFrom.
unwrapAndTransferPreApproved (L368-370) also does NOT check.
This is intentional because WETH is not a fee-on-transfer token, but if the
wrappedNativeCurrency is ever set to a non-standard wrapper with fees, this breaks.

validIntent hashes intent fields using abi.encodePacked (L80-93). The packed encoding
of adjacent dynamic-length or variable-width fields can produce collisions. However,
examining the fields: recipientAmount (uint256), deadline (uint256), recipient (address),
recipientCurrency (address), refundDestination (address), feeAmount (uint256),
id (bytes16), operator (address), chainid (uint256), sender (address), address(this).
All fields are fixed-size (uint256=32B, address=20B, bytes16=16B). With abi.encodePacked,
fixed-size types are packed without padding between addresses/bytes16.
Key concern: address (20B) + bytes16 (16B) + address (20B) = 56 bytes packed.
An attacker could potentially craft different (refundDestination, id, operator) tuples
that produce the same 56 packed bytes.

Transfers inherits Sweepable which allows a sweeper to sweep all ERC20 or ETH
from the contract. The transfer flow is: (1) receive funds to contract,
(2) transferFundsToDestinations sends to recipient + feeDestination. If sweeper
calls sweepToken between step 1 and step 2, the funds would be stolen. However,
nonReentrant prevents re-entrancy within the same tx. The sweeper would need to
front-run between the two internal calls, which is impossible within a single
atomic transaction. Between separate transactions, the contract should hold zero
balance (all funds are forwarded in the same tx).

wrapAndTransfer wraps ETH into WETH, then calls transferFundsToDestinations
which checks recipientCurrency. Since recipientCurrency = address(wrappedNativeCurrency)
(L277 check), transferFundsToDestinations enters the ERC20 branch (L728-735)
and sends WETH to recipient and feeDestination. However, succeedPayment (L289)
reports spentCurrency = NATIVE_CURRENCY (address(0)). The event is misleading —
the payer spent ETH but the recipient/fee received WETH. This is by design
(event tracks what payer sent, not what recipient received), but could confuse
off-chain accounting systems.

In swapTokens, after Uniswap execution, the code checks fee-on-transfer for both
feeDestination (L670-675) and recipient (L676-681) separately. If recipient ==
feeDestinations[operator], both checks measure the balance change of the SAME address.
The first check expects feeAmount increase, finds recipientAmount + feeAmount increase
(both transfers went to same address), and would see a LARGER increase than expected.
revertIfInexactTransfer checks balanceAfter - balanceBefore != expectedDiff — so
if the diff is recipientAmount + feeAmount but expected is feeAmount, it would REVERT.
This means payments where recipient == feeDestination would always fail in swap paths.

Custom signature prefix enables cross-protocol signature replay. At L97-103, if _intent.prefix is non-empty, the signed message hash is keccak256(abi.encodePacked(_intent.prefix, hash)) — an arbitrary prefix chosen by the caller (not the signer). An attacker could choose a prefix such that the resulting signedMessageHash matches a hash the operator previously signed for a DIFFERENT purpose (e.g., EIP-712 typed data, another dApp's personal_sign, or a Gnosis Safe tx). The operator's signature from that other context would then validate here, allowing the attacker to forge a TransferIntent the operator never authorized.

feeDestination is NOT included in the operator's signed hash (L81-93). The operator signs over: recipientAmount, deadline, recipient, recipientCurrency, refundDestination, feeAmount, id, operator, chainId, sender, address(this). But feeDestinations[operator] is resolved at EXECUTION time (L588, L674, L725-727, L731-735). If the operator's feeDestination is changed between signing and execution (by anyone who calls registerOperatorWithFeeDestination from the operator's address, or if the operator's key is compromised for registration but not for intent signing), fees go to an unexpected address.

Malicious recipient can grief/DOS payments via revert in receive(). sendNative (L757-766) uses .call{value}("") to send ETH. If the recipient is a contract that reverts in receive(), the entire transferNative/unwrapAndTransfer tx reverts. The operator signed the intent with this recipient, but the recipient could become malicious AFTER the intent was signed (e.g., upgradeable proxy recipient, or a contract that conditionally reverts).

subsidizedTransferToken EIP-2612 permit can be frontrun, causing the subsidized tx to revert. At L530-536, the contract calls IERC7597.permit() with the user's signature. If a frontrunner extracts the permit signature from the mempool and calls permit() directly on the token contract first, the nonce is consumed. When the original subsidizedTransferToken tx executes, the permit call reverts (nonce already used). However, the allowance WAS set by the frontrunner's tx, so the transfer would work if the permit didn't revert. But standard ERC-2612 permit reverts on replayed nonce.

abi.encodePacked hash collision between different TransferIntents. The hash at L80-93 uses abi.encodePacked with multiple adjacent address/uint256 fields. While all individual types are fixed-size, bytes16(id) is 16 bytes followed by address(operator) which is 20 bytes. In abi.encodePacked, bytes16 occupies exactly 16 bytes and address occupies 20 bytes — both are fixed size, so there is no collision risk from packed encoding with these types. HOWEVER, the hash does NOT include a domain separator or type hash. Two different Transfers contract deployments on the same chain (different addresses) are protected by address(this) in the hash. But there is no EIP-712 domain separator, making the signature scheme non-standard and harder to verify off-chain.

Operator can unregister AFTER signing intents, then re-register with a different feeDestination to redirect fees. The operator registration is permissionless (anyone can register as operator). The unregisterOperator function (L794-798) deletes the feeDestination mapping. If the operator re-registers with a new feeDestination, all pending signed intents will now direct fees to the new destination. Combined with T-TB-02, this is a fee redirection attack vector.

USDC/USDT blocklist can permanently DOS payments. If the Transfers contract address is added to USDC or USDT's blocklist, ALL token transfers through the contract fail permanently. The contract receives tokens first (safeTransferFrom to address(this)) then forwards them — a blocklisted address cannot receive tokens. This is a centralization risk inherent to the custodial flow.

Zero-amount intent bypass — when recipientAmount + feeAmount = 0, multiple functions skip all transfers but still mark the intent as processed and emit Transferred. transferToken (L189), transferTokenPreApproved (L247), unwrapAndTransfer (L315), subsidizedTransferToken (L544) — all have `if (neededAmount > 0)` guards that skip the actual transfer. A zero-amount intent gets marked as processed (succeedPayment at end) without any value transfer. This could be used to burn valid intent IDs.

neededAmount = _intent.recipientAmount + _intent.feeAmount se calcula en múltiples funciones
(L136, L183, L235, L309, L356, L400, L430, L483, L523, L574). Con Solidity ^0.8.17, esta
suma tiene checked overflow nativo — revertirá si recipientAmount + feeAmount > type(uint256).max.
Sin embargo, el operador firma el intent incluyendo ambos valores. Un operador malicioso podría
firmar un intent con valores que sumen > uint256.max, causando que TODA llamada con ese intent
revierta — DoS sobre el payer que no puede completar el pago.
ANÁLISIS: overflow revert es el comportamiento correcto aquí. No hay pérdida de fondos.
El operador firmaría su propio DoS. Solidity 0.8+ protege correctamente.

En el modifier exactValueSent (L137-140):
  revert InvalidNativeAmount(int256(msg.value - neededAmount));   // L138
  revert InvalidNativeAmount(-int256(neededAmount - msg.value));  // L140

El cast int256(uint256_value) hace overflow silencioso si el valor uint256 > type(int256).max
(2^255 - 1). Esto NO causa pérdida de fondos porque la transacción SIEMPRE revierte en
ambos paths — el error es solo que el mensaje de error sería incorrecto (valor erróneo
en el revert reason). Con Solidity 0.8.17, el cast de uint256 a int256 NO es checked —
es un truncamiento silencioso. PERO esto solo afecta el revert data, no la lógica.

EXCEPCIÓN POTENCIAL: si neededAmount overflow (T-M-01 lo protege), o si msg.value
es extremadamente grande (> 2^255 wei ≈ 5.7e58 ETH — imposible en la práctica).

En swapTokens L699:
  return (payerBalanceBefore + routerBalanceBefore) - (payerBalanceAfter + routerBalanceAfter);

El cálculo intenta capturar "cuánto del input token consumió el swap". Incluye el balance
del router para compensar tokens que el router ya tenía (swept al payer como refund).

VECTOR DE ATAQUE: Si un tercero dona tokens al router DURANTE la ejecución del swap
(antes de que se mida routerBalanceAfter), routerBalanceAfter sería mayor de lo esperado,
causando que el return value sea MAYOR que lo realmente consumido. Esto se reportaría
en el evento Transferred como spentAmount inflado — pero NO causa pérdida de fondos
porque el payer ya pagó y los fondos ya se distribuyeron vía Uniswap.

OTRO VECTOR: Si routerBalanceBefore tiene tokens residuales, esos se incluyen en el
cálculo. El contrato maneja esto correctamente (L684-687 comentario explícito).

RIESGO REAL: underflow si (payerBalanceAfter + routerBalanceAfter) >
(payerBalanceBefore + routerBalanceBefore). Esto podría pasar si alguien envía tokens
al payer o al router durante la tx. Solidity 0.8 revertirá → DoS del swap.
¿Quién puede hacer esto? Solo con un callback — pero ReentrancyGuard está activo.

En swapTokens cuando msg.value > 0 (L602):
  payerBalanceBefore = _msgSender().balance + msg.value;

Cuando el payer llama una función payable, su ETH balance ya se redujo por msg.value
ANTES de la ejecución del contrato. Así que _msgSender().balance es el balance POST-envío.
El contrato suma msg.value para reconstruir el balance PRE-envío. Esto es CORRECTO.

Luego en L691:
  payerBalanceAfter = _msgSender().balance;

Después del swap, cualquier ETH no consumido se devuelve al payer vía UNWRAP_WETH + SWEEP.

return = (balancePre + msg.value + routerBefore) - (balancePost + routerAfter)

Si el swap consume X ETH (wrapeados como WETH), el router devuelve (msg.value - X) ETH al payer.
payerBalanceAfter = payerBalanceBefore_real + (msg.value - X) = (_msgSender().balance) + (msg.value - X)

return = (_msgSender().balance + msg.value + routerBefore) - ((_msgSender().balance + msg.value - X) + routerAfter)

Si routerBefore == routerAfter (router no retiene nada): return = X. CORRECTO.

PERO: gas costs reducen _msgSender().balance entre las dos mediciones. El gas pagado
NO se refleja aquí porque balance se mide dentro de la misma tx — no hay gas entre mediciones.
CORRECTO: el balance del payer dentro de la misma tx no cambia por gas (gas se cobra al final).

En L603:
  routerBalanceBefore = address(uniswap).balance + IERC20(wrappedNativeCurrency).balanceOf(address(uniswap));

El contrato suma ETH nativo + WETH del router. Lo mismo en L692-694 para routerBalanceAfter.

PROBLEMA POTENCIAL: Si el router tiene X ETH y X WETH, y durante la ejecución UNWRAPS
el WETH a ETH, la suma ETH+WETH permanece constante — correcto.
Pero si el router WRAPS ETH a WETH (como hace WRAP_ETH en L609), la suma también
permanece constante — correcto.

EDGE CASE: Si un tercero envía ETH directamente al router durante la tx (no posible
en una tx atómica a menos que el router tenga un receive/fallback vulnerable).

Este diseño es ROBUSTO contra conversiones ETH<->WETH internas del router.

Funciones directas (transferNative, wrapAndTransfer) usan modifier exactValueSent que
requiere msg.value == recipientAmount + feeAmount exactamente.

PERO swapAndTransferUniswapV3Native (L384) NO usa exactValueSent. Esto es BY DESIGN
porque el payer no sabe exactamente cuánto ETH costará el swap — envía un máximo
(slippage) y el exceso se devuelve via UNWRAP_WETH + SWEEP.

RIESGO: Si el SWEEP falla o no devuelve todo el exceso, el payer pierde ETH.
El contrato delega esto completamente a Uniswap UniversalRouter.

OTRO ÁNGULO: msg.value = 0 pero neededAmount > 0. El swap se ejecutaría con 0 ETH input
intentando obtener neededAmount output — Uniswap revertirá con V3TooMuchRequested.
No hay validación explícita de msg.value > 0 para swap nativo, pero la lógica
if (neededAmount > 0) en L403 solo procede si hay algo que swappear, y Uniswap
se encargará de revertir si no hay suficiente input.

swapTokens usa V3_SWAP_EXACT_OUT (L610, L639, L649) que pide exactamente neededAmount
de output y paga hasta maxAmountWillingToPay de input. Uniswap V3 redondea UP la
cantidad de input necesaria (favor del pool).

Esto significa que para tokens de baja precisión (USDC 6 decimals, WBTC 8 decimals),
el rounding del input puede ser significativo en términos relativos.

EJEMPLO: neededAmount = 1 wei de un token 18-dec. El swap pide exactamente 1 wei.
Con un pool de baja liquidez, el input requerido podría redondearse a 2 wei del
input token — 100% de sobrepago en el tick boundary.

IMPACTO: El payer paga ligeramente más de lo mínimo teórico. Pero maxWillingToPay
protege al payer — no pagará más de lo que autorizó.

EN LA PRÁCTICA: para montos razonables (>$1), el rounding de Uniswap V3 es
negligible (< 1 wei del token de mayor precisión).

revertIfInexactTransfer (L768-778) compara balanceAfter - balanceBefore contra expectedDiff.

Si el target recibe tokens de otra fuente entre balanceBefore y balanceAfter (rebasing,
airdrop mid-block, o donation), la diferencia sería > expectedDiff → revert.

El contrato RECHAZA fee-on-transfer tokens (diferencia < expected → revert) Y también
rechaza rebasing/donating tokens (diferencia > expected → revert).

MATH EDGE CASE: Si balanceBefore > balanceAfter (token deflationary/rebasing negativo),
la resta L775 underflows → revert. Solidity 0.8 lo protege.

Esto es BY DESIGN — el contrato quiere transferencias exactas. Pero rechazar
tokens rebasing como stETH podría ser un problema de UX si no se documenta.

El contrato Transfers NO hace ninguna operación que dependa de los decimales del token:
- No hay multiplicación/división de precios
- No hay conversión de decimales
- No hay cálculos de share price o exchange rate
- recipientAmount y feeAmount son montos absolutos definidos por el operador

La ÚNICA math es la suma recipientAmount + feeAmount y las restas para calcular
diferencias de balance. Estas operaciones son agnósticas a los decimales.

El swap via Uniswap maneja internamente la conversión de precios con sus propios
mecanismos de precisión.

CONCLUSIÓN: No hay riesgo de precision loss por diferencia de decimales en este contrato.

Cuando el recipient quiere ETH nativo (recipientCurrency == NATIVE_CURRENCY) y el payer
paga con un token (no ETH), swapTokens:
1. Swap exacto tokenIn → WETH (neededAmount de WETH output)
2. UNWRAP_WETH con amount = neededAmount (L640)
3. TRANSFER feeAmount al feeDestination (como ETH)
4. TRANSFER recipientAmount al recipient (como ETH)

PERO collectFees (L586-590) usa recipientCurrency = NATIVE_CURRENCY = address(0) para
el TRANSFER command. En UniversalRouter, TRANSFER con token=address(0) debería transferir
ETH nativo. Si el router interpreta address(0) diferente → fondos stuck.

VERIFICACIÓN: En el path msg.value == 0, L629 confirma recipientCurrency == NATIVE_CURRENCY.
collectFees y transferToRecipient usan _intent.recipientCurrency = NATIVE_CURRENCY = address(0).
UniswapConstants.ETH en L643 es el marcador para ETH nativo. Si address(0) != UniswapConstants.ETH,
los TRANSFER commands fallarían.

UniswapConstants.ETH = address(0) en Uniswap V3. CORRECTO.

Si recipientAmount = 0 y feeAmount = 0, neededAmount = 0. Todas las funciones de
transferencia tienen if (neededAmount > 0) o if (msg.value > 0) guards. Cuando
neededAmount = 0, se SALTA la transferencia pero se ejecuta succeedPayment()
que marca processedTransferIntents[operator][id] = true.

IMPACTO: Un operador podría crear un intent con recipientAmount=0, feeAmount=0.
Un payer ejecuta la tx (gratis, sin tokens). El intent se marca como procesado.
Si el recipient esperaba recibir fondos → no recibe nada y el intent ya no puede
re-ejecutarse (AlreadyProcessed).

PERO: El operador FIRMA el intent. Si recipientAmount=0, el operador lo consintió.
No hay ataque de un payer no autorizado porque la firma incluye sender.

¿Puede un payer front-run con el intent firmado? La firma incluye _msgSender()
(L92: sender en el hash), así que otro sender no puede reusar la firma.

CONCLUSIÓN: By design. Operador que firma amount=0 lo hace intencionalmente.

L699: return (payerBalanceBefore + routerBalanceBefore) - (payerBalanceAfter + routerBalanceAfter);

Si el router tenía tokens residuales de otro usuario (depositados por otro tx en el mismo
bloque ANTES de esta tx), esos tokens se incluyen en routerBalanceBefore.

Después del swap, SWEEP devuelve TODOS los tokens residuales del router al payer
(incluyendo los que no eran del payer). Entonces:
- routerBalanceBefore = R (tokens residuales) + 0 (no se transfirió nada aún)
- payerBalanceBefore = P + maxWillingToPay
- Después del swap y SWEEP:
  - routerBalanceAfter = 0 (todo swept)
  - payerBalanceAfter = P + maxWillingToPay - swapCost + R (recibió residuales)

return = (P + maxWillingToPay + R) - (P + maxWillingToPay - swapCost + R + 0)
       = swapCost

Los R se cancelan. El cálculo es CORRECTO incluso con tokens residuales.
El contrato es MÁS inteligente de lo que parece — el comment en L684-687 lo explica.

In subsidizedTransferToken (L505-559), the validIntent modifier receives
_signatureTransferData.owner as the sender parameter instead of _msgSender().
This means the operator signs an intent for a specific token owner, and ANYONE can
call subsidizedTransferToken to execute the payment. This is by design for gasless
transactions. However, the EIP-2612 permit signature (L530-536) is also provided by
the user. An attacker who observes the pending tx in the mempool can front-run it:
1. Extract the permit signature from the mempool
2. Call permit() directly on the token contract with the same params
3. Then call subsidizedTransferToken with the same intent
The permit call in step 2 would set the allowance. The subsidizedTransferToken call
in step 3 would also call permit() which would either succeed (idempotent) or revert
depending on the token's permit implementation (nonce already used).
If the token's permit uses nonces, the front-run permit consumes the nonce, and the
subsidizedTransferToken's internal permit call reverts. This is a griefing/DoS vector.

The validIntent modifier (L80-93) includes block.chainid in the keccak256 hash.
This prevents cross-chain replay attacks where a signature valid on chain A could be
reused on chain B. The hash also includes address(this) which prevents cross-contract
replay on the same chain. Both are correctly implemented.
Note: block.chainid is used (not a cached immutable), so this is safe even across
hard forks that change the chain ID.

Replay protection uses processedTransferIntents[operator][id] (L119-121).
This is scoped per operator, meaning two different operators can have the same intent ID.
This is correct — each operator manages their own ID namespace.
The ID is bytes16, giving 2^128 possible values — collision-resistant.
The processed flag is set in succeedPayment (L753) AFTER the transfer logic executes
in the modifier's _;. This ordering is safe because nonReentrant prevents re-entry.

OpenZeppelin's ECDSA.recover (v4.x) normalizes the s-value to the lower half of the
curve, preventing signature malleability attacks. Even if a malleable signature existed,
the processedTransferIntents replay protection would prevent double-execution.
Both layers of defense are present and correctly applied.

The hash in validIntent uses abi.encodePacked with mixed types (L80-93):
uint256, uint256, address, address, address, uint256, bytes16, address, uint256, address, address.
All types are fixed-size (uint256=32B, address=20B, bytes16=16B). There are NO adjacent
dynamic-size types, so abi.encodePacked collision via variable-length concatenation ambiguity
is NOT possible here. The encoding is deterministic and unique for any distinct set of inputs.
However, there IS a subtle concern: address types are 20 bytes and bytes16 is 16 bytes.
In abi.encodePacked, these are tightly packed without padding. The sequence
[refundDestination(20B) | feeAmount(32B) | id(16B) | operator(20B)] is unambiguous because
uint256 feeAmount always occupies exactly 32 bytes, creating a fixed boundary.

At L530-536, subsidizedTransferToken calls IERC7597.permit() without try/catch.
If the permit call reverts for any reason (nonce already used, signature invalid,
token doesn't support ERC-7597), the entire transaction reverts.
This is coupled with TR-SIG-02: a front-run attacker consuming the permit nonce
causes permanent DoS for that specific intent. The operator would need to create
a new intent with a new ID and the user would need to sign a new permit.
A safer pattern would be try/catch around the permit call, then verify allowance
is sufficient regardless. DAI-style permits and some tokens have non-standard
behavior that could also cause unexpected reverts.

In swapAndTransferUniswapV3Native (L384), swapAndTransferUniswapV3Token (L413), and
swapAndTransferUniswapV3TokenPreApproved (L458), the `poolFeesTier` parameter is entirely
caller-controlled. The operator signs the TransferIntent which locks recipientAmount,
feeAmount, recipientCurrency, and deadline, but does NOT sign poolFeesTier.

The swap uses V3_SWAP_EXACT_OUT (L580: swapPath = abi.encodePacked(tokenOut, poolFeesTier, tokenIn)).
EXACT_OUT means the router will consume whatever amount of tokenIn is needed to produce
exactly `neededAmount` of tokenOut. The `maxAmountWillingToPay` serves as the slippage cap.

Attack vector: The payer (msg.sender) IS the caller, so they choose poolFeesTier themselves.
A malicious payer could pick a pool with extremely thin liquidity (e.g., fee tier 10000 = 1%
pool that has almost no liquidity). In a thin pool, the price impact is massive, so the
swap consumes far more tokenIn.

However: the payer is paying with THEIR OWN tokens. Using a worse pool only hurts the payer
(they spend more of their own tokens for the same output). The recipient and fee destination
always receive exactly recipientAmount and feeAmount of the recipientCurrency. So the payer
has no incentive to pick a bad pool — it only costs them more.

The real risk is: a third-party relayer submitting the transaction on behalf of the payer.
If the payer pre-signs a Permit2 signature for maxWillingToPay, a malicious relayer could
choose a bad poolFeesTier to maximize the payer's input consumption. The relayer could
sandwich the swap to extract the excess. But: the payer controls maxWillingToPay via the
permit2 signature, which caps maximum extraction.

For the Native variant (swapAndTransferUniswapV3Native): the payer sends msg.value directly,
and any excess ETH is swept back to the payer via SWEEP. So there's no extraction — the
payer gets the unused ETH back.

Conclusion: The payer self-selects the pool and bears the cost of bad selection. The protocol
is designed so that recipient always gets exact amounts. This is by-design, not a vulnerability.

En transferNative() y unwrapAndTransfer*(), los fondos nativos se envían al recipient vía
sendNative() (L762) que usa `payable(destination).call{value: amount}("")`. Si el recipient
es un contrato que revierte en receive()/fallback(), TODA la transacción revierte. El intent
ya fue firmado por el operador con ese recipient fijo — no se puede cambiar. El pago queda
permanentemente bloqueado porque el intent ID no puede re-usarse (processedTransferIntents
no se marca en caso de revert) PERO el recipient tampoco puede cambiar sin nueva firma.

Impacto: El merchant (recipient) que deploya un contrato sin receive() o que revierte
nunca puede recibir pagos nativos. Si el operador firmó intents para ese recipient,
los pagadores no pueden completar esos pagos. Los fondos del pagador no se pierden (tx revierte)
pero el servicio/producto no se entrega.

En transferFundsToDestinations() L726, si feeAmount > 0 y recipientCurrency == NATIVE_CURRENCY,
se llama sendNative(feeDestinations[_intent.operator], feeAmount, false). Si el feeDestination
es un contrato que revierte, TODOS los pagos nativos con fee > 0 para ese operador quedan bloqueados.

A diferencia del recipient (que varía por intent), el feeDestination es GLOBAL para el operador.
Si el operador registró un feeDestination problemático, TODOS sus intents nativos fallan.

El operador puede arreglarlo llamando registerOperatorWithFeeDestination() con una nueva dirección,
pero los intents ya firmados con la firma vieja seguirán fallando si el operador cambió de dirección
(la firma incluye el operator address, no el feeDestination).

En swapTokens() L667, el swap a Uniswap se ejecuta con try/catch. Si el swap falla
(slippage, pool inexistente, liquidez insuficiente, pool manipulado), se revert con
SwapFailedString o SwapFailedBytes. NO hay fallback: el pago se cancela completamente.

Un atacante podría manipular el pool de Uniswap justo antes de la tx del pagador
(sandwich attack) para causar que el swap falle. El pagador pierde gas, el pago no
se completa. El atacante puede repetir esto indefinidamente si monitorea el mempool.

Además, si el poolFeesTier especificado no corresponde a un pool existente, el swap
siempre fallará. Esto es un parámetro del pagador, no del intent, así que un pagador
informado puede corregirlo, pero la UX es mala.

Si el recipientCurrency es un token con blocklist (USDC, USDT) y el recipient o
feeDestination está en la blocklist, safeTransfer revierte y el pago se bloquea.

En transferFundsToDestinations() L731: requestedCurrency.safeTransfer(_intent.recipient, amount)
Si el recipient fue añadido a la blocklist de USDC después de que el operador firmó el intent,
el pago ya no puede completarse. El intent ID no se puede reusar porque la tx completa revierte
(processedTransferIntents no se marca).

Mismo problema en L734 para feeDestination.

pause() y unpause() son onlyOwner (L801-808). El modifier whenNotPaused está en todas
las funciones de pago. Cuando se pausa, ningún pago nuevo puede procesarse.

Esto es safe porque: (1) el contrato no retiene fondos entre transacciones (los fondos
se transfieren en la misma tx), (2) unpause() existe y es funcional, (3) solo owner puede
pausar/despausar.

No hay fondos atrapados por el pause porque el contrato no tiene balances persistentes
de usuarios. El peor caso es que los pagos se retrasen hasta que se despause.

El mapping processedTransferIntents (L37) crece con cada pago procesado y nunca se limpia.
Sin embargo, como es un mapping (no array), el acceso es O(1) y no hay iteración.
No hay función que itere sobre los intents procesados.

Storage bloat sí existe (cada intent = 1 SSTORE de 32 bytes = 20K gas first time),
pero no afecta la funcionalidad. No es un vector de DoS.

En subsidizedTransferToken() (L505), el msg.sender es el relayer, no el payer.
El payer solo firma un EIP-2612 permit. Si la tx revierte (por cualquiera de los
vectores anteriores), es el relayer quien pierde gas, no el payer.

Sin embargo, si un atacante grief-ea repetidamente las txs del relayer (manipulando
pool, blocklisting, etc.), el relayer podría dejar de servir ese intent, bloqueando
el pago subsidiado. El payer tendría que usar otro método de pago.

El permit firmado tiene deadline = intent.deadline, así que eventualmente expira.
No hay fondos atrapados.

El contrato hereda Sweepable, que presumiblemente permite al owner recuperar tokens
o ETH atrapados en el contrato. Esto mitiga el riesgo de fondos permanentemente bloqueados
en caso de un bug o edge case que deje fondos en el contrato.

Verificar que sweep funciona para ETH nativo también (el receive() solo acepta WETH).

En swapTokens (L668-681), después de que Uniswap ejecuta el swap, el contrato verifica
que los tokens de salida llegaron correctamente via revertIfInexactTransfer. Lo hace en
DOS llamadas separadas: una para feeDestination (L670-675) y otra para recipient (L676-681).

El problema crítico: si _intent.recipient == feeDestinations[_intent.operator], AMBAS
llamadas miden el balance de la MISMA dirección. El flujo es:

1. Pre-swap: feeBalanceBefore = IERC20(tokenOut).balanceOf(feeDestinations[operator])
             recipientBalanceBefore = IERC20(tokenOut).balanceOf(_intent.recipient)
   → Si recipient == feeDestination, feeBalanceBefore == recipientBalanceBefore

2. Uniswap ejecuta TRANSFER(feeAmount → feeDestination) y TRANSFER(recipientAmount → recipient)
   → Ambas van a la MISMA dirección. Balance aumenta en feeAmount + recipientAmount.

3. Primera check (L670-675):
   balanceAfter = token.balanceOf(feeDestinations[operator])
                = feeBalanceBefore + feeAmount + recipientAmount  (AMBOS transfers llegaron)
   expectedDiff = feeAmount
   balanceAfter - balanceBefore = feeAmount + recipientAmount ≠ feeAmount
   → REVERT con InexactTransfer()

El pago falla aunque los fondos estuvieran siendo entregados correctamente a la dirección
correcta. El operador legítimo que usa su propia dirección como recipient Y feeDestination
(caso común en comercios que quieren simplificar — reciben todo en una wallet) nunca
puede usar las funciones de swap. Solo afecta a swapAndTransferUniswapV3Native,
swapAndTransferUniswapV3Token, swapAndTransferUniswapV3TokenPreApproved cuando
recipientCurrency != NATIVE_CURRENCY (el path token-to-token y native-to-token).

El path token-to-native (recipientCurrency == NATIVE_CURRENCY) NO está afectado porque
el check solo se ejecuta para recipientCurrency != NATIVE_CURRENCY (L669:
if (_intent.recipientCurrency != NATIVE_CURRENCY)).

Los pagos non-swap (transferToken, transferTokenPreApproved, etc.) NO están afectados
porque transferFundsToDestinations NO hace revertIfInexactTransfer después de enviar
— simplemente hace safeTransfer directamente.

6 hunters detectaron el vector pero solo lo analizaron como "griefing al relayer".
La investigación profunda revela el escenario completo:

subsidizedTransferToken (L505-559) llama permit() en L530 SIN try/catch. Cualquier
actor puede front-run la tx del relayer de dos formas:

FORMA 1 — Front-run completo del pago:
El front-runner extrae del mempool: intent + EIP-2612 sig + permit data.
Llama subsidizedTransferToken directamente (es permisionless — L505 no tiene restricción
de caller). La tx del front-runner ejecuta primero: permit consume nonce, allowance
se establece, safeTransferFrom toma los fondos del owner, el intent se marca processed.
La tx del relayer legítimo llega: validIntent falla con AlreadyProcessed(). Outcome:
el pago fue ejecutado, los fondos fueron a recipient/feeDestination correctos, pero
el relayer original (si tenía incentivos off-chain) pierde su compensación.

FORMA 2 — Grief del nonce:
El front-runner extrae solo la firma de permit y llama T.permit(owner, Transfers, amount, deadline, sig)
directamente en el token. El nonce se consume. Cuando la tx del relayer llega,
L530 llama permit() → revierte (nonce stale). El allow check (L539-542) falla porque
no se estableció el allowance. Toda la subsidizedTransferToken revierte.
Outcome: pago bloqueado, operador debe crear nuevo intent con nuevo ID, owner
debe firmar nuevo permit.

CASO CRÍTICO NO EXAMINADO — Token que NO implementa IERC7597:
La línea L530 hace un cast forzado: IERC7597(_intent.recipientCurrency).permit(...)
Si el token NO implementa ERC-7597 (la mayoría de ERC20 no lo hacen), la llamada
a permit() sobre una dirección que no tiene esa función puede:
a) Revertir con "function not found" → toda la tx revierte → grief permanente
   para esa combinación de token+intent.
b) En tokens con fallback(), ejecutar código arbitrario del fallback → no hay
   validación de que el call tuvo el efecto esperado (el allowance check L539
   SÍ valida que el allowance fue establecido, lo cual mitiga esto parcialmente).

La función succeedPayment en subsidizedTransferToken usa _signatureTransferData.owner
como el "sender" del evento Transferred (L558). Esto es correcto en la mayoría
de los casos, pero si el relayer es también el payer (por algún escenario de
batch), el evento puede ser misleading.

registerOperatorWithFeeDestination (L781-785) NO valida _feeDestination != address(0):

    function registerOperatorWithFeeDestination(address _feeDestination) external {
        feeDestinations[_msgSender()] = _feeDestination;
        emit OperatorRegistered(_msgSender(), _feeDestination);
    }

Si el operador llama registerOperatorWithFeeDestination(address(0)):
- feeDestinations[operator] = address(0)
- operatorIsRegistered modifier: feeDestinations[operator] == address(0) → revert OperatorNotRegistered()
- PERO se emite OperatorRegistered(operator, address(0))

El evento dice que el operador ESTÁ registrado con feeDestination=address(0), pero
el modifier dice que NO está registrado. Esta contradicción afecta a:
1. Off-chain sistemas que monitorizan OperatorRegistered para saber qué operadores
   están activos — verían al operador como "registered" cuando en realidad no puede
   procesar pagos.
2. El operador podría confundirse y pensar está activo.
3. Contraste con registerOperator() (L788-792) que usa msg.sender como feeDestination
   (nunca puede ser 0) y con unregisterOperator() que emite OperatorUnregistered.

La combinación peligrosa: un operador registra con address(0) (accidentalmente o
por bug en su dApp). Emite OperatorRegistered. Luego firma 50 intents y los distribuye.
Los pagadores intentan ejecutar → todo revierte con OperatorNotRegistered.
Ningún evento indica que el operador se "auto-des-registró" — el último evento es
OperatorRegistered, lo cual es misleading.

Diferencia clave con unregisterOperator(): unregisterOperator emite OperatorUnregistered
(correcto, sistemas pueden rastrear). registerOperatorWithFeeDestination(0) emite
OperatorRegistered con feeDestination=0 (incorrecto, sistemas no pueden distinguir).

Este DD sintetiza y profundiza el hallazgo convergente más fuerte (5 hunters):
feeDestination no está en el hash firmado + puede cambiar entre signing y ejecución.

El vector preciso que ningún hunter articuló completamente:

El feeDestination NO es un campo del TransferIntent firmado. La única forma que tiene
un payer de "conocer" el feeDestination en el momento del pago es consultarlo on-chain
ANTES de enviar su tx, pero entre su consulta y su tx, el operador puede haber cambiado.

ESCENARIO DE EXPLOTACIÓN DE KEY PARCIAL COMPROMETIDA:
En sistemas de seguridad empresariales, un operador puede tener:
  - Key A (hot wallet): firma intents de alto volumen, capacidad limitada
  - Key B (cold wallet): registra/actualiza feeDestination, capacidad total

Si un atacante compromete Key A (pero no Key B), no puede firmar nuevos intents
maliciosos porque no controla la lógica de negocio. PERO si el operador tiene
Key A == Key B (que es el caso para EOA simples), un compromiso total del operador
permite:

1. Atacante compromete la clave del operador.
2. Firma nuevos intents maliciosos (o usa los existentes pendientes).
3. Llama registerOperatorWithFeeDestination(attackerWallet).
4. Todos los intents pendientes (ya distribuidos a merchants) ejecutan ahora
   con fees → attackerWallet.
5. El atacante no puede redirigir recipientAmount (está firmado), solo feeAmount.

IMPACTO ESCALADO: Si el operador tiene 10,000 intents pendientes con feeAmount=5 USDC
cada uno, el atacante puede extraer hasta $50,000 simplemente cambiando feeDestination.
Los pagadores ejecutan intents válidos (signatures son correctas), pero los fees
van al atacante en lugar del merchant.

EL CASO MÁS PELIGROSO: Un operador que usa address(this) como feeDestination:
registerOperatorWithFeeDestination(address(transfers)):
- Para pagos ERC20: fees quedan atrapados en el contrato (solo el sweeper puede rescatar).
- Para pagos nativos: sendNative al contrato propio → receive() requiere
  msg.sender == wrappedNativeCurrency → revert NativeTransferFailed.
  TODO el pago falla. Operador efectivamente hace DoS en sus propios pagos nativos
  al registrar address(this) como feeDestination.

En swapTokens (L586-590), el comando collectFees para el Uniswap router se construye
ANTES del try/catch:

    bytes memory collectFees = abi.encode(
        _intent.recipientCurrency,
        feeDestinations[_intent.operator],  // ← resolución aquí
        _intent.feeAmount
    );

El modifier operatorIsRegistered (L128-132) verifica que feeDestinations[operator] != 0
ANTES de entrar a swapTokens. Esto parece seguro. Pero hay un race condition teórico:

En teoría, dentro de una función nonReentrant, ningún estado externo puede cambiar
entre L128 (check) y L588 (captura del valor). Sin embargo, hay un escenario específico:

ESCENARIO: ¿Puede feeDestinations[operator] ser 0 durante la construcción de collectFees?

Respuesta: NO bajo ejecución normal single-threaded de EVM. El nonReentrant garantiza
que no hay re-entrada, y la función es lineal. El valor de feeDestinations[operator]
no puede cambiar entre el modifier y la ejecución de swapTokens.

PERO: hay una implicación más interesante. Los comandos Uniswap para el swap
codifican feeDestinations[operator] como una dirección fija en el bytes payload.
Si esta dirección es address(0) por algún edge case, el comando TRANSFER de
Uniswap intentaría transferir fees a address(0). El UniversalRouter de Uniswap
típicamente interpreta address(0) como "no transfer" o como ETH para TRANSFER commands.

Para el path de tokenOut != NATIVE (L644-660):
- collectFees = abi.encode(tokenOut, address(0), feeAmount)
- TRANSFER(tokenOut, address(0), feeAmount) → Uniswap envía feeAmount de tokenOut a address(0)?

Si el Uniswap UniversalRouter TRANSFER command para ERC20 envía a address(0), los tokens
van a la dirección quemada. El revertIfInexactTransfer luego verifica el balance de address(0):
balanceAfter - balanceBefore == feeAmount. Si el token permite transferir a address(0) (la
mayoría lo hace), esto no revertirá, y los fees serán quemados permanentemente.

Sin embargo, el modifier operatorIsRegistered previene que lleguemos aquí si
feeDestinations[operator] == 0. Así que este escenario NO es alcanzable.

LO QUE SÍ ES ALCANZABLE: el operador registra con una dirección que PARECE válida pero
es contract address(0)-like: por ejemplo, una dirección que devuelve true en address.call
pero no acepta tokens. Esto ya está cubierto en DD-T-04.

HALLAZGO REAL DE ESTE DD: La construcción de collectFees usa feeDestinations lookup
DOS VECES: una en L588 y otra en L674 (revertIfInexactTransfer). Si entre estas
dos líneas el feeDestination cambiara (imposible en nonReentrant), el check
mediría el balance de una dirección diferente a donde fue el fee. Esto confirma
la importancia de nonReentrant para la correctness del swap accounting.

VECTOR CONCRETO: swapAndTransferUniswapV3Token cuando feeAmount == 0. En ese caso:
- collectFees encoda feeAmount=0
- L671: revertIfInexactTransfer(0, feeBalanceBefore, tokenOut, feeDestinations[operator])
- Si feeDestinations[operator] cambió a una dirección con tokens de tokenOut preexistentes,
  el check podría fallar (balance cambió por razón externa al swap). Pero nonReentrant
  previene esto.

subsidizedTransferToken (L505-559) hace un cast forzado a IERC7597 en L530:

    IERC7597(_intent.recipientCurrency).permit({...})

Si recipientCurrency NO implementa IERC7597.permit(), hay tres outcomes posibles:

OUTCOME A — El token tiene fallback() que acepta la llamada silenciosamente:
La llamada a permit() no revierte pero tampoco establece ningún allowance.
L539-542 luego verifica: allowance = erc20.allowance(owner, address(this)).
Si allowance < neededAmount → revert InsufficientAllowance.
La tx revierte. No hay pérdida de fondos. El usuario está protegido.

OUTCOME B — El token revierte (no tiene fallback compatible):
L530 revierte. Toda la tx revierte. Griefing: cualquier usuario que intente
usar subsidizedTransferToken con este token siempre falla. Debe usar
transferTokenPreApproved en su lugar.

OUTCOME C — El token tiene un fallback() que establece allowance de forma diferente:
Extremadamente improbable, pero si el fallback ejecuta setApproval o similar,
el allowance check podría pasar. Luego safeTransferFrom (L549) transferiría tokens.
Este es el escenario más peligroso pero requiere un token específicamente malicioso.

LA VERDADERA IMPLICACIÓN: La función ASUME que recipientCurrency es IERC7597.
No hay validación on-chain. El operador decide qué token es pagable via
subsidizedTransferToken. Si el operador crea un intent con un token no-IERC7597,
la función siempre falla para ese intent. El operador debe conocer qué tokens
soportan ERC-7597 (ERC-20 con permit de tipo {r, s, v, deadline}).

Nota: ERC-7597 es la interfaz de permit estilo {bytes signature} (distinta de
EIP-2612 que usa {uint8 v, bytes32 r, bytes32 s}). La mayoría de tokens usan
EIP-2612, pero el contrato espera la interfaz de {bytes signature}.
